sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Expect a high-risk cardiovascular population. One observational study summarized in the review found less intraoperative hypotension and vasopressor administration with regional anesthesia than with alternative modalities, but the regional group combined spinal anesthesia and peripheral blocks; this does not establish a technique-specific effect.

Consider tourniquet-related discomfort and ischemic pain when selecting regional coverage. The evidence describes stable hemodynamics in a small high-risk BKA study without a tourniquet, but does not establish that result for other patients or tourniquet conditions.
The surgical approach may be staged in unstable or septic patients to obtain source control; coordinate timing and anesthetic decisions with the surgical team as clinical status evolves.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review
Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Major concerns include cardiopulmonary complications, wound infection, prolonged ICU care, and revision. Risk context includes cardiac disease, renal impairment, infection, and proximal amputation; reported mortality varies by population and should not be treated as an individual prediction.

If stump pain persists, consider non-anesthetic causes as well as inadequate analgesia, including infection, wound dehiscence, reduced blood flow, osteomyelitis, hematoma, or inadequate tissue coverage.

Peripheral blocks require attention to coverage and local-anesthetic toxicity risk, especially when multiple nerves or substantial volumes are involved. The review’s case reports do not establish routine management for patients with sepsis, thrombocytopenia, or respiratory infection.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The sources do not establish a procedure-specific fluid regimen, transfusion threshold, or blood-ordering rule. Assess bleeding and resuscitation needs in the clinical context; the chapter specifically identifies hemostasis and adequate resuscitation for traumatic injuries.

The review summarizes studies associating regional anesthesia with reduced blood loss or transfusion in some settings, but the comparative evidence is mixed and does not provide a patient-specific estimate or mandate an anesthetic technique.
Perfusion and tissue viability inform level selection and healing potential; TcPO₂ may contribute to assessment but does not capture the whole patient or limb condition.

sources.label: Lower Extremity Amputation — StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Plan acute stump analgesia before the anesthetic or block regresses. The review favors regional anesthesia for acute stump pain and describes multimodal planning, while noting that opioids alone may be insufficient; the sources do not establish one universal drug regimen.

For BKA, combined saphenous/adductor-canal and sciatic coverage is described for perioperative pain; continuous catheters may extend analgesia. Evidence for long-term prevention of phantom limb pain remains limited.

Discuss phantom limb pain and residual limb pain as distinct but potentially overlapping recovery problems. Early acute-pain-service involvement and a preemptive approach are emphasized in the review; no intervention is guaranteed to prevent chronic pain.

A retrospective BKA comparison reported lower pain scores, opioid use, and postoperative nausea and vomiting with combined femoral and sciatic blocks than with general anesthesia; this observational finding does not establish a universal technique choice.

sources.label: The Perioperative Challenges of Major Lower Extremity Amputation and the Impact of Regional Anesthesia on Morbidity, Mortality, and Pain Management: A Narrative Review

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The procedure-specific sources do not specify emergence or extubation criteria. For general anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, apply quantitative recovery guidance; do not impose that requirement on cases without blockade.

After anesthesia, use PACU or equivalent care, including ICU when appropriate. Continue condition-appropriate monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; evaluate pain and the operative wound.

Provide a structured handoff covering the preoperative condition, surgical and anesthetic course, adverse events, blood loss and resuscitative measures, and the planned destination. A receiving clinician should accept responsibility before anesthesia-team departure.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal anesthesia review is a narrative review focused on major lower-extremity amputation and regional anesthesia, especially peripheral nerve blocks; it is not a guideline or meta-analysis. Its summarized studies vary in design and population.

Comparative outcome evidence is unresolved: studies report possible morbidity advantages with regional techniques, while mortality findings are controversial. Many studies combine neuraxial and peripheral techniques, limiting technique-specific conclusions.

The StatPearls chapter is an educational surgical review rather than an anesthesia reference. ASA monitoring and postanesthesia standards provide general requirements, not amputation-specific anesthetic plans.

The available sources do not resolve individualized airway/ventilation planning, anesthetic technique selection for a particular patient, or perioperative anticoagulant management for regional procedures.
The procedure-specific chapter does not specify vascular-access strategy or monitoring standards.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Perforation can combine full-stomach aspiration risk, hypovolemia, vasodilation and septic myocardial dysfunction.
Coordinate urgent source control, antibiotics and active resuscitation; induction may precipitate cardiovascular collapse.
Prepare reliable access, blood when indicated, vasopressors, warming and close perfusion/acid-base monitoring.
The endpoint may be definitive repair or damage control with an open abdomen; postoperative ventilation/ICU may be necessary.

sections.title: Source, severity & organ dysfunction
bullets: Review site/cause of perforation, contamination, shock, lactate, renal function and respiratory status. Identify anticoagulants, frailty and preexisting organ dysfunction.
Begin the source-control and antibiotic pathway while resuscitating. Do not postpone life-saving surgery merely to achieve normal laboratory values.

sources.label: ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: Aspiration-risk induction in shock
bullets: Coordinate decompression when appropriate, preoxygenation, suction and an airway backup plan. Prepare induction with rapidly available vasoactive support and drugs titrated to the patient’s reserve.
Positive-pressure ventilation and anesthetic vasodilation may remove compensatory mechanisms. Where feasible obtain useful monitoring before induction without delaying urgent source control.

sources.label: ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: Perfusion, fluids & electrolytes
bullets: Account for vomiting, bowel preparation, poor intake, bleeding and measured gastric/wound losses. Give fluid for evidence of hypovolemia or fluid responsiveness and reassess; do not replace a presumed fixed “third-space deficit.”

Avoid both excess crystalloid and under-resuscitation. Balanced crystalloid is often appropriate; distinguish vasodilatory hypotension from hemorrhage or low output and use vasoactive support when indicated. Correct potassium, sodium and acid-base disturbances with attention to renal function.

sections.title: Source control & ongoing vasoplegia
bullets: Reassess perfusion repeatedly using examination, blood pressure, lactate trends and other available hemodynamic information. Persistent hypotension may require norepinephrine-based support rather than continued unselected fluid boluses.
Antibiotics, hemodynamic resuscitation and source control proceed together. New deterioration can also reflect hemorrhage, ventilation problems or cardiac dysfunction.

sources.label: ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: Repair, resection & damage control
bullets: Clarify primary repair, resection, diversion or staged laparotomy. Bowel discontinuity and temporary closure require an explicit ICU, nutrition and re-exploration plan.
Track blood loss, core temperature, acid-base state, coagulation and electrolytes during prolonged contamination control.

sources.label: ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: Analgesia with sepsis and coagulopathy
bullets: Consider systemic multimodal analgesia and appropriate wound/abdominal wall techniques. Epidural placement requires careful assessment of infection, coagulation, antithrombotics and hemodynamic tolerance.
Avoid renal-toxic or bleeding-promoting analgesic choices in patients with AKI or active hemorrhage. Titrate opioids to respiratory reserve and anticipated ventilation.

sources.label: ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: ICU handoff & persistent deterioration
bullets: Handoff source control achieved, remaining contamination, vasopressors, cultures/antibiotics, drains, bowel continuity and any planned second look.
Worsening lactate, oliguria, abdominal distension or escalating support requires reassessment for ongoing sepsis, bleeding, ischemia or abdominal compartment physiology.

sources.label: ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: Monitoring, access & temperature
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring and temperature surveillance when significant changes are anticipated. Major bleeding, shock, prolonged surgery or limited reserve may warrant an arterial line, repeated blood gases and additional venous access.

Choose access for the anticipated blood and vasoactive requirements; a central line is not automatically necessary for every abdominal operation. Warm exposed patients and significant fluid/blood infusions, and reassess glucose and electrolytes according to illness and procedure.

sources.label: ASA Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: Extubation, respiratory recovery & disposition
bullets: Before extubation, assess wakefulness, airway protection, ventilation, oxygenation, temperature, perfusion and ongoing bleeding. If neuromuscular blockers were used, verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; head lift alone is insufficient.

Plan monitored or ICU recovery for persistent shock, major resuscitation, respiratory failure or an open abdomen. CPAP/NIV for postoperative hypoxemia requires an appropriate patient with low aspiration risk, skilled monitoring and prompt escalation if it fails.

bullets: Adult clinical-review draft, not an individualized order set or independently approved protocol. Emergency, elective, endoscopic and vascular pathways have different evidence bases; do not transfer every ERAS recommendation between them.

Use current institutional airway, transfusion, anticoagulation and rescue policies. The date marks source checking, not a guarantee that every linked review is new; older educational sources and institutional pathways are labeled.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pilonidal surgery ranges from drainage of an acute abscess to definitive treatment of chronic disease. The operative approach matters: these sources describe local anesthesia for selected drainage and pit-picking procedures, and general anesthesia for the reviewed modified cleft-lift technique.
For definitive excision and closure, the review supports off-midline techniques over midline closure; it reports no evidence that one off-midline method is superior to the others.

Prone positioning is reported for the reviewed cleft-lift operation, but the surgical reviews provide no anesthesia-specific airway technique, physiologic targets, or complication-management protocol. Do not infer a routine airway or anesthetic recipe from them.

Recovery priorities in the available evidence are surgical wound healing and follow-up: open wounds can require prolonged healing and frequent dressing changes, while dehiscence and recurrence are reported after closure procedures.

sources.label: The Management of Pilonidal Sinus
Practical Management of Pilonidal Disease

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Acute abscess management is distinct from definitive treatment of chronic sinus disease. The surgical review favors simple incision and drainage for an acute abscess; complete excision during acute swelling may create a very large wound defect.

Definitive options include excision with healing by secondary intention or closure. Midline primary suture is not recommended in the reviewed guidelines; off-midline closure options include Karydakis, cleft lift, and Limberg flap.

For the authors’ modified Bascom cleft lift, the described workflow uses general anesthesia and prone positioning with moderate waist flexion. This is a description of that technique, not a universal anesthetic requirement for pilonidal procedures.

sources.label: The Management of Pilonidal Sinus
Practical Management of Pilonidal Disease

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify whether the planned procedure is acute abscess drainage, a minimally invasive intervention, or definitive excision and closure; these are distinct approaches, and the sources do not provide one anesthesia plan applicable to all of them.

The available sources do not provide procedure-specific anesthesia selection criteria or a preoperative risk-stratification protocol. Assess and plan according to the individual patient and intended operation; no case-specific algorithm can be derived here.

bullets: The modified cleft-lift description places the patient prone with moderate waist flexion. It also describes lateral taping of the buttocks to the table as a surgical exposure technique; the source does not provide anesthesia-specific positioning or pressure-injury guidance.

For any anesthetic, ASA basic monitoring standards call for continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes. Apply ventilation monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and airway device.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The surgical technique description identifies induction of general anesthesia followed by prone positioning for the modified cleft lift. It does not specify anesthetic maintenance, physiologic targets, or phase-specific management.

Continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature during anesthesia in accordance with the applicable monitoring standard; the case-specific reviews add no pilonidal-specific targets.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Wound problems are relevant surgical outcomes, not an anesthesia protocol: the cleft-lift authors describe minor dehiscence requiring local wound care as their most common complication and report a recurrence requiring reoperation in their experience.

Reported recurrence and wound-healing outcomes vary across procedures and studies. The review notes substantial disagreement and inadequate comparative evidence for some techniques; do not present a single recurrence estimate as a guaranteed individual outcome.

bullets: The pilonidal surgical sources do not report an anesthesia fluid regimen or case-specific blood-loss guidance. Individualize management to the patient and operation rather than adopting an unsupported fixed volume or blood-loss estimate.

bullets: No procedure-specific anesthetic analgesic regimen or PONV guidance is supplied by the pilonidal reviews. The cleft-lift authors report minimal postoperative narcotic requirements in their outpatient experience; this is not a comparative analgesia protocol.

bullets: The surgical reviews do not specify an emergence or extubation plan. For any patient who received neuromuscular blocking drugs, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirming TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply as a routine requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

bullets: The two pilonidal sources are surgical reviews, not anesthesia references. They support procedure selection and describe surgical technique and wound outcomes, but do not establish an anesthesia protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Port placement is typically performed through venous access using a Seldinger technique, with the catheter connected to a subcutaneous pocket; removal is mentioned in the evidence, but its technique is not described.

Anesthesia varies: local anesthesia or superficial cervical plexus block with intravenous sedoanalgesia has been studied, while another cohort reports general anesthesia. These sources do not establish one preferred technique.
Key procedural hazards include arterial puncture, pneumothorax, arrhythmia, and catheter malposition; guidewire and catheter position need attention during placement.
Recovery priorities include monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic, assessment for access-related complications, and confirmation of recovery status before discharge from postanesthesia care.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Placement involves venous access, guidewire passage, catheter placement and connection to a subcutaneous port pocket. The supplied sources describe Seldinger placement; access may be landmark-guided or ultrasound-guided.
The internal jugular vein was the preferred route in the prospective study, and all patients in the audit had IJV access. Route selection should not be inferred as universal from these reports.

Assess the intended access and implant site for suitability; local infection or tumor at the intervention site were exclusion criteria in the prospective study.
The anesthesiologist determines medical status and develops the anesthesia-care plan. The supplied standards excerpt does not enumerate port-specific assessment requirements.

bullets: Agree the emergency access/undocking workflow before the robot restricts the head and torso. Table movement must follow the specific platform’s coordinated safety process.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Soft-tissue mass excision ranges from a localized excision under local anesthesia to larger or complex procedures; the available procedure study reports local anesthesia or monitored controlled anesthesia, but does not establish which patients need which technique.

Priorities supported by the procedure sources are careful dissection near neurovascular structures, hemostasis, and limiting traction or thermal injury; reported complications include seroma, hematoma, and nerve injury.

Do not assume general anesthesia, an advanced airway, or neuromuscular blockade for a small superficial mass; the supplied sources do not define case-specific selection criteria or an anesthesia regimen.
Recovery should include assessment appropriate to the anesthetic and patient condition; the procedure literature does not define a specific emergence, analgesic, or PACU protocol.

Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operative approach depends on lesion site and extent. Excision may be diagnostic as well as therapeutic when complete tissue architecture is needed; the supplied sources do not specify a single approach for all soft-tissue masses.

For lipomas, one described limited-incision method uses circumferential dissection, full mobilization before delivery, meticulous hemostasis, irrigation, and layered closure. This is a reported technique, not a universal standard.

For a rapidly growing presumed lipoma, the source describes radiologic evaluation to help distinguish it from malignant neoplasms. The available material does not establish a sarcoma staging, margin, or frozen-section protocol.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify lesion location, depth, size, vascularity, and proximity to neurovascular structures with the surgical team; these factors affect planning, but the sources provide no universal anesthesia-selection rule.

Consider whether complete excision is appropriate or whether a diagnostic alternative is needed for a large or complex lesion near vital structures. This is a source-described concern, not a fixed contraindication to excision.
Assess patient-specific medical status and develop the anesthesia plan; the provided standards identify this responsibility but do not supply a procedure-specific assessment protocol.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Positioning and room setup are site-dependent. A cutaneous excision reference calls for comfortable positioning, appropriate surgical lighting, and a setup at the surgeon’s appropriate height; it does not establish positioning for every deep mass.
For MAC or general anesthesia, apply the applicable basic anesthetic monitoring standards, including continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature.
The supplied sources do not support routine invasive monitoring or a particular vascular-access plan for this procedure.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The lipoma series includes local anesthesia or monitored controlled anesthesia but gives no regimen or criteria for choosing between them. Do not infer that all excisions require general anesthesia or an airway device.
Airway device selection, general-anesthetic technique, and ventilation strategy are not addressed by the procedure-specific evidence.
When moderate or deep sedation is used, the ASA monitoring standard calls for continual clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the method is precluded or invalidated.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: For local infiltration in the described lipoma technique, the authors emphasize allowing time for epinephrine vasoconstriction and using hydrodissection to facilitate dissection and reduce bleeding. These are technique details from a retrospective series, not an anesthesia protocol.
Avoid unnecessary traction and thermal injury during limited-incision dissection; the source describes careful mobilization and preference for scissors or forceps over electrocautery for dissection.
No procedure-specific physiologic targets or phase-based anesthetic management are established in the supplied evidence.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Relevant reported procedural complications include seroma, hematoma, and nerve injury. In the single retrospective lipoma series, the nerve injury occurred in a large mass and resolved spontaneously; these data do not establish general rates for all soft-tissue excisions.

Maintain attention to bleeding and potential hematoma. The excisional-biopsy reference identifies bleeding as the most common intraoperative concern and notes that persistent bleeding may require further local control.

For expanding, tense postoperative hematoma, the reference describes prompt evacuation and wound-bed re-exploration to reduce risk of tissue ischemia, infection, and edge necrosis; this is procedural guidance, not an anesthetic algorithm.

bullets: The available sources do not establish an intravenous-fluid volume or resuscitation approach for soft-tissue mass excision; individualize to the clinical circumstances rather than adopting a fixed total.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Postanesthesia care applies after general, regional, or monitored anesthesia care. During transport, the patient should be evaluated and treated with monitoring and support appropriate to condition; on PACU arrival, reassessment and handoff are required.
During the initial recovery phase, the postanesthesia standard requires a quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry; ongoing observation should reflect the patient’s condition.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is recommended and recovery to a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 should be confirmed before extubation; this does not apply to cases without blockade.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most procedure-specific source is a retrospective series of lipoma excisions using one technique; it is not an anesthesia reference and did not compare the technique directly with other minimal-incision approaches.

The excisional-biopsy source is an educational narrative review and is not an anesthesia reference; its discussion of cutaneous lesions does not resolve anesthesia choices for deep or complex soft-tissue masses.
The ASA sources provide general standards for monitoring, preanesthesia responsibility, and postanesthesia care, not procedure-specific anesthetic prescriptions.

The lipoma series reports local anesthesia or monitored controlled anesthesia but does not specify which patients received each technique or describe a monitored-anesthesia regimen; it therefore does not establish a case-specific anesthetic plan.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Plan around thyroid function and airway compression, not gland size alone; positional symptoms or substernal extension can change induction and rescue options.
Coordinate the EMG tube and neuromuscular-blocker strategy when recurrent laryngeal nerve monitoring is planned.
Expanding neck hematoma with airway compromise is an immediate emergency; recognize early swallowing, swelling and breathing changes.
After surgery, distinguish hematoma, bilateral vocal-cord dysfunction, edema, hypocalcemia and rare tracheomalacia rather than calling all stridor laryngospasm.

sections.title: Extent, neck dissection & substernal disease
bullets: Clarify lobectomy versus total/completion thyroidectomy, cancer-related nodal dissection, reoperation and any substernal component. Extensive dissection changes airway, nerve and parathyroid risks.

Review imaging when compression or retrosternal extension is suspected, including level/extent of tracheal narrowing. Establish whether positioning worsens symptoms and whether specialist airway or thoracic backup is needed.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)

sections.title: Thyroid state & elective optimization
bullets: Review thyroid function, symptoms, rate/rhythm, heart failure and antithyroid or replacement treatment. Aim to control significant overt hyperthyroidism before elective surgery; avoid assuming an apparently calm patient is biochemically optimized.

Severe hypothyroidism can affect cardiac function, ventilation, drug sensitivity and recovery. Coordinate endocrine optimization and the urgency decision rather than using one abnormal TSH result as a universal cancellation rule.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)

sections.title: Compressive goiter & induction strategy
bullets: Assess voice, dysphagia, stridor, orthopnea, supine intolerance and neck mobility; review prior vocal-cord assessment. Tracheal deviation alone does not mandate awake intubation, but symptoms and meaningful compression warrant a deliberate plan.

For an anticipated difficult airway or intolerance of apnea, consider awake intubation with appropriate oxygenation, topicalization and skilled backup. Confirm tracheal placement visually and with capnography before induction; do not assume maintaining spontaneous breathing guarantees safety.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
APSF: 2022 ASA difficult-airway guideline update

sections.title: Monitoring, access & escalation
bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Choose arterial monitoring, reliable additional IV access and serial laboratory testing for anticipated instability, major surgery or rapid metabolic change rather than for the endocrine label alone.

Agree who communicates hormone-related interventions, key surgical transitions and abnormal laboratory results. Have the required rescue drugs, blood access and postoperative monitoring destination ready before a predictable high-risk phase.

sections.title: Positioning, airway access & exposure
bullets: Check cervical mobility before extending the neck. Pad pressure points, protect eyes, secure the airway and IVs, and recheck ventilation after final positioning and draping. Avoid forcing extension in cervical disease.

Account for restricted airway access after the table turns. Extensive central/lateral neck dissection, reoperation or substernal disease changes the duration and airway plan; it is not interchangeable with a small focused operation.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)

sections.title: Nerve-monitoring tube & neuromuscular blockade
bullets: If laryngeal EMG monitoring is planned, position the tube electrodes correctly at the vocal cords and verify contact after neck positioning. Tube movement, electrode contact and residual blockade can cause poor signals; loss of signal is not automatically surgical nerve injury.

Coordinate adequate intubating conditions with recovery before stimulation. Neuromuscular blockers suppress EMG amplitude, so agree on the induction/reversal strategy and any additional doses rather than applying an indiscriminate “never use relaxant” rule.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring; a usable surgical EMG signal is not proof of complete systemic recovery. When blockade was used, confirm adductor-pollicis train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
APSF: neuromuscular blockade guideline summary (2023)

sections.title: Thyroid storm or unexplained instability
bullets: Unexplained tachyarrhythmia, hyperthermia and cardiovascular deterioration should raise concern for thyroid storm in the appropriate setting, while also evaluating other causes. Altered mental status and gastrointestinal findings may be unavailable under anesthesia.

Stop provoking stimulation where feasible, call for help and initiate the local thyroid-storm pathway with supportive cooling, hemodynamic care, endocrine-directed antithyroid therapy and glucocorticoids. Rate-control drugs require caution in decompensated cardiac failure; a beta blocker is not the whole treatment.

sources.label: Thyroid surgery anesthesia review (2013; historical narrative review)

sections.title: Analgesia, nausea & smooth recovery
bullets: Use multimodal analgesia with acetaminophen, local infiltration or a selected superficial cervical plexus technique, and NSAID/COX-2 therapy when renal, bleeding and other risks permit. Reserve titrated opioids for additional need, particularly with OSA or airway concerns.

Plan risk-based PONV prevention and prompt treatment. Aim for a controlled emergence without severe coughing or retching, but do not sacrifice ventilation or airway protection merely to suppress the response.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)

sections.title: Extubation & postoperative voice/airway
bullets: Plan extubation from the preoperative airway and operative course. Significant compression, difficult intubation, swelling or nerve concerns may require delayed extubation or a staged specialist plan rather than routine immediate removal.

Bilateral RLN dysfunction can cause acute stridor and airway obstruction; unilateral dysfunction may cause hoarseness or impaired airway protection. Escalate new voice or respiratory changes, and do not use a reassuring nerve-monitor trace as a substitute for clinical assessment.

Tracheomalacia is an uncommon consideration after longstanding compression, not an assumed finding in every large goiter. A cuff-leak assessment cannot by itself rule out every cause of extubation failure.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
APSF: 2022 ASA difficult-airway guideline update
Thyroid surgery anesthesia review (2013; historical narrative review)

sections.title: Neck hematoma: recognize & act
bullets: Look for DESATS: difficulty swallowing/discomfort, rising early-warning score, swelling, anxiety, tachypnea/difficulty breathing and stridor. Stridor may be late; a small hematoma can still produce dangerous airway compression and venous congestion.

Call surgical and senior anesthesia help, give oxygen and assess the airway with the patient head-up. Rapidly expanding swelling or airway compromise requires immediate emergency management; do not delay decompression for imaging or routine transfer.

For airway compromise from suspected hematoma, trained clinicians should open and evacuate the wound using the local emergency protocol. SCOOP means skin exposure, cut sutures, open skin, open muscles including the strap layer, and pack the wound. Merely opening superficial skin may not decompress the deeper collection.

If compromise persists, proceed with expert airway management, limited attempts and immediate front-of-neck rescue capability. Definitive surgical hemostasis and close monitored care are still required after initial decompression. The thyroid consensus is the direct source; adapt through the local neck-surgery pathway for parathyroid cases.

sources.label: DAS/BAETS/ENT-UK: thyroid hematoma consensus guideline (2021)
StatPearls: Parathyroidectomy (2024)

sections.title: Hypocalcemia & hormone replacement
bullets: Monitor postoperative calcium/PTH according to extent of surgery and local protocol. Paresthesia, muscle spasm, tetany, QT prolongation or laryngospasm can signal hypocalcemia; severe symptomatic cases require monitored urgent treatment.

Total thyroidectomy requires thyroid-hormone replacement; after partial surgery assess residual function rather than assuming the same regimen for everyone. Document endocrine follow-up and any calcium/calcitriol plan at discharge.

sections.title: Observation & discharge safeguards
bullets: Ensure staff can recognize hematoma and access emergency neck-opening equipment. The DAS consensus recommends at least hourly observations initially for 6 hours after thyroid surgery, with subsequent frequency and discharge individualized to risk and local policy.
Provide explicit emergency advice for neck swelling, swallowing/breathing difficulty and hypocalcemic symptoms. An uneventful PACU period does not eliminate later hematoma risk.

Guidelines, narrative reviews and device/procedure-specific evidence are not interchangeable. Hormone status, organ reserve and postoperative trends determine the plan; a tumor label alone does not establish safe anesthesia or discharge.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Tracheostomy establishes an airway through the anterior tracheal wall by an open surgical or percutaneous approach. Open procedures are usually performed in an operating room; percutaneous placement is commonly performed at the bedside in an ICU.

The key anesthetic priorities are coordinated airway transition, reliable confirmation of tracheostomy-tube position, and avoidance of loss of ventilation or airway access. End-tidal carbon dioxide and, for percutaneous placement, bronchoscopic visualization support confirmation.

Important hazards include operative bleeding, false passage or airway loss during tube exchange, posterior-wall injury, and rare airway fire when electrocautery is used in an oxygen-enriched environment.

Recovery planning centers on a secured, patent tracheostomy airway, surveillance for bleeding, obstruction or displacement, and appropriate postanesthesia or ICU care. The source does not establish a specific anesthetic emergence or analgesia regimen.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Tracheostomy creates an opening in the anterior tracheal wall, usually between the second and third rings. The approaches described are open surgery and percutaneous placement using a modified Seldinger technique.

Open tracheostomy is traditionally performed in the operating room; selected cases may be performed under local anesthesia. Percutaneous placement is usually performed at the ICU bedside, though it may also be done in the operating room.

The choice of approach depends on the clinical situation, anatomy, procedural expertise and setting. In the COVID-era review, evidence did not establish superiority of open over percutaneous technique; that review’s infection-control context should not be treated as a general approach mandate.
Initial placement generally uses a cuffed, nonfenestrated tracheostomy tube. The operative technique and airway plan should be coordinated between the proceduralist and airway operator.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify the indication and whether the patient is already intubated; assess current airway access, neck anatomy, prior surgery or radiation, and coagulation status. These factors can affect approach and procedural difficulty.

For a planned case, review whether the patient can tolerate the brief ventilation interruption that may be needed during tracheal entry or dilation. The available sources do not establish a universal threshold for tolerance.

In life-threatening airway emergencies, the source states that no condition is an absolute contraindication to tracheostomy; management remains dependent on the emergency and available airway options.

The COVID-era review recommends multidisciplinary discussion for its population and describes infectious-risk planning. Those recommendations are specific to COVID-19-era practice and do not establish routine timing or testing requirements for other patients.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For neck access, supine positioning with neck extension is described; a shoulder roll or chest bump can improve anterior tracheal access. Individualize positioning when neck mobility or anatomy limits extension.

Have tracheostomy equipment and appropriate tube options available. For percutaneous placement, the described technique uses flexible bronchoscopy to visualize needle and guidewire placement and confirm tube position.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. ASA standards call for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature; for general anesthesia, expired carbon dioxide monitoring is continued unless invalidated by the patient, procedure or equipment.

For a transmissible respiratory pathogen or other aerosol-risk context, use infection precautions and room controls appropriate to the circumstance and local policy; the COVID-era review describes negative-pressure rooms when available.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Open procedures are usually performed under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation, but selected upper-airway-compromise cases may be managed awake under local anesthesia with spontaneous breathing. Percutaneous procedures are typically performed in intubated, sedated patients, with or without neuromuscular blockade.

For percutaneous placement, the described conventional technique withdraws the ETT under bronchoscopic guidance before needle entry; coordinate ETT movement and tracheal access with the proceduralist. The precise airway sequence may vary by approach.

Ventilation may be interrupted briefly during tracheal entry or percutaneous dilation if clinically feasible. Once the tracheostomy tube is inserted, confirm placement with end-tidal carbon dioxide and reconfirm ventilation.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This recommendation is conditional on blockade use; it does not impose paralysis for every tracheostomy.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: The airway transition is a critical phase: coordinate ETT withdrawal, tracheal entry, tracheostomy-tube insertion and connection to the breathing circuit. Confirm tube position and ventilation after the transition.

Bleeding can obscure the operative field or impede bronchoscopy. The source emphasizes correction of coagulopathy when possible and meticulous hemostasis; it does not supply a universal fluid or transfusion regimen for this reference.

When electrocautery is used, coordinate with the surgical team to reduce airway-fire risk from oxygen and ignition sources. The supplied sources do not establish a universal inspired-oxygen threshold for all tracheostomies.
Tracheostomy may reduce airway resistance and facilitate ventilator weaning, but the source does not provide case-specific physiologic targets or a ventilation prescription.

sources.label: Tracheostomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Anticipate bleeding, false passage, tube obstruction, displacement and loss of airway access. Tube displacement into soft tissue or a false passage may require airway re-establishment; the source identifies flexible-laryngoscopic guidance as preferable for reintubation when required.
Posterior-wall disruption, false passage or apical injury can lead to pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum. Bronchoscopy can help prevent posterior-wall injury during percutaneous placement.

If airway fire occurs, the source describes immediate circuit removal, mask ventilation and airway inspection for thermal injury. This is a source-reported response, not a substitute for local emergency protocols.

Early tube changes are discouraged unless necessary because the immature tract increases the risk of false passage and airway compromise. The source describes the initial tube change as typically occurring on postoperative days 5 to 7; this is not a universal timing instruction for an individual patient.

sources.label: Tracheostomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Bleeding is identified as the most common intraoperative complication. Assess and manage hemostasis in the context of the patient’s coagulation status and procedural findings.

The tracheostomy overview provides no fluid regimen or specific fluid-management guidance. Fluid administration and perfusion goals therefore remain patient- and context-dependent rather than fixed by these sources.

The COVID-era review likewise does not specify fluid-management regimens, blood-product thresholds or transfusion practice; its discussion of anticoagulation is specific to COVID-associated illness and does not define a general perioperative anticoagulation protocol.

sources.label: Tracheostomy
Perioperative Considerations for Tracheostomies in the Era of COVID-19

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: The tracheostomy source provides no analgesic regimen or specific postoperative pain-management recommendation. It therefore does not support a standard drug or dose for this procedure.

The supplied sources do not provide a procedure-specific PONV assessment or prophylaxis regimen; manage these issues according to the patient and applicable practice guidance rather than infer a tracheostomy-specific protocol.

sources.label: Tracheostomy

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The procedure establishes a tracheostomy airway, which is connected to the ventilator as appropriate. Confirm placement with end-tidal carbon dioxide and reassess ventilation; the source does not specify when or how anesthesia should be discontinued or the ETT removed.

Plan recovery in a PACU or equivalent area such as an ICU, with transport monitoring and handoff appropriate to the patient’s condition. The ASA postanesthesia standards call for attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness and temperature.

Postprocedure surveillance includes tube patency and position, bleeding, and subcutaneous air. Humidified gas, suctioning and routine stoma or cannula care are described as measures to reduce obstruction risk.

sources.label: Tracheostomy

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal procedure source is a clinical overview, not an anesthesia-specific guideline or formal systematic review. It describes approaches, airway considerations and complications but does not provide detailed anesthetic emergence, analgesia or fluid protocols.

The second procedure source concerns COVID-19-associated respiratory failure and is a narrative review combining prior outbreak literature with institutional experience. Its timing and infection-control discussion should not be generalized as routine practice outside its scope.

ASA basic monitoring, postanesthesia-care and neuromuscular-blockade sources support general monitoring and recovery principles, not a tracheostomy-specific anesthetic plan. The supplied ERAS sources concern gastrointestinal surgery and provide no tracheostomy recommendations.

A specific cuff-pressure target is not adopted here: the tracheostomy overview gives discordant pressure statements in different sections and uses different units. Case-specific anesthetic targets and an analgesia or emergence protocol are not established by the available procedure sources.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Large ventral defects and loss of domain can make closure physiologically important, not just technically difficult.
GA is usual for laparoscopic/robotic reconstruction; plan limited airway access, prolonged positioning and possible open conversion.
Evaluate OSA, pulmonary reserve, aspiration risk and antithrombotics; obstructed patients need an emergency-abdominal plan.
Watch for worsening ventilation and organ perfusion after reduction/closure; plan multimodal pain control and an appropriate monitored recovery.

sections.title: Defect, urgency & patient reserve
bullets: Review defect size, loss of domain, prior mesh/infection, expected adhesiolysis, bowel involvement and reconstruction duration. Obesity/OSA and limited respiratory reserve affect both induction and closure tolerance.

Review antithrombotics, frailty and cardiopulmonary disease. In an obstructed or septic patient, prepare for resuscitation and bowel resection rather than treating this as an isolated abdominal wall operation.

sections.title: Local, regional or general anesthesia
bullets: For suitable open inguinal repair, an experienced team may use local infiltration/field block with or without carefully titrated sedation. Patient acceptance and the planned dissection matter.

Do not extrapolate open inguinal PROSPECT recommendations to all femoral, ventral or robotic repairs. Complex laparoscopic/robotic repair generally requires controlled ventilation, immobility and a secured airway.

sources.label: PROSPECT open inguinal hernia repair recommendations (2019; procedure-specific)

Abdominal wall reconstruction anesthesia (2012 review; limited direct evidence)

sections.title: OSA, aspiration & airway access
bullets: Assess OSA/obesity, regurgitation and obstruction. Preoxygenate and position to optimize ventilation; plan the airway before robotic docking.
With incarceration and vomiting, use an individualized aspiration-risk induction, gastric decompression when indicated and readily available suction; sedation does not provide aspiration protection.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: laparoscopic and robotic surgery (2024 educational review)
ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum, positioning & ventilation
bullets: CO₂ insufflation reduces respiratory compliance/FRC, increases CO₂ load and can alter SVR and venous return; the direction of cardiac-output change depends on pressure, position and volume status. Use predicted/ideal, not actual, body weight for lung-protective tidal volume.

Individualize PEEP and minute ventilation to mechanics, oxygenation and CO₂. Reverse Trendelenburg may worsen hypotension; Trendelenburg may worsen airway pressures and edema. Sudden severe bradycardia during insufflation warrants immediate communication, stopping the stimulus/deflation and treatment as clinically indicated.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: laparoscopic and robotic surgery (2024 educational review)

sections.title: Perfusion, fluids & electrolytes
bullets: Account for vomiting, bowel preparation, poor intake, bleeding and measured gastric/wound losses. Give fluid for evidence of hypovolemia or fluid responsiveness and reassess; do not replace a presumed fixed “third-space deficit.”

Avoid both excess crystalloid and under-resuscitation. Balanced crystalloid is often appropriate; distinguish vasodilatory hypotension from hemorrhage or low output and use vasoactive support when indicated. Correct potassium, sodium and acid-base disturbances with attention to renal function.

sources.label: ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)
ASCRS/SAGES elective colorectal ERAS guideline (2022/2023)

sections.title: Reduction, loss of domain & closure
bullets: After reduction and closure, a rise in airway pressure, reduced compliance, oliguria or circulatory compromise may signal harmful intra-abdominal pressure. Discuss tension and organ dysfunction immediately; an isolated airway pressure is not a diagnostic criterion for abdominal compartment syndrome.

Compare respiratory mechanics and perfusion before and after closure. Avoid reflex large fluid loads that may worsen edema; coordinate reassessment of closure, abdominal pressure when indicated and postoperative ventilation.

sources.label: Abdominal wall reconstruction anesthesia (2012 review; limited direct evidence)
ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: Regional options & recovery priorities
bullets: Infiltration, ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric block or TAP techniques can reduce opioid needs for appropriate incisions. Match the technique to the actual surgical field and account for all local-anesthetic doses.

Use nonopioid analgesics when safe, with opioids as rescue. Screen for urinary retention, nausea, uncontrolled pain and respiratory depression; major reconstruction may need inpatient respiratory support and VTE planning.

sources.label: PROSPECT open inguinal hernia repair recommendations (2019; procedure-specific)
Abdominal wall reconstruction anesthesia (2012 review; limited direct evidence)

sections.title: Monitoring, access & temperature
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring and temperature surveillance when significant changes are anticipated. Major bleeding, shock, prolonged surgery or limited reserve may warrant an arterial line, repeated blood gases and additional venous access.

Choose access for the anticipated blood and vasoactive requirements; a central line is not automatically necessary for every abdominal operation. Warm exposed patients and significant fluid/blood infusions, and reassess glucose and electrolytes according to illness and procedure.

sources.label: ASA Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
ERAS emergency laparotomy Part 2 (2023; excludes vascular, trauma, appendicitis and cholecystitis)

sections.title: Extubation, respiratory recovery & disposition
bullets: Before extubation, assess wakefulness, airway protection, ventilation, oxygenation, temperature, perfusion and ongoing bleeding. If neuromuscular blockers were used, verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; head lift alone is insufficient.

Plan monitored or ICU recovery for persistent shock, major resuscitation, respiratory failure or an open abdomen. CPAP/NIV for postoperative hypoxemia requires an appropriate patient with low aspiration risk, skilled monitoring and prompt escalation if it fails.

bullets: Adult clinical-review draft, not an individualized order set or independently approved protocol. Emergency, elective, endoscopic and vascular pathways have different evidence bases; do not transfer every ERAS recommendation between them.

Use current institutional airway, transfusion, anticoagulation and rescue policies. The date marks source checking, not a guarantee that every linked review is new; older educational sources and institutional pathways are labeled.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Debridement ranges from bedside sharp removal to surgical excision in the operating room. Surgical debridement removes nonviable tissue down to intact structures; the extent and method depend on the wound and patient.

For surgical cases, plan adequate anesthesia and account for pain and bleeding. Tissue and vessel injury with bleeding are common during surgical debridement; wound-care sources do not establish an anesthetic technique for a particular patient or wound.

Choose the anesthetic and monitoring to fit the planned procedure and patient; available sources do not establish a default airway, ventilation strategy, invasive monitoring plan, or fluid regimen for debridement.

After anesthesia, use an appropriate postanesthesia-care setting and monitor recovery according to the patient's condition. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited guideline supports quantitative confirmation of recovery before extubation.

A Primer on Wound Bed Preparation

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Debridement removes adherent dead tissue, scabs, or foreign bodies; the selected method should reflect the wound and patient rather than assume one technique is suitable for all cases. Debridement supports wound assessment and healing, but repeated, unselected surgical removal may impair healing.

Sharp debridement may be performed on an outpatient basis and can leave nonviable tissue behind. Surgical debridement is more extensive and, in the cited wound primer, is performed in the operating room; pronounced findings warrant adequate anesthesia in an operating room in the position paper.

The wound primer notes that surgical debridement often requires general anesthesia or local infiltrate. The position paper advises discussing general anesthesia as an option; neither source establishes a universal anesthetic technique.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
A Primer on Wound Bed Preparation

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify wound extent, the proposed method and setting, patient comorbidities, pain, and the patient's overall condition. The cited position paper also identifies available resources and clinician competencies as factors in method selection.

Assess bleeding risk before surgical debridement, including coagulation disorders and anticoagulant treatment, and incorporate findings into procedural planning. The source identifies significant bleeding as a particular complication but gives no thresholds or medication-interruption schedule.

Assess pain and consider individualized, adequate analgesia. Pyoderma gangrenosum during its inflammatory phase is identified as a condition in which debridement may worsen disease through pathergy; the source says medically controlled inflammation changes that consideration.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
A Primer on Wound Bed Preparation

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For pronounced findings requiring surgical debridement, the wound-care position paper recommends an operating-room setting with adequate anesthesia. It does not provide positioning, access, warming, or room-equipment specifications.

Apply the relevant basic anesthesia monitoring standards for the anesthetic delivered: oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature are continually evaluated, with blood pressure and heart rate assessed at least every five minutes.

Do not infer that an arterial line is routinely required for this procedure. The monitoring standard describes intra-arterial pressure as one possible means of continually evaluating circulation during general anesthesia, not a debridement-specific indication.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The provided wound-debridement sources do not specify airway choice, induction, ventilation, or criteria for general versus local anesthesia beyond noting that surgical debridement may require general anesthesia or local infiltrate. Select technique for the individual procedure and patient; no routine intubation or paralysis is established here.

For general anesthesia, follow the basic ventilation-monitoring standard, including continual evaluation of ventilation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the standard's stated exceptions apply.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, the cited ASA-guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not apply as a requirement to local-anesthetic or other cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Surgical debridement may involve removal down to intact tissue, with tissue and vessel injury and bleeding commonly occurring. The supplied wound sources do not define physiologic targets or procedure-specific critical phases.
After surgical debridement, the position paper describes hemostasis by manual compression or hemostatic wound dressings and recommends a short-term clinical check that bleeding is controlled.

The primer notes that sharp or surgical debridement often causes bleeding; it provides no bleeding rate or quantified complication risk. Avoid extrapolating this observation to an expected blood loss for an individual case.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
A Primer on Wound Bed Preparation

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Bleeding is a recognized complication of surgical debridement. Reassess hemostasis clinically after the procedure; the wound position paper does not supply a blood-loss threshold or a transfusion algorithm.
Consider pathergy in susceptible wounds, particularly pyoderma gangrenosum during active inflammation. The source advises that debridement can be performed when inflammation is medically controlled.
Worsening wound findings may include increased exudate, pain, odor, bleeding, and tissue friability.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
A Primer on Wound Bed Preparation

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Individualize fluid and blood-product planning to the patient, wound, and observed losses. The supplied sources do not establish a fluid volume, transfusion threshold, or blood-product preparation rule for debridement.

Account for bleeding risk before the procedure and assess hemostasis after surgical debridement. The wound paper describes clinical bleeding control rather than a quantitative perfusion or blood-loss endpoint.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)
A Primer on Wound Bed Preparation

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Assess pain regularly with an appropriate instrument and plan analgesia individually. The position paper gives visual analog and numeric rating scales as examples.
For minor procedures, topical lidocaine–prilocaine cream may be sufficient; the position paper specifies an adequate application time of not less than 30–60 minutes.
Discuss general anesthesia as an option for surgical debridement when appropriate. No PONV prevention or treatment regimen is supplied for this procedure.

sources.label: Position paper of the Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. on the nomenclature of debridement in chronic wounds (German title: Positionspapier der Initiative Chronische Wunde (ICW) e. V. zur Nomenklatur des Débridements chronischer Wunden)

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The supplied debridement sources do not provide emergence criteria or procedure-specific postoperative anesthesia care. Use the appropriate postanesthesia-care setting unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise.

During recovery, evaluate the patient continually with monitoring appropriate to medical condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. A quantitative oxygenation method such as pulse oximetry is required in the initial recovery phase under the cited standard.

If neuromuscular blockade was used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation as described in the cited guideline overview. The source does not establish a debridement-specific discharge or extubation protocol.

New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most procedure-relevant source is an ICW professional-society position paper on chronic-wound debridement nomenclature and wound-care practice, not an anesthesia reference. It supports debridement-method selection, analgesia considerations, bleeding risk, and clinical bleeding checks, but does not provide an anesthetic plan.

The second wound source is a primer/review covering acute and chronic wounds; it describes debridement approaches but supplies no anesthesia-specific recommendations. Neither wound source specifies an adult-only population.

ASA sources provide general standards for monitoring, preanesthesia responsibility, and postanesthesia care, not debridement-specific technique or risk management. The neuromuscular-blockade source is an overview of ASA guidance and applies only when neuromuscular blocking drugs are used.
The supplied GI ERAS sources concern gastrointestinal surgery and provide no debridement-specific recommendations in the supplied content; they do not resolve the case-specific anesthesia gaps.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Routine diagnostic EGD and emergency EGD for bleeding or obstruction are different anesthesia scenarios.
The scope shares the mouth/pharynx; preplan oxygen delivery, suction, ventilation monitoring and scope withdrawal for rescue.
Use patient- and procedure-specific sedation or GA, with a protected-airway strategy when aspiration/protection needs justify it.
Assess recovery for aspiration, bleeding, perforation and residual sedation rather than time alone.

sources.label: BSG adult endoscopy sedation guideline (2023/2024)

sections.title: Diagnostic versus urgent therapeutic EGD
bullets: Confirm whether the procedure is diagnostic, dilation, biopsy, hemostasis or foreign-body retrieval. Identify active bleeding, gastric outlet obstruction or severe dysphagia.
Escalate to the dedicated bleeding, foreign-body or advanced endoscopy reference when needed; routine outpatient assumptions are unsafe in those settings.

sources.label: BSG adult endoscopy sedation guideline (2023/2024)
ESGE peptic-ulcer bleeding guideline update (May 2026)

sections.title: Shared airway and anesthetic technique
bullets: No sedation, topical anesthesia, moderate/deep sedation or GA may be appropriate depending on the patient and planned examination. Coordinate the bite block, scope and airway devices.

Plan intubation selectively for protection/aspiration or procedural needs; an EGD label alone does not mandate an ETT. If an awake difficult-airway approach is indicated, plan it before loss of protective reflexes.

sources.label: BSG adult endoscopy sedation guideline (2023/2024)

sections.title: Frailty, OSA and physiologic reserve
bullets: Review previous sedation problems, OSA/obesity, baseline oxygen/ventilatory support and cardiopulmonary reserve. Frail or older patients often need smaller, slower sedative increments with time to assess the effect.

Assess fasting losses, bowel preparation, renal/hepatic dysfunction and concurrent sedating medicines. Hypotension or apnea may reflect excessive drug effect, but persistent deterioration also requires a procedural differential.

sources.label: BSG adult endoscopy sedation guideline (2023/2024)

sections.title: GLP-1 and retained contents
bullets: Assess dose escalation, significant GI symptoms and other delayed-emptying disorders. Most low-risk elective patients can continue GLP-1 therapy under the multisociety approach; universal withholding is not the default.

Higher-risk patients may need a coordinated liquid-only diet strategy, altered anesthesia, trained gastric ultrasound or elective delay. Neither fasting nor a held dose guarantees absent retained contents; urgency and the underlying disease still matter.

sources.label: ASA summary of multisociety GLP-1 guidance (2024; updated 2025)
BSG adult endoscopy sedation guideline (2023/2024)

sections.title: Diagnostic versus therapeutic bleeding risk
bullets: Confirm the actual planned intervention: diagnostic examination/biopsy, EUS without sampling and stent-only ERCP differ from sphincterotomy, EUS sampling, polypectomy and EMR/ESD. A low-risk booking may become therapeutic.

Balance bleeding against thrombosis with the prescribing/procedural team, particularly for coronary stents or mechanical valves. Do not give a blanket “stop all blood thinners” instruction; drug, renal function, intervention and current guidance determine interruption, bridging and restart.

sources.label: BSG/ESGE endoscopy antithrombotic guideline (2021; individualize and check current protocol)
ASGE gastrostomy feeding tube guideline (2025)

sections.title: Respiratory events and postoperative warning signs
bullets: Obstruction, apnea, laryngospasm, bronchospasm or aspiration can occur during upper-airway stimulation. Stop and regain airway control rather than repeatedly deepening sedation without reassessment.
Chest/abdominal pain out of proportion, fever, bleeding, dyspnea or persistent instability after instrumentation warrants evaluation for a procedural injury or aspiration.

sources.label: BSG adult endoscopy sedation guideline (2023/2024)

sections.title: Remote-location preparation & shared airway
bullets: Before starting, verify oxygen, suction, bag-mask ventilation, airway devices, resuscitation equipment, trained assistance and the transfer route. Arrange the patient, scope, tubing and monitors so the airway remains reachable.

Agree how the endoscopist will stop, withdraw the scope and help reposition the patient if ventilation or resuscitation is needed. High-flow oxygen may support oxygenation in selected patients but does not prevent aspiration or substitute for ventilation monitoring.

sources.label: ASA Statement on Nonoperating Room Anesthesia Services (2023)
BSG adult endoscopy sedation guideline (2023/2024)

sections.title: Monitoring, sedation depth & respiratory rescue
bullets: MAC describes an anesthesia service, not a fixed depth of sedation. Moderate/deep sedation can progress to apnea or loss of airway reflexes; the anesthesia plan must include rescue and possible conversion to GA.

Use ECG, pulse oximetry and blood pressure/heart rate at least every five minutes for anesthesia care. Monitor exhaled CO₂ during moderate/deep sedation unless precluded or invalidated; oxygen saturation alone may miss hypoventilation. Temperature monitoring depends on anticipated changes and procedure/anesthetic requirements.

sources.label: ASA Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
BSG adult endoscopy sedation guideline (2023/2024)
ASA sedation terminology reproduced in CMS document (definition only; not GI coverage guidance)

sections.title: Recovery, complications & discharge
bullets: Continue monitoring until consciousness, ventilation and circulation recover adequately. Persistent pain, hypoxemia, fever, bleeding or instability requires assessment for a procedural complication rather than automatic discharge.

bullets: ERCP combines upper shared-airway instrumentation with prone/semi-prone or lateral positioning and potentially limited rescue access.
MAC with planned sedation and GA with tracheal intubation are both options; higher aspiration risk or prolonged complex work may favor GA.
Review cholangitis/sepsis, obstruction, cardiopulmonary reserve and the planned intervention before choosing technique.
Prepare for pancreatitis, hemorrhage, perforation and infection; sudden deterioration also requires an airway/ventilation and cardiovascular assessment.

sections.title: Biliary disease, sepsis and complexity
bullets: Clarify duct stones, obstruction, cholangitis, stent exchange, sphincterotomy or combined EUS/ERCP. Review labs and organ function appropriate to illness.
Sepsis may produce vasodilation, hypovolemia and myocardial dysfunction; coordinate antibiotics, drainage and active resuscitation rather than treating this as routine ambulatory sedation.

sections.title: MAC versus GA: individualized choice
bullets: The 2023 modified-Delphi consensus favors MAC in many scenarios but identifies increased aspiration risk and prolonged high-complexity procedures as reasons to favor GA with intubation. This is expert consensus, not proof that one technique is best for every patient.

Age or ASA classification alone does not settle the decision. Consider airway access, gastric outlet obstruction, major bleeding risk, respiratory reserve, provider experience and the consequences of emergency conversion.

sections.title: Prone/semi-prone positioning and conversion
bullets: Agree the final position and how the team will withdraw the scope and turn the patient if ventilation fails. Secure the airway/circuit if intubated; pad eyes and pressure points and maintain line access.

sections.title: Stenting versus sphincterotomy
bullets: Biliary/pancreatic stenting without sphincterotomy is classified differently from ERCP with sphincterotomy. If sphincterotomy may be needed, clarify the higher-risk antithrombotic pathway before starting.
Coordinate interruption/restart with bleeding and thrombotic risk; avoid automatic discontinuation in coronary-stent or other high-risk patients.

sections.title: Instability, bleeding and perforation
bullets: Check airway/ventilation and perfusion immediately when instability occurs; ask about bleeding, perforation or other procedural events. Persistent hypotension is not necessarily simply propofol effect.
Massive post-sphincterotomy bleeding may require airway control, major-hemorrhage support and endoscopic/IR/surgical rescue. Have a transfer/escalation plan before the first intervention.

sections.title: Pancreatitis, infection and PONV

Postprocedure abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, bleeding or instability requires evaluation for pancreatitis, cholangitis or perforation. Use risk-based antiemetic/analgesic treatment without masking deterioration.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Transvaginal cerclage is the usual approach. When appropriate, regional anesthesia is commonly favored over general anesthesia with tracheal intubation; either technique may be used when carefully selected.

Priorities include confirming the indication and excluding labor, ruptured membranes, and infection; pregnancy-related aspiration risk and aortocaval compression should inform anesthetic and positioning decisions.

Lithotomy, with Trendelenburg when needed to reduce bulging membranes, is described for transvaginal placement. Fetal heart rate is assessed before and after; continuous intraoperative fetal monitoring is generally not performed.

Recovery priorities are obstetric reassessment and observation for contractions, bleeding, membrane rupture, infection, and neuraxial-block resolution; pain is often limited and acetaminophen is commonly used.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for cervical cerclage
Anesthesia for Cervical Cerclage

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Cerclage reinforces the cervix for cervical insufficiency, with the aim of reducing second-trimester loss or preterm birth. The usual approach is transvaginal; transabdominal cerclage is a distinct option for selected anatomical limitations or prior failed cerclage.

The cited ACOG indications include a relevant second-trimester loss history, physical-examination findings, or an ultrasound indication in a patient with prior preterm birth. Timing depends on indication and guidance; it is not a single universal window.

Transabdominal cerclage is not interchangeable with routine transvaginal placement: laparoscopic or robotic abdominal procedures generally require general anesthesia, while an open approach may use general or neuraxial anesthesia.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Cervical Cerclage
Anaesthesia for cervical cerclage

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Confirm the indication and coordinate with obstetrics to assess for labor, ruptured membranes, infection, bleeding, and fetal demise or lethal anomaly before proceeding. These findings may preclude cerclage or materially change the risk assessment.

Assess maternal health, airway, back if neuraxial anesthesia is considered, gestational age, patient preference, and the need for uterine relaxation. For general anesthesia, airway security should reflect body habitus, airway examination, and fasting status—not a routine intubation rule.

Pregnancy-related aspiration risk warrants individualized assessment and prophylaxis when indicated. The supplied sources do not support treating any fasting status as eliminating risk or applying one airway strategy to every patient.

sources.label: Anesthesia for Cervical Cerclage
Anaesthesia for cervical cerclage

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Transvaginal placement may occur in a general operating theatre or a labor-and-delivery unit, depending on institutional practice. Lithotomy is described, with left uterine displacement as clinically appropriate.
Trendelenburg can facilitate reduction of bulging membranes, but may increase neuraxial spread; coordinate positioning and block timing with the procedural team.

Assess fetal heart rate before and after placement. Continuous intraoperative fetal monitoring is generally not performed in this setting, reflecting viability and interpretive limitations described in the review; this is not a claim that fetal assessment is unnecessary.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for cervical cerclage
Anesthesia for Cervical Cerclage

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Regional anesthesia avoids airway instrumentation and reduces exposure to general anesthetic agents; the review favors regional techniques over general anesthesia with tracheal intubation in its discussion. This is a preference when suitable, not an absolute requirement.

Spinal anesthesia is described as technically straightforward and reliably providing dense sensory block; an epidural or combined spinal–epidural may be considered when duration or the ability to extend a block matters. The supplied evidence does not establish one neuraxial technique as mandatory.

If general anesthesia is selected, use the airway approach appropriate to the individual assessment. The source allows a laryngeal mask or natural airway for appropriately fasted patients; it does not prescribe routine rapid-sequence induction or intubation for every cerclage.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for cervical cerclage

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Bulging membranes and uterine relaxation can shape the anesthetic plan. Volatile agents may relax uterine smooth muscle under general anesthesia; if regional anesthesia is used and relaxation is needed, the review describes intravenous nitroglycerin as an option.

Trendelenburg may help the obstetrician reduce bulging membranes; avoid assuming it is physiologically neutral because it can increase neuraxial spread. Coordinate the maneuver and anesthetic assessment with the operator.

Maintain standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the technique and patient. The cerclage-specific sources do not establish a distinct monitoring protocol beyond fetal assessment before and after the procedure.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Recognized maternal and procedural risks include infection, bleeding, cervical injury, uterine irritability or contractions, rupture of membranes, and preterm labor. Escalate new or worsening findings with the obstetric team.

Fetal and obstetric risks include pregnancy loss, PPROM, and preterm birth despite placement. New fetal bradycardia or membrane concerns warrant prompt obstetric reassessment; the supplied sources do not provide a cerclage-specific rescue algorithm.

If neuraxial anesthesia is used, Trendelenburg and hyperbaric solution positioning can affect block height. Reassess block extent when position changes or unexpected symptoms occur; the review does not give a detailed treatment pathway for a high block.
