sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The cerclage-specific review provides no fluid regimen, expected blood loss, or bleeding-management approach. Do not infer a fixed fluid volume, blood-loss estimate, or transfusion plan from the supplied evidence.
When gestational physiology makes aortocaval compression relevant, left uterine displacement is described to mitigate hemodynamic effects. Individualize positioning to the patient and procedure.
Transabdominal approaches have distinct potential for hemorrhage and visceral injury; the supplied sources give no procedure-specific blood-loss or transfusion algorithm.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Uterine cramping may occur regardless of anesthetic technique. Paracetamol is usually prescribed; the review does not establish long-acting intrathecal opioids as routine practice.
Most patients are described as having minimal pain; acetaminophen or a small oral opioid dose may be used if needed. No cerclage-specific PONV regimen is provided.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Assess fetal status after the procedure, using gestation-appropriate obstetric assessment. The review specifies fetal heart-rate assessment before and after placement, regardless of anesthetic technique.

Observe for contractions, bleeding, hemodynamic instability, and neuraxial-block resolution; continue to assess for infection or membrane rupture as recovery proceeds. Disposition should follow the responsible obstetric and anesthesia teams’ assessment.
The cerclage-specific review does not provide a detailed emergence protocol or universal discharge criteria; do not infer these from the procedure description alone.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal procedure-specific source is an educational clinical review, not a guideline or systematic review. It reports that available evidence found no long-term maternal or fetal outcome difference between regional and general anesthesia when carefully performed, while discussing regional techniques as preferred over general anesthesia with tracheal intubation; these statements support individual selection, not a universal mandate.

The second procedure-specific source is an educational clinical summary, not original research or a guideline; it explicitly notes that its supplied content omits a detailed intraoperative monitoring protocol and fluid regimen. Use the clinical claims here within those limits.

Procedure-specific evidence in the supplied material does not establish detailed algorithms for bleeding, fluid management, fetal or maternal deterioration, or discharge. These remain areas for local specialist judgment; this draft is not a complete or approved clinical protocol.

bullets: Often a brief procedure with local anesthesia, sedation or GA depending on extent and tolerance.
Immobility during excision must be balanced with airway safety; a brief case can still cause apnea under deep sedation.
Cervical bleeding and responses to locally injected vasoactive medication require communication.
Recovery focuses on bleeding, pain/nausea control and clear return precautions.

bullets: Clarify loop excision versus a larger cone, estimated bleeding and intended local anesthetic/vasoconstrictor. Confirm allergies and cumulative local-anesthetic exposure with the team; communicate before injections and monitor for cardiovascular changes.

Unexpected bradycardia or hypotension during cervical manipulation requires stopping the stimulus and assessing ventilation, perfusion and blood loss. If vasopressin is proposed, its systemic cardiovascular toxicity applies even to local injection; the cited evidence is a safety signal, not a cervical dosing standard.

bullets: Quantify vaginal blood loss and clarify the location and adequacy of surgical hemostasis. A cervical laceration or excisional vessel injury is not treated by assuming uterine atony alone.

Persistent bleeding or instability requires access/resuscitation escalation and a definitive surgical plan. Before discharge, reconcile anticoagulant restart instructions and expected versus concerning bleeding.

Assess vomiting, pain/opioids, reflux, obstruction, fasting and gestational stage individually. bullets: Use appropriate ECG, blood pressure, oxygenation and ventilation monitoring; exhaled CO₂ is expected during moderate/deep sedation unless precluded or invalidated. Monitor temperature when clinically significant changes are intended, anticipated or suspected.

Match venous access, arterial monitoring and blood availability to hemorrhage risk and physiologic reserve, not the procedure name alone. Warm patients and substantial fluid/blood infusions; reassess hemoglobin, electrolytes, glucose and acid-base status as indicated.

sections.title: Lithotomy, pressure points & nerve protection
bullets: Document mobility limits and neuropathy; lift and lower legs together with adequate personnel. Protect the fibular head, heels and calves, avoid excessive hip flexion/abduction or external rotation, and avoid traction/compression on the brachial plexus or tucked arms.

Minimize time in lithotomy and steep Trendelenburg, reassess supports and perfusion when feasible, and avoid prolonged hypotension or concentrated calf pressure. Severe postoperative leg pain, swelling or weakness can signal compartment syndrome even with palpable pulses; obtain urgent assessment rather than attributing it automatically to a block.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & fluid balance
bullets: Target euvolemia with reassessment of perfusion and measured losses; avoid both indiscriminate crystalloid loading and rigid restriction during bleeding. Distinguish vasodilation from hypovolemia or low cardiac output before choosing fluid, blood or vasoactive support.

Account for poor intake, bowel preparation, ascites drainage and irrigation absorption when relevant. Oliguria during pneumoperitoneum or pelvic manipulation is not by itself a mandate for repeated fluid boluses; inspect the catheter, hemodynamics and surgical context.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV prevention
bullets: Use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia with acetaminophen and an NSAID when renal function, bleeding risk and other contraindications permit. Local infiltration or an appropriate regional block may reduce incisional pain; blocks do not reliably eliminate visceral pelvic pain.

Assess PONV risk and use multimodal prophylaxis from different drug classes when indicated; consider propofol-based anesthesia and opioid reduction. Choose rescue antiemetics from a different class where possible and account for QT risk, sedation, urinary retention and other patient-specific effects.

bullets: Before extubation, confirm consciousness, airway protection, gas exchange, temperature and hemodynamic stability. After neuromuscular blockade verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; prolonged Trendelenburg also requires assessment for airway edema and a safe reintubation plan.

Arrange observation or higher-acuity care for persistent shock, major bleeding, airway swelling or respiratory compromise. Discharge requires controlled pain/nausea, appropriate bleeding assessment and procedure-specific voiding/catheter and return-precaution plans.

bullets: Review gestational age when relevant, bleeding severity, retained tissue, infection, prior uterine surgery and placental location. Scar plus complete previa after the first trimester increases concern for placenta accreta spectrum and may require a higher-acuity center.

sections.title: Uterine perforation & concealed injury
bullets: Unexpected loss of resistance, a sudden fluid-deficit increase, abdominal distension, bleeding or instability should trigger concern for perforation. Under anesthesia, pain may be absent; quantify bleeding and ask about instrument/energy use and possible extrauterine injury.

Stop and reassess with the surgical team; bowel, bladder or vascular injury may require laparoscopy/laparotomy and resuscitation. Stable suspected perforation and perforation with electrosurgery, ongoing bleeding or organ injury are not interchangeable scenarios.

sections.title: Hemorrhage recognition & resuscitation
bullets: For substantial anticipated bleeding, establish suitable access, type/crossmatch and a blood-delivery plan before incision. During active hemorrhage activate the local pathway early, follow perfusion and serial laboratory trends, and address hypothermia, hypocalcemia, fibrinogen/platelet deficits and coagulopathy as indicated.

A normal initial hemoglobin does not exclude acute major blood loss. Resuscitation and definitive surgical control proceed together; vasopressors may support perfusion but do not replace blood or correction of the bleeding source.

sections.title: Uterotonics & hemorrhage medication cautions
bullets: Uterotonics treat appropriate uterine-atony scenarios, not every surgical bleeding source. Methylergonovine is contraindicated in hypertension/toxemia and can cause coronary vasospasm; routine IV use is unsafe. Do not assume its role in rescue bleeding supports prophylactic use: SFP advises against prophylactic methylergonovine for D&E at 20–24 weeks.

Carboprost can cause bronchoconstriction; its label contraindicates active pulmonary disease and cautions with an asthma history, so select alternatives or follow a specialist protocol where relevant. Oxytocin/misoprostol selection and TXA use should follow the indication-specific hemorrhage pathway; direct evidence for TXA in abortion hemorrhage is limited and partly extrapolated.

Rapid IV oxytocin can cause hypotension, flushing and reflex tachycardia, with potential ischemia or arrhythmia in vulnerable patients. Follow the product-specific and indication-specific protocol; avoid an unplanned rapid bolus and communicate administration to anesthesia.

Misoprostol can cause shivering and fever. Consider timing and the full clinical picture rather than automatically diagnosing infection from fever alone, while still evaluating persistent fever, instability or other evidence of sepsis.

bullets: Hysteroscopic resection or hydrothermal systems may involve circulating liquid and require fluid accounting. Nonresectoscopic radiofrequency or balloon methods have different failure modes; do not impose hysteroscopic saline deficit limits on every device indiscriminately.

sections.title: Uterine perforation & concealed injury
bullets: Unexpected loss of resistance, a sudden fluid-deficit increase, abdominal distension, bleeding or instability should trigger concern for perforation. Under anesthesia, pain may be absent; quantify bleeding and ask about instrument/energy use and possible extrauterine injury.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Distension-fluid absorption is the defining risk: identify the medium, track the deficit and agree a patient-specific stop limit.
Hypotonic electrolyte-free media can cause hyponatremia; isotonic saline can still cause dangerous overload.
Anesthetic depth varies with diagnostic versus operative work, anticipated duration and patient tolerance.
A sudden deficit increase, hemorrhage or instability also raises concern for uterine perforation and extrauterine injury.

sections.title: Distension medium & absorption physiology
bullets: Confirm the exact distension medium and energy system before starting. Electrolyte-free hypotonic media can cause dilutional hyponatremia and hypo-osmolality; isotonic saline generally avoids this mechanism but can still cause severe volume overload and pulmonary edema.

Absorption increases with high intrauterine pressure, opened vessels and prolonged/resective procedures. Use the lowest pressure that provides adequate visualization and communicate rapid deficits; do not equate a saline-based system with unlimited fluid safety.

sources.label: BSGE/ESGE operative hysteroscopy distension-media guideline (2016)

sections.title: Fluid-deficit limits & stop communication
bullets: Agree a patient-specific stop limit before surgery. The 2016 BSGE/ESGE guideline uses 1000 mL for hypotonic and 2500 mL for isotonic media in healthy patients; stop earlier for symptoms, rapid absorption or instability. These are maximum deficit thresholds, not proven safe intravascular doses.

For older patients or cardiac/renal disease, suggested lower limits are 750 mL hypotonic and 1500 mL isotonic, with further reduction as appropriate. In healthy patients, notify anesthesia and reassess at 750/1500 mL respectively. Track infused minus recovered fluid at least every 10 minutes and at bag changes; spills, peritoneal loss, bleeding and measurement errors mean the deficit is not identical to intravascular absorption.

sections.title: Lithotomy, pressure points & nerve protection
bullets: Document mobility limits and neuropathy; lift and lower legs together with adequate personnel. Protect the fibular head, heels and calves, avoid excessive hip flexion/abduction or external rotation, and avoid traction/compression on the brachial plexus or tucked arms.

Minimize time in lithotomy and steep Trendelenburg, reassess supports and perfusion when feasible, and avoid prolonged hypotension or concentrated calf pressure. sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum & Trendelenburg physiology
bullets: CO₂ insufflation and head-down positioning reduce FRC/compliance, increase airway pressures and CO₂ load, and alter SVR and venous return. Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight, individualize PEEP and minute ventilation, and reassess ETT depth after positioning. sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & fluid balance

sections.title: Intramyometrial vasopressin: cardiovascular warning
bullets: Agree on and communicate the agent, concentration, total intended dose and injection timing before local vasopressin. Systemic absorption or intravascular injection can produce severe bradycardia, hypertension, coronary/peripheral vasospasm, arrhythmia, pulmonary edema or cardiac arrest; negative aspiration does not eliminate risk.

Stop injection and assess ECG, central perfusion and blood pressure immediately if instability occurs. An unreadable cuff or absent peripheral pulse may reflect intense vasospasm rather than systemic hypotension; do not give reflex large vasopressor doses without assessment. Treat true pulseless arrest immediately. Case reports do not establish a universally safe dose.

sections.title: Blood conservation without fixed hemodynamic targets
bullets: Discuss anticipated vascularity, surgical tourniquet or other local hemostatic strategies, and whether cell salvage is appropriate under institutional policy. Correct preoperative anemia when feasible and define a contingency for uncontrolled bleeding.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Postpartum tubal ligation is commonly performed through an infraumbilical mini-laparotomy; the enlarged postpartum uterus can bring the tubes within reach of the incision.

When feasible, consider neuraxial anesthesia, including a functional labor epidural; individualize technique and timing to the patient’s condition and preferences. The evidence does not establish a universally superior technique.

Key perioperative concerns include aspiration risk, postpartum hemodynamic status and blood loss, and the possibility that labor epidural anesthesia may be inadequate or fail as time from delivery increases.

After anesthesia, admit the patient to the PACU or an equivalent area unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise. Re-evaluate the patient on arrival and continually in recovery; monitor according to the patient’s medical condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature. Use a quantitative method of assessing oxygenation, such as pulse oximetry, during the initial phase of recovery.

bullets: The described surgical access is an infraumbilical mini-laparotomy. In the immediate postpartum period, the fundus is near the umbilicus and the salpinges are readily accessible through a small incision.
ACOG categorizes PPTL as urgent and ideally performed within 24 hours after delivery. Individualize timing and anesthetic technique according to anesthetic and obstetric risks and patient preference.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess maternal condition and anesthetic risks, including hemodynamic status and blood loss. The obstetric anesthesia guideline recommends a focused history and examination, including airway, heart and lung assessment, and baseline blood pressure.

Before elective PPTL, avoid solid food for 6 to 8 hours depending on food type and consider aspiration prophylaxis. For laboring patients with aspiration risks, consider additional oral-intake restrictions case by case.

Consider aspiration prophylaxis with a nonparticulate antacid, an H2-receptor antagonist, and/or metoclopramide as appropriate. The guideline reports effects on gastric acidity and peripartum nausea, but does not establish that prophylaxis changes aspiration frequency or outcomes.

A functional labor epidural may be considered, but assess its adequacy rather than assuming it will provide surgical anesthesia. Failure becomes more likely as the postdelivery interval lengthens; the guideline does not give a fixed reactivation protocol.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Neuraxial or general anesthesia may be used; individualize according to anesthetic and obstetric risk and patient preference. Available guidance favors considering neuraxial techniques for most PPTL procedures but does not establish comparative superiority.

A labor epidural is an option only if it is functional and provides an adequate surgical block. A T4 pinprick level is identified as indicated for surgical anesthesia in the OpenAnesthesia review; confirm block adequacy before proceeding.

bullets: Assess hemodynamic status in the context of postpartum blood loss and the patient’s current condition; the sources do not establish a PPTL-specific hemodynamic target.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Reassess if neuraxial anesthesia is incomplete or deteriorates; labor epidural reactivation may fail, particularly with increasing time since delivery. The available guideline supports individualized technique selection rather than a fixed rescue sequence.

Recognize neuraxial adverse effects including hypotension, nausea, itching, and postdural puncture headache; general anesthesia carries airway, aspiration, and other risks. The supplied PPTL sources do not provide a complication-specific treatment algorithm.

Defer or reconsider PPTL in acutely ill patients or when the procedure could compromise care for other labor-and-delivery patients. The review lists ongoing postpartum hemorrhage, sepsis, coagulopathy, and critical-care admission among contraindications.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum & Trendelenburg physiology
bullets: CO₂ insufflation and head-down positioning reduce FRC/compliance, increase airway pressures and CO₂ load, and alter SVR and venous return. Cardiac output responses depend on insufflation pressure, position, volume status and ventricular reserve; decreases are not inevitable in every patient.

Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight, individualize PEEP and minute ventilation, and reassess ETT depth after positioning. Sudden bradycardia with insufflation requires communication, stopping the stimulus/deflation and treatment; unexplained hypoxemia or collapse warrants evaluation for hemorrhage, gas embolism or thoracic gas complications.

sections.title: Intramyometrial vasopressin: cardiovascular warning
bullets: Agree on and communicate the agent, concentration, total intended dose and injection timing before local vasopressin. Systemic absorption or intravascular injection can produce severe bradycardia, hypertension, coronary/peripheral vasospasm, arrhythmia, pulmonary edema or cardiac arrest; negative aspiration does not eliminate risk.

Stop injection and assess ECG, central perfusion and blood pressure immediately if instability occurs. An unreadable cuff or absent peripheral pulse may reflect intense vasospasm rather than systemic hypotension; do not give reflex large vasopressor doses without assessment. Treat true pulseless arrest immediately. Case reports do not establish a universally safe dose.

sections.title: Lithotomy, pressure points & nerve protection
bullets: Document mobility limits and neuropathy; lift and lower legs together with adequate personnel. Protect the fibular head, heels and calves, avoid excessive hip flexion/abduction or external rotation, and avoid traction/compression on the brachial plexus or tucked arms.

Minimize time in lithotomy and steep Trendelenburg, reassess supports and perfusion when feasible, and avoid prolonged hypotension or concentrated calf pressure. Severe postoperative leg pain, swelling or weakness can signal compartment syndrome even with palpable pulses; obtain urgent assessment rather than attributing it automatically to a block.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum & Trendelenburg physiology
bullets: CO₂ insufflation and head-down positioning reduce FRC/compliance, increase airway pressures and CO₂ load, and alter SVR and venous return. Cardiac output responses depend on insufflation pressure, position, volume status and ventricular reserve; decreases are not inevitable in every patient.

Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight, individualize PEEP and minute ventilation, and reassess ETT depth after positioning. Sudden bradycardia with insufflation requires communication, stopping the stimulus/deflation and treatment; unexplained hypoxemia or collapse warrants evaluation for hemorrhage, gas embolism or thoracic gas complications.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & fluid balance
bullets: Target euvolemia with reassessment of perfusion and measured losses; avoid both indiscriminate crystalloid loading and rigid restriction during bleeding. Distinguish vasodilation from hypovolemia or low cardiac output before choosing fluid, blood or vasoactive support.

Account for poor intake, bowel preparation, ascites drainage and irrigation absorption when relevant. Oliguria during pneumoperitoneum or pelvic manipulation is not by itself a mandate for repeated fluid boluses; inspect the catheter, hemodynamics and surgical context.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV prevention
bullets: Use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia with acetaminophen and an NSAID when renal function, bleeding risk and other contraindications permit. Local infiltration or an appropriate regional block may reduce incisional pain; blocks do not reliably eliminate visceral pelvic pain.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Cubital tunnel release treats ulnar nerve compression or traction at the elbow after conservative management has failed; the operation may involve decompression, transposition, or both.
Local, regional, and general anesthesia have all been used. The supplied evidence does not establish one usual or preferred anesthetic technique for every release.

Prioritize reliable operating conditions and awareness of inadequate regional analgesia, conversion to general anesthesia, and nerve-related complications; avoid treating any one technique as risk-free.

In the PACU, continually evaluate the patient and monitor by methods appropriate to the patient’s medical condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature. The sources do not establish a cubital-tunnel-specific recovery protocol.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The procedure addresses compression or traction of the ulnar nerve at the elbow. Release may be decompression or transposition; the supplied sources do not define criteria for choosing between these approaches.

Anesthesia options represented in the evidence include local, regional, and general anesthesia. Selection is case- and procedure-dependent; the review does not provide selection criteria or a comprehensive anesthetic protocol.
Comparative safety findings from the retrospective cohort apply to in-situ decompression, not transposition or revision surgery.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Confirm the planned operation and anesthetic approach with the surgical team. The cohort included patients diagnosed from history and examination, with or without electrodiagnostic evidence; it does not establish a mandatory testing pathway.

Establish baseline ulnar-distribution symptoms and relevant neurologic history when assessing the patient. The study discusses theoretical concern about peripheral neuropathy or cervical radiculopathy with regional block, but does not resolve that concern generally.
Discuss the possibility that regional anesthesia may provide inadequate analgesia and require conversion. The observed cohort result is not a universal prediction for an individual patient.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The procedure-specific source reports tourniquet use in nearly all cases in the cohort, but does not specify patient positioning or a preferred setup. Confirm the planned access and tourniquet arrangement with the operative team.

For MAC or regional anesthesia, apply the applicable basic monitoring standards. These include continuous ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and quantitative oxygenation assessment.
During moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the patient, procedure, or equipment makes this invalid or precluded.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Do not infer a required airway technique from the procedure. The comparative study describes general anesthesia as requiring intubation and regional anesthesia as avoiding intubation, but gives no individual airway techniques.

If general anesthesia is used, assess ventilation throughout; when an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask is inserted, verify placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide and continue quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis as specified by the monitoring standards.
The supplied procedure-specific evidence does not establish a ventilation strategy or an indication for airway instrumentation for this operation.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain communication with the surgical team regarding operative progress and adequacy of anesthesia. The evidence identifies inadequate intraoperative pain control as a reason for conversion from regional to general anesthesia.
Nerve-related injury is a relevant operative concern, particularly during nerve mobilization; the procedure review does not quantify risk by surgical approach.
No procedure-specific physiologic targets or detailed intraoperative sequence are established by the supplied sources.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Be prepared to reassess inadequate analgesia during regional anesthesia and coordinate escalation of the anesthetic approach if required. Conversion occurred in the retrospective cohort; its observed rate should not be treated as a patient-specific estimate.

Postoperative complications reported in the in-situ cohort included worsening pain, edema, medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve neurapraxia, wound problems, rash, and hematoma. Overall complication rates did not differ significantly between anesthesia groups.
The cohort authors reported that complications were not directly attributed to anesthetic type. Its retrospective design and limited ability to detect rare nerve injuries constrain reassurance.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The procedure-specific study provides no fluid regimen, blood-loss, or transfusion data. Do not derive a fixed fluid or blood-management plan from these sources.
The study reports tourniquet use but does not describe a perfusion-management protocol or tourniquet-management recommendations.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Local and regional techniques may provide intraoperative feedback, but the review does not specify how that feedback was used or recommend a particular technique or drug regimen.

One included study reported less postoperative pain with local anesthesia than general anesthesia; the abstract does not provide pain scores, timing, or analgesic regimens, so it does not support a comparative analgesic protocol.

The cohort reports that some regional-anesthesia patients were discharged with continuous anesthetic delivery catheters, but this is an observed practice rather than a general recommendation. Procedure-specific PONV prevention guidance is not provided.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Use the applicable postanesthesia-care standards: continually evaluate the patient, monitor according to condition, and use quantitative oxygenation assessment during the initial recovery phase.
Assess for pain, swelling, wound complications, and new or worsening neurologic symptoms in the context of reported procedure complications; no specific surveillance schedule is established.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring and confirmation of recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis apply; these requirements do not imply that blockade is needed for this operation.

bullets: The anesthesia-comparison evidence includes a scoping review whose supplied page provides an abstract and a retrospective single-institution cohort limited to in-situ decompression. Neither establishes a comprehensive protocol or settles management for transposition and revision cases.
The cohort was underpowered for rare nerve injuries and had six-week follow-up; its findings should not be interpreted as proof that a technique is free of risk.
Procedure-specific evidence does not establish positioning, detailed anesthetic selection, fluid management, or a postoperative analgesia and surveillance protocol.
Case-specific targets and protocols are not established in the available sources.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Digit revision amputation can be performed with local infiltration or regional blockade, but the available sources do not establish one preferred technique for this operation. The choice depends on the procedure and patient; a digital block is one described option for digit procedures.

Priorities include selecting an approach compatible with the patient’s circulation, avoiding inadvertent vascular or nerve injection, and recognizing local-anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). Use particular caution with vasoconstrictor-containing anesthetic when circulation is compromised.

The anesthetic setting and monitoring should match the technique and sedation used. For anesthesia care, apply the relevant basic monitoring standards; do not infer that a local-anesthetic digit procedure requires general anesthesia or an advanced airway.

Recovery priorities supported here are reassessment and observation appropriate to the patient’s condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature after anesthesia care. Procedure-specific phantom-digit pain prevention and counseling are not established by these sources.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The available hand-procedure review includes digit revision amputation and describes bedside local infiltration and regional blocks, including digital blocks. It does not assign an anesthetic method to revision amputation or ray resection; select an approach in coordination with the procedural team rather than treating any one technique as standard.
A digital nerve block provides local anesthesia for fingers and toes. The supplied references do not identify a preferred block approach for a particular amputation level or ray resection.

Intravenous regional anesthesia is discussed as an option for hand and forearm surgery in a systematic review, but that evidence compares tourniquet approaches and does not provide an amputation-specific selection protocol or recommended local-anesthetic regimen.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess the patient’s medical status and develop an anesthesia plan. For a digital block, confirm consent and local-anesthetic allergy status; the block reference also lists infection at the injection site and distorted landmarks among contraindications.

Consider circulation before choosing an injection approach or vasoconstrictor-containing solution. The hand review advises caution with compromised circulation; it does not supply a procedure-specific vascular risk score or a universal prohibition.

Consider hepatic disease when planning amide local anesthetic exposure. The digital-block reference notes hepatic metabolism and advises close attention to potential systemic toxicity in end-stage liver disease; it does not establish a digit-amputation dosing protocol.

The supplied anesthesia sources do not establish surgical candidacy for replantation, amputation indications, or a replantation consultation pathway. Those decisions are outside the evidence available for this draft.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For regional anesthesia or monitored anesthesia care, qualified anesthesia personnel must remain present and continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. Apply the standard appropriate to the anesthetic actually delivered.

With local anesthesia without sedation, ventilation adequacy is evaluated by continual observation of qualitative clinical signs under the basic monitoring standards. The digital-block reference does not specify a routine monitoring protocol.

When anesthesia is administered, the standards call for continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, subject to the standards’ stated exceptions. These requirements are not a reason to imply that every digit procedure requires anesthesia beyond local anesthesia.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The case-specific sources describe local and regional techniques but do not establish an airway plan for digit amputation or ray resection. Do not infer a need for an LMA, endotracheal tube, or general anesthesia from the operation name alone.

If sedation is used, assess ventilation in accordance with its depth. The monitoring standards call for continual clinical observation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring during moderate or deep sedation unless the nature of the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes it.

If general anesthesia is selected for an individual case, use the applicable general-anesthesia monitoring standards; the supplied procedure sources do not specify induction, maintenance, ventilation, or airway-device choices for this operation.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: During digital block placement, use patient feedback to identify possible nerve contact. The hand review advises immediate withdrawal if the patient reports an electric-shock sensation or paresthesia in the nerve distribution.

Avoid direct intraneural injection and aspirate before injection to check for intravascular placement, as described in the digital-block reference. This is technique guidance for a digital block, not an amputation-specific anesthetic recipe.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For a felon with abscess, tension, or fluctuance, the source-supported procedure is incision and drainage; cellulitis without abscess is managed differently.
A digital block before I&D is the only anesthetic technique specifically described for felon drainage; a finger tourniquet may aid visualization.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: For felon with abscess formation, tension, or fluctuance, drain the infected material. Cellulitis without abscess is not described as an I&D indication in this source.

The described approach targets maximal volar swelling and tenderness. Deep felon drainage uses a lateral incision with specified separation from the DIP joint and nail plate; superficial felon may use a volar longitudinal incision.

Bluntly separate fingertip septae as needed for complete drainage, irrigate, and pack and splint the wound. The source discourages fish-mouth, hockey-stick, and transverse palmar incisions because of reported injury and scarring.
This approach is supported for felon only; it should not be treated as a procedure description for flexor tendon sheath infection or palmar-space abscess.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The supplied procedure-specific evidence is principally about flexor tendon repair; it describes primary repair and selected delayed repairs, but does not establish an extensor-tendon anesthesia approach.

Anesthesia preference varies. A UK surgeon survey’s Results section reports regional anesthesia as the most commonly preferred approach, but its table conflicts with that result; the survey does not establish a best technique.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The flexor-tendon literature describes primary repair and, for delayed presentation, consideration of delayed primary repair, grafting, or staged reconstruction based on intraoperative findings. It is not a source for extensor-tendon technique.

WALANT permits active flexion-extension testing during repair. The authors use the movement assessment to evaluate gliding and gapping and to tailor the repair; this describes their practice, not comparative proof of superiority.
Retrieval of a retracted tendon stump may affect access and operative complexity. The survey reports several retrieval approaches but does not establish one as an anesthesia-related requirement.

Assess local-anesthetic exposure and the possibility of systemic toxicity when local anesthetic is used; the supplied review describes toxicity as dose-dependent but is not a tendon-repair dosing protocol.

bullets: For general anesthesia, regional anesthesia, or monitored anesthesia care, ASA basic standards call for ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with the specified monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and circumstances.

bullets: The supplied sources do not establish a tendon-repair-specific airway technique or ventilation plan. Do not infer a need for an airway device from the operation alone.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: If WALANT is chosen, active movement provides the surgeon an opportunity to assess tendon excursion and repair integrity during the operation. It is not a substitute for the anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the care provided.

The review describes reinforcing observed gapping and adjusting pulley release or reconstruction when gliding is impaired. These are surgical decisions informed by movement testing, not anesthesia instructions.
No tendon-repair-specific physiologic targets or anesthetic critical-phase protocol are established in the supplied evidence.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Repair gapping and rupture are relevant surgical concerns. The flexor-tendon review links intraoperative movement testing and reinforcement of observed gapping with rupture-risk reduction; it does not provide an anesthesia rescue algorithm.

Adhesions are a significant postoperative concern in the review, particularly with accompanying bone or severe soft-tissue injuries. The surgeon and therapy team address these risks through operative and rehabilitation decisions.

With local anesthetic exposure, recognize possible LAST; the supplied review lists early neurologic symptoms and severe neurologic or respiratory effects. It does not establish a tendon-case-specific monitoring or treatment protocol.

A hand-anesthesia review describes epinephrine-related vasoconstriction as potentially limiting blood loss and advises caution with compromised circulation; it does not specifically validate a tendon-repair regimen.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Define resection extent, vascular involvement and future liver remnant in the context of cirrhosis, steatosis or treatment-related injury.
Prepare for rapid hemorrhage and coordinated inflow/outflow clamping or release.
A selective low venous-pressure strategy during transection must preserve organ perfusion and be reassessed after resection.
Monitor gas embolism, coagulation/metabolic changes and postoperative liver/renal failure, not only surgical blood loss.

sections.title: Future liver remnant & liver cancer context
bullets: Clarify functional remnant assessment, portal hypertension, steatosis, chemotherapy-related injury and planned vascular reconstruction. Do not apply one remnant-volume threshold to every normal, cirrhotic or chemotherapy-exposed liver.

Coordinate postoperative level of care around remnant function, complexity and patient reserve. Liver cancer surgery can involve both extensive bleeding and pre-existing dysfunction; small-incision access does not imply a small physiologic resection.

sources.label: Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)
ERAS Society liver surgery guideline (2022)

sections.title: Low venous pressure during transection
bullets: ERAS supports low CVP during transection with close monitoring and phase-specific fluid management. CVP is affected by ventilation, position and cardiac function; it is not a direct measure of circulating blood volume.

Do not chase a CVP number by indiscriminate dehydration or vasodilation. Reassess if hypotension, ischemia or inadequate organ perfusion develops; restore appropriate perfusion after the low-pressure phase rather than maintaining restriction through the entire case.

sources.label: ERAS Society liver surgery guideline (2022)

sections.title: Vascular control & release
bullets: Confirm whether the team plans portal triad inflow occlusion, selective vascular control or total vascular exclusion. Their effects on venous return and afterload differ; communicate before clamping, releasing or changing the strategy.

Be ready for reduced preload/output during major caval exclusion and hemodynamic/metabolic changes on release. Use serial assessment, appropriate vasoactive support and surgical coordination rather than applying one fixed fluid bolus or MAP target to every maneuver.

sources.label: Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)

sections.title: Major bleeding & transfusion readiness
bullets: Match crossmatched blood, access, rapid infusion and cell-salvage planning to vascular involvement, portal collaterals and surgical extent. Cell-salvage use in malignancy or contamination requires institutional selection and processing policy, not an automatic blanket ban or mandate.

During uncontrolled bleeding, activate the hemorrhage protocol and pursue source control while following perfusion and serial hemoglobin/coagulation trends. Warm products, monitor ionized calcium, potassium and acid-base status, and move toward targeted therapy when timely tests are available.

sources.label: Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)
Liver transplantation anesthesia update (2020 narrative review)

sections.title: Venous air / gas embolism: recognition & response
bullets: Open hepatic veins and low venous pressure can permit air entrainment; laparoscopic venous injury can also allow CO₂ embolism. Sudden ETCO₂ fall, hypoxemia, hypotension or arrhythmia warrants immediate team assessment alongside hemorrhage, circuit and cardiac causes; none is diagnostic alone.

Alert the surgeon, stop air entry or insufflation and occlude/flood the source as appropriate; give 100% oxygen, stop nitrous oxide if used, and support ventilation/circulation. Use resuscitation for arrest and consider echo. Aspiration through an already suitably positioned catheter or repositioning may help in selected circumstances, but must not delay source control or CPR.

sources.label: WFSA air embolism and anesthesia (2016 educational tutorial)
Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)

sections.title: Post-hepatectomy liver failure surveillance
bullets: Watch for impaired lactate clearance, worsening bilirubin/coagulation, hypoglycemia, encephalopathy, ascites and renal dysfunction after substantial resection. Remnant volume/function, cirrhosis, steatosis, chemotherapy injury and perioperative insults influence risk.

Do not wait for a formal postoperative-day diagnostic definition before escalating clinical deterioration. Evaluate bleeding, sepsis, vascular compromise and obstruction as potentially treatable causes; severe dysfunction may require ICU organ support.

sources.label: Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum & surgical position
bullets: CO₂ absorption, reduced compliance and increased abdominal pressure change ventilation and circulation. Titrate minute ventilation/PEEP, check airway pressures and tube position, and recognize that reverse Trendelenburg may reduce venous return.

Sudden bradycardia during insufflation requires immediate communication, stopping the stimulus/deflation and appropriate treatment. Prolonged or unexpected hypoxemia, hypercarbia or collapse requires evaluation for gas complications, hemorrhage and cardiopulmonary causes.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: laparoscopic and robotic surgery (2024 educational review)

sections.title: Hepatic reserve & patient assessment
bullets: Review cirrhosis/portal hypertension, bilirubin, albumin, coagulation, platelets, renal function, sodium, nutrition and functional capacity. Distinguish hepatocellular injury tests from synthetic function and the amount/function of liver expected to remain.

Assess ascites, encephalopathy, infection, cardiomyopathy and pulmonary complications. Hepatopulmonary syndrome involves abnormal pulmonary vascular dilation/hypoxemia; portopulmonary hypertension adds pulmonary vascular and RV risk. They require different evaluation and are not interchangeable diagnoses.

sources.label: Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)
Portal hypertension perioperative considerations (2023 ANZCA review)

sections.title: Aspiration, induction & ventilation
bullets: Assess vomiting, obstruction, ascites, encephalopathy, fasting and urgency. Choose airway protection and induction technique for the actual risk, with adequate preoxygenation and vasoactive/blood support available when perfusion is fragile.

Use controlled ventilation for major surgery with lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight and individualized PEEP. Ascites, pleural effusions, abdominal exposure and pneumoperitoneum can alter mechanics; protect oxygenation without ignoring RV and venous-pressure effects.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: laparoscopic and robotic surgery (2024 educational review)
Portal hypertension perioperative considerations (2023 ANZCA review)
OpenAnesthesia adult liver transplantation (2023 educational review)

sections.title: Access, monitoring & temperature
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring and temperature assessment when significant change is anticipated. Major resection, shock or substantial anticipated transfusion often warrants an arterial line, adequate large-bore access and repeated point-of-care laboratory assessment.

Prepare rapid blood delivery, warming and appropriate vasoactive infusions before high-risk phases. Choose central access and additional cardiac monitoring for the individual procedure and reserve; they are not obligatory for every routine cholecystectomy.

sources.label: ASA Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)

sections.title: Perfusion, renal protection & fluid balance
bullets: Avoid both excessive crystalloid loading and rigid under-resuscitation. Reassess actual blood/fluid losses, perfusion and fluid responsiveness, interpreting dynamic measures within their limitations rather than treating CVP as a direct blood-volume measurement.

Balance organ perfusion against hepatic venous congestion; use vasoactive support for vasodilation when indicated. Track renal function and electrolytes and avoid unnecessary nephrotoxins; oliguria requires clinical assessment, not automatic repeated boluses.

sources.label: ERAS Society liver surgery guideline (2022)
Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)

sections.title: Rebalanced coagulation & targeted transfusion
bullets: Cirrhosis can predispose to both hemorrhage and thrombosis. INR alone does not measure overall bleeding risk, and prophylactic plasma solely to normalize chronic cirrhotic INR is not recommended; anticoagulant-related INR elevation and active massive hemorrhage require different assessment.

Integrate surgical bleeding, platelets, fibrinogen, temperature, ionized calcium and acid-base status. TEG/ROTEM can guide targeted transfusion in major bleeding/transplantation but does not reliably predict every procedure-related bleed or certify neuraxial safety. Avoid a universal platelet/INR target for all HPB procedures.

sources.label: AASLD procedural bleeding in cirrhosis (2024 educational guidance)
ALTA North American practice-based TIPS recommendations (2022 consensus)

sections.title: Drug handling, analgesia & regional choices
bullets: Hepatic dysfunction can change clearance, protein binding and sensitivity; titrate rather than simply excluding every hepatically metabolized drug. Avoid unnecessary prolonged sedation, reassess neuromuscular blockade quantitatively and account for simultaneous renal dysfunction.

Use multimodal analgesia suited to hepatic/renal reserve and the incision. Acetaminophen requires an appropriate hepatic plan; NSAIDs may be unsuitable with renal injury or bleeding risk. Epidural benefit must be weighed against hypotension and evolving post-resection coagulation, including a safe catheter-removal plan.

sources.label: ERAS Society liver surgery guideline (2022)
Portal hypertension perioperative considerations (2023 ANZCA review)
APSF: 2023 neuromuscular blockade monitoring and reversal guidelines

sections.title: Glucose, electrolytes & acid-base trends
bullets: Monitor glucose during major hepatic/pancreatic procedures and severe liver dysfunction. Stress hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia with poor hepatic reserve can both occur; use measured values and a local protocol rather than assuming a single predictable direction.

Trend potassium, ionized calcium, sodium, lactate and other electrolytes according to severity and transfusion. Interpret poor lactate clearance in the context of perfusion and liver function; protect against excessively rapid sodium correction in chronically hyponatremic patients.

sources.label: Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)
OpenAnesthesia adult liver transplantation (2023 educational review)

sections.title: Emergence & postoperative surveillance
bullets: Extubate only when consciousness, airway protection, ventilation, oxygenation, temperature and perfusion are adequate. If neuromuscular blockade was used, verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; shock, edema or respiratory failure may require continued ventilation.

Handoff bleeding, transfusion, glucose/electrolyte trends, liver/renal function, drains and analgesia. Escalate persistent lactate elevation, worsening bilirubin/coagulation, hypoglycemia, encephalopathy, fever or abdominal findings for possible organ failure, bleeding or bile/pancreatic leak.

APSF: 2023 neuromuscular blockade monitoring and reversal guidelines

sections.title: VTE prevention, nutrition & mobilization
bullets: An elevated INR does not protect against VTE. Coordinate mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with bleeding, renal function and neuraxial procedures using the current institutional pathway.

Use individualized PONV prevention, early mobilization and enteral intake when clinically appropriate. Adapt recovery milestones to obstruction, reconstruction, ongoing shock and complications rather than applying one ERAS pathway indiscriminately.

sections.title: Evidence scope & clinical review
bullets: Adult clinical-review draft, not an independently approved protocol or individualized order set. Resection, donation, transplantation, biliary sepsis and endoscopy have different evidence bases; clinical review must preserve those distinctions.

bullets: Organize the anesthetic around dissection, anhepatic and reperfusion phases, with repeated reassessment of perfusion and metabolic state.

bullets: Review current liver disease severity, encephalopathy, ascites, infection, renal replacement, sodium and cardiopulmonary testing. Understand the actual graft/operative approach and expected vascular reconstruction rather than applying one clamping model to every recipient.

Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy, hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension can markedly change risk. Discuss additional monitoring and support with the transplant team; avoid outdated allocation formulas or universal pulmonary-pressure eligibility rules in an anesthesia reference.

sections.title: Transplant access & cardiac monitoring
bullets: Plan arterial and adequate large-bore/central access, rapid warming/infusion, serial blood gases/coagulation and immediate resuscitation capability. Anticipate altered reliability of peripheral pressures during vasoplegia or major shifts.

TEE or pulmonary artery monitoring can be valuable according to RV/pulmonary vascular risk, expertise and contraindications. Review esophageal pathology/varices when considering TEE; monitoring choices differ among centers and neither device is automatically required for every patient.

sections.title: Pre-anhepatic phase: dissection & bleeding
bullets: Portal collaterals, adhesions and diseased-liver dissection may cause rapid hemorrhage; caval compression or torque can also reduce preload. Communicate maneuvers and use blood/perfusion trends to distinguish causes of instability.

Coordinate ascites drainage, transfusion and warming while avoiding excessive congestion. Correct important electrolyte/acid-base derangements and plan ahead for clamping; the dissection phase is not a reason for unmeasured prophylactic plasma loading.

sections.title: Anhepatic phase: clamping & metabolism
bullets: Caval clamping and surgical technique determine the fall in venous return/output; piggyback, bypass and temporary shunts change the response. Treat actual hemodynamic consequences rather than assuming a fixed percentage fall in cardiac output.

Consider hemorrhage, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, air/thrombus embolism, RV failure and myocardial dysfunction as well as vasoplegia; use echo/other monitoring and local resuscitation pathways where appropriate.

Reassess arterial pressure at the correct reference level, oxygenation/ventilation, blood loss/hemoglobin, temperature, anesthetic delivery and residual/new neuromuscular blockade. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Patient understanding, cooperation, comfort and a workable airway-rescue plan are essential.
Select awake-throughout or asleep-awake techniques around mapping and patient factors.

sections.title: Preparation and mapping cooperation
bullets: Discuss positioning, noises, stimulation, expected tasks and periods of wakefulness with the patient and team. Assess anxiety, communication ability, baseline deficits, OSA and tolerance of the planned position; candidacy is individualized.
Coordinate scalp/local analgesia and sedative timing with testing. Adequate comfort should not depend on deep sedation that prevents cooperation or compromises ventilation.

sections.title: Rescue with the head fixed
bullets: Agree how to access the mouth, release drapes/fixation if necessary and secure the airway despite limited head movement. Prepare mask/SGA/intubation options appropriate to the patient rather than assuming spontaneous ventilation will remain reliable.

If airway obstruction, persistent hypercapnia, seizure or inability to cooperate prevents safe mapping, prioritize oxygenation and conversion over completion of awake testing. Sedation adjustments should be communicated to the mapping team.

sections.title: Seizure prevention & rescue

sections.title: CPP, pressure targets & venous drainage
bullets: The usual bedside model is CPP = MAP − ICP; brain-level arterial pressure, venous pressure and autoregulation affect interpretation. sections.title: Brain relaxation, CO₂ & osmotherapy
bullets: Avoid hypoxemia and unintended hypercapnia; confirm PaCO₂ when ETCO₂ may be misleading. Routine profound or prolonged hyperventilation can reduce cerebral blood flow. A brief rescue strategy for threatened herniation is different from prophylactic hypocapnia in every craniotomy.

sections.title: Indication and anesthetic scope
bullets: Review imaging and whether the goal is stable chronic collection drainage, urgent decompression or a different procedure. Anticipate changes if bleeding, swelling or operative findings require wider exposure.

sections.title: EVD leveling, drainage & transport
bullets: Verify ordered drainage height, reference point, patency and open-versus-clamped plan. Level an EVD at the external auditory meatus with an appropriate leveling device; relevel after position changes and never connect a pressurized flush system.

sections.title: Prone positioning, eyes & peripheral nerves
bullets: Before and after turning, verify the airway, ventilation, lines, neutral neck alignment and padded pressure points. Keep the abdomen free of avoidable compression and avoid excessive arm abduction or plexus stretch; reassess supports throughout a long case.

No device or fixed transfusion threshold guarantees prevention.

sections.title: SSEP / MEP / EMG-compatible anesthesia
bullets: Agree modalities and baseline acquisition before incision and, when useful, before/after positioning. TIVA is commonly chosen for robust evoked potentials; volatile agents and nitrous oxide can suppress signals, while neuromuscular blockade especially affects myogenic MEP/EMG rather than sensory conduction itself.

Restore agreed perfusion and correct reversible abnormalities with the team; no single universal rescue MAP or alarm percentage applies to all modalities and lesions.

sections.title: Ruptured aneurysm, nimodipine & DCI
bullets: For unsecured aneurysmal SAH, use frequent monitoring and short-acting treatment to avoid severe hypertension, hypotension and variability. The 2023 guideline does not establish one universal BP target; consider ICP/hydrocephalus, presenting pressure and comorbidity.

Coordinate enteral nimodipine, euvolemia and neurocritical follow-up. Symptomatic delayed cerebral ischemia may need individualized BP augmentation after team assessment, but prophylactic hypervolemia/hemodynamic augmentation is not recommended; new deficits also require evaluation for other causes.

sections.title: Temporary occlusion and rupture preparedness
bullets: Agree phase-specific goals before temporary clipping and during restoration of flow. Avoid hypotension that worsens ischemia; anesthetic burst suppression, when selected, must not undermine hemodynamic stability.

For rupture, communicate immediately, support oxygenation/circulation and surgical control, and prepare blood/resuscitation. Deliberate profound hypotension or adenosine-induced pause is not a routine default; specialized rescue requires a coordinated plan and contraindication assessment.

sections.title: SSEP / MEP / EMG-compatible anesthesia
bullets: Agree modalities and baseline acquisition before incision and, when useful, before/after positioning. TIVA is commonly chosen for robust evoked potentials; volatile agents and nitrous oxide can suppress signals, while neuromuscular blockade especially affects myogenic MEP/EMG rather than sensory conduction itself.

Keep anesthetic concentrations and physiology stable and communicate all boluses or blocker doses. TIVA still requires reliable delivery, hypnosis assessment and awareness prevention; neither TIVA nor a preserved SSEP guarantees intact motor function.

sections.title: Seizure prevention & rescue
bullets: Reconcile seizure history, recent events and antiseizure medication timing; continue indicated therapy unless the epilepsy team deliberately modifies it for recording. Have a communicated rescue plan before cortical stimulation.

If a seizure occurs, alert the surgeon and stop stimulation, support oxygenation/ventilation and protect the patient. Exposed-cortex irrigation with chilled sterile solution may stop stimulation-induced activity; persistent/generalized seizures require prompt medication and airway rescue under the local protocol even if recording must be interrupted.

sections.title: Severe TBI targets and their limits
bullets: Brain Trauma Foundation guidance recommends treating ICP above 22 mmHg and targeting CPP 60–70 mmHg in severe TBI, informed by autoregulation, exam and imaging. These are not blanket targets for every elective craniotomy or spinal operation.

Avoid aggressive attempts to maintain CPP above 70 mmHg with fluids/pressors because of respiratory risk. Prolonged prophylactic PaCO₂ at or below 25 mmHg is not recommended; high-dose methylprednisolone increases mortality and is contraindicated in severe TBI.

sections.title: Associated injury and time-critical preparation
bullets: Assess cervical spine risk, blood loss elsewhere, anticoagulants and the neurologic trajectory. Protect oxygenation/perfusion during airway management and positioning while coordinating prompt decompression.

Hyperosmolar therapy and brief rescue ventilation for threatened herniation require a specific team plan with hemodynamic/electrolyte monitoring. Do not let routine invasive-line placement or nonessential testing delay definitive emergency treatment.

sections.title: EVD leveling, drainage & transport
bullets: Verify ordered drainage height, reference point, patency and open-versus-clamped plan. Level an EVD at the external auditory meatus with an appropriate leveling device; relevel after position changes and never connect a pressurized flush system.

Do not routinely clamp every EVD for transport. Agree a plan using clamp tolerance, ICP and drainage needs; prevent overdrainage during movement and restore ordered settings with trained monitoring. Accurate fluid-coupled pressure measurement and simultaneous open drainage are not interchangeable states.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For concern about severe TBI, the review supports definitive tracheal intubation. RSI may reduce aspiration risk; modified RSI with low-volume/low-pressure breaths may be considered when ICP is high. These statements do not make RSI compulsory in every patient.

Video laryngoscopy may facilitate intubation; have difficult-airway equipment available and maintain cervical stabilization when indicated. Avoid nasotracheal intubation when skull-fracture status is unknown or fracture is suspected.

Do not use 30–35 mmHg as a routine PaCO₂ target for every TBI patient. ACS 2024 guidance gives an initial PaCO₂ target of 35–45 mmHg when intracranial hypertension is absent; raised ICP, severe metabolic acidosis and significant pulmonary disease require an individualized strategy. Therapeutic hyperventilation belongs in an ICP-directed rescue or tiered pathway, not a universal ventilation recipe.
Use arterial blood gas assessment when CO₂ abnormality is suspected or the end-tidal value may be unreliable, particularly during hypotension.

bullets: Clarify awake mapping versus asleep image-guided placement and whether microelectrode or clinical stimulation testing is planned.

bullets: Awake/MAC and GA strategies are used according to targeting and testing requirements. Sedatives can alter neuronal recordings or tremor testing; agree drug reductions or pauses with the team rather than copying a fixed washout interval.

If motor testing requires Parkinson medication adjustment, document the exact plan and prompt postoperative resumption. Avoid unplanned withdrawal or agents that worsen the patient’s movement-disorder treatment.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Reconcile seizure burden, antiseizure medications and any planned changes for electrophysiologic recording.
ECoG and functional mapping need a stable, specifically coordinated anesthetic.
Anesthetic suppression or activation can obscure interpretation; discuss changes before boluses.
Treat prolonged seizures and airway compromise promptly even when rescue interrupts recording.

sections.title: ECoG recording and anesthetic effects
bullets: Confirm whether awake functional testing, ECoG or other monitoring is required. Avoid unnecessary deep suppression or abrupt agent changes during recordings; drug effects and washout timing differ by recording goal and center.

Medication withholding or pharmacoactivation must be an explicit epilepsy-team plan with rescue medication and cortical irrigation available. Do not infer that every epilepsy operation requires awake anesthesia or the same sedative-free interval.

sources.label: Intraoperative electrocorticography anesthesia review (2013)
Awake craniotomy anesthesia review (2018)

sections.title: Seizure prevention & rescue
bullets: Reconcile seizure history, recent events and antiseizure medication timing; continue indicated therapy unless the epilepsy team deliberately modifies it for recording. Have a communicated rescue plan before cortical stimulation.

If a seizure occurs, alert the surgeon and stop stimulation, support oxygenation/ventilation and protect the patient. Exposed-cortex irrigation with chilled sterile solution may stop stimulation-induced activity; persistent/generalized seizures require prompt medication and airway rescue under the local protocol even if recording must be interrupted.

sections.title: Baseline neurologic status & preparation
bullets: Document consciousness, pupils, language, strength/sensation and relevant pre-existing deficits before anesthesia when feasible. Review imaging, urgency, seizures, antithrombotics, cardiopulmonary disease, renal function and prior airway/cervical issues.

Clarify the surgical/monitoring plan and usual antiseizure, steroid, Parkinson or chronic pain medications. Continue or modify medications through an explicit specialist plan; mapping-related changes are not permission for indiscriminate withholding.

sections.title: Airway control & restricted access
bullets: Choose airway technique for aspiration risk, consciousness, cervical stability and anticipated access after fixation/positioning. Use the approach most likely to secure oxygenation safely while limiting unnecessary cervical movement; awake intubation is selective, not mandatory for every cervical case.

Secure and recheck the ETT, circuit and lines before draping, pinning or turning prone. Plan rescue, release of fixation or repositioning with the team; sedation with limited access still requires capnography and the ability to rescue apnea or obstruction.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & reference level
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring, temperature surveillance when indicated and access matched to hemorrhage or vasoactive needs. Arterial pressure monitoring is often useful for major cranial/cord-risk surgery; it must not create avoidable delay in emergency reperfusion or decompression.

Document the arterial transducer reference level, especially with the head elevated; pressure measured at heart level may overestimate brain-level arterial pressure. Recheck airway/lines after positioning and arrange access to blood, laboratory testing and emergency equipment.

sections.title: CPP, pressure targets & venous drainage
bullets: The usual bedside model is CPP = MAP − ICP; brain-level arterial pressure, venous pressure and autoregulation affect interpretation. Hypotension can reduce perfusion even when ICP is not rising. Agree targets for the actual pathology and operative phase rather than using one number for all neurosurgery.

Keep the head/neck positioned to support venous drainage without excessive rotation, flexion or external compression. Coordinate head elevation and PEEP with oxygenation and perfusion; zero PEEP or indiscriminate volume loading is not a universal neuroprotective strategy.

sections.title: Brain relaxation, CO₂ & osmotherapy
bullets: Avoid hypoxemia and unintended hypercapnia; confirm PaCO₂ when ETCO₂ may be misleading. Routine profound or prolonged hyperventilation can reduce cerebral blood flow. A brief rescue strategy for threatened herniation is different from prophylactic hypocapnia in every craniotomy.

Mannitol or hypertonic saline may be used for a defined indication with surgical/neurocritical coordination. Monitor perfusion, sodium/osmolality, renal function and volume consequences; neither drug nor a fixed regimen is automatically appropriate for every swollen brain.

sections.title: Head fixation, stimulation & position
bullets: Coordinate analgesia/anesthesia for laryngoscopy, pin placement, incision and emergence while protecting perfusion. If local/scalp block is used, track total dose and communicate timing; sudden hemodynamic changes still need assessment rather than automatic anesthetic deepening.

Protect eyes and pressure points, secure lines and preserve airway access as far as practical. With the head above the heart, consider venous air entrainment risk; communicate any need to release fixation or reposition during an emergency.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & metabolic care
bullets: Maintain appropriate intravascular volume and cerebral/cord perfusion without excessive fluid loading. Use measured bleeding, hemoglobin and physiology to guide blood/fluid therapy; deliberate hypotension is not a default blood-conservation strategy in a perfusion-vulnerable patient.

Avoid unnecessary hypo-osmolar fluid in intracranial disease, and monitor glucose, sodium, hemoglobin, temperature and acid-base status according to case severity. Treat hypoglycemia when present; a blanket prohibition on all glucose-containing fluid would be unsafe.

sections.title: Analgesia, PONV & examination quality
bullets: Provide multimodal analgesia matched to the incision and patient, considering local/scalp or appropriate regional techniques. Check cumulative local-anesthetic exposure and bleeding considerations; opioid-sparing care should not mean inadequate analgesia.

Prevent and treat PONV while avoiding unnecessary sedation that obscures the neurologic exam. Balance smooth emergence and blood-pressure control with ventilation, airway protection and reliable assessment.

sections.title: Emergence, neurologic examination & disposition
bullets: Aim for a smooth, timely neurologic exam when safe, but do not force immediate extubation in a patient with impaired airway protection, brainstem dysfunction, severe swelling, shock or respiratory failure. Verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis after neuromuscular blockade.

Handoff baseline and new deficits, pupils/mental status, blood-pressure goals, drain settings, bleeding, seizures and airway concerns. New weakness, delayed awakening or respiratory deterioration requires urgent assessment for reversible physiology and surgical/neurologic complications.

sections.title: Evidence scope & clinical-review boundary
bullets: Adult clinical-review draft, not an independently approved protocol. TBI, aSAH, spontaneous ICH, ischemic stroke and chronic spine disease have different targets; do not transfer one guideline’s pressure or drug recommendations indiscriminately to another.

Institutional handbook numbers are not universal mandates; the 2026 AHA/ASA stroke guideline takes precedence over older conflicting post-thrombectomy BP targets. Older mapping reviews and low-level rescue evidence are labeled. Device-specific instructions, local protocols and clinician signoff remain necessary.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Urgent CSF diversion may be required for symptomatic hydrocephalus or selected intracranial hypertension.
Choose local/sedation or GA according to consciousness, cooperation and airway safety, not the drain name alone.
Confirm coagulation, infection prevention and neurosurgical drainage/pressure orders.
Level, monitor and transport the drain using an individualized plan that prevents both obstruction and overdrainage.

sections.title: EVD leveling, drainage & transport
bullets: Verify ordered drainage height, reference point, patency and open-versus-clamped plan. Level an EVD at the external auditory meatus with an appropriate leveling device; relevel after position changes and never connect a pressurized flush system.

Do not routinely clamp every EVD for transport. Agree a plan using clamp tolerance, ICP and drainage needs; prevent overdrainage during movement and restore ordered settings with trained monitoring. Accurate fluid-coupled pressure measurement and simultaneous open drainage are not interchangeable states.

sources.label: SNACC perioperative EVD/lumbar drain guideline (2017)

sections.title: Insertion preparation and complication surveillance
bullets: Assess urgency, imaging, coagulation/antithrombotics and airway protection. Coordinate correction and insertion prophylaxis under the current institutional policy without unnecessary delay in deteriorating hydrocephalus.

Watch for catheter-related hemorrhage, malposition, obstruction and infection. New neurologic deterioration or abnormal drainage requires immediate neurosurgical assessment; do not flush or manipulate the system without an authorized protocol.

sections.title: Explicit drain handoff
bullets: Communicate the prescribed reference height, open/closed status, recent output, ICP trend and tolerance of clamping. Verify the system with the receiving team and relevel after transfers or head-position changes.

Pressure transducer and drainage configurations need trained handling. Do not apply a generic fixed hourly drainage goal to every pathology; the neurosurgical order and clinical response govern drainage.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Ruptured and elective unruptured aneurysms require different BP, antithrombotic and ICU plans.
Immobility and reliable airway access may favor GA, but technique remains patient/procedure specific.
Coordinate heparin and antiplatelet strategy, especially when a stent or flow diverter is used.
Watch for perforation, thromboembolism, access-site bleeding and new neurologic deficits.

sections.title: Ruptured aneurysm, nimodipine & DCI
bullets: For unsecured aneurysmal SAH, use frequent monitoring and short-acting treatment to avoid severe hypertension, hypotension and variability. The 2023 guideline does not establish one universal BP target; consider ICP/hydrocephalus, presenting pressure and comorbidity.

Coordinate enteral nimodipine, euvolemia and neurocritical follow-up. Symptomatic delayed cerebral ischemia may need individualized BP augmentation after team assessment, but prophylactic hypervolemia/hemodynamic augmentation is not recommended; new deficits also require evaluation for other causes.

sources.label: AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH guideline (2023)

sections.title: Antithrombotics, contrast & catheter complications
bullets: Clarify planned heparin/antiplatelet therapy, prior thrombolysis and any procedure-specific reversal strategy with the neurointerventional team. Do not order routine anticoagulation holds or reversal without considering intracranial device thrombosis and bleeding risks.

Account for renal function, contrast exposure, access-site/retroperitoneal bleeding, perforation and cerebral thromboembolism. Sudden neurologic or hemodynamic change needs immediate communication, imaging/procedural assessment and rescue, not automatic attribution to sedation.

sources.label: AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH guideline (2023)
AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline (2026)

sections.title: Neurointerventional suite & immobility
bullets: Check oxygen, suction, difficult-airway equipment, blood/resuscitation access and the transfer route before draping. C-arm equipment, radiation shielding and sterile coverage can limit airway access; secure equipment and coordinate a rapid access plan.

Choose GA or sedation for airway protection, cooperation and procedural requirements. If sedation fails because of movement, vomiting, seizure or impaired ventilation, convert promptly with the team rather than preserving sedation at the expense of safety.

University of Iowa neuroanesthesia handbook (2025 institutional guidance; not universal targets)

sections.title: Coil versus stent / flow-diverter strategy
bullets: Clarify the actual device and antiplatelet requirements before anesthesia. Emergency hemorrhage rescue may conflict with thrombosis prevention, so reversal and drain/procedure timing require the neurovascular team.
After deployment, document neurologic findings and planned BP/antithrombotic monitoring. Do not use an identical medication-hold plan for simple coiling and an intracranial stent.

sections.title: Prone positioning, eyes & peripheral nerves
bullets: Before and after turning, verify the airway, ventilation, lines, neutral neck alignment and padded pressure points. Keep the abdomen free of avoidable compression and avoid excessive arm abduction or plexus stretch; reassess supports throughout a long case.

Avoid direct eye pressure and periodically confirm eye/head position. For high-risk prolonged or high-blood-loss spine surgery, discuss visual-loss risk, preserve perfusion and oxygen delivery, and assess vision when awake; new visual symptoms require urgent ophthalmologic evaluation. No device or fixed transfusion threshold guarantees prevention.

sections.title: SSEP / MEP / EMG-compatible anesthesia
bullets: Agree modalities and baseline acquisition before incision and, when useful, before/after positioning. TIVA is commonly chosen for robust evoked potentials; volatile agents and nitrous oxide can suppress signals, while neuromuscular blockade especially affects myogenic MEP/EMG rather than sensory conduction itself.

Keep anesthetic concentrations and physiology stable and communicate all boluses or blocker doses. TIVA still requires reliable delivery, hypnosis assessment and awareness prevention; neither TIVA nor a preserved SSEP guarantees intact motor function.

sections.title: Cord perfusion & immediate signal-loss response
bullets: For a significant monitoring change, immediately announce it, pause the provoking surgical maneuver and initiate the agreed team response. Check surgical compression/hardware/traction, technical leads/stimulation and anesthetic/physiologic causes in parallel; do not wait to notify the surgeon until an anesthesia checklist is finished.

Reassess arterial pressure at the correct reference level, oxygenation/ventilation, blood loss/hemoglobin, temperature, anesthetic delivery and residual/new neuromuscular blockade.
