sections.title: 2026 guidance: technique and avoiding delay
bullets: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline supports either GA or procedural sedation for EVT. Loss of airway protection, vomiting, severe agitation or movement may favor GA; sedation needs rapid conversion capability.

Correct hypotension/hypovolemia and avoid delays solely for optional monitoring. If eligible for both IV thrombolysis and EVT, IVT should be given rapidly without waiting to assess response or delaying EVT; coordinate with the stroke team.

sections.title: Peri-EVT and post-reperfusion BP
bullets: The 2026 guideline considers BP at or below 185/110 mmHg reasonable before EVT without preceding IVT, and at or below 180/105 during EVT and for 24 hours afterward. IVT has its own pre/post thresholds; confirm the actual reperfusion treatment and individualized target.

For successfully recanalized anterior-circulation LVO (mTICI 2b, 2c or 3) without another BP indication, intensive SBP reduction below 140 mmHg for the first 72 hours is harmful and not recommended. This supersedes older routine low-target protocols; it does not mean ignoring severe hypertension or a separate emergency indication.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: MEPs assess motor pathways; myogenic recordings depend on neuromuscular transmission and can be suppressed by blockade.
Coordinate anesthetic delivery, stimulation and baseline acquisition with neurophysiology.
Stable TIVA often supports signals, but hypotension, anemia, technical issues or surgical injury can still cause loss.

sections.title: SSEP / MEP / EMG-compatible anesthesia
bullets: Agree modalities and baseline acquisition before incision and, when useful, before/after positioning. TIVA is commonly chosen for robust evoked potentials; volatile agents and nitrous oxide can suppress signals, while neuromuscular blockade especially affects myogenic MEP/EMG rather than sensory conduction itself.

Keep anesthetic concentrations and physiology stable and communicate all boluses or blocker doses. TIVA still requires reliable delivery, hypnosis assessment and awareness prevention; neither TIVA nor a preserved SSEP guarantees intact motor function.

sections.title: Percutaneous trial versus surgical implantation
bullets: The 2023 consensus advises against inserting percutaneous SCS trial leads under GA or deep sedation unless technical challenges or patient factors justify it. The recommendation has low-certainty evidence and is not a blanket prohibition for all surgical paddle-lead operations.

If GA/deep sedation prevents feedback, document the indication and use an appropriate monitoring strategy; IONM should be considered for paresthesia-dependent placement. Uncontrolled movement or a difficult airway can alter the risk-benefit balance.

sections.title: Prone sedation, bleeding and infection
bullets: Confirm the ability to communicate during testing and access the airway while prone. Avoid drifting into deep sedation without a rescue plan; coordinate conversion if safety demands it.

Reconcile antithrombotic management and infection-prevention requirements with the implanting team and current neuraxial/interventional-pain guidance. Do not apply a generic medication hold interval to every trial or implantation.

sections.title: Existing device, electrosurgery & reactivation
bullets: Identify manufacturer, leads/generator location, controller and specialist contact. Most systems need deactivation or a manufacturer-specific surgery mode; magnet responses vary, so never assume a magnet universally turns an SCS off.

Prefer bipolar cautery when feasible and follow device-specific precautions for monopolar use. Pad the generator and protect recent leads from excessive movement; restore the correct mode/settings and verify therapy with the responsible team after surgery.

sections.title: Baseline neurologic status & preparation
bullets: Document consciousness, pupils, language, strength/sensation and relevant pre-existing deficits before anesthesia when feasible. Review imaging, urgency, seizures, antithrombotics, cardiopulmonary disease, renal function and prior airway/cervical issues.

Clarify the surgical/monitoring plan and usual antiseizure, steroid, Parkinson or chronic pain medications. Continue or modify medications through an explicit specialist plan; mapping-related changes are not permission for indiscriminate withholding.

bullets: Choose airway technique for aspiration risk, consciousness, cervical stability and anticipated access after fixation/positioning. bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring, temperature surveillance when indicated and access matched to hemorrhage or vasoactive needs. Arterial pressure monitoring is often useful for major cranial/cord-risk surgery; it must not create avoidable delay in emergency reperfusion or decompression.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & metabolic care
bullets: Maintain appropriate intravascular volume and cerebral/cord perfusion without excessive fluid loading. Use measured bleeding, hemoglobin and physiology to guide blood/fluid therapy; deliberate hypotension is not a default blood-conservation strategy in a perfusion-vulnerable patient.

sections.title: Prone positioning, eyes & peripheral nerves
bullets: Before and after turning, verify the airway, ventilation, lines, neutral neck alignment and padded pressure points. Keep the abdomen free of avoidable compression and avoid excessive arm abduction or plexus stretch; reassess supports throughout a long case.

sections.title: SSEP / MEP / EMG-compatible anesthesia
bullets: Agree modalities and baseline acquisition before incision and, when useful, before/after positioning. TIVA is commonly chosen for robust evoked potentials; volatile agents and nitrous oxide can suppress signals, while neuromuscular blockade especially affects myogenic MEP/EMG rather than sensory conduction itself.

Keep anesthetic concentrations and physiology stable and communicate all boluses or blocker doses. TIVA still requires reliable delivery, hypnosis assessment and awareness prevention; neither TIVA nor a preserved SSEP guarantees intact motor function.

sections.title: Cord perfusion & immediate signal-loss response
bullets: For a significant monitoring change, immediately announce it, pause the provoking surgical maneuver and initiate the agreed team response. Reassess arterial pressure at the correct reference level, oxygenation/ventilation, blood loss/hemoglobin, temperature, anesthetic delivery and residual/new neuromuscular blockade. Restore agreed perfusion and correct reversible abnormalities with the team; no single universal rescue MAP or alarm percentage applies to all modalities and lesions.

bullets: Distinguish expanding acute trauma from a stable chronic subdural; urgency and anesthetic options differ.
Assess mass effect, neurologic decline, anticoagulants and associated injury.

Prepare for decompression, reversal/resuscitation and postoperative examination or continued ventilation as indicated.

sections.title: Acute versus chronic presentation
bullets: Rapid deterioration, pupillary changes or herniation signs require coordinated emergency airway/perfusion support and surgical decompression. Do not assume limited external blood loss means stable intracranial physiology.

Chronic subdural drainage may be performed with a different anesthetic than emergency craniotomy, but impaired cooperation, aspiration or airway risk may still favor GA. Reconcile anticoagulant/antiplatelet exposure and current reversal protocol with the team.

bullets: Review renal clearance and timing of the actual anticoagulant, baseline cognition and comorbid disease. Use drug-specific contemporary reversal guidance; spontaneous-ICH recommendations are not automatically identical to traumatic hematoma management.

sections.title: CPP, pressure targets & venous drainage
bullets: The usual bedside model is CPP = MAP − ICP; brain-level arterial pressure, venous pressure and autoregulation affect interpretation. Hypotension can reduce perfusion even when ICP is not rising. Agree targets for the actual pathology and operative phase rather than using one number for all neurosurgery.

Keep the head/neck positioned to support venous drainage without excessive rotation, flexion or external compression. Coordinate head elevation and PEEP with oxygenation and perfusion; zero PEEP or indiscriminate volume loading is not a universal neuroprotective strategy.

sections.title: Brain relaxation, CO₂ & osmotherapy
bullets: Avoid hypoxemia and unintended hypercapnia; confirm PaCO₂ when ETCO₂ may be misleading. Routine profound or prolonged hyperventilation can reduce cerebral blood flow. A brief rescue strategy for threatened herniation is different from prophylactic hypocapnia in every craniotomy.

Mannitol or hypertonic saline may be used for a defined indication with surgical/neurocritical coordination. Monitor perfusion, sodium/osmolality, renal function and volume consequences; neither drug nor a fixed regimen is automatically appropriate for every swollen brain.

sections.title: Head fixation, stimulation & position
bullets: Coordinate analgesia/anesthesia for laryngoscopy, pin placement, incision and emergence while protecting perfusion. If local/scalp block is used, track total dose and communicate timing; sudden hemodynamic changes still need assessment rather than automatic anesthetic deepening.

Protect eyes and pressure points, secure lines and preserve airway access as far as practical. With the head above the heart, consider venous air entrainment risk; communicate any need to release fixation or reposition during an emergency.

sections.title: Anterior, oblique and posterior branches
bullets: Confirm access surgeon involvement, levels, revision, vascular anatomy concerns and whether the patient will be repositioned for posterior instrumentation. Ensure rapid access to blood and a rescue plan for major vessel injury.

sections.title: Major spine / cranial hemorrhage readiness
bullets: Correct elective anemia when feasible and plan crossmatch, large-bore access, warming, cell salvage and antifibrinolytic use for high-blood-loss operations. TXA selection and regimen should account for renal function, seizure/thrombotic context and the procedure rather than copying a universal dose.

During major loss, reassess hemoglobin, coagulation, platelets/fibrinogen, ionized calcium and temperature. Restoring MAP with fluid/pressors alone does not restore oxygen-carrying capacity; transfusion decisions integrate bleeding, perfusion and neurologic risk.

sections.title: Approach-specific postoperative surveillance
bullets: Compare lower-extremity neurologic function with baseline and monitor unexplained abdominal distension, falling hemoglobin or hemodynamic changes for concealed bleeding.

sections.title: Baseline neurologic status & preparation
bullets: Document consciousness, pupils, language, strength/sensation and relevant pre-existing deficits before anesthesia when feasible. Review imaging, urgency, seizures, antithrombotics, cardiopulmonary disease, renal function and prior airway/cervical issues.

Clarify the surgical/monitoring plan and usual antiseizure, steroid, Parkinson or chronic pain medications. Continue or modify medications through an explicit specialist plan; mapping-related changes are not permission for indiscriminate withholding.

bullets: Choose airway technique for aspiration risk, consciousness, cervical stability and anticipated access after fixation/positioning. sections.title: Monitoring, access & reference level
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring, temperature surveillance when indicated and access matched to hemorrhage or vasoactive needs. Arterial pressure monitoring is often useful for major cranial/cord-risk surgery; it must not create avoidable delay in emergency reperfusion or decompression.

Document the arterial transducer reference level, especially with the head elevated; pressure measured at heart level may overestimate brain-level arterial pressure. Recheck airway/lines after positioning and arrange access to blood, laboratory testing and emergency equipment.

sections.title: Prone positioning, eyes & peripheral nerves
bullets: Before and after turning, verify the airway, ventilation, lines, neutral neck alignment and padded pressure points. Keep the abdomen free of avoidable compression and avoid excessive arm abduction or plexus stretch; reassess supports throughout a long case.

Avoid direct eye pressure and periodically confirm eye/head position. For high-risk prolonged or high-blood-loss spine surgery, discuss visual-loss risk, preserve perfusion and oxygen delivery, and assess vision when awake; new visual symptoms require urgent ophthalmologic evaluation. No device or fixed transfusion threshold guarantees prevention.

sections.title: SSEP / MEP / EMG-compatible anesthesia
bullets: Agree modalities and baseline acquisition before incision and, when useful, before/after positioning. TIVA is commonly chosen for robust evoked potentials; volatile agents and nitrous oxide can suppress signals, while neuromuscular blockade especially affects myogenic MEP/EMG rather than sensory conduction itself.

Keep anesthetic concentrations and physiology stable and communicate all boluses or blocker doses. TIVA still requires reliable delivery, hypnosis assessment and awareness prevention; neither TIVA nor a preserved SSEP guarantees intact motor function.

sections.title: Cord perfusion & immediate signal-loss response
bullets: For a significant monitoring change, immediately announce it, pause the provoking surgical maneuver and initiate the agreed team response. Check surgical compression/hardware/traction, technical leads/stimulation and anesthetic/physiologic causes in parallel; do not wait to notify the surgeon until an anesthesia checklist is finished.

Reassess arterial pressure at the correct reference level, oxygenation/ventilation, blood loss/hemoglobin, temperature, anesthetic delivery and residual/new neuromuscular blockade. Restore agreed perfusion and correct reversible abnormalities with the team; no single universal rescue MAP or alarm percentage applies to all modalities and lesions.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & metabolic care
bullets: Maintain appropriate intravascular volume and cerebral/cord perfusion without excessive fluid loading. Use measured bleeding, hemoglobin and physiology to guide blood/fluid therapy; deliberate hypotension is not a default blood-conservation strategy in a perfusion-vulnerable patient.

Avoid unnecessary hypo-osmolar fluid in intracranial disease, and monitor glucose, sodium, hemoglobin, temperature and acid-base status according to case severity. Treat hypoglycemia when present; a blanket prohibition on all glucose-containing fluid would be unsafe.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: The hormone phenotype matters as much as the surgical route: assess acromegaly, Cushing disease and hypopituitarism separately.
Plan a secured oral airway, access despite draping and a smooth emergence with early visual/neurologic assessment.
After surgery, distinguish AVP deficiency from other polyuria and monitor for delayed hyponatremia after discharge.
Steroid coverage, sodium follow-up and CPAP/airway support must be explicitly agreed with endocrinology and the skull-base team.

sections.title: Functional tumor, mass effect & route
bullets: Clarify tumor type, size, suprasellar/cavernous extension, baseline vision and anticipated skull-base repair. A functioning adenoma and a nonfunctioning compressive lesion have different systemic risks.

Review prior surgery, radiation and nasal access issues. Confirm the surgical approach and any planned CSF diversion rather than assuming every sellar lesion follows a routine transsphenoidal pathway.

sections.title: Pituitary axes, cortisol & thyroid replacement
bullets: Review cortisol/adrenal reserve, free T4 and other relevant axes, sodium, glucose, visual findings and prior hormone replacement. Functional phenotype and mass effect may coexist with deficiencies.

When ACTH deficiency and central hypothyroidism coexist, establish glucocorticoid coverage before starting thyroid replacement: thyroid hormone can increase cortisol clearance and precipitate crisis in untreated adrenal insufficiency.

Document perioperative steroid coverage or a supervised steroid-sparing testing pathway when adrenal reserve is intact. Do not withhold needed steroids solely to obtain a cleaner postoperative cortisol result.

sections.title: Acromegaly, OSA & anticipated difficulty
bullets: Assess macroglossia, pharyngeal/laryngeal tissue enlargement, jaw changes, goiter and OSA in acromegaly. Have an explicit difficult-airway strategy, including an awake option when indicated.
Cushing-related obesity, myopathy and OSA also affect induction and recovery. Baseline cardiomyopathy or pulmonary hypertension may require additional assessment and monitoring.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & escalation
bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Choose arterial monitoring, reliable additional IV access and serial laboratory testing for anticipated instability, major surgery or rapid metabolic change rather than for the endocrine label alone.

Agree who communicates hormone-related interventions, key surgical transitions and abnormal laboratory results. Have the required rescue drugs, blood access and postoperative monitoring destination ready before a predictable high-risk phase.

sections.title: Transsphenoidal access & secured oral airway
bullets: The endoscopic transsphenoidal route shares the nose and skull base with the surgeon. A secured oral tracheal tube usually keeps the nasal operative field clear; position the circuit away from instruments and recheck after the head is positioned.

Avoid blind nasal instrumentation after skull-base surgery. If a throat pack is specifically indicated, document insertion/removal and clear blood or secretions before extubation; routine anesthetist-inserted packs are not recommended by the adult throat-pack consensus.

sections.title: Surgical field, perfusion & vascular injury
bullets: Use controlled, titratable anesthesia while maintaining cerebral perfusion and oxygenation. TIVA may improve the operative field, but no single low MAP is appropriate for all patients; account for baseline pressure, cardiovascular disease and intracranial pathology.
Communicate topical nasal vasoconstrictor/local-anesthetic administration and cumulative exposure. Abrupt hypertension or arrhythmia may reflect systemic absorption rather than inadequate anesthesia.

Unexpected major bleeding raises concern for carotid injury and requires immediate surgical control, resuscitation and vascular/neurointerventional escalation. Prepare suitable access and blood support for complex or invasive lesions; a routine low-blood-loss expectation must not delay rescue.

sections.title: Fluid, glucose and urine-output interpretation
bullets: Use controlled fluid management while following hemodynamics, glucose and urine output. Mark timing of substantial fluids, diuretics, steroids and tumor removal so later polyuria can be interpreted correctly.

A urinary catheter and serial laboratories are particularly useful when the operation is complex or water-balance disturbance is anticipated. Do not treat urine volume alone with either unlimited fluid or automatic DDAVP.

sections.title: AVP deficiency: assess before treating polyuria
bullets: Arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D; central diabetes insipidus) causes inappropriately dilute polyuria. Assess urine output trend, fluid balance, thirst, serum sodium and paired serum/urine osmolality rather than diagnosing from urine volume alone.

A proposed postoperative screen is urine output >300 mL/hour for 3 consecutive hours with urine specific gravity <1.005 plus excessive thirst, serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg or sodium >145 mmol/L. These are assessment criteria, not an automatic DDAVP order; sodium may remain normal with intact thirst and water access.

Exclude mobilization of perioperative fluids, hyperglycemia/osmotic diuresis, mannitol/diuretics and rapid fluid loss after successful acromegaly surgery. Glucocorticoid replacement can unmask AVP-D that cortisol deficiency had obscured.

If thirst is intact and drinking is safe, allow access to water with surveillance. Significant losses, rising sodium, impaired consciousness or inability to drink may require individualized fluid replacement and desmopressin. Initially use reassessment-driven dosing rather than automatic repeated doses; monitor sodium and urine response.

sources.label: JCEM: Disorders of salt and water balance after pituitary surgery (2022/2023)

sections.title: Delayed hyponatremia, DDAVP & discharge checks
bullets: Delayed SIAD-related hyponatremia often develops after initial recovery, commonly around postoperative day 7 within a reported day 4–14 window. Arrange a sodium check around one week and give explicit symptom/return instructions, even if inpatient sodium was normal.

Before labeling hyponatremia SIAD, assess adrenal insufficiency, thyroid deficiency, medications including desmopressin, fluid exposure and volume status. Severe symptoms, confusion or seizures require urgent hospital assessment and controlled correction.

Do not apply a blanket postoperative fluid restriction to a patient with active AVP-D or impaired thirst. Excess DDAVP plus fluid intake can cause dangerous hyponatremia, especially if a later antidiuretic phase develops.

sections.title: Emergence, OSA & skull-base repair
bullets: Clear blood/secretions, verify pack removal and quantitative recovery if relaxants were used, and plan awake extubation with a defined reintubation strategy for difficult airways or OSA. A smooth wake-up should still allow prompt neurologic and visual assessment.

Postoperative CPAP/noninvasive positive pressure needs an individualized agreement with the skull-base team: defect/repair integrity, CSF-leak risk and OSA severity matter. Do not prescribe a universal restart date or simply leave significant obstruction untreated; provide an appropriate monitored rescue plan.

New visual loss, diplopia, depressed consciousness, major epistaxis or suspected CSF rhinorrhea requires urgent neurosurgical assessment. Avoid nose blowing and straining according to the repair-specific instructions.

bullets: Use non-opioid analgesia and small titrated opioid doses as needed; avoid excessive sedation in OSA or when neurologic assessment is important. NSAID use should follow the surgeon’s bleeding/repair policy rather than an automatic routine.

Provide antiemetic prophylaxis because vomiting/retching can stress hemostasis and the skull-base repair. Airway difficulty, OSA, hormonal instability, major blood loss or neurologic concerns warrant higher-acuity observation.

sections.title: Discharge and endocrine follow-up
bullets: Specify steroid prescription/testing, sodium check timing, fluid advice and any desmopressin plan in the handoff. Normal immediate recovery does not eliminate delayed sodium or cortisol problems.

Give clear return instructions for thirst/polyuria, persistent nausea or headache, confusion, visual change, clear nasal drainage or significant bleeding. Persistent symptoms need clinical evaluation rather than reassurance based on the operation’s apparent success.

sections.title: CPP, pressure targets & venous drainage

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: ECT induces a generalized tonic-clonic seizure using scalp electrodes under general anesthesia and neuromuscular blockade. Ventilation is generally assisted by face mask; tracheal intubation is not routine.

The key physiologic pattern is early parasympathetic bradycardia or, rarely, asystole, followed by seizure-associated sympathetic tachycardia and hypertension. Monitor closely and be prepared to manage clinically important instability.
Select and titrate anesthesia to the patient: anesthetic dose and choice can affect seizure generation, hemodynamics, and recovery. The available review does not establish one universal regimen.
After stimulation, assess oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and level of consciousness. Headache and nausea are common post-ECT complaints; postictal delirium or agitation may occur.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
Electroconvulsive Therapy Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: ECT delivers an electrical stimulus through scalp electrodes under general anesthesia and neuromuscular blockade to induce a therapeutic generalized seizure. Electrode placement and stimulus properties affect seizure threshold and treatment effects.
Common electrode placements are bitemporal, bifrontal, and right unilateral; selection is part of the ECT treatment approach rather than an anesthetic positioning instruction.

Assess seizure duration using EEG, electromyography, or observed muscle movement. The review reports an appropriate motor duration range, but this should not be conflated with a universal anesthetic target or an EEG duration.
Treatment is commonly delivered in repeated sessions, but course length and frequency vary with response and urgency; do not infer a fixed course from the anesthetic sources.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess psychiatric and medication history, physical status, airway, and relevant investigations. The review describes evaluation comparable to other general anesthesia and notes that difficult mask ventilation, aspiration risk, or prolonged ventilation may require unplanned intubation.

Review ongoing medicines with the treating team. The review says usual medications are generally continued through the morning, with specified exceptions; it does not support blanket benzodiazepine or antihypertensive holding rules.

Consider cardiovascular and respiratory comorbidity carefully. The review identifies several conditions associated with relatively high risk during ECT, so individualized assessment and preparation are important.

Fasting guidance in the review allows clear liquids, including oral antihypertensive medication, up to the stated interval; apply relevant institutional policy and patient-specific aspiration assessment.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: For ECT delivered in a NORA setting, account for potential limitations in equipment, patient monitoring, and access to emergency support; conduct careful risk assessment and preparation.

Recommended ECT intra-procedure monitoring includes non-invasive blood pressure, pulse oximetry, ECG, and capnography; continue observation for motor seizure activity and coordinate EEG assessment with the ECT team.
Protect teeth and soft tissues: the stimulus can activate jaw muscles despite relaxation, so place the bite block carefully before stimulation.

sources.label: Safety of nonoperating room anesthesia: a narrative review
Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Face-mask ventilation with a simple bag-valve-mask system is generally used. Routine tracheal intubation is not recommended, but airway difficulty, aspiration risk, prolonged ventilation, or special circumstances may change the approach.

Provide oxygenation and assess ventilation throughout anesthesia. The ECT review recommends capnography; it does not establish a universal end-tidal carbon dioxide target or endorse a fixed hyperventilation protocol.
A bite block is important because forceful jaw clenching can occur despite neuromuscular relaxation. Check placement before the electrical stimulus and remain alert to dental or oral injury.

When neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring where available and confirm adequate recovery before extubation if an airway device is used; these are general NMB recommendations, not a mandate for intubation in ECT.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Between stimulus and seizure onset, parasympathetic predominance can produce hypotension, bradycardia, or asystole; during the seizure, rebound sympathetic activity produces tachycardia and hypertension.

The cardiovascular response can be substantial, particularly for patients with cardiovascular disease. Track hemodynamics and respond to clinically significant instability in the context of the individual patient.

Antihypertensives may blunt seizure generation, while anesthetic agents also differ in anticonvulsant and hemodynamic effects. Select and adjust agents to balance seizure quality and patient risk; no single drug is appropriate for every patient.
Seizures also increase cerebral blood flow, intracranial pressure, and cerebral oxygen demand; account for relevant neurologic and cardiovascular comorbidity in anesthetic planning.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy
Electroconvulsive Therapy Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Watch for significant hypertension, tachycardia, bradycardia, or hypotension, especially in patients at risk of ischemia or other cardiovascular complications. Escalate and manage according to observed severity and local emergency processes.

Potential complications include pulmonary edema, ventricular tachycardia, myocardial infarction, aspiration, respiratory failure, cerebral hemorrhage, dental injury, and tongue or gingival laceration. Serious events are not the expected course, but require recognition and escalation.

Transient postictal agitation or delirium may occur. Assess for reversible contributors and maintain patient and staff safety; the review describes behavioral measures and medication options without establishing a single required treatment.
An implanted cardiac device is not by itself a reason to assume ECT cannot proceed; device function and interference risk require case-specific planning.

sources.label: Anesthetic care for electroconvulsive therapy
Electroconvulsive Therapy Anesthetic Considerations

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The ECT review does not provide a fluid-management or bleeding-management protocol. No routine fluid total, blood preparation, or access gauge is established by the available ECT-specific evidence.
Monitor circulation during the procedure and recovery; prioritize recognition of hemodynamic instability rather than assuming a particular fluid intervention.
Oral and dental trauma, including tongue laceration, is a reported complication; inspect and address clinically apparent injury rather than anticipating routine hemorrhage.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Headache is a common post-ECT complaint; the OpenAnesthesia review reports prophylactic ketorolac and/or acetaminophen as usual options. Individualize for contraindications and patient context.
Nausea is reported after ECT, and ondansetron is described as a prophylactic option. The source gives a regimen, but this reference omits dosing and does not treat it as mandatory.
Myalgia can follow succinylcholine; the review describes NSAIDs, including ketorolac, as options for prevention or treatment. Consider patient-specific risks when selecting analgesia.
Post-ECT nausea and vomiting are reported complications; consider prophylaxis in context, particularly when patient or anesthetic factors increase risk.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Continue appropriate assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and consciousness through recovery. The ECT review recommends monitoring standard non-invasive hemodynamic variables and oxygen saturation for a post-treatment observation period.
Expect possible transient confusion or agitation, headache, nausea, and muscle pain; reassess the patient and escalate if recovery is not consistent with the observed course.
If neuromuscular blockade has been used, assess recovery appropriately; general ASA guidance recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.
The ECT-specific source does not establish a universal discharge time or discharge protocol. Discharge readiness should follow applicable local postanesthesia standards and physician assessment.

bullets: The ECT-specific evidence is educational review material and a narrative review, not a single standardized protocol or formal evidence-graded guideline. Individual anesthetic choices and doses therefore require clinical judgment.

The review gives no specific patient positioning or vascular-access recommendations.

title: ICU Bedside Procedures Under Anesthesia / Sedation

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: ICU bedside procedural anesthesia covers a varied set of procedures; the anesthetic approach ranges from sedation and analgesia to monitored anesthesia care or TIVA, selected for the patient and procedure.
Prioritize cardiopulmonary stability: critically ill patients may tolerate transient hypoxemia or hypercarbia poorly, and anesthesia can increase respiratory and hemodynamic support needs.
Anticipate remote-location constraints—limited workspace, equipment, personnel, and emergency support—and coordinate the procedural and ICU teams before starting.
Plan recovery in the ICU or equivalent postanesthesia-care area, with condition-appropriate monitoring, reassessment, and a clear handoff.

Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Bedside care may be appropriate when transport could cause decompensation or interrupt critical care. It avoids transport but does not remove the need to assess whether the location can support the procedure and rescue needs.

The supplied evidence includes ICU bedside GI endoscopy and interventional pulmonology procedures such as bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage. It does not establish an anesthetic protocol for every procedure listed in the case description.
Anesthetic depth is procedure- and patient-dependent. The review describes a spectrum from sedation and analgesia through monitored anesthesia care to TIVA; it does not supply a universal regimen.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

Procedural anesthesia at the bedside

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess current organ dysfunction and support needs, including hemodynamic instability, shock, arrhythmias, respiratory failure, renal dysfunction, bleeding, electrolytes, ventilation status, and vascular access.

Consider procedure urgency, comorbidities, and whether the ICU environment can support the planned care. Critically ill patients may be more susceptible to anesthetic adverse effects in the setting of multiorgan dysfunction.

Discuss the plan and consent with the patient or family as appropriate, and coordinate with ICU staff and relevant procedural and surgical teams, including anticipated complications and escalation options.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Before a bedside procedure, account for limited space, fewer available personnel and tools, and potentially limited ability to escalate care if complications arise.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic: continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; during moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the circumstances invalidate it.

Maintain continuous ECG display and determine blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes during anesthesia. The available sources do not specify a universal bedside position or monitoring package for all procedures.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For an already ventilated patient, protect the existing airway and avoid accidental extubation during the procedure. The ICU endoscopy review specifically identifies this risk for patients with an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy receiving ventilation.

For endoscopy, consider airway compression, positioning-related respiratory limitation, and aspiration risk. The NORA review describes a secure endotracheal airway for patients not appropriately nil per os or with specified GI pathology; this is not a universal intubation instruction for bedside procedures.

During general anesthesia, verify airway-device placement clinically and by expired carbon dioxide. With mechanical ventilation, use a device that detects breathing-system disconnection and provides an audible alarm.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Titrate anesthetic and analgesic effects cautiously in the context of limited physiologic reserve and existing respiratory or hemodynamic support. The available review does not define drug doses or targets for this case.

Watch for transient hypoxemia or hypercarbia and worsening hemodynamics; these may be poorly tolerated in critically ill patients. Escalation should be guided by the patient’s condition and local critical-care resources, rather than an unsupported universal algorithm.

Preserve coordination with the proceduralist and ICU team through critical portions of the procedure; the sources do not establish procedure-specific anesthetic phases or physiologic targets for the full range of bedside procedures.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Remote-location anesthesia has recognized hazards including oversedation and inadequate respiratory management, associated in cited claims analysis with workspace, staffing, and unfamiliar-equipment limitations. This is a general safety signal, not an ICU-specific risk estimate.

Maintain awareness of respiratory compromise, arrhythmia, and hemodynamic deterioration, and ensure the team knows how to access available emergency support. The supplied evidence does not provide a single rescue algorithm for this heterogeneous case.
For ventilated patients, treat circuit-disconnection detection and audible alarm availability as part of the setup, rather than relying on recognition after deterioration.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use the existing ICU assessment and support plan as context for perfusion management; anticipate that anesthesia may increase hemodynamic support needs. The sources do not specify a universal fluid strategy or vasopressor regimen.

Review anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy with the procedural team when relevant. The review notes that interruption may not be possible before an emergency procedure and that endoscopic interventions can have increased bleeding risk in treated patients.

sources.label: Navigating gastrointestinal endoscopy challenges in the intensive care unit: A mini review

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Anesthesia or sedation may reduce anxiety, discomfort, and pain and improve cooperation. Select the approach according to patient condition and procedural requirements.
The source set does not establish an ICU bedside analgesic regimen or PONV-prevention strategy. Avoid treating the case-field drug list as a supported recipe.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After anesthesia care, use the ICU or another area providing equivalent postanesthesia care. Recovery observation should reflect the patient’s condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

Reassess on arrival, provide a verbal handoff, and transmit the preoperative condition and anesthetic/procedural course to the receiving nurse. Continue appropriate monitoring during transport if transport is required.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The general bedside procedural-anesthesia source is a review whose supplied abstract does not describe individual procedures, drug regimens, doses, monitoring parameters, or outcomes. It supports planning and risk assessment, not a detailed procedure protocol.

The ICU GI endoscopy source is a mini review and explicitly lacks standardized anesthesia protocols and procedure-specific anesthetic regimens; its scope cannot establish management for tracheostomy, chest tubes, feeding tubes, or debridement.

Basic monitoring and postanesthesia standards supply general safety requirements, not procedure-specific selection, airway, fluid, or complication protocols. Case-specific targets are not established in the available sources.
The supplied sources do not establish a case-wide blood-product threshold, crossmatch policy, fluid total, or procedure-specific bleeding plan.
The supplied sources do not establish a universal return-to-prior-sedation or ventilator-setting protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult MRI is nonpainful; minimal or light sedation may be sufficient, while some patients need deeper sedation or general anesthesia to remain still. The sources do not establish one preferred drug regimen.
Prioritize MRI-device screening, MRI-appropriate equipment, and monitoring that remains observable despite restricted access and possible signal artifacts.

Key hazards include airway or ventilation compromise that is difficult to detect, projectile injury, burns, and monitoring interference. Plan how to summon help and move the patient out of zone IV for emergencies.
Recovery should follow the facility’s postanesthesia-care standards, with appropriate monitoring and discharge assessment; the sources do not define an MRI-specific emergence protocol.

sources.label: Non-Operating Room Anesthesia: Patient Selection and Special Considerations
Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Anesthetic care may range from moderate sedation to general anesthesia, depending on patient factors, scan needs, and the ability to remain still. MRI itself is generally nonpainful; avoid assuming that every adult requires general anesthesia.
Select depth and airway strategy for the individual and the scan. Lighter anesthesia can still be complicated by airway compromise and may require interruption of imaging and treatment.
Coordinate the plan with radiology and support staff, including scan duration, patient position, monitoring and equipment needs, and emergency roles.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Identify implants, embedded foreign bodies, and patient-attached metal before entry into the controlled MRI areas. Establish the status of each relevant device with the responsible MRI team; do not infer compatibility from the device category alone.

For a pacemaker or defibrillator, the advisory describes substantial hazard but also recognizes MRI-conditional devices and exceptional MRI circumstances. If MRI is considered essential, it calls for a device-specific management plan with the appropriate clinicians and device expertise.

Assess respiratory function, hemodynamic stability, comorbidities, and the need for special monitoring or airway equipment. For acute or severe renal insufficiency, the advisory cautions against gadolinium administration because of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use equipment identified as MRI safe or conditional for its intended location. Work with MRI personnel to establish equipment locations and ensure equipment does not compromise image acquisition.

Maintain observation of the patient and physiologic monitors directly or by video, and make vital signs viewable from zone III when the provider is not in zone IV. Position leads carefully because heating and burns can occur even with nonferromagnetic leads.

Apply basic anesthesia monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and patient. MRI can distort signals; ECG interpretation may be limited, and pulse-oximetry or temperature-probe readings may be affected.
Account for acoustic noise and extended distance from the patient; use communication and tubing arrangements appropriate to the scanner and local setup.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Plan airway management before imaging because access and direct assessment of ventilation can be difficult in the scanner. If the patient is at risk of airway compromise, the advisory supports more aggressive airway management, including a tracheal tube or laryngeal mask airway.

For moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the procedure, patient, or equipment invalidates that monitoring. Pulse oximetry alone does not assess ventilation.
Have MRI-appropriate alternative airway devices and immediately accessible suction available. Perform complex airway management in a controlled environment outside zone IV.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain vigilance during scanning: noise, limited line of sight, equipment interference, and distance from the patient can delay recognition of deterioration. Ensure that monitoring remains visible and that a means of rapid intervention is available.

Consider airway obstruction, apnea, hypoventilation, and hemodynamic instability during the scan. MRI-related ECG artifacts can make interpretation unreliable; suspected cardiac events warrant assessment outside the scanner zone.

Be alert to heating and temperature changes, especially during longer scans and in patients with relevant risk factors. The available sources do not establish a universal MRI temperature-management regimen.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Projectile injury is a life-threatening environmental hazard. Restrict entry to screened personnel and objects, and follow local MRI emergency procedures if a projectile event occurs.

A quench can release cryogen gas and displace oxygen if venting fails; escaping gas may also raise pressure and impede opening the zone-IV door. Follow institutional protocol and remove the patient from zone IV if possible; magnetic-field hazards may persist afterward.

For a medical emergency, summon help and move the patient out of zone IV to the designated safe area; emergency equipment and resuscitation should be available there. Do not assume non-MRI-safe equipment can be brought into zone IV.

Burns can result from heated or looped monitoring cables and probes. Investigate discrepant monitor readings with awareness of MRI artifact and remove the patient from the scanner zone when needed for accurate assessment.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Safety: Advanced

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The MRI advisory does not provide procedure-specific fluid, bleeding, or perfusion regimens. Manage these according to the patient’s condition and the requirements of the planned anesthetic rather than applying an MRI-specific total.
Plan access and infusion delivery around the MRI environment; use MRI-appropriate equipment or an arrangement approved for its location.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: MRI is generally nonpainful, but the advisory does not establish an analgesic regimen or an MRI-specific PONV prevention strategy. Avoid importing a routine analgesic prescription from this evidence.
Assess and manage recovery symptoms according to the patient’s clinical needs and local postanesthesia care practice; these sources do not provide MRI-specific PONV guidance.

sources.label: Practice Advisory on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Anesthetic Care for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The MRI advisory does not specify emergence technique or timing. Coordinate recovery location and handoff with radiology and receiving staff, with monitoring, oxygen, suction, and resuscitation capability appropriate to the patient.
Use applicable postanesthesia standards: transport with a knowledgeable anesthesia team member, reassess on arrival, hand off the course and current status, and continue monitoring through recovery.
If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, apply the cited quantitative monitoring recommendations before extubation; they are conditional on blocker use and do not imply routine paralysis for MRI.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The ASA MRI advisory is consensus-based practice advice, not an absolute requirement; it states that evidence is limited and that local policy and clinical circumstances matter.
The MRI safety review is an educational summary rather than a procedure-specific anesthetic protocol. The general NORA review also notes limited outcome data and varied practices.
The basic monitoring and postanesthesia sources provide general standards, not MRI-specific drug selection, airway choices, fluid plans, or emergence timing.
Adult MRI-specific drug selection and device-specific clearance protocols are not resolved by the supplied material; apply institutional MRI safety processes and individualized anesthetic judgment.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For adults receiving cranial SRS, treatment commonly proceeds with the patient awake or lightly sedated; MAC is often sufficient. General anesthesia is reserved for selected patients who cannot tolerate or remain still for treatment.

The defining anesthetic challenge is reliable immobility in a remote treatment environment with restricted access during irradiation. Plan observation, communication, and a safe route for team access before treatment begins.

Prioritize standard oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature assessment; remote observation does not remove the need to reconcile radiation-room access with applicable anesthesia monitoring standards.

After treatment, assess recovery in an appropriate postanesthesia-care setting. For cranial frame-based SRS, frame removal and pin-site care precede discharge or further observation; the source describes most patients as outpatients.

16 Anesthesia in the Radiation Oncology Suite, in Anesthesia Outside the Operating Room, 2nd edition

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Cranial SRS uses imaging and computer planning to direct focused radiation at an intracranial target; it is not conventional surgery. Adults generally do not require general anesthesia and may remain awake with light sedation.

For frame-based Gamma Knife, local anesthetic is administered before a stereotactic frame is secured to the skull with pins. The team analyzes images and formulates a radiation plan; for treatment, the frame is secured to an apparatus. Some devices, such as CyberKnife, use masks rather than frames to hold the head in place.

SBRT and proton therapy are within the requested case scope, but the supplied adult-specific evidence chiefly describes conventional radiation therapy and cranial SRS. Do not assume its SRS workflow or anesthetic approach applies unchanged to those modalities.

sources.label: Stereotactic Radiosurgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish whether the patient can tolerate the immobilization device and remain still, and discuss the planned level of sedation or anesthesia with the procedural team. Claustrophobia, anxiety, movement disorders, and painful treatment-planning procedures are described as factors that may make anesthetic support necessary.

For frame-based SRS, clarify the sequence and tolerance of frame placement under local anesthesia before proceeding with the treatment plan. The AANS source notes possible pin-site bleeding or infection, but does not provide an anticoagulant-management protocol.
When MRI is part of the workflow, screen for metallic implants and foreign bodies and arrange MRI-compatible equipment and monitoring; follow the site's MRI safety process.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan the equipment layout and patient observation with the radiation team before treatment. The radiation-oncology chapter describes closed-circuit cameras directed at the patient and monitors, and notes that circuit extensions may be needed when equipment placement is constrained.

Use monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and setting, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature assessment. The XRT chapter lists ECG, noninvasive blood pressure, pulse oximetry, and qualitative end-tidal CO₂ monitoring in its remote-monitoring description.

Resolve room-evacuation procedures against applicable anesthesia standards before treatment. The chapter describes evacuation during irradiation, while ASA monitoring standards require continuous presence of qualified anesthesia personnel, with a specific provision for hazards that may require intermittent remote observation. The sources do not establish a universal compliant workflow for every radiation vault.

Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: For a cooperative adult undergoing SRS, awake or lightly sedated management is described; the supplied sources do not establish a single airway device or anesthetic drug regimen for adults.

If general anesthesia is selected, account for limited airway access from immobilization and the remote setting. For frame-based treatment, the chapter specifically notes that the frame restricts airway access and calls for a means to remove it quickly if access becomes necessary.

During moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless the procedure, patient, or equipment invalidates that monitoring. The ASA standards also require exhaled carbon dioxide confirmation after placement of an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Immobility is central to accurate targeting. Inadequate immobilization can cause treatment failure or injury to normal tissue; coordinate any interruption or repositioning with the radiation team rather than assuming treatment can continue through movement.

Maintain reliable remote observation and communication during irradiation. The chapter describes camera views for breathing and movement and notes that the patient and monitors may not be directly visible from the usual remote location.

Radiation exposure is a staff-safety hazard to address through the site’s radiation-safety procedures. The supplied standards do not define radiation-vault entry thresholds or a specific emergency-entry algorithm.

sources.label: 16 Anesthesia in the Radiation Oncology Suite, in Anesthesia Outside the Operating Room, 2nd edition
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Respiratory compromise or airway obstruction is especially consequential when access is restricted. The NORA review identifies oversedation and inadequate ventilation or oxygenation as risks in remote locations; ensure that the team has a coordinated way to stop treatment and reach the patient.

For frame-based treatment, pin-site bleeding or infection is described as rare. Swelling around a tumor may occur; the AANS article describes Decadron use in that context, but does not establish an anesthetic treatment protocol.

Seizure and delayed radiation effects, including tissue necrosis and edema, are described as possible complications of cranial SRS. These are radiation-treatment risks requiring coordination with the treating clinical team, not evidence for a routine anesthetic intervention.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The radiation-oncology chapter characterizes typical XRT cases as having no blood loss or fluid shift and provides no routine fluid-management regimen. Individualize fluid care to the patient and treatment context rather than inferring a fixed requirement.
Frame-pin bleeding is mentioned as rare, but the sources do not provide an anticoagulant management, blood preparation, or transfusion protocol for this case.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Ordinary external-beam XRT is described as generally painless. For frame placement, local anesthetic is used at the pin sites; the AANS article also mentions possible IV morphine for comfort, without specifying a regimen.

The radiation-oncology chapter suggests considering antiemetic therapy at the end of treatment days because radiation-related emesis may add to chemotherapy- or stress-related nausea. It does not establish a universal prophylaxis plan for adult SRS, SBRT, or proton treatment.
The AANS source describes steroid treatment for swelling around a tumor as directed by the radiation team; this is not an anesthetic analgesia regimen.

sources.label: 16 Anesthesia in the Radiation Oncology Suite, in Anesthesia Outside the Operating Room, 2nd edition

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After irradiation has ended, the radiation team can re-enter; for frame-based SRS the frame is removed and pin sites dressed. Recovery location and observation should reflect the anesthetic and the patient’s status.

Postanesthesia care standards require appropriate monitoring, initial-phase quantitative oxygenation assessment, and a receiving PACU or equivalent unless the responsible anesthesiologist specifically orders otherwise.

For cranial SRS, the AANS article describes outpatient care for most patients, with possible observation or overnight stay and follow-up. It does not provide an anesthesia-specific discharge scoring protocol.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The most procedure-specific anesthesia source is a narrative textbook chapter covering several radiation procedures. It is not a guideline, has no stated systematic-review methods, and focuses substantially on children; its practice descriptions should not be treated as adult-specific standards.

The AANS patient-education article supports procedural details of cranial SRS but explicitly is not an anesthesia reference and supplies no anesthesia protocol. ASA sources provide general monitoring and postanesthesia-care standards, not a radiation-specific workflow.

Adult, modality-specific anesthetic approaches for SBRT and proton therapy, and a radiation-vault workflow that reconciles room evacuation with anesthesia personnel-presence standards, are not established by the supplied evidence.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For scheduled cesarean delivery, neuraxial anesthesia is generally preferred; select spinal, epidural, or combined techniques according to the clinical situation, patient preference, and anesthesiologist judgment.
Prioritize uterine displacement and prevention or prompt treatment of neuraxial hypotension; vasopressors are central, with fluid use individualized rather than tied to a fixed preload.

Before incision, assess and document neuraxial block adequacy. Treat reported pain as clinically significant: pause when feasible, address the cause, and escalate support if regional supplementation is inadequate.

Anticipate uterine atony and bleeding, and plan recovery around ongoing assessment, neuraxial-opioid effects where used, and multimodal analgesia. Use institutional pathways for hemorrhage and postanesthesia care.

sources.label: Practice Guidelines for Obstetric Anesthesia: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Obstetric Anesthesia and the Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology
Statement on Pain During Cesarean Delivery
Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology: Consensus Statement and Recommendations for Enhanced Recovery After Cesarean
Statement on the Use of Adjuvant Medications and Management of Intraoperative Pain During Cesarean Delivery

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Cesarean delivery is delivery of the fetus through uterine incision. For an elective case, neuraxial anesthesia is generally preferred; general anesthesia remains an individualized alternative when clinical circumstances warrant it.

Spinal, epidural, and combined spinal-epidural techniques are among the neuraxial approaches described. An indwelling epidural may be considered for urgent delivery; these sources do not establish a single technique for every patient.

sources.label: Practice Guidelines for Obstetric Anesthesia: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Obstetric Anesthesia and the Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology
Statement on Pain During Cesarean Delivery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Conduct a focused maternal, obstetric, and anesthetic history and examination, including airway, heart, lungs, baseline blood pressure, and the back when neuraxial anesthesia is planned. Discuss significant risk factors with the obstetric team.

Assess bleeding history and individualize platelet testing and neuraxial eligibility to the clinical context; a routine platelet count is not necessary in a healthy parturient. For thrombocytopenia, weigh bleeding concerns and competing general-anesthesia risks rather than applying a cutoff from this reference.

Review fasting and aspiration risk, including airway difficulty and relevant comorbidity. Consider timely aspiration prophylaxis before cesarean delivery; the provided sources do not establish that prophylaxis eliminates aspiration risk.
Use maternal history, anticipated hemorrhagic risk, and institutional policy to decide on type-and-screen or crossmatch; routine crossmatch is not required for healthy, uncomplicated parturients.

sources.label: Practice Guidelines for Obstetric Anesthesia: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Obstetric Anesthesia and the Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology
The Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology Interdisciplinary Consensus Statement on Neuraxial Procedures in Obstetric Patients With Thrombocytopenia

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Maintain uterine displacement, usually to the left, until delivery. Ensure the labor-and-delivery operating suite has resources and support personnel comparable to a main operating suite.
Establish and maintain IV access before neuraxial anesthesia or general anesthesia. The guideline does not require a fixed fluid volume before neuraxial initiation.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring and maintain qualified anesthesia personnel throughout anesthesia. Use fetal monitoring in accordance with the clinical setting and local obstetric practice; the supplied cesarean guideline does not specify a universal monitoring timeline.

sources.label: Practice Guidelines for Obstetric Anesthesia: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Obstetric Anesthesia and the Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring
Guidelines for Neuraxial Analgesia or Anesthesia in Obstetrics

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Neuraxial anesthesia is preferred for most cesarean deliveries, but prepare for possible conversion to general anesthesia. Make airway equipment, suction, and skilled assistance available; the obstetric suite should support management of failed intubation and respiratory complications.

If general anesthesia is required, select and conduct the airway approach according to urgency, aspiration risk, airway assessment, and available expertise. The supplied sources do not provide a complete patient-specific airway or ventilation protocol.

sources.label: Practice Guidelines for Obstetric Anesthesia: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Obstetric Anesthesia and the Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology
Statement on Pain During Cesarean Delivery

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Check and document neuraxial block level before incision. If the patient reports pain, consider appropriate neuraxial or systemic supplementation; when feasible, pause surgery until comfort is restored.

Spinal hypotension is a central physiologic concern. Maintain blood pressure near baseline using an individualized prophylactic vasopressor strategy; fluid preload or coload may be used, but should not delay spinal anesthesia for a fixed volume.

Use the lowest effective uterotonic dose that achieves adequate uterine tone. Avoid large, rapidly administered oxytocin boluses; dosing and administration should follow applicable specialty guidance and institutional practice.

Prevent intraoperative nausea and vomiting through hypotension prevention and appropriate antiemetic prophylaxis; coordinate with the surgical team on uterine exteriorization, for which evidence is not definitive.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For inadequate neuraxial anesthesia, assess pain and block adequacy, communicate with the patient and surgical team, and consider neuraxial or systemic adjuvants. Convert to general anesthesia when pain remains refractory to appropriate supplementation.

Remain alert to hypotension and respiratory compromise after neuraxial drug administration; rapid recognition and treatment are important. The cited guideline identifies these hazards but does not supply a complete complication-management algorithm.

For uterine atony or hemorrhage, escalate through the institution’s obstetric hemorrhage pathway and coordinate promptly with the obstetric team; no universal resuscitation algorithm is established here.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Use IV fluid preload or coload as clinically appropriate, alongside vasopressor management of spinal hypotension. Do not delay neuraxial anesthesia to deliver a predetermined volume.

Assess hemorrhage risk before surgery and make blood-product preparation proportionate to maternal history, placental findings, anticipated bleeding, and local policy. The sources do not support a universal crossmatch or fluid total.

Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology: Consensus Statement and Recommendations for Enhanced Recovery After Cesarean

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia, consider neuraxial opioid analgesia and continue multimodal nonopioid analgesia where appropriate. Individualize opioid rescue and use the applicable specialty pathway for neuraxial-opioid monitoring.

Use antiemetic prophylaxis with different mechanisms and address hypotension as a contributor to intraoperative nausea and vomiting. Specific drug selection should follow patient factors and institutional guidance.
Manage pain and anxiety as distinct problems; anxiolytics or hypnotics alone are not a substitute for treating surgical pain.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: After general anesthesia, extubation should occur when the patient is fully awake and airway reflexes are maintained. This is general-anesthesia review guidance, not a cesarean-specific extubation algorithm.

Provide postanesthesia care after cesarean neuraxial or general anesthesia, with evaluation appropriate to the patient’s condition. Assess motor-block recovery; persistent motor blockade warrants anesthesia-provider evaluation under the obstetric neuraxial guideline.
Recovery priorities include assessment for bleeding, uterine tone, pain, nausea, and neuraxial-opioid effects, alongside maternal-infant and breastfeeding support as circumstances permit.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: This draft draws on obstetric anesthesia guidance, SOAP consensus recommendations, ASA standards, and reviews. The SOAP ERAC authors note that obstetric-specific high-quality evidence is limited and some recommendations rely on expert consensus or extrapolation.

The ASA pain statements identify blank best-practice sections in the supplied material. Their background supports recognition, communication, and consideration of supplementation, but does not provide a complete dosing or treatment algorithm.
The general-anesthesia article is a review, not a comprehensive perioperative protocol; the basic anesthetic monitoring standards are not procedure-specific.
Case-specific targets for several workflow details are not established in the available sources; use individualized clinical judgment and applicable institutional protocols.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: An epidural blood patch (EBP) places autologous blood in the epidural space to seal a dural tear and may also raise intracranial pressure through mass effect.

For PDPH, consider EBP when headache is moderate to severe and refractory to conservative treatment; assess severity, treatment response, incapacitation, and the patient’s activities rather than treating every dural puncture.
Prioritize asepsis, appropriate level selection and localization, and patient tolerance; stop injection for intolerable pain or a neurologic deficit.

Recovery priorities include supine positioning after the patch, assessment for symptom response and neurologic change, and recognition that a changed, recumbency-worsened headache may represent rebound intracranial hypertension.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: EBP is a therapeutic neuraxial procedure using the patient’s own blood to seal a CSF leak; the review describes both epidural plug formation and pressure-related effects.

For PDPH, the review describes selecting the same interspace as the dural tear or one space below. It recommends fluoroscopic localization and contrast confirmation; these are review recommendations, not a universally established technique for every setting.
The review describes prone positioning. It does not establish lateral or sitting positioning as equivalent approaches.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Confirm that the clinical problem is a headache attributed to low CSF pressure and that conservative treatment has not provided adequate relief. The review describes an initial conservative-treatment period, but the decision to patch remains individualized.
Screen for contraindications, particularly febrile illness, bacteremia or septicemia, infection at the puncture site, coagulation disorder, and patient refusal.

Do not treat prophylactic patching after accidental dural puncture as routine: the review finds the evidence insufficient. It also notes uncertainty around platelet thresholds; its cited studies and author recommendation do not establish one universally supported cutoff.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Maintain strict asepsis for both blood collection and epidural access. The review describes an experienced operator and fluoroscopic guidance, but does not define a universal room configuration.
The review describes prone positioning for EBP. It does not specify a routine monitoring set, vascular-access requirement, or monitoring frequency for an EBP performed without anesthesia care.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The review presents EBP as a procedure, not a general anesthetic technique, and provides no airway or ventilation protocol. Do not infer a need for airway instrumentation, paralysis, or general anesthesia from these sources.
The available EBP review does not establish a sedation regimen or define when sedation is appropriate; any anesthetic care requires a separate clinical assessment and applicable standards.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Use careful epidural localization and assess injectate spread; the review describes fluoroscopy and contrast for confirming needle-tip location and detecting possible intravascular injection.
Inject slowly and use patient-reported symptoms as a procedural safety signal. Stop for intolerable pain or neurologic deficit rather than pursuing a predetermined volume.
Avoid early therapeutic EBP before recovery from neuraxial blockade; the review cautions that an epidural pressure surge could cause unpredictable cephalad spread of local anesthetic.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Important procedural hazards include infection, nerve-root irritation, seizure associated with rare intravascular injection, and rare cauda equina syndrome. Avoid injecting blood in systemic infection.
Backache is common after EBP and is usually transient; assess severity and associated neurologic symptoms rather than assuming all post-procedure pain is benign.

A new headache that is worse lying down or changes location after apparent leak closure raises concern for rebound intracranial hypertension; the review describes medical treatments but does not provide a patient-specific diagnostic or treatment algorithm.
If an initial patch has no clinical benefit, the review advises waiting before repeat patching and reconsidering the diagnosis when repeat procedures are needed.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The procedure uses the patient’s autologous blood. The review does not establish routine prophylactic fluid supplementation as PDPH treatment; do not convert hydration advice into a mandatory fluid regimen.
No EBP-specific blood-loss, transfusion, or perfusion-management protocol is supplied in the procedure review.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Before EBP, conservative measures described for low-CSF-pressure headache include caffeine and analgesics; the review does not establish these as procedural analgesia or as substitutes for evaluation of persistent or severe symptoms.

The review does not provide a specific PONV-prevention regimen for EBP. Analgesic and anxiolytic selection should not be inferred from medication lists discussed for other low-CSF-pressure headache contexts.

After the procedure, the review advises avoiding straining, Valsalva, intense exercise, twisting, and bending for a period intended to reduce clot dislodgement and recurrence; individualize instructions to the clinical context.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Anesthetic emergence is not described for EBP. If anesthesia care is provided, apply the relevant postanesthesia standards rather than treating this review as a recovery protocol.
The review recommends supine positioning after EBP and monitoring for neurologic symptoms, headache response, and transient back pain. It does not set a formal observation or discharge protocol.

sources.label: Recent update on epidural blood patch

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal EBP source is a narrative review of current literature, not a guideline or trial. Its reported outcomes vary across populations and techniques; numerical success estimates should not be treated as a guaranteed result.
A second supplied PDPH review is explicitly retracted and is excluded as a basis for clinical recommendations in this draft.

The primary review itself identifies insufficient evidence for prophylactic EBP and a need for a qualified trial; practice details should therefore be interpreted within the review’s scope and local expertise.
Available sources do not establish a complete EBP-specific protocol for atypical postpartum headache evaluation, sedation, routine monitoring, or recovery disposition.
