sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Recognize surgical complications described in the guideline, including anterior or posterior capsule rupture, dropped nucleus, zonular dialysis, iris or IOL damage, and suprachoroidal hemorrhage. The executive summary does not provide an anesthesia-specific management algorithm.

Ophthalmic blocks carry technique-specific risks. Sharp-needle blocks can cause rare serious injury, while sub-Tenon’s block avoids a sharp instrument but still has reported complications; select and perform a block only with appropriate expertise.

With suspected local-anesthetic toxicity or central spread after a block, recognize that severe neurologic and cardiovascular manifestations are possible and escalate for airway and cardiovascular support. The cited review describes the hazard but does not establish a cataract-specific response protocol.

bullets: The sources describe cataract surgery as minimally stressful with minimal blood loss, but give no cataract-specific fluid regimen or bleeding-management protocol. Individualize fluid and access decisions to patient factors and the anesthetic actually planned.

For locoregional blocks, the review identifies orbital or retrobulbar hemorrhage as a possible serious complication. It does not provide a general cataract-surgery transfusion, blood-loss, or perfusion target.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Topical anesthesia is commonly used; intracameral lidocaine may be added to reduce intraoperative pain. The guideline does not provide a dose or a broader systemic analgesic regimen.

The guideline recommends an intracameral cefuroxime injection at the end of surgery to reduce postoperative endophthalmitis, within its stated European regulatory context. This is a surgical infection-prevention recommendation, not an anesthetic analgesic regimen.

The review describes less postoperative nausea and vomiting with total intravenous anesthesia than with some alternatives, but this does not justify selecting TIVA routinely for cataract surgery. sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: For GA, avoid coughing, straining, and retching where possible because these can increase IOP. The review describes this as an emergence concern but does not prescribe a specific emergence regimen.

After anesthesia, use postanesthesia care appropriate to the patient’s condition. The ASA standard calls for continual evaluation, attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, with quantitative oxygenation assessment during the initial recovery phase.

Provide eye-drop and eye-protection instructions, including avoiding eye rubbing. Advise patients to seek assessment for decreased vision after improvement, new flashes or floaters, increased pain, or redness.

bullets: The cataract guideline is an executive summary of selected recommendations, not an anesthesia reference. It explicitly leaves airway management, positioning, monitoring requirements, physiologic targets, and anesthesia-specific postoperative monitoring unspecified.

The ophthalmic anesthesia review covers adults and multiple eye procedures, but some technique advice is preference-based or theoretical, and practice varies internationally. Apply its general airway and block discussion in scope rather than treating it as a cataract-specific standard.
This 2012 regional-anaesthesia review does not state a formal search method or evidence-grading approach; interpret its technique and risk statements in that context.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Open-globe repair closes a full-thickness ocular wound. General anesthesia is preferred for repair when possible, but the supplied procedure sources do not establish a specific anesthetic or airway regimen.

The immediate ocular hazard is expulsion of intraocular contents. Minimize pressure on the eye and avoid manipulating prolapsed contents; surgical choices such as anterior-chamber reformation also have pressure and wound-leak trade-offs.

Stillness and avoidance of coughing, straining, or retching are important considerations: a general ophthalmic anesthesia review links these events at emergence with increased intraocular pressure, but does not define an open-globe-specific airway strategy.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia observation and attention to nausea or vomiting that could provoke pressure increases. The provided sources do not specify an open-globe-specific emergence, analgesia, or PONV regimen.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Open-globe injury (OGI) repair addresses a full-thickness corneal or scleral wound. The surgical review covers corneal-wound closure, anterior-chamber reformation, and scleral exploration and visualization.

For corneal wounds, the surgeon may reform the anterior chamber with filtered air or ophthalmic viscosurgical device (OVD). Air may deflate through a wound; OVD can maintain the chamber but may elevate IOP and obscure wound edges.
Scleral exploration may require conjunctival peritomy; posterior exploration and extraocular-muscle handling are surgical considerations rather than a basis for a universal anesthetic technique.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess overall fitness for general anesthesia and obtain consent when circumstances permit. Ocular or orbital trauma may accompany head, neck, or other bodily injuries; life-threatening injuries take priority.
A suspected open globe warrants a rigid shield. Avoid preoperative retrobulbar block in an open globe; eye movement assessment may also be limited for posterior wounds when movement risks expulsion.
Consider pre- and intraoperative antibiotics as part of the surgical infection-prevention plan. The supplied sources do not establish a single regimen for every OGI.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Prepare an operating microscope and ophthalmic instruments appropriate to the anticipated wound and trauma burden; the surgical reference describes a typical institutional setup and notes that equipment should be customized.

For general anesthesia, follow basic anesthetic monitoring standards: continually evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; use ECG, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment, and quantitative oxygenation monitoring as specified by the standard.
The procedure sources do not specify patient or operating-table positioning; do not infer a position from this evidence.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is preferred for open-globe repair when possible, but the procedure-specific sources do not state an airway device or intubation technique. Select airway management based on the clinical context rather than treating a generic ophthalmic airway observation as an OGI rule.

The general ophthalmic review associates supraglottic devices with fewer emergence problems than laryngoscopy and intubation, but this is not an open-globe-specific recommendation and does not resolve the device choice for this operation.

If neuromuscular blockade is used, quantitative monitoring and confirmation of adequate recovery before extubation are supported by the ASA guideline overview; these recommendations do not make paralysis obligatory for every case.

bullets: Minimize external pressure on the injured eye and avoid manipulating prolapsed vitreous or other intraocular contents, which may be adherent to surrounding structures.
Coordinate with the surgeon during extraocular-muscle manipulation. The oculocardiac reflex can cause bradycardia, pain, and nausea; communicate promptly if it occurs.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Retinal-detachment repair may use vitrectomy, scleral buckling, or other vitreoretinal approaches. Adult vitrectomy is often performed with monitored anesthesia and a regional block; general anesthesia is selected when cooperation or procedural factors require it.
If intraocular gas is present, nitrous oxide must not be administered: diffusion into the gas can rapidly raise intraocular pressure and cause ocular morbidity.
Globe manipulation can provoke the oculocardiac reflex, including bradycardia and hypotension. Recognize a change promptly and communicate with the surgeon.

Recovery priorities include avoiding coughing, straining, and retching that can increase intraocular pressure, assessing for pressure elevation, and following the surgeon-prescribed postoperative position.

bullets: Retinal-detachment surgery encompasses different surgical approaches, including pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) and scleral buckling. The operation and tamponade choice are surgical decisions; the supplied sources do not establish a single approach for this combined-procedure label.

For adult vitrectomy, monitored anesthesia with a retrobulbar block is a common approach in the procedure-specific review; general anesthesia is used selectively, including when the patient cannot cooperate. bullets: Establish whether the patient can maintain the anticipated postoperative position. Neck, back, rheumatological, or cardiopulmonary limitations may affect the feasibility of face-down or specified head-tilt positioning.

Discuss anticipated air travel and high-altitude exposure when the surgical team is choosing tamponade. Patients with intraocular gas should avoid air travel and other activities involving atmospheric-pressure shifts while gas remains.

Assess medical comorbidity and ability to cooperate, and select preoperative testing based on clinical indication rather than routine testing for all patients. Diabetes is relevant to perioperative assessment, but the sources do not establish a retinal-surgery-specific glucose target.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult strabismus surgery aims to realign the eyes by weakening, strengthening, or repositioning extraocular muscles. General anaesthesia is commonly used; selected cooperative adults may have topical or other limited techniques for suitable procedures.

Key intraoperative concerns are the oculocardiac reflex (OCR) during muscle traction and airway/ventilation factors that can increase its likelihood. Coordinate with the surgeon; stop traction if the reflex occurs and escalate treatment if it persists or is severe.

PONV is a relevant adult recovery issue, but the available evidence does not support describing it as uniformly the highest-risk procedure or prescribing one regimen for every adult. Use individualized prophylaxis and opioid-sparing analgesia.

Plan recovery around assessment of pain, nausea/vomiting, and alignment-related symptoms such as diplopia; diplopia is common early and often improves. Apply standard postanaesthesia monitoring and handoff requirements.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Surgery changes extraocular muscle force or position: recession weakens, resection strengthens, and transposition changes muscle position. Procedure complexity, laterality, prior surgery, and whether adjustable sutures are planned inform anaesthetic selection.

General anaesthesia is suitable across ages and commonly used, particularly for complex, repeated, or bilateral surgery. Topical anaesthesia is an option only for selected cooperative adults and suitable procedures; muscle traction and detachment can be uncomfortable.

Adjustable-suture cases may involve a later awake alignment assessment and adjustment under topical anaesthesia after anaesthetic effects resolve. Avoid assuming that a long-acting block is neutral for this pathway, as it may delay the second stage.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Clarify adult-onset symptoms and assess for underlying causes. The anaesthesia review specifically identifies thyroid function, bleeding disorders, and anticoagulant use as areas for assessment; thyroid eye disease should be stable and the patient euthyroid before surgery.

Review prior strabismus or other ocular surgery, relevant comorbidity, patient cooperation, and the planned technique. These factors may affect suitability for topical/regional techniques and the potential for difficult access or block spread.

Do not treat strabismus itself as an established malignant-hyperthermia risk factor or infer that volatile anaesthesia must be avoided. The review reports no association and describes volatile agents as commonly used in children; adult-specific comparative MH evidence is not established here.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use standard anaesthesia monitoring appropriate to the technique. During anaesthesia, ECG is continuously displayed and blood pressure and heart rate are determined and evaluated at least every five minutes; use quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

For general anaesthesia, follow standard monitoring requirements for ventilation and airway-device placement, including expired carbon-dioxide monitoring. Keep the patient and surgical field observable as required by the selected approach.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Either a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) or endotracheal tube may be used for general anaesthesia. If LMA patency is in doubt, address the airway before surgery begins; mid-case exchange may contaminate the surgical field.

The review favours assisted or controlled ventilation over spontaneous breathing because hypercarbia can increase OCR risk. Maintain attention to oxygenation and ventilation and avoid factors that promote hypercarbia or hypoxaemia.

When neuromuscular blockade is used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery to a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply as a requirement to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: OCR is triggered by pressure on the globe or traction on extraocular muscles and may present as bradycardia or arrhythmia. Adult reported incidence in the review is lower than in children, but the reflex remains clinically relevant.

Coordinate muscle traction with the surgeon. If OCR occurs, ask for immediate release of traction; this often restores rhythm. If it persists or recurs, anticholinergic treatment may be considered, with escalation guided by the clinical state.

OCR generally diminishes with repeated stimulation, but do not rely on this to prevent an event. The review reports that acute traction is more reflexogenic than gradual traction and that opioid and dexmedetomidine use can potentiate OCR.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For marked bradycardia, arrhythmia, or failure to recover promptly after traction stops, communicate with the surgeon and escalate anaesthetic management. The available sources describe possible severe rhythm disturbances but do not establish a single treatment sequence for every event.

Recognize that globe perforation, slipped or lost muscle, retinal detachment, and infection are reported surgical complications. Suspected globe injury or muscle loss requires prompt communication with the ophthalmic surgeon and reassessment of the anaesthetic approach if further exploration or repair is needed.
After surgery, diplopia is common in the first week and often resolves. Persistent or concerning visual symptoms warrant ophthalmic assessment rather than an assumption that symptoms are expected.

bullets: The review describes vision-threatening bleeding risk as low, including with continued antithrombotic treatment, but recommends preoperative assessment of bleeding disorders and anticoagulant use. Orbital fat manipulation can cause postoperative bleeding and inflammation; the source does not quantify blood loss or provide a fluid or blood-loss protocol.

bullets: Use an individualized multimodal, opioid-sparing approach. The review supports paracetamol, intravenous NSAIDs, topical local anaesthetic, and limited opioid use; supplementary regional block is a team decision, not a required component.
The review reports adult PONV at 30%, independent of general anaesthetic technique, and notes that ondansetron plus dexamethasone is often given prophylactically to adults.

Inferior oblique surgery tends to be more uncomfortable and often induces more postoperative nausea. Short-acting narcotics in the recovery room are a possible cause of nausea and vomiting in some patients.

Provide postanaesthesia care with continual assessment appropriate to the patient's condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. The initial recovery phase requires quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

bullets: ACL reconstruction is usually arthroscopic and often outpatient; the available evidence describes general, regional, and combined anesthetic approaches but does not establish one as routine for every patient.
Postoperative pain is a major recovery concern. Graft-related pain may differ, and available comparisons do not establish a single analgesic regimen as superior.

Regional analgesia can be part of a multimodal plan. Adductor canal and femoral blocks have broadly similar pain outcomes in most cited comparisons, but femoral block is associated with greater quadriceps weakness.

Prioritize functional recovery and safe mobilization while monitoring for pain, nausea, and residual motor impairment; PACU observation and discharge decisions should follow applicable local standards.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For adults with an unstable ankle mortise and suitable soft tissues, ankle ORIF restores alignment and stability; fixation is fracture-specific and may involve plates, screws, or syndesmotic stabilization.

Neuraxial techniques may provide surgical anesthesia for foot/ankle surgery. Peripheral nerve blocks may be used for postoperative analgesia or as adjuncts to general or neuraxial anesthesia; a popliteal sciatic block is commonly combined with a saphenous block for foot/ankle surgery. Choose an approach based on patient and procedural factors; the supplied review does not establish a preferred approach for ankle ORIF.

The dominant case-specific concerns are soft-tissue condition and wound healing, neurovascular integrity, and comorbidities such as diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and neuropathy. Timing should reflect the soft-tissue envelope rather than a fixed interval.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia monitoring and reassessment of the operated foot’s neurovascular status, swelling, and splint. Regional analgesia may support postoperative pain control, but motor block and safe mobility require attention.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: ORIF is generally selected for an unstable mortise in a patient fit for surgery when the soft tissues are favorable. The operative aim is anatomical restoration with stable fixation; fracture pattern determines the construct.

Fixation options described include plates and screws for fibular fractures, fracture-specific medial or posterior malleolar fixation, and screws or tightropes for syndesmotic diastasis. These are surgical options, not a universal construct.

Intraoperative imaging is used to assess alignment and syndesmotic stability; the described options include the Hook (Cotton) test and external-rotation stress views. Posterior malleolar anatomy may require preoperative CT for operative planning.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess fracture pattern, mortise stability, syndesmotic involvement, skin and swelling, and relevant comorbidities. Diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and neuropathy can adversely affect healing; assess vascular status and baseline neurologic function.

Fracture blisters and substantial swelling signal soft-tissue risk. Definitive fixation may be delayed while swelling subsides; the evidence supports judging timing by tissue condition, not applying a fixed wait.

Complete individualized VTE risk assessment, including prior DVT, immobilization or nonweight bearing, and other relevant patient risk factors; sources do not support a universal prophylaxis regimen for all ankle-fracture patients.

Recognize possible local-anesthetic systemic toxicity from early neurologic symptoms or evolving cardiac instability and escalate promptly to appropriate emergency support. The supplied review discusses lipid-emulsion rescue, but its dosing details are intentionally not reproduced here.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Hip fracture repair may use general or neuraxial anesthesia; select the approach for the patient, fracture, comorbidities, and expected procedure rather than treating spinal anesthesia as universally superior.

Frail older adults are common in this population. Prioritize assessment of cardiovascular, respiratory, neurologic, volume, and cognitive status, and weigh the consequences of hypotension and respiratory compromise.

Neuraxial sympathectomy can cause hypotension and bradycardia; general anesthesia can worsen atelectasis and hypoxia risk. Maintain perfusion and oxygenation while anticipating technique-specific hazards, including bone cement implantation syndrome with cemented hemiarthroplasty.

Recovery priorities include adequate analgesia, early ambulation when feasible, and surveillance for respiratory or cardiovascular deterioration and altered cognition. Regional analgesia may support pain control and mobilization; it does not eliminate the need for individualized recovery monitoring.

bullets: Assess associated injuries and decision-making capacity, and obtain informed consent from the patient or an appropriate surrogate. Review advance directives as relevant to the anesthetic and perioperative plan.

Review antithrombotic medications, coagulation status, and renal function when considering neuraxial or peripheral regional techniques. Apply current agent- and patient-specific guidance; the available sources do not justify a universal interruption schedule.

bullets: Neuraxial sympathetic blockade can reduce arterial and venous tone, lowering preload and causing hypotension or bradycardia. Maintain attention to perfusion and respond to evolving hemodynamics using the clinical context; no case-specific target is established here.

For cemented hemiarthroplasty, anticipate possible bone cement implantation syndrome around cement insertion. Acute hypotension, hypoxemia, or cardiac instability warrant prompt recognition and escalation; the supplied review describes this as a potentially serious cement-related event.

Long-bone fracture and instrumentation can be associated with fat embolism syndrome. Be alert to respiratory distress, altered mental status, and petechial rash, including delayed postoperative presentation.

Neuraxial hematoma is rare but potentially devastating, and anticoagulation is an important risk factor. New neurologic concerns after neuraxial procedures require urgent evaluation; consult applicable specialty guidance.

For a regional technique, consider airway rescue feasibility, patient cooperation, expected duration, and the intended number of levels. The lumbar review describes these as selection considerations for elective lumbar surgery, not as criteria for general anesthesia.

bullets: For minor spine procedures classified by the review as up to two-level decompression without instrumentation, it describes an 18–20G IV and an arterial line only when medically indicated. Do not generalize access recommendations for major or complex operations to every decompression.

When prone, use team communication, appropriate equipment, padding, and positioning checks; reassess positioning as the case proceeds. The review describes risks ranging from soft-tissue injury to visual loss and peripheral nerve injury.

bullets: With general anesthesia, plan a secured airway suitable for prone surgery and verify its position after placement. Cervical or upper-thoracic surgery may make airway management challenging, but the supplied sources do not compare specific airway techniques for this operation.

Maintain required ventilation monitoring during general anesthesia, including quantitative expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring from airway placement through extubation or transfer. bullets: Avoid treating deliberate hypotension as a routine blood-conservation measure. The spine review found no adult evidence demonstrating its effectiveness and notes potential organ-ischemia and visual-loss risks; another supplied review discusses pressure support to preserve cord perfusion. Individualize hemodynamic goals to the patient, operation, and neuromonitoring.

For cases using evoked potentials, coordinate anesthetic technique and changes in anesthetic or hemodynamic conditions with the monitoring team. The source favors TIVA for spinal fusion monitoring; this does not establish that TIVA is required for every decompression.

bullets: Position-related visual loss and peripheral nerve injury are recognized hazards of prone spine surgery. Maintain attention to pressure points, head and eye positioning, hemodynamics, anemia, and volume status; the cited review does not provide a laminectomy-specific risk estimate.

Dural tear is recognized in the lumbar anesthesia review. It reports no significant difference in durotomy risk between spinal and general anesthesia in comparative studies, but the supplied evidence does not establish a specific intraoperative response or postoperative protocol.

If a new postoperative neurologic finding is detected, promptly compare it with the documented baseline and communicate with the surgical and anesthesia teams. The supplied sources support baseline documentation and postoperative examination, but do not specify an imaging or reoperation algorithm.

bullets: The supplied sources do not support a fixed fluid total, routine cell salvage, or universal transfusion preparation for laminectomy. TXA and cell salvage are discussed in the broad spine review as blood-conservation options, particularly in larger procedures; the evidence supplied does not establish routine use for a limited decompression or provide a procedure-specific regimen here.

bullets: Multimodal analgesia may combine neuraxial or peripheral nerve blocks with NSAIDs, acetaminophen, gabapentinoids, and patient-controlled analgesia. Bilateral ultrasound-guided erector spinae plane block has been reported to reduce postoperative opioid requirements and improve patient satisfaction in lumbar surgery.

Do not infer that NSAIDs are universally appropriate or inappropriate after decompression from fusion-related evidence. The supplied spine review says selective COX-2 effects were reported while non-union and bleeding concerns remained debatable; it does not resolve drug choice for this individual procedure.

bullets: After general anesthesia, facilitate an early neurologic examination where clinically feasible. Compare motor and sensory findings with the preoperative record; the supplied sources do not establish a specific extubation sequence for lumbar or cervical laminectomy.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm TOF recovery of at least 0.9 before extubation. This applies when blockade is used, not to local-anesthetic or neuraxial cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide postanesthesia care with ongoing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; use quantitative oxygenation assessment during the initial recovery phase. Escalation and discharge decisions remain subject to clinical assessment and facility policy.

bullets: Suspect FES when respiratory distress, altered mental status, or petechiae develop after long-bone injury or instrumentation; hypotension and fever may also occur. Escalate promptly for respiratory or hemodynamic support rather than relying on an unsupported case-specific algorithm.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Toe, ray, and transmetatarsal amputation removes diseased tissue while aiming to preserve functional limb length when possible. The available amputation review does not establish a specific operative or anesthetic approach for these exact levels.

General or regional anesthesia are described options; selection is individualized. A popliteal sciatic block combined with saphenous coverage is described for foot/ankle surgery, but the sources do not establish it as a reliable sole anesthetic for every amputation at these levels.

Healing potential, infection, and perfusion at the chosen level are central concerns. In patients with diabetes, the review emphasizes glycemic control and early antibiotics; it cautions that perfusion measures do not capture all factors relevant to healing.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring and plan recovery around the patient’s condition, pain, wound, and perfusion assessment. The supplied sources do not support a universal glucose target, fluid volume, block recipe, or discharge plan for this operation.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Lumbar discectomy includes different surgical approaches. In an adult observational study of elective microdiscectomy, general anesthesia (GA) involved tracheal intubation and prone positioning; spinal anesthesia was also studied. The evidence does not establish one technique as universal.

Select anesthesia case by case, considering patient preference and cooperation, comorbidities, and surgical complexity. For endoscopic procedures, local anesthesia with or without sedation, epidural anesthesia, and GA are described; these findings should not be assumed to define practice for every discectomy approach.

Prioritize safe positioning and appropriate anesthetic monitoring. Awake feedback may help identify possible nerve irritation during some endoscopic procedures; GA removes that immediate feedback, and the review describes neuromonitoring as a possible aid while noting limited procedure-specific evidence.

Recovery priorities include evaluating pain and the patient's condition after anesthesia, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. When neuromuscular blockers are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

A broad orthopedic review describes multimodal analgesia as combining regional techniques with non-opioid and opioid options. This is general orthopedic context, not a validated discectomy-specific regimen.

In the adult observational study, PONV was associated with submaximal satisfaction, and GA patients reported more throat irritation and mouth dryness. These findings inform counseling and recovery observation but do not establish comparative risk for all discectomy populations.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The adult microdiscectomy study reports patients awakened in the operating room and transferred to PACU with stable vital signs. This is a study protocol, not a universal extubation or emergence requirement.

PACU care should include continual assessment appropriate to the patient's condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; a quantitative oxygenation method is required during the initial recovery phase under the cited standard.

When a neuromuscular blocker has been used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation are recommended by the cited ASA guideline overview. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

After anesthesia, admit the patient to a PACU or equivalent unless the responsible anesthesiologist orders otherwise. Continually evaluate and monitor the patient as appropriate, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, level of consciousness, and temperature; use pulse oximetry during the initial phase of recovery.

bullets: The most procedure-specific anesthesia review concerns full-endoscopic discectomy and cautions that its underlying studies provide limited evidence. Its conclusions should not be generalized without qualification to all open or microscopic discectomy.

The blood-pressure and regional-anesthesia reviews are broad orthopedic sources, not discectomy-specific guidelines. Their general findings are used only with explicit scope limits.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pelvic fracture fixation is a spectrum: provisional external fixation and staged damage-control orthopedics are described for hemodynamically unstable patients; early definitive fixation is described for stable or adequately resuscitated patients.
The dominant immediate physiologic threat is major retroperitoneal hemorrhage with hemodynamic collapse; rapid mechanical stabilization and coordinated hemorrhage control are central priorities.

In unstable polytrauma, damage-control strategy aims to limit physiologic deterioration, including hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy; timing and extent of fixation depend on injury and response to resuscitation.

Recovery priorities include reassessment for ongoing bleeding and associated complications, appropriate postanesthesia monitoring, and coordination of thromboprophylaxis and mobilization when clinically appropriate. The available sources do not establish a routine extubation or ICU pathway for every patient.

sources.label: Advances in Managing Pelvic Fractures in Polytrauma: A Comprehensive Review

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Stabilization may be provisional or definitive. External fixation is described as a rapid means of provisional pelvic stabilization and hemorrhage control in damage-control orthopedics; the choice of fixation is based on the clinical situation and injury pattern.

For stable or adequately resuscitated patients, early total care with definitive fixation is described as an option. The review characterizes this approach, including its timing, for selected patients; it does not establish a universal schedule for an individual case.

Percutaneous fixation and open reduction and internal fixation have different trade-offs in exposure, reduction, and potential complications. The supplied review discusses these comparatively but does not provide a patient-specific selection rule.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Establish current physiologic stability, injury burden, and response to initial resuscitation when framing the damage-control versus definitive-fixation strategy. Lactate clearance and base deficit are identified as markers used to assess perfusion and resuscitation adequacy.

Review available imaging and the clinical trajectory for injury pattern and ongoing hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced CT is described as providing information on these issues; the source does not define an anesthesia-specific imaging or testing protocol.
Maintain a high index of concern for associated urogenital injury as part of the polytrauma assessment. The review reports these injuries but does not set out a screening algorithm.

The sources do not establish a universal preoperative risk score, airway evaluation pathway, or laboratory schedule specific to pelvic fixation; assess and coordinate according to the patient’s injuries and local trauma process.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The provided evidence does not prescribe a pelvic-fixation room layout, vascular-access configuration, or positioning. These depend on the planned approach, imaging needs, and the patient’s condition; the cited review supplies no procedure-specific setup standard.

During anesthesia, maintain continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. ECG is continuously displayed and blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes under the ASA basic monitoring standards.

Additional invasive or advanced monitoring is not established as routine for this procedure by the supplied sources; select it for the clinical context rather than treating it as a universal requirement.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The available pelvic-fracture review does not specify an airway device, intubation technique, or ventilation strategy for fixation. No universal airway approach can be derived from these sources; select a technique for the patient's physiology, injuries, and planned procedure.

For general anesthesia, verify airway-device position clinically and by expired carbon dioxide, and continue quantitative end-tidal carbon-dioxide analysis until extubation or transfer begins, consistent with ASA basic monitoring standards.
The sources do not establish that general anesthesia, neuromuscular blockade, or tracheal intubation is mandatory for every pelvic fracture procedure.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Major pelvic-ring bleeding can arise from the posterior pelvic venous plexus and may cause rapid hemodynamic collapse. Treat deterioration as a potential hemorrhage emergency and coordinate promptly with the surgical and trauma teams for control and stabilization.

In damage-control orthopedics, rapid mechanical stabilization is described as reducing mortality and helping prevent progression of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. The review does not specify an anesthetic sequence or physiologic target for achieving this.
Fixation timing and extent should remain linked to physiologic status and response to resuscitation; instability is not a reason to extrapolate a fixed anesthetic or operative recipe from the review.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Severe retroperitoneal bleeding can cause hemodynamic collapse.

The review identifies hemorrhage, venous thromboembolism, and postoperative infection among early complications. Prophylaxis and mobilization require coordination with bleeding risk, fixation, and the overall injury plan.

Percutaneous techniques may reduce soft-tissue disruption but are associated in the review with risks including malunion, screw malposition, and neurovascular injury. These are procedural hazards for the team to account for, not anesthesia-specific management instructions.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The review describes hemorrhage control and mechanical stabilization as key elements in pelvic trauma, but provides no transfusion ratio, fluid regimen, or blood-product threshold. Do not treat a fixed resuscitation recipe as established by this evidence.
Lactate clearance and base deficit are identified as measures for assessing perfusion and resuscitation adequacy. The source does not define thresholds or a target-directed protocol for their use.
Near-infrared spectroscopy and continuous cardiac-output analysis are mentioned as possible assessment technologies in the review, not as required monitoring or validated pelvic-fixation targets.

bullets: The supplied pelvic-fracture review does not provide a surgical anesthetic analgesia regimen. Analgesic selection should be individualized to injury, coagulation status, and the intended recovery pathway rather than inferred from the review’s discussion of conservative care.

Neuraxial or regional techniques require individualized assessment of bleeding risk and neurologic context. The broad regional-anesthesia review identifies coagulopathy as a concern for neuraxial procedures because bleeding may cause spinal hematoma and neurologic injury.

bullets: No emergence or extubation guidance is stated.

Provide postanesthesia care in a PACU or equivalent area, with continuing assessment appropriate to the patient’s condition, attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, and a documented handoff.
Monitor for hemorrhage and DVT/PE. The review describes mechanical compression and low-molecular-weight heparin as prophylactic measures and says early mobilization can reduce thromboembolic risk.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair addresses partial- or full-thickness tears; the operation and its duration vary with tear size, acuity, associated pathology, and repair complexity.
General anesthesia combined with regional analgesia is a common approach for significant, longer repairs; beach-chair and lateral-decubitus positioning are both used.

Priorities include protecting cerebral perfusion in the beach-chair position, anticipating interscalene-related diaphragmatic impairment, and detecting irrigation-fluid extravasation that may threaten the airway.
Plan recovery around airway reassessment when extravasation is suspected and sustained multimodal analgesia to support rehabilitation; use opioids as rescue rather than the sole analgesic strategy.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Repair may be arthroscopic or open; the procedure-specific guideline recommends an arthroscopic approach whenever possible because it is associated with less postoperative pain.
The operation may involve partial or complete repair, debridement with acromioplasty, or graft-based reconstruction; choices depend on tear characteristics and patient factors.
Significant tears may require longer, more complex surgery. Anticipated duration and complexity should inform the anesthetic technique and analgesia plan.

sources.label: PROSPECT guideline for rotator cuff repair surgery: systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess comorbidities and cardiorespiratory reserve, age, tear acuity and size, associated injuries, anticoagulation, and positioning/analgesia needs. For traumatic tears, assess for other injuries.

Before interscalene block, consider pulmonary reserve and pre-existing diaphragmatic dysfunction because phrenic involvement can impair respiratory function. Discuss alternatives when that risk is clinically important.
Agree on positioning and regional technique with the patient, surgeon, and anesthesiologist after weighing block coverage, duration, adverse effects, and rehabilitation implications.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Beach-chair and lateral-decubitus positions are used. Select with the surgeon and team, plan positioning together, and avoid extreme head rotation in beach-chair positioning.

In beach-chair positioning, anticipate hypotension, bradycardia, and reduced cerebral perfusion; respond promptly to blood-pressure falls while accounting for the pressure gradient between the heart and brain.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring. Arterial pressure monitoring and cerebral oximetry are not established as obligatory for every repair; individualize additional monitoring to patient risk and clinical circumstances.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia with an endotracheal tube is favored in the review when airway access will be limited by positioning; anesthetic technique remains individualized to the patient and operation.
For regional analgesia, interscalene block is a first-choice technique in the procedure-specific guideline, but counsel and assess for hemidiaphragmatic paresis and respiratory symptoms.

Apply standard ventilation monitoring during general anesthesia. Do not assume a regional technique eliminates respiratory risk, particularly where phrenic blockade or fluid-related airway compromise is possible.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Beach-chair positioning can reduce cerebral perfusion and cause hypotension or bradycardia. Maintain vigilance through positioning and surgery; avoid deliberate hypotension as a routine analgesic strategy.

Arthroscopic irrigation creates a specific airway hazard: extravasated fluid may produce neck or mediastinal swelling, airway edema, or tracheal compression. Risk increases with prolonged surgery, poor positioning, high irrigation pressure, and obesity.
Track irrigation fluid used and collected, and follow airway pressure/compliance and neck swelling when extravasation is a concern. Consider a cuff-leak assessment before extubation in that context.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Suspected cerebral hypoperfusion in beach-chair positioning warrants prompt assessment of hemodynamics, head/neck position, and oxygenation, with escalation according to the clinical situation; the available sources do not establish a universal pressure target.

New neck swelling, rising airway pressures, or concern for airway obstruction after substantial irrigation should prompt reassessment before extubation and readiness to manage airway compromise. Do not treat extubation as routine when edema is suspected.
After interscalene block, assess dyspnea in the context of possible hemidiaphragmatic paresis; block selection should account for respiratory reserve.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Arthroscopy uses substantial irrigation; monitor fluid input and collected output because local extravasation and systemic absorption can have clinically important consequences. No fixed irrigation balance or IV fluid total is established here.
Avoid assuming that a specific crystalloid volume or vasopressor regimen applies to every patient. Manage perfusion in light of position, baseline physiology, and observed hemodynamics.
Although blood loss may occur, the supplied procedure-specific material gives no transfusion threshold or repair-specific blood-loss protocol.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use multimodal analgesia unless contraindicated: paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2-specific inhibitor, with opioids reserved for rescue. Individualize agents to patient factors and local practice.

Offer single-shot or continuous interscalene block as first-choice regional analgesia when appropriate; the guideline discussion favors continuous block, while diaphragm-sparing alternatives may be considered when interscalene block is unsuitable.

A single-shot block may wear off with rebound pain; maintain regular non-opioid analgesia through that transition. Intravenous dexamethasone is recommended by the guideline to prolong block analgesia and provide antiemetic effects.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Before extubation, reassess for irrigation-related airway edema when there is neck swelling or other concern; use airway pressure/compliance, neck assessment, and cuff-leak evaluation as relevant to the clinical picture.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm adequate recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this requirement does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide postanesthesia observation appropriate to the patient's condition, including attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; reassess pain and respiratory symptoms.

title: Scoliosis Correction (Posterior Spinal Fusion with Instrumentation) (Adult)

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult posterior spinal fusion with instrumentation is used to correct and stabilize spinal deformity, including adult degenerative deformity; multilevel procedures may involve substantial blood loss.
Prone positioning and the correction itself create risks to spinal neural structures; positioning also affects ventilation, venous return, peripheral nerves, and eyes.

Priorities include documenting baseline neurologic function, maintaining reliable conditions for any planned neuromonitoring, anticipating bleeding, and avoiding hypotension that could threaten spinal cord or other-organ perfusion.

Recovery requires appropriate respiratory and hemodynamic observation and prompt assessment of new neurologic or visual symptoms; the sources do not establish a single extubation or disposition pathway.

Anesthesia Pitfalls and Considerations for Spine Surgery
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Posterior spinal fusion may be performed alone or with other approaches and osteotomies to address adult spinal deformity. The extent of correction and levels treated depend on the deformity and operative plan; do not assume every case includes an osteotomy.
Adult degenerative deformity is within scope. Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis recommendations in the supplied sources cannot establish adult selection criteria or practice.
Surgical complexity matters: longer multilevel constructs, severe deformity, revision surgery, and osteotomies are relevant contexts for increased neurologic or bleeding risk.

sources.label: Neurological complications in adult spinal deformity surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess cardiopulmonary comorbidity, functional capacity, and surgical invasiveness. Severe scoliosis can be associated with restrictive physiology and reduced lung volumes; pulmonary disorders are relevant to perioperative risk.
Record baseline motor and sensory findings for comparison after surgery. Identify pre-existing neurologic deficit and review imaging and deformity features that may affect neural risk.

Review anemia and anticipated blood loss when planning preparation and access. Adult elective thoracolumbar surgery data identify multilevel fusion, osteotomy, age, and low hemoglobin as transfusion predictors; these support individualized preparation, not a universal crossmatch or transfusion threshold.

sources.label: Anesthesia Pitfalls and Considerations for Spine Surgery

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Prone positioning should permit exposure while minimizing abdominal and thoracic compression, pressure injury, and abnormal limb positioning. Consider the effects of prone positioning on venous return, cardiac output, and ventilation, particularly with relevant comorbidity.

Protect eyes from direct pressure and secure eyelids closed; protect peripheral nerves by avoiding excessive arm abduction, neck rotation, elbow pressure, and pressure near the anterior superior iliac spine.

Choose invasive pressure monitoring and vascular access according to expected blood loss, comorbidity, and the need to assess perfusion. If neuromonitoring is planned, coordinate signals with the anesthesia and surgical teams; SSEP and MEP provide complementary information.

sources.label: Anesthesia Pitfalls and Considerations for Spine Surgery

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Plan airway management around the patient's airway, cervical mobility, neurologic findings, and positioning needs. The sources do not establish a single preferred intubation method for all spine patients.

After prone positioning, verify airway-device position and secure the circuit to reduce displacement risk. Unintended extubation is especially consequential because access and reintubation may be difficult while prone.

Maintain ventilation assessment appropriate to general anesthesia and positioning; the supplied basic monitoring standard specifies continual evaluation and expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by the circumstances.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: When evoked-potential monitoring is used, inhaled anesthetics can impair signal quality; propofol with an opioid infusion is described as a typical technique. Keep anesthetic depth consistent to support interpretation rather than treating one technique as universally mandatory.
Neuromuscular blockade affects MEPs and EMG. Coordinate any blocker use and recovery with the monitoring plan; the source allows use for intubation or exposure and notes reversal may be needed.

Correction, implant placement, and osteotomy closure are critical phases. For a signal change, coordinate prompt surgical pause and assessment; consider technical, anesthetic, blood-pressure, and neural causes rather than assuming a single mechanism.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Neurologic injury may arise from correction-related stretch or ischemia, neural compression, or malpositioned instrumentation. A new postoperative deficit needs urgent evaluation because a compressive hematoma is a potentially reversible cause of deterioration.

Visual loss and ocular injury are uncommon but serious concerns in prolonged prone surgery, particularly when combined with blood loss or hypotension. Avoid direct eye pressure and assess promptly if visual symptoms are reported.

Other relevant hazards include peripheral nerve injury, hypothermia in lengthy cases, and airway displacement during positioning or imaging. Monitor and troubleshoot in context; the sources do not provide a single procedure-specific rescue algorithm.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Multilevel deformity surgery can involve major blood loss. Anticipate blood conservation and resuscitation needs from the planned procedure and patient factors; cell salvage is described as useful when predicted blood loss is high.

Antifibrinolytics have evidence supporting use in spine surgery, but the supplied source gives no case-specific dose or universal indication. Individualize use, including consideration of hypercoagulable disorders.

Balance hemostasis against spinal cord, optic nerve, cardiac, and renal perfusion. The sources caution against induced hypotension in spinal cord compression or neurologic deficit; a newer review describes controlled hypotension in spinal surgery, so this is not a universal target and requires case-specific judgment.

Use goal-directed fluid and blood-product decisions based on evolving losses, physiology, and coagulation assessment. Available sources do not specify a universal fluid volume or transfusion threshold for this operation.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Shoulder arthroplasty may be performed with general anesthesia, regional anesthesia, or a combination; interscalene block is a commonly described regional technique, but the choice must reflect patient and procedural factors.

For beach-chair positioning, prioritize cerebral perfusion and recognize that apparently stable routine vital signs may not exclude reduced cerebral oxygenation; available blood-pressure findings are review-level, not a universal target.
Interscalene block can provide substantial analgesia, but phrenic nerve effects and other block complications matter, particularly when pulmonary reserve is limited.

Plan recovery around respiratory assessment, effective analgesia as the block resolves, and appropriate postanesthesia observation; no shoulder-arthroplasty-specific emergence or PACU regimen is established in these sources.

bullets: Shoulder arthroplasty includes total, reverse, hemiarthroplasty, and revision procedures. The supplied sources identify these procedure types but do not provide a surgical approach or implant-selection protocol.

Anesthetic options include regional anesthesia, general anesthesia, or a combination. Interscalene block is described for total shoulder arthroplasty and proximal humeral prosthetic replacement; selection depends on coverage, patient factors, and the planned operation.

bullets: Assess cardiopulmonary reserve, cardiovascular disease, anemia, comorbidity burden, and factors that may increase postoperative medical risk; arrange specialty review or optimization when indicated by the patient’s condition.

Clarify neurologic, pulmonary, and cardiovascular history before considering an upper-extremity block. In particular, assess pulmonary function where phrenic involvement could be consequential; pre-existing diaphragmatic dysfunction is also relevant.

Review antithrombotic therapy, coagulation status, and pre-existing neurologic disease when regional techniques are contemplated. Apply current, relevant specialty guidance to the actual block and medication rather than using a generic interval from this reference.

bullets: Beach-chair positioning is associated with reduced cerebral oxygenation and perfusion in the available review. Positioning protocols, head fixation details, and a universal blood-pressure correction for the arm-to-brain gradient are not specified by these sources.

If beach-chair positioning is used, consider cerebral oximetry as an adjunct and establish a baseline before positioning when feasible. The supplied beach-chair review describes continuous cerebral oximetry and a relative alert threshold; it does not establish NIRS as mandatory for every case.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA basic standards require ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and oxygenation assessment during anesthesia.

For general anesthesia, follow basic monitoring standards for ventilation and confirm airway-device position with clinical assessment and expired carbon dioxide. During moderate or deep sedation, use expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes it.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Avoid hypotension that could compromise cerebral perfusion during beach-chair positioning. One study summarized in a 2025 clinical review suggested cerebral blood flow was maintained above a particular MAP; that finding is not a universal patient-specific target or a procedure guideline.

The beach-chair review describes gradual table elevation and attention to venous return as measures discussed for perfusion management. Their use should be individualized; the shoulder-arthroplasty complication review provides no specific physiologic protocol.

Cerebral desaturation or suspected neurologic compromise warrants prompt assessment of pressure, oxygenation, and head position, with escalation to the anesthesia and surgical team. The source describes these as responses to desaturation, not a complete rescue algorithm.
Routine blood-loss expectations, specific critical surgical phases, and a standard hemodynamic protocol for arthroplasty are not provided in the procedure-specific sources.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Interscalene block can cause hemidiaphragmatic paresis, Horner syndrome, hoarseness, and other complications; respiratory consequences depend on the patient’s reserve. New dyspnea requires clinical assessment rather than automatic attribution to the block.

Other reported block hazards include local-anesthetic systemic toxicity, pneumothorax, venous air embolism, and neurologic injury. Maintain appropriate monitoring and readiness to escalate; the incidence figures in the review are not a shoulder-arthroplasty-specific risk estimate.

Medical complications after shoulder arthroplasty vary across studies and include cardiovascular, genitourinary, respiratory, and thromboembolic events. Risk assessment should account for indication and comorbidity, rather than treating a pooled rate as an individual prediction.

For suspected serious cardiopulmonary or neurologic events, recognize the deterioration, summon appropriate help, and follow applicable institutional emergency pathways; these sources do not establish a shoulder-specific resuscitation algorithm.

sources.label: Anesthesiological Considerations in Shoulder Surgery
Medical complications following shoulder arthroplasty: a review of the evidence

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The supplied arthroplasty review does not provide a typical blood-loss estimate, fluid prescription, transfusion threshold, or case-specific blood-product preparation rule. Individualize these decisions to patient risk, procedure, and observed bleeding.

Transfusion is reported in heterogeneous arthroplasty cohorts, and transfused patients often had greater comorbidity and longer operative times; the review does not establish that transfusion itself causes the associated complications.

For major procedures with substantial blood loss or fluid shifts, the orthopedic blood-pressure review discusses goal-directed fluid therapy. It does not supply a shoulder-arthroplasty-specific fluid volume or mandate that approach for every case.

sources.label: Medical complications following shoulder arthroplasty: a review of the evidence
Perioperative Blood Pressure Optimization to Improve Outcomes in Orthopedic Patients: A Clinical Review

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Interscalene block is a regional analgesic option for shoulder surgery. The review presents multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia as necessary and describes continuous interscalene infusion as its preferred technique for most shoulder-surgery patients, with catheters indicated in almost all open procedures, particularly rotator-cuff repair. These are review conclusions, not a universal protocol.

Single-shot block duration is finite, and pain may increase as it regresses. Ensure a transition plan using appropriate non-opioid and rescue analgesia; the supplied sources do not establish a specific arthroplasty medication regimen or dose.

Consider block alternatives when phrenic nerve effects are undesirable. The review describes suprascapular with or without axillary nerve block as less likely to cause phrenic blockade, while noting that analgesia may be inferior to interscalene block.
No shoulder-arthroplasty-specific PONV prevention regimen is provided in the fetched sources; assess and manage PONV according to the patient and applicable local guidance.

sources.label: Anesthesiological Considerations in Shoulder Surgery
Medical complications following shoulder arthroplasty: a review of the evidence

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: No procedure-specific emergence or extubation approach is supplied. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation follow the cited ASA guideline summary.

Provide postanesthesia care with ongoing assessment appropriate to condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Pulse oximetry is required during the initial phase of recovery under the cited standard, subject to its stated exception and waiver provisions.

Assess respiratory symptoms in the context of the block and the patient’s pulmonary reserve, and provide analgesia as the block regresses. The shoulder-surgery review does not provide a specific PACU observation duration or discharge protocol.
Transport and handoff should preserve monitoring and support appropriate to the patient’s condition, with transfer of the perioperative course to the receiving nurse.

Standards for Postanesthesia Care

Anesthesiological Considerations in Shoulder Surgery

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The shoulder-anesthesia source is a 2012 review, not a guideline or trial, and combines evidence from different shoulder procedures. Its technique and analgesia descriptions should not be treated as validated arthroplasty-specific prescriptions.

The arthroplasty complications review draws on heterogeneous evidence with inconsistent definitions and reporting. Its pooled rates have substantial limitations and should not be used as individualized predictions.
The 2025 blood-pressure article is a clinical review; beach-chair numeric findings and management descriptions rely on cited studies, not a shoulder-arthroplasty-specific trial or society protocol.

The fetched sources do not resolve a case-specific airway device, positioning protocol, blood-loss expectation, or arthroplasty analgesic regimen. This draft is a source-limited reference and is not a complete or approved clinical protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Shoulder arthroscopy may be performed with regional anesthesia, sedation, or general anesthesia; patients may be positioned sitting or lateral. Select the anesthetic and airway approach for the operation, patient, and positioning rather than assuming one standard technique.

Interscalene block is a frequently used shoulder analgesic technique, but its respiratory effect is an important selection risk: phrenic blockade is common and depends on approach and volume. Assess pulmonary reserve and consider alternatives when respiratory impairment would be poorly tolerated.

Beach-chair positioning is associated with reduced cerebral oxygenation and blood flow and neurological complications. The review describes gradual table elevation, pre-emptive vasopressor infusion to stabilize MAP ≥70 mmHg, and continuous cerebral oximetry as a management strategy; this is not a universal MAP target.

Irrigation-fluid extravasation is common during shoulder arthroscopy, particularly in subacromial procedures. Severe cervical edema and airway problems have been reported; airway obstruction may not be recognized in an intubated patient until extubation. Plan for severe pain after block resolution.

Perioperative Blood Pressure Optimization to Improve Outcomes in Orthopedic Patients: A Clinical Review

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Shoulder arthroscopy encompasses varied procedures and surgical stimulation. The anesthetic may range from awake or sedated regional techniques to general anesthesia, with or without regional analgesia; selection should account for the planned procedure and patient factors.

Interscalene block is a common shoulder analgesic approach, but it does not guarantee success or eliminate the possibility of conversion to general anesthesia. Discuss the selected technique, expected sensory or motor effects, and an alternative plan.
Position may be sitting or lateral. The sources do not establish a single position or anesthetic technique as appropriate for every arthroscopic shoulder procedure.

sources.label: Current Concepts in Anaesthesia for Shoulder Surgery
Anesthesiological Considerations in Shoulder Surgery

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess pulmonary function and pre-existing diaphragmatic dysfunction before an upper-extremity block that may affect the phrenic nerve. Consider respiratory reserve when selecting block approach and anesthetic technique.

Explain the potential for dyspnea or other block effects, block failure, and pain as the block resolves; establish how rescue analgesia will be accessed. Avoid presenting phrenic blockade incidence as identical across all block techniques and volumes.

Review neurologic, pulmonary, cardiovascular, hematologic, and medication history as part of regional-anesthesia selection. The choice should be shared and reflect block coverage, duration, comorbidities, and consequences of postoperative motor blockade.

sources.label: Regional anesthesia for orthopedic procedures: What orthopedic surgeons need to know
Current Concepts in Anaesthesia for Shoulder Surgery

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Prepare for the selected sitting or lateral position and ensure monitoring and access remain workable after positioning. The available shoulder reviews do not give a detailed positioning-injury or room-layout protocol.

In beach-chair positioning, recognize that upper-body elevation can impair cerebral oxygenation and blood flow. A clinical review describes gradual table elevation, blood-pressure support, and cerebral oximetry; select monitoring intensity to the patient and clinical context rather than treating an arterial line or NIRS as universally required.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic: continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, with ECG and blood pressure/heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes under the cited ASA standard.

sources.label: Current Concepts in Anaesthesia for Shoulder Surgery
Anesthesiological Considerations in Shoulder Surgery
Perioperative Blood Pressure Optimization to Improve Outcomes in Orthopedic Patients: A Clinical Review

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Do not infer a mandatory endotracheal tube for beach-chair cases or a laryngeal mask for lateral cases from these sources. Airway choice depends on the intended anesthetic, patient, surgical access, and the ability to manage airway complications.

Irrigation-fluid extravasation can produce cervical edema, laryngeal edema, tracheal compression, or airway obstruction. Keep this hazard in mind even when the airway is secured, because swelling may not be apparent until emergence.
When a tracheal tube or laryngeal mask is used, follow standard verification and ventilation monitoring requirements, including expired carbon-dioxide monitoring as specified by the ASA standard.

sources.label: Current Concepts in Anaesthesia for Shoulder Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Treat beach-chair elevation as a cerebral-perfusion risk, particularly in older patients or those with cerebrovascular disease. Avoid hypotension and monitor for cerebral desaturation or neurologic change; the cited review describes interventions including raising MAP, increasing inspired oxygen, or repositioning the head if desaturation occurs.

Expect that interscalene block may impair ipsilateral diaphragmatic function. Respiratory impact varies with technique and volume; monitor clinically and do not assume a low-volume approach will preserve function in every patient with limited reserve.

Watch for fluid tracking beyond the operative space, especially with prolonged procedures, lateral positioning, high pump pressures, or subacromial work. The source reports that the exact incidence of extravasation is unknown and does not define a validated surveillance protocol.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: If neck or chest swelling, respiratory distress, or concern for airway compression develops, recognize possible irrigation-fluid extravasation and escalate airway evaluation and support. Case reports establish a serious hazard, not its routine incidence or a single rescue pathway.

Assess respiratory symptoms after interscalene block in light of expected phrenic involvement, but do not dismiss significant or worsening dyspnea as routine. Pneumothorax is also a recognized, uncommon block complication.

For inadequate block or unexpected neurologic symptoms, reassess block effect and consider alternative analgesia or conversion as clinically indicated. Block-related neurologic injury is uncommon but may be serious; the sources do not define a shoulder-arthroscopy-specific troubleshooting algorithm.

sources.label: Current Concepts in Anaesthesia for Shoulder Surgery
Anesthesiological Considerations in Shoulder Surgery
Regional anesthesia for orthopedic procedures: What orthopedic surgeons need to know

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Do not assume a fixed crystalloid volume or blood-loss strategy for shoulder arthroscopy from the supplied evidence. A broader orthopedic review describes more restrictive intake/output management for less invasive arthroscopy; individualize fluid administration to the patient and clinical course.

Separate intravenous fluid management from arthroscopy irrigation: irrigation can extravasate into tissue and contribute to edema, including airway-threatening edema. The available sources provide no case-specific irrigation volume or pump-pressure target.

In patients receiving sevoflurane in the beach-chair position, one study suggested cerebral blood flow was maintained only when MAP exceeded 70 mmHg. This is a study-specific finding, not a universal target.

Anesthesiological Considerations in Shoulder Surgery
Current Concepts in Anaesthesia for Shoulder Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Regional analgesia can reduce postoperative pain and opioid requirements. Single-shot interscalene block has limited duration, so prepare patients for block regression and ensure a rescue oral analgesia plan is understood.

When phrenic effects are a concern, suprascapular and axillary nerve blocks are described as alternatives, with potentially incomplete joint coverage and evidence that is limited and largely observational. Select alternatives with awareness of coverage and rescue-analgesia needs.

Do not treat intra-articular local-anesthetic infusion as routine: reviews describe concern for post-arthroscopic chondrolysis and advise against such infusions. The evidence about harm from a single injection in humans is less certain than the concern around infusion.

Use an individualized PONV prevention approach; the supplied shoulder-specific sources do not establish a preferred prophylaxis regimen. The review reports nausea differences in some analgesia comparisons, not a universal preventive protocol.

sources.label: Current Concepts in Anaesthesia for Shoulder Surgery

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Before emergence, reassess for tissue swelling and potential airway compromise after substantial irrigation, particularly if the procedure was prolonged or involved subacromial work. Edema may become clinically apparent only at extubation.

Plan postanesthesia observation around the patient’s condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. The ASA standard requires appropriate monitoring and a quantitative oxygenation method during the initial recovery phase.

Provide a clear handoff and ensure the receiving team understands the block, respiratory considerations, and plan for analgesia as the block regresses. Discharge readiness is determined through facility-approved processes and appropriate physician responsibility.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: Shoulder-specific evidence is primarily narrative review and includes studies of differing designs and strength; it is not a unified procedural guideline. Reported techniques and results should not be interpreted as mandatory practice.

The beach-chair recommendations come from a clinical review, not a procedure-specific society standard in the supplied sources. The reported MAP and cerebral-oximetry values should therefore be interpreted in context, not as universal thresholds.

Shoulder-specific sources do not provide a formal airway-management protocol, routine monitoring protocol, or detailed fluid and blood-loss guidance. Local practice and patient-specific assessment remain necessary where the evidence does not establish a case-specific standard.
The supplied ASA documents provide general monitoring and postanesthesia-care standards, not shoulder-specific airway, positioning, or analgesia instructions.
