overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Implantation is a surgical option for erectile dysfunction after conservative treatments fail. Devices are malleable or inflatable; the three-piece inflatable implant is described as the current gold standard. Infrapubic and penoscrotal approaches are used according to surgeon preference and patient anatomy.

The procedural review specifies general anesthesia. Spinal anesthesia is reported in a single case, but the available evidence does not establish it as the preferred or routine technique; the choice requires clinical judgment.

Infection prevention is a dominant priority: infection can present late and may require removal of all prosthesis components. Other important procedural hazards include urethral injury, corporal perforation, sizing-related problems, and erosion.

Recovery priorities include assessment for urinary retention, pain, wound complications, and device-related concerns. The source describes catheter and dressing care and later pump instruction; it does not establish an anesthesia-specific analgesic or emergence protocol.

sources.label: Penile Prosthesis Implantation
Vasovagal Syncope in Penoscrotal Inflatable Penile Prosthesis Implantation Following Spinal Anesthesia

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Implantation is generally considered after less invasive ED therapies have not worked. Other stated indications include Peyronie disease with ED, corporal fibrosis, and selected priapism-related conditions.
Implants may be malleable or inflatable. The three-piece inflatable system comprises corporal cylinders, a fluid reservoir, and a scrotal pump; the source describes it as the current gold standard.

For three-piece implantation, infrapubic and penoscrotal/high scrotal approaches are described. Approach depends on surgeon preference and patient anatomy; prior pelvic surgery may affect reservoir placement.

The operation includes corporal dilation, cylinder measurement and placement, reservoir and pump placement, and device testing. Bladder decompression is specified before reservoir placement; cylinder sizing and positioning are critical to avoid crossover, injury, pain, or erosion.

sources.label: Penile Prosthesis Implantation

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess ED history and prior treatment, relevant surgical history, medication and medical history, and cardiovascular risk. Prior injections or priapism matter because corporal fibrosis may complicate implantation.

Identify active infection, unresolved voiding problems, and serious comorbidities that could make sexual activity dangerous. The source lists these as contraindications; surgical history may also change incision or reservoir planning.

Aim for optimal glucose control; HbA1c above 8.5% is associated with increased postoperative infection. Address smoking cessation early because tobacco use is associated with higher surgical-site infection rates.

Counsel about the permanent nature and goals of implantation, potential infection, erosion and revision, and realistic expectations for penile length. The source states that the procedure does not lengthen the penis and that slight shortening may occur.

sources.label: Penile Prosthesis Implantation

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The surgical description specifies preparation from the umbilicus to the midthigh and sterile draping. It describes Foley catheter placement for bladder drainage, injury-risk reduction, and urethral identification.

Infection-prevention measures described include chlorhexidine-based skin preparation, double gloving with clean undergloves for implant handling, and coated or hydrophilic implants. Antibiotic prophylaxis is described as targeted and weight-based, but optimal regimens remain uncertain.

The procedure source does not state a patient position or monitoring protocol. Apply the relevant basic anesthetic monitoring standards to the chosen anesthetic; these require continuous ECG display and blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes.

sources.label: Penile Prosthesis Implantation
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The procedural chapter specifies general anesthesia but provides no airway device, induction, maintenance, or emergence protocol. These details should not be inferred from the procedure description.

Spinal anesthesia is documented in a single case report, not as comparative evidence establishing routine preference. That report describes a vasovagal event; it does not provide an airway-management protocol.

The available procedure-specific evidence does not establish a need for neuromuscular blockade. If blockade is used, the cited ASA guideline overview recommends quantitative monitoring and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation, measured at the adductor pollicis.

sources.label: Penile Prosthesis Implantation
Vasovagal Syncope in Penoscrotal Inflatable Penile Prosthesis Implantation Following Spinal Anesthesia
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Corporal dilation and cylinder placement are critical phases for sizing and avoiding crossover, urethral injury, perforation, erosion, and pain. The surgical source describes sequential dilation and checks for crossover.
Reservoir placement requires a decompressed bladder. The source describes space of Retzius placement and a submuscular alternative, including after prior pelvic surgery or complicated hernia repair.

For neuraxial cases, remain alert to abrupt bradycardia or hypotension. A single case report describes this during closure; tissue handling and traction were stopped, and the event was treated by the team. It cannot establish incidence or routine prophylaxis.

sources.label: Penile Prosthesis Implantation
Vasovagal Syncope in Penoscrotal Inflatable Penile Prosthesis Implantation Following Spinal Anesthesia

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Urethral injury may be indicated by irrigation around the catheter and out of the meatus. The source advises stopping surgery and describes catheter drainage and injury-specific repair as surgical management.

Infection may present acutely or subtly months to years later. The source describes broad-spectrum antibiotics and complete component removal as common treatment; suspected infection warrants prompt surgical-team assessment.
Improper cylinder sizing can cause poor appearance, pain, or erosion; significant erosion may require explantation. Cranial pump migration can affect function and sensation.
Postoperative urinary retention affects up to 27% of patients. Management typically includes Foley catheterization or clean intermittent self-catheterization.

sources.label: Penile Prosthesis Implantation

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: No procedure-specific systemic fluid regimen, blood-loss estimate, transfusion guidance, or bleeding-management details are provided. Individualize fluid and perfusion management to the patient and operative course; do not infer a fixed total from procedural irrigation or device-filling volumes.
The urologic anesthesia chapter gives general advice to correct hypovolemia and dose drugs according to renal function, but it supplies no penile-prosthesis-specific fluid or perfusion targets.

Anesthesia for Urological Surgery

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: The procedure-specific source provides no anesthesia-specific analgesic regimen. It notes that a short course of narcotic medication may be given postoperatively, without establishing a preferred regimen.
No penile or perineal block, NSAID-based plan, stool-softener requirement, or PONV prophylaxis regimen is established in the supplied procedure-specific evidence.

sources.label: Penile Prosthesis Implantation

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The procedure source provides no emergence protocol. When neuromuscular blockade has been used, follow quantitative monitoring and reversal guidance applicable to the agent and block depth; confirm TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.

After anesthesia, use the appropriate postanesthesia care setting, transfer with an anesthesia-team member who can evaluate and treat the patient, and provide a handoff. During initial recovery, use quantitative oxygenation assessment such as pulse oximetry.

Surgical postoperative care described includes catheter and dressing management, assessment of bladder emptying, and instruction to pull the scrotal pump downward to reduce proximal migration. The source also describes avoiding heavy lifting until follow-up.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The primary procedure source is a StatPearls educational clinical review, not an anesthesia reference; it does not provide an anesthetic protocol or formal evidence grading.

The neuraxial evidence is a single surgical case report and cannot establish comparative safety, routine technique, or prophylaxis. Its reported vasovagal event is relevant as a hazard, not as a management standard.

Basic monitoring and postanesthesia standards apply across anesthetic care, while the neuromuscular-blockade guidance applies only when blockade is used. None supplies a penile-prosthesis-specific airway, fluid, analgesia, or emergence protocol.

Antibiotic prophylaxis remains an area of uncertainty in the procedure review; it reports that further research is needed to identify optimal prophylaxis. Regimen selection should rely on applicable current specialty guidance and local policy.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: PCNL removes renal stones through a percutaneous tract; it is commonly used for large or complex stones, including staghorn calculi. The standard approach described is prone, with either general or regional anesthesia selected for the patient and procedure.

Key anesthetic priorities are maintaining a secure airway and safe ventilation during prone positioning, protecting pressure points and eyes, and recognizing pleural injury, bleeding, fluid absorption, and infection-related deterioration.

GA secures the airway and permits control of ventilation in prone position; regional techniques may improve early postoperative analgesia in selected patients. Neither technique is established as universally preferable.

Recovery priorities include assessing oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; evaluating for bleeding, pleural complications, fluid-related disturbance, and infection; and confirming adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation if a blocker was used.

sources.label: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Current Clinical Opinions and Anesthesiologists Perspective
Standards for Postanesthesia Care
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: PCNL is described as an established minimally invasive option for renal calculi generally larger than 2 cm. The review also lists large renal calculi (>1.5–2 cm), staghorn calculi, and upper-tract calculi not responding to other treatment among its indications.

In standard PCNL, a tract is created from the back into the kidney, enlarged to accept a sheath, and used for nephroscope-guided stone extraction or fragmentation. A nephrostomy tube and urinary drainage catheter are commonly placed after removal.

Prone is the standard position described, but anesthesia choice depends on patient factors, team expertise, preferred operative position, and expected duration and stone burden. The sources support both GA and regional approaches; selection is not a universal rule.

sources.label: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Current Clinical Opinions and Anesthesiologists Perspective
Anesthetic considerations for urologic surgeries

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess stone burden and anatomy, renal function, hydronephrosis, comorbidities, and capacity to tolerate prone positioning. The review describes renal-function confirmation and stabilization of existing comorbidities as part of preparation.

Identify and address active infection before proceeding; infection, positive pelvic-urine or stone cultures, larger stone burden, and multiple punctures are associated with postoperative SIRS or sepsis in the review. This supports vigilance and risk assessment, not a patient-specific antibiotic regimen.

Review bleeding risk, renal reserve, cardiopulmonary status, and prone-position tolerance. The available sources describe these as relevant modifiers but do not establish a universal vascular-access, transfusion-preparation, or positioning-clearance threshold.

sources.label: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Current Clinical Opinions and Anesthesiologists Perspective

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan for prone positioning and fluoroscopic access, with the surgical team coordinating the turn and confirming that ventilation is unhampered after positioning. Secure the airway before the turn and reassess it afterward.

Protect eyes from pressure and pad the ears, elbows, wrists, knees, and ankles; position and support the arms to reduce brachial-plexus stretch. Avoid neck-vein torsion and pressure on breasts where applicable.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the technique. ASA standards require continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; arterial-line placement is not established as routine by the PCNL sources.

sources.label: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Current Clinical Opinions and Anesthesiologists Perspective
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: With GA, a secured airway is an important advantage in prone position, but tube displacement or kinking during the turn is a potentially serious hazard. Secure the tube and reassess position and ventilation after positioning.

GA permits control of tidal volume during percutaneous access to reduce pleural and lung injury risk. Upper-pole or supracostal access increases intrathoracic risk; coordinate with the surgeon and watch for rising airway pressures, changing end-tidal CO₂, or falling oxygen saturation during higher or multiple punctures.

Regional anesthesia, including spinal anesthesia, is described as an alternative in selected cases. The evidence does not support treating endotracheal intubation or GA as mandatory for every PCNL; prolonged or complicated procedures may favor GA according to the review authors.

sources.label: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Current Clinical Opinions and Anesthesiologists Perspective

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Position change and renal puncture are key phases for airway and respiratory reassessment. Upper-pole access can injure pleura or lung; the review describes ventilatory standstill during access as an approach used to facilitate an ideal working-sheath position, not as a universal protocol.

During irrigation and collecting-system manipulation, consider fluid extravasation or absorption if irrigation drainage falls or hemodynamics change. The review identifies electrolyte disturbance and intravascular volume overload as possible consequences.

Maintain awareness of infection-related deterioration during and after decompression of a potentially infected collecting system; the supplied evidence emphasizes early recognition but does not define a PCNL-specific universal trigger or response algorithm.

sources.label: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Current Clinical Opinions and Anesthesiologists Perspective

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Pleural injury may present as hydrothorax, pneumothorax, or hydropneumothorax, particularly with supracostal access. Suspect it with respiratory or oxygenation change; the review describes intraoperative chest imaging and postoperative chest radiography as ways to detect injury.

Bleeding can arise from renal capsule or parenchyma, with risk affected by access and patient factors. A new hemodynamic change or significant bleeding warrants prompt communication with the surgeon and escalation; the sources do not establish a universal transfusion threshold.

Fluid absorption may produce volume overload, electrolyte disturbance, altered mental status, or hemodynamic change. The review advises monitoring electrolytes and blood gases when concerned; suspected pelvic perforation may require stopping surgery and drainage, coordinated with the surgical team.

Fever, SIRS, or sepsis can follow PCNL, with risk associations including stone burden, multiple punctures, and positive pelvic-urine or stone cultures. Recognize deterioration early and escalate for appropriate critical-care assessment; the review's management discussion is not a formal guideline.

sources.label: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Current Clinical Opinions and Anesthesiologists Perspective

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Fluid management must account for both operative losses and potential irrigation-fluid absorption. Reduced drainage, hemodynamic change, or altered mental status should raise concern; the sources do not establish a universal intravenous-fluid total.

The review describes isotonic irrigation, fluoroscopic guidance, and continuous or open irrigation as approaches to minimize collecting-system injury. It also describes restricting IV fluids and considering diuretics when overload occurs under GA; these are source-reported considerations, not a patient-specific prescription.

Renal bleeding can be substantial because of hilar-vessel proximity and limited parenchymal tamponade. Assess readiness for hemorrhage management in light of stone, access, and patient factors; no universal blood-ordering or transfusion threshold is supplied.

sources.label: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Current Clinical Opinions and Anesthesiologists Perspective

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Regional anesthesia may reduce early postoperative pain and systemic analgesic requirements compared with GA in the cited studies, but the observed advantage is technique- and study-dependent and does not establish a required anesthetic or postoperative regimen.

PONV was more frequent with GA than regional anesthesia in one randomized comparison. The supplied sources do not specify a PCNL-specific antiemetic or analgesic protocol; individualize care to the patient and procedure.

sources.label: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy: Current Clinical Opinions and Anesthesiologists Perspective
Comparison of percutaneous nephrolithotomy under epidural anesthesia versus general anesthesia: A randomized prospective study

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The PCNL review does not supply a specific emergence or extubation protocol. After anesthesia, evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; PACU or equivalent postanesthesia care is required by the cited ASA standards.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, quantitative monitoring is recommended, with TOF ratio at least 0.9 confirmed before extubation. This recommendation applies when NMB has been used, not to regional or local anesthesia without blockade.

In recovery, assess for pleural injury, bleeding, renal dysfunction, fever or sepsis, and irrigation-fluid-related volume or electrolyte disturbance. Use monitoring and escalation appropriate to clinical status; PCNL-specific discharge criteria are not provided.

New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal PCNL anesthesia source is a narrative review, not a formal guideline; it reports heterogeneous studies and no formal study-quality appraisal. Its comparative conclusions should therefore be interpreted as review-author synthesis, not binding standards.

The GA-versus-epidural trial was single-center and selected adults with negative urine cultures; its findings do not establish management for infected stones, higher-risk excluded patients, or all PCNL techniques.

Generic ASA monitoring, preanesthesia, postanesthesia, and neuromuscular-blockade standards inform their respective domains but do not establish PCNL-specific airway, line-placement, fluid, or extubation protocols.
Case-specific adult targets for arterial access, ventilation settings, fluid totals, and a universal emergence sequence are not established in the supplied evidence.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Prostate biopsy is usually performed under transrectal ultrasound guidance; transperineal biopsy is an alternative. Positioning may be left lateral decubitus or lithotomy.
For TRUS-guided biopsy, periprostatic local-anesthetic infiltration or nerve block is the supported analgesic approach. The sources do not establish routine sedation or a particular airway technique.
Priorities include awareness of infectious complications, bleeding, and vasovagal episodes. Major complications are uncommon in the cited review, but infection can include urosepsis.
Recovery planning should account for bleeding and infectious symptoms. A procedure-specific emergence or postoperative monitoring protocol is not established in the biopsy sources.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: TRUS-guided systematic needle biopsy is the usual approach described for suspected prostate cancer. Transperineal biopsy is an alternative; selection of route is procedural and patient-context dependent.

TRUS-guided sampling uses ultrasound assessment and needle cores. For transrectal biopsy, the source describes left lateral decubitus or lithotomy positioning according to surgeon preference and circumstances.
The review recommends at least 10 systematically directed cores for an initial biopsy and more for larger glands; this is a biopsy sampling recommendation, not an anesthesia plan.

Techniques for Local Anesthesia in Transperineal and Transrectal Prostate Biopsy: An Image-based Step-by-Step Guide With Dedication to Anatomy

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: The cited review describes biopsy consideration in the setting of persistent suspicion based on DRE, elevated PSA, or related PSA measures, and says biopsy should be pursued when results could affect management.

Infectious risk and prophylaxis merit review against current local guidance. The available review summarizes trials supporting antibiotic prophylaxis but is not a current resistance-specific protocol.

The supplied sources do not establish anticoagulant interruption, restart timing, or a biopsy-specific bleeding-risk protocol; assess these issues individually with the relevant procedural team and applicable guidance.

sources.label: Using Biopsy to Detect Prostate Cancer

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Position for procedural access and patient comfort: left lateral decubitus or lithotomy are described for transrectal biopsy. The transrectal ultrasound probe and biopsy needle are procedural equipment.
The biopsy references do not specify routine anesthetic monitoring. If monitored anesthesia care or another anesthetic is provided, applicable basic anesthetic monitoring standards apply.
For anesthesia care, the ASA standards call for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; specific monitoring should reflect the anesthetic and patient context.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Local-anesthetic biopsy techniques do not have a source-established airway plan. Do not infer a need for intubation or general anesthesia from the procedure description.

The technical guide notes that intravenous sedation, epidural, or intubation anesthesia may be considered for high pain sensitivity or more complex procedures, while associating these approaches with greater side-effect risk and longer post-procedure monitoring. It supplies no regimen.
No biopsy-specific ventilation strategy is provided in the available sources.

sources.label: Techniques for Local Anesthesia in Transperineal and Transrectal Prostate Biopsy: An Image-based Step-by-Step Guide With Dedication to Anatomy

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Periprostatic infiltration or nerve block is the review-supported pain-control approach for TRUS-guided biopsy. The technical source describes ultrasound-guided placement and cautions against urethral or prostatic-capsule perforation.

Vasovagal episodes are a recognized biopsy complication. The sources do not provide a specific physiologic management algorithm; respond to observed instability using the clinical context and appropriate escalation.

The technical guide emphasizes careful needle placement under ultrasound and avoiding adjacent-structure injury during optional injections; these details do not constitute a universal anesthesia technique.

sources.label: Using Biopsy to Detect Prostate Cancer
Techniques for Local Anesthesia in Transperineal and Transrectal Prostate Biopsy: An Image-based Step-by-Step Guide With Dedication to Anatomy

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Relevant complications include infection, urethral or rectal bleeding, hematuria, hematospermia, pain, and vasovagal episodes. Urosepsis is reported as a rare major complication in the cited series.

Fever and urinary infection appear among reported delayed post-biopsy outcomes. The sources do not establish a specific threshold, workup, or treatment pathway; clinical concern warrants timely assessment and escalation.

Local-anesthetic complications described include hematoma, infection, hypotension, and rare systemic toxicity. The source stresses correct dosing but does not supply a universal dose limit for this reference.

sources.label: Using Biopsy to Detect Prostate Cancer
Techniques for Local Anesthesia in Transperineal and Transrectal Prostate Biopsy: An Image-based Step-by-Step Guide With Dedication to Anatomy

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Biopsy-related bleeding may be rectal, urethral, or urinary; the available sources report these complications but do not establish a case-specific blood-management protocol.
No routine fluid regimen or procedure-specific perfusion target is provided for prostate biopsy in the supplied evidence.

Techniques for Local Anesthesia in Transperineal and Transrectal Prostate Biopsy: An Image-based Step-by-Step Guide With Dedication to Anatomy

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: For TRUS-guided biopsy, periprostatic infiltration or nerve block is the review-supported analgesic technique. The source does not prescribe a universal dose or procedural recipe here.

Intrarectal lidocaine gel evidence was mixed in the review, and several randomized studies found it inferior to periprostatic block. Do not treat the gel as an equivalent substitute based on the available evidence.

The technical report describes transperineal biopsy as more painful than transrectal biopsy in cited discussion and notes pain may rise with puncture number; it does not establish a universal regimen for this route. PONV guidance is not supplied.

bullets: Local anesthesia is described as minimizing postoperative recovery time, but no biopsy-specific emergence protocol or monitoring duration is given. Sedation or deeper anesthetic techniques may entail longer monitoring.

When anesthesia care is provided, postanesthesia standards call for appropriate observation, evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, and quantitative oxygenation assessment during initial recovery.
Provide recovery counseling and follow-up consistent with local practice for bleeding or infectious symptoms; the biopsy review reports outcomes but does not prescribe a post-biopsy care pathway.

bullets: The 2025 local-anesthesia source is a technical report and image-based guide, not a comparative trial; its authors note variable effectiveness across studies and need for further research.
The biopsy review is narrative and dates to 2008. Its prophylaxis and complication data should not be read as a current institution-specific antibiotic protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Pyeloplasty is surgical correction of ureteropelvic-junction obstruction; the comparative series describes Anderson–Hynes repair under general anesthesia, by open or laparoscopic approach. It does not establish a robotic-specific anesthetic protocol.

Open surgery was performed in lateral decubitus. For a robotic/laparoscopic approach, account for the general effects of insufflation and positioning, while recognizing that the available sources do not give pyeloplasty-specific targets.
Preservation of renal function is a central procedural goal. Assess renal status and avoid assuming that urine output alone reflects perfusion during pneumoperitoneum.

Recovery priorities include appropriate postanesthesia monitoring, pain and nausea assessment, and observation of urinary catheter output. The comparative study found longer hospital stays and greater analgesic requirements after open than laparoscopic repair, but gives no procedure-specific emergence pathway.

sources.label: Comparison of Laparoscopic and Open Pyeloplasty Impact on Comfort and Success: A Retrospective, Single Center Study
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Postanesthesia Care

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The comparative study describes Anderson–Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty for ureteropelvic-junction obstruction, using a retroperitoneal approach for open and laparoscopic surgery. Its findings do not independently establish details for robotic pyeloplasty.
In the reported open approach, patients were placed lateral and a subcostal incision was used. The source does not provide a comparable detailed description of robotic access.
In this retrospective, single-center cohort, success was 84% after open and 87% after laparoscopic pyeloplasty; the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.631).

sources.label: Comparison of Laparoscopic and Open Pyeloplasty Impact on Comfort and Success: A Retrospective, Single Center Study

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review the indication, hydronephrosis and available renal-function assessment. The surgical study prioritized patients using imaging, renographic, functional and symptomatic criteria; these are reported surgical selection features, not anesthesia thresholds.

Renal preservation is an explicit treatment goal. General urologic anesthesia guidance emphasizes renal-function-based drug dosing and avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs; apply these as considerations in the individual assessment, not as a case-specific regimen.
The available pyeloplasty cohort included children and adults and does not supply a complete adult-specific anesthetic risk assessment. Do not infer adult practice from its pediatric subgroup.

sources.label: Comparison of Laparoscopic and Open Pyeloplasty Impact on Comfort and Success: A Retrospective, Single Center Study
Anesthesia for Urological Surgery

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Use the planned approach to guide positioning: lateral decubitus is reported for open pyeloplasty. For robotic surgery, provide adequate space and protect the patient from robot-arm contact; these are general robotic considerations, not pyeloplasty-specific findings.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA standards call for continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature; blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes.

The study reports placement of a urethral catheter, ureteral J catheter and surgical drain. Their use and postoperative management should be confirmed with the operating team; this report does not establish that every patient or approach requires the same configuration.

sources.label: Comparison of Laparoscopic and Open Pyeloplasty Impact on Comfort and Success: A Retrospective, Single Center Study
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The pyeloplasty series states that general anesthesia was used but does not report airway technique or ventilation management. For laparoscopic/robotic surgery generally, an endotracheal tube is preferred in the cited educational review to permit higher ventilatory pressures and PEEP; this does not establish a case-specific mandate.

If insufflation is used, anticipate reduced compliance and changes in CO₂ handling described for laparoscopic/robotic procedures; adjust ventilation to the observed physiology rather than importing a fixed target from a general review.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring is preferred, with recovery confirmed at TOF ratio ≥0.9 before extubation. This recommendation does not apply to cases conducted without NMB.

sources.label: Comparison of Laparoscopic and Open Pyeloplasty Impact on Comfort and Success: A Retrospective, Single Center Study
Anesthesia for Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery
New Practice Guidelines for Neuromuscular Blockade

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: For a laparoscopic or robotic approach involving pneumoperitoneum, consider the general effects on venous return, cardiac loading and respiratory mechanics. The pyeloplasty sources do not characterize these effects specifically for this operation.

Insufflation can reduce renal perfusion and urine output in laparoscopic surgery generally. Interpret urine output alongside the broader clinical picture and surgical context rather than as a stand-alone perfusion measure.
No pyeloplasty-specific critical-phase, ventilation-target or intraoperative renal-protection protocol is reported in the available procedure study.

bullets: The comparative study reports bleeding, urinary infection and stricture among surgical complications, with no significant difference in overall complication rates by approach. These are surgical outcomes, not quantified anesthesia risks.

During insufflation, remain alert to acute hemodynamic or respiratory change and escalate assessment if it occurs. General laparoscopic references describe vagal bradyarrhythmia, hypercarbia-related effects and access-related hemorrhage; they do not provide a pyeloplasty-specific rescue algorithm.

bullets: The comparative study used different analgesic agents according to age, so its reported analgesic consumption cannot establish an adult, approach-specific postoperative regimen. Select adult analgesia individually rather than adopting the study’s treatment doses.

Use an individualized multimodal analgesic strategy. A general urologic review describes TAP block as an option in urologic surgery, but does not establish its efficacy or required use for pyeloplasty specifically.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Radical cystectomy removes the bladder for invasive cancer and is commonly combined with urinary diversion using bowel; approaches include open and robot-assisted surgery.

Expect a major, often prolonged operation with substantial bleeding potential. Priorities supported by the evidence include perfusion without fluid overload, normothermia, and attention to blood loss and transfusion decisions.

Anesthetic technique should reflect the surgical approach and patient factors. Thoracic epidural analgesia is described chiefly for open surgery; routine omission is supported by consensus for many robot-assisted cases, not as a universal rule.

Recovery priorities include opioid-sparing analgesia, prevention and early recognition of gastrointestinal dysfunction, and appropriate postanesthesia monitoring. Ileus and thromboembolism are relevant postoperative concerns.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Cystectomy may remove part or all of the bladder for invasive bladder cancer. Radical cystectomy may be open or robot-assisted; diversion approaches discussed in the sources include ileal conduit, neobladder, and other urinary diversions.

Open surgery and minimally invasive approaches differ in operative demands. The review associates minimally invasive surgery with less blood loss and bowel handling, while a meta-analysis found longer operative time for robot-assisted than open surgery.

Urinary diversion using ileum can be associated with hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis through urinary solute reabsorption; this is a postoperative metabolic consideration, particularly with an ileal conduit.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess and optimize relevant medical risks, including cardiac, pulmonary, kidney disease, hypertension, diabetes, anemia, nutrition, smoking, and alcohol use. The review supports counseling and prehabilitation but does not establish a cystectomy-specific selection threshold.
Treat iron deficiency, with or without anemia, when predicted blood loss is >500 mL, as recommended in the anesthesia review.

For bowel preparation, the ERAS review reports no gastrointestinal or wound-infection advantage from mechanical and antibiotic preparation for small-bowel diversion; it distinguishes colon-based diversion, for which preparation is recommended based on colorectal literature.

Plan VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis in the context of the operation and individual risk. The review supports mechanical measures for major abdominal surgery and considers extended prophylaxis for patients at increased risk.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Anticipate a major urologic operation with potential for significant blood loss and ensure the room and team can respond to changing clinical status. The available sources do not establish a universal access configuration or case-specific equipment list.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and patient; the ASA standard calls for continuous evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. Blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes under that standard.

bullets: The sources describe general anesthesia and neuraxial techniques but do not establish a single airway device or ventilation strategy for cystectomy. Select airway management for the operation, approach, and patient rather than treating a specific device as universal.

For general anesthesia, follow basic monitoring standards for ventilation, including continual assessment and expired carbon-dioxide monitoring unless invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment.
A small, nonrandomized open-cystectomy study reports feasibility of combined spinal-epidural anesthesia in a selected cohort; its design and size do not establish this as routine technique.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Maintain perfusion while avoiding fluid overload. The review reports reduced blood loss, length of stay, and overall complications with net-even fluid balance, and cites cystectomy trial evidence that goal-directed fluid therapy reduced ileus and PONV.
Prevent hypothermia throughout the operation. The review links hypothermia with greater wound-infection incidence, cardiac events, and bleeding, and recommends active warming measures.

Use antibiotic prophylaxis consistent with local policy and the chosen agent’s pharmacology. The review recommends pre-incision prophylaxis and notes that repeat dosing may be beneficial during prolonged surgery or increased blood loss; it does not endorse prolonged postoperative administration.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Ileus is a prominent recovery concern. Minimize avoidable fluid overload and opioid exposure where feasible, and coordinate early recognition and management with the surgical team; the sources do not provide a cystectomy-specific rescue algorithm.

Bleeding can be substantial. Interpret transfusion decisions in the clinical context: observational cystectomy studies associate transfusion with adverse outcomes, while other adjusted analyses found no significant association.

Keep urinary-diversion complications in view during postoperative assessment, including ileal-conduit acid-base disturbance. Evaluate concerning deterioration promptly with the surgical team; no case-specific diagnostic or treatment pathway is established here.
Consider VTE among important postoperative risks; the review reports that many events occur after discharge. Apply individualized prophylaxis and follow local pathways.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Set fluid management around intravascular volume, cardiac output, and tissue perfusion while avoiding fluid overload. Goal-directed therapy is supported by cystectomy trial evidence for reducing ileus and PONV, not as a fixed-volume recipe.

Expect meaningful blood-loss potential and reassess perfusion and blood loss as the case evolves. A narrative anesthesia review gives a broad average blood-loss range for cystectomy, but this does not predict an individual case.
In major urologic surgery, intraoperative urine output may not be measurable; the ERAS review describes stroke-volume-guided therapy as an alternative means of guiding fluid management.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia to support mobilization, gastrointestinal recovery, and oral nutrition. Thoracic epidural is described in ERAS protocols chiefly for open surgery; it is not a universal requirement across approaches.

TAP block is one opioid-sparing option described for cystectomy; the review reports lower opioid use, earlier flatus, and shorter length of stay compared with conventional pain management, without differences in complications or readmissions.

Anticipate PONV as a barrier to mobilization and oral intake. Use risk-informed multimodal prevention and opioid minimization; the review describes combining antiemetic classes rather than relying on a single measure.

NSAIDs may be part of multimodal analgesia, but weigh analgesic benefit against renal function in the individual patient; the anesthesia review notes both common avoidance because of nephrotoxicity and reported opioid-sparing benefit.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Disposition should reflect the patient’s condition and operative course; the available evidence does not establish routine ICU admission for every cystectomy patient. An ICU is an example of an equivalent postanesthesia-care location when appropriate.

During initial recovery, monitor oxygenation quantitatively and evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; provide handoff and continued observation appropriate to condition.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this recommendation does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Support early oral nutrition and mobilization as tolerated within the recovery pathway; the review associates early feeding with potential reduction in postsurgical complications and higher first-day step counts with lower probability of prolonged stay.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Robot-assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy uses pneumoperitoneum and head-down positioning; the supplied review describes a steep Trendelenburg position, with chest banding used to prevent patient movement.

The dominant physiologic challenge is reduced respiratory compliance with possible hypercapnia, alongside cardiovascular effects of pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg. Ventilation and hemodynamics require ongoing reassessment.

Priorities include safe positioning and access before docking, managing fluid to preserve the operative view, and watching for facial or airway edema and ocular complications after prolonged head-down positioning.
During recovery, assess airway patency and oxygenation, and confirm adequate neuromuscular recovery before extubation when a neuromuscular blocking drug was used.

bullets: RALP is a robotic-assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy. The anesthetic implications arise principally from robotic access, pneumoperitoneum, head-down positioning, and a prolonged period in position; the available sources do not establish one universal anesthetic technique.

The procedure-specific review describes restricted fluid administration while the bladder–urethra anastomosis is being performed to avoid excess urine interfering with the surgical view. sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess cardiovascular and pulmonary reserve in relation to pneumoperitoneum and head-down positioning. The RALP review identifies pulmonary dysfunction, particularly COPD, as a risk for high airway pressures; limited cardiac reserve may make hemodynamic changes less well tolerated.

Consider cerebrovascular and ocular history when evaluating tolerance of Trendelenburg. The review advises caution with a history of aneurysm or stroke because intracranial pressure may rise; it also describes possible intraocular pressure elevation.

Assess functional status, comorbidities, and renal function as part of the overall perioperative evaluation. The general urologic review emphasizes these considerations but does not establish RALP-specific selection thresholds.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Plan positioning and pressure protection before docking. One RALP review describes modified lithotomy with arms and hands padded and tucked; it also warns that patients can slip during table-position changes and describes chest binding in its institutional practice.

Complete access checks before docking, since positioning and the robot can restrict access. Consider whether a higher-risk patient or an anticipated prolonged case warrants additional monitoring; the source describes this as a consideration, not a universal requirement.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring standards, including ongoing evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature. Arterial pressure and heart rate are to be determined and evaluated at least every five minutes under the cited ASA standard.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Anticipate reduced lung compliance and increased airway pressures with pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg. The RALP review reports impaired respiratory mechanics and recommends attention to peak airway pressure; the supplied sources do not establish one ventilation mode for every patient.

Reassess ventilation and carbon-dioxide elimination as the case progresses. The review notes that prolonged carbon-dioxide pneumoperitoneum can cause hypercarbia and describes increasing ventilation rate as a response; use clinical and monitored findings to guide adjustments.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm adequate recovery before extubation. The cited guidance recommends monitoring at the adductor pollicis and a TOF ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation; this does not imply paralysis for every anesthetic technique.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg can have interacting respiratory and cardiovascular effects. The RALP review reports increased airway pressures and reduced compliance; another review describes possible competing effects on venous return and cardiac output. Interpret changes in the context of position, insufflation, ventilation, and the patient’s reserve.

Maintain awareness of positioning-related ocular and neurologic effects as well as possible subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax, or pneumomediastinum. The supplied reviews identify these hazards but do not provide a single case-specific surveillance protocol.
The transition from head-down positioning and pneumoperitoneum toward supine recovery is a key point for reassessing ventilation, hemodynamics, and fluid needs.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Facial, pharyngeal, or laryngeal edema may follow prolonged Trendelenburg. Reassess airway findings before extubation; the review says a cuff-leak test may be warranted when edema is a concern.

Ocular injury is a relevant positioning hazard. The historical institutional series reported corneal abrasion despite eye taping; its subsequent practice change and observed incidence are not a universal estimate or standard for current practice.

If unexpected respiratory or hemodynamic deterioration occurs, consider effects of position and insufflation as well as the complications identified in the reviews. Escalate assessment and management to the clinical situation; the available sources do not establish a universal emergency algorithm.

bullets: Fluid restriction is described to limit urine that could obscure the operative field and facial edema during prolonged Trendelenburg. The reviews give differing practice suggestions; do not convert them into a universal fluid total.

Balance operative-view considerations against perfusion and the patient’s hemodynamic response. The available evidence does not establish a universal fluid amount or a single vasopressor preference for RALP.

The institutional series describes generally limited blood loss but also reports postoperative intra-abdominal bleeding requiring additional surgery. These observations do not establish an expected loss or a transfusion threshold for an individual case.

When neuromuscular blockade has been used, verify quantitative recovery before extubation; residual blockade is associated with airway obstruction and reintubation.

During transfer and initial recovery, continue monitoring and provide an appropriate handoff. PACU standards require ongoing assessment, with particular attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Robotic partial or radical nephrectomy removes part or all of a kidney for renal tumors. Robotic partial nephrectomy is performed in lateral decubitus; the available robotic-surgery review specifies flank elevation for the partial procedure.

Plan for restricted patient access after docking and prevent movement while instruments are engaged. Positioning, pressure, and nerve injury are concerns; the team should be prepared to detach the robot rapidly if access is needed.

Assess cardiopulmonary comorbidity and residual renal function before surgery. During recovery, prioritize oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, temperature, and evaluation for bleeding and renal function.

The supplied sources do not establish a nephrectomy-specific anesthetic recipe, fluid total, arterial-line requirement, or partial-nephrectomy clamp regimen. Individualize these decisions; do not infer mannitol or steep Trendelenburg as routine from the supplied evidence.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Partial versus radical nephrectomy is selected according to tumor characteristics. The source notes partial nephrectomy may be used for smaller renal masses, but supplies no patient-specific selection algorithm.

Patients are commonly positioned lateral decubitus. For robot-assisted partial nephrectomy, the robotic review describes 45° lateral decubitus with flank elevation; it does not specify a corresponding setup for radical nephrectomy.
The robot is bulky and docking restricts access; establish a team plan for rapid detachment before the case. Movement with instruments docked risks internal tissue or vascular injury.

bullets: Assess cardiovascular, pulmonary, and cerebrovascular disease, functional reserve, and expected residual renal function. Many nephrectomy patients are older and may have comorbidities.
Review positioning and pressure-injury risks, including dependent-side nerve injury and venous congestion; plan padding and neutral neck alignment for the intended lateral position.
The supplied evidence does not establish a procedure-specific preoperative protocol beyond these assessment considerations; adapt evaluation to patient condition and planned extent of resection.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Allow sufficient space for the bulky robotic system; protect the patient’s head from robot-arm collisions and secure lines, monitors, and protective devices beforehand to reduce the risk of kinking or displacement.

Protect eyes and ears from pressure, use an axillary roll on the dependent side, and maintain neutral neck position in lateral decubitus. Recheck pressure points and extremities after positioning and before docking.

Use applicable basic anesthetic monitoring. The evidence does not establish routine arterial-line placement for robotic nephrectomy; select additional monitoring according to patient status and clinical judgment.

bullets: A general anesthetic with endotracheal intubation is a reasonable approach for robotic abdominal surgery, where controlled ventilation and restricted access are relevant; the general laparoscopic/robotic reference describes general anesthesia as standard and prefers an ETT.

Secure the airway and circuit before lateral positioning and docking, then reassess ventilation after positioning and insufflation. The supplied nephrectomy-specific sources do not prescribe ventilation settings or a particular maintenance agent.

Ensure immobility while robotic instruments are docked. Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and confirm recovery before extubation when a neuromuscular blocker has been used; these requirements do not apply to cases without such blockade.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Restricted access can delay recognition and response to deterioration. Rehearse emergency undocking with the operating-room team before docking; the sources do not supply a nephrectomy-specific undocking sequence.

Positioning risks include pressure sores, nerve damage, and venous congestion; protect the patient’s head from robot-arm collisions. In one center, positioning injuries occurred in 6.6% of 334 adult robot-assisted urological procedures; this is not a nephrectomy-specific incidence.

Hemorrhage is a recognized nephrectomy concern. If instability or suspected bleeding develops, prioritize recognition, communication, and restoring access; specific transfusion triggers and a procedural rescue algorithm are not supplied.

bullets: Estimate residual renal function and account for removal of all or part of a kidney when assessing perfusion and selecting perioperative medications. The sources provide no universal fluid total or nephrectomy-specific fluid target.

Reconcile NSAID use with renal considerations rather than applying a blanket rule: the review notes nephrotoxic concerns but also reports a live-donor study with postoperative ketorolac and no observed reduction in renal function.

NSAIDs are commonly avoided because of nephrotoxic effects, although the review also describes postoperative analgesic and opioid-sparing effects. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Suprapubic catheterization provides bladder drainage through the lower abdominal wall. It may be performed by open cystotomy or percutaneously; it is used when urethral catheterization is not possible, unsuccessful, contraindicated, or undesirable.

The central procedural hazard is injury to bowel or adjacent vessels, particularly with a nondistended bladder or altered anatomy after abdominal or pelvic surgery. Distention and appropriate imaging help assess and reduce this risk.

Anesthesia depends on the approach and circumstances: local anesthesia is described for percutaneous techniques, while open cystotomy typically uses general or regional anesthesia. The available procedure source does not establish a routine airway technique or anesthetic drug regimen.

Recovery priorities include monitoring for catheter displacement, hematuria, infection, and urine leakage, while applying postanesthesia monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic and the patient’s condition.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The catheter enters the bladder through the lower abdominal wall above the pubic symphysis. Approaches include open cystotomy and percutaneous trocar or Seldinger techniques; approach selection is based on patient and procedural factors, available equipment and imaging, urgency, and clinician experience.
Adequate bladder filling is important before insertion. The source suggests a minimum volume, but does not establish that figure as a universal target for every patient or approach.

Cystoscopic confirmation is recommended when feasible. Percutaneous placement should not be described as requiring ultrasound in every case: the source describes imaging as helpful and states that radiographic guidance for Seldinger placement is desirable but optional.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Confirm the drainage indication and assess whether urethral access is impossible, unsafe, unsuccessful, or otherwise unsuitable. Indications include acute retention when urethral catheterization cannot be safely performed and selected longer-term drainage needs.

A nondistended bladder, suspected or confirmed bladder cancer, and uncorrected coagulopathy are listed as absolute contraindications to percutaneous placement in the source. These are approach-specific statements and should not be generalized into a prohibition on all suprapubic access.

Prior abdominal or pelvic surgery warrants caution because adhesions or altered anatomy may place bowel between the bladder and abdominal wall. Consider preprocedural imaging, particularly when this history is present.

Other relative contraindications include local skin infection or cellulitis, ascites, pubic osteomyelitis, and relevant mesh, hardware, or vascular grafts at the site. Assess anticoagulation and coagulopathy in the context of the planned approach; the source does not provide a perioperative medication-management schedule.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The described position is supine with a slight Trendelenburg tilt to move bowel away from the bladder. Rigid cystoscopy requires dorsal lithotomy; flexible cystoscopy can be performed supine.

Use imaging and cystoscopy as appropriate to the chosen technique and anatomy. Ultrasound with color Doppler is described as useful for assessing intervening bowel or obstructing vascular structures, especially where anatomy may be altered.

For general anesthesia, regional anesthesia, or monitored anesthesia care, apply the applicable basic anesthetic monitoring standards. During moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless precluded or invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment.

bullets: Ensure adequate bladder distention before access; distention brings the anterior bladder closer to the skin and moves bowel superiorly away from the expected catheter path. Confirm entry and catheter position using the technique-appropriate method, with cystoscopy when feasible.

The critical access concern is avoiding bowel, vascular, and bladder injury while establishing the tract and confirming catheter position. Preprocedural imaging and intraoperative ultrasound may reduce bowel-injury risk; neither the supplied evidence nor the case-specific source establishes a universal imaging mandate.

The source identifies postobstructive diuresis after decompression as a possible issue in chronic obstruction. Monitor the clinical course when substantial chronic retention is relevant; the source provides no detailed fluid-management protocol.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Potential intraoperative complications include bowel or vascular injury, intraperitoneal violation, hemorrhage, bladder injury, catheter misplacement, and failure to enter the bladder. Maintain awareness of these access-related hazards and confirm position where feasible.

Early postoperative problems include pain, hematuria, infection, dislodgement, and urine leakage. Leakage around the tube may indicate blockage or bladder spasms; the source describes irrigation, exchange, infection treatment, or medication for spasms as possible responses, without a case-specific algorithm.

Incorrect balloon position may cause migration into the urethra, pain, and tissue damage on inflation. A displaced or malfunctioning catheter warrants prompt assessment by the responsible procedural team; the supplied source does not provide an anesthesia-specific rescue protocol.

bullets: Hemorrhage and vascular injury are recognized complications, but the procedural source gives no expected blood loss, transfusion guidance, hemodynamic targets, or intraoperative fluid protocol. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: TURBT is an endoscopic bladder-tumor resection performed under spinal or general anesthesia, with the aim of removing visible tumor when feasible and obtaining tissue for diagnosis and staging.

Lateral-wall resection carries a specific obturator-reflex hazard: sudden adductor movement can increase bladder-perforation risk. Coordinate the anesthetic approach and prevention measures with the surgeon.

Spinal anesthesia does not reliably prevent a directly stimulated obturator jerk. When neuromuscular blockade is indicated for this risk, the cited review favors general anesthesia; other surgical prevention measures also matter.

Recovery priorities include assessing for bleeding, bladder perforation, and catheter-related bladder discomfort, and following standard postanesthesia monitoring. A specific TURBT analgesia or recovery regimen is not established by these sources.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: TURBT is an endoscopic procedure used for bladder-cancer diagnosis and treatment. Resection aims to remove visible tumor when feasible and obtain an adequate specimen for histology; high-grade disease generally requires assessment that includes detrusor muscle.

The patient is placed in dorsal lithotomy after induction. Spinal and general anesthesia are both described; the choice depends on the patient, procedure, and whether blockade is needed to mitigate obturator-reflex risk.

For lateral-wall tumors, discuss obturator-reflex prevention with the surgeon before resection. Avoid bladder overfilling; surgical approaches described also include reducing cutting current, short intermittent bursts, bipolar electrocautery, and neuromuscular blockade.

Assess relevant history and fitness for spinal or general anesthesia. The TURBT review specifically identifies hematuria, lower urinary tract symptoms, and urothelial-cancer risk factors in the preoperative history.

bullets: The key procedure-specific event is electrical stimulation near the obturator nerve during lateral-wall resection, which can produce abrupt adductor spasm. Coordinate resection timing and prevention with the surgeon.

Spinal anesthesia does not block direct electrical stimulation of the obturator nerve. Prevention may involve anesthetic blockade or surgical measures; the sources do not support relying on neuraxial anesthesia alone to abolish this reflex.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: TURP is an endoscopic treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia. It may be performed under spinal or general anesthesia; spinal anesthesia is often favored because an awake patient can report early symptoms of TURP syndrome.
TURP syndrome can result from irrigation-fluid absorption and involve dilutional hyponatremia, fluid overload, and glycine toxicity.
Priorities are to recognize evolving neurologic, visual, respiratory, or hemodynamic changes; communicate promptly with the surgeon; and assess sodium and osmolality when the syndrome is suspected.
Recovery requires attention to delayed TURP syndrome as well as respiratory status, circulation, consciousness, temperature, and catheter-related bladder discomfort.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: TURP is performed with a resectoscope and a wire loop connected to monopolar or bipolar electrocautery. Irrigating fluid distends the bladder and provides a surgical view.

The anesthetic may be spinal or general. Spinal anesthesia can preserve awareness of early symptoms; general anesthesia remains an option when neuraxial anesthesia is unsuitable or other patient/procedural factors favor it.
Bipolar resectoscopes permit electrolyte-containing irrigation, including normal saline.

bullets: Assess medical status and develop an anesthesia plan; consider age, comorbidity, functional status, procedure duration, and anticipated blood loss as part of general urologic perioperative assessment.
Identify pre-existing hyponatremia and relevant contributors; the TURP review advises diagnosing and treating pre-existing hyponatremia and establishing euvolemia before the procedure.

Absorption risk increases with prolonged resection, larger prostate size, higher irrigation pressure, bleeding/open veins, and capsular or bladder perforation. Keep these factors in view when discussing operative progress with the surgeon.

With general anesthesia, early subjective symptoms are unavailable and diagnosis may rely on nonspecific cardiovascular changes and laboratory assessment. Maintain appropriate oxygenation and ventilation if TURP syndrome is suspected.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Irrigation-fluid uptake can be rapid through exposed venous channels or slower from peri-vesical and retroperitoneal spaces. Absorption varies with pressure, duration, irrigation volume, and bleeding.
TURP syndrome reflects more than dilutional hyponatremia: volume overload, electrolyte/osmolality disturbance, and irrigant solute toxicity may coexist.

Risk can arise early and may present after the operation. Coordinate with the surgeon to limit prolonged resection and avoid unnecessarily high irrigation pressure while maintaining adequate surgical conditions.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Possible manifestations of TURP syndrome include nausea, headache, confusion or agitation, visual disturbance, seizures, coma, pulmonary edema, arrhythmia, and hemodynamic instability. A conscious patient may report visual symptoms early.

For suspected syndrome, promptly alert the surgeon, stop irrigation/resection as appropriate, assess sodium and osmolality, and evaluate respiratory and cardiovascular status. Escalate support according to severity; the sources do not establish one universal treatment sequence.

Consider bladder or capsular perforation when clinical changes occur; it can permit rapid absorption. The available sources describe the hazard but do not provide a specific diagnostic or repair protocol.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Ureteral stenting is performed to drain an obstructed upper urinary tract; the available evidence primarily describes cystoscopic placement, including urgent placement for obstructing stones. It does not establish a preferred technique for routine stent removal.

Anesthetic approaches vary with setting and clinical context. Local anesthetic gel, sometimes with sedation, is reported for non-OT placement; an emergency cohort mostly received general anesthesia. Neither source establishes a single approach for routine placement or removal.

Key procedural hazards reported include difficult or failed access, patient pain or distress, haematuria, infection, stent displacement, and ureteral or collecting-system injury. Obstruction accompanied by infection or acute kidney injury warrants attention to the patient's underlying illness as well as the procedure.

Plan recovery according to anesthetic and patient condition, with appropriate postanesthesia monitoring and attention to reported urinary complications. If neuromuscular blockade is used, confirm quantitative recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this does not apply to cases without blockade.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Ureteroscopy is an endoscopic diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for stones and other upper-tract problems. Retrograde access is through the urethra and bladder; rigid or semi-rigid scopes suit distal ureteral work, while flexible scopes reach the upper ureter and kidney.

Provide adequate anesthesia and minimize movement during scope advancement. General anesthesia is recommended in the procedure-specific review; combined spinal-epidural is described as an alternative. The sources do not establish a routine airway device or anesthetic drug regimen.

Prioritize infection assessment and careful control of irrigation. Active UTI should be treated and resolved before ureteroscopy; high irrigation pressure may increase bacteremia risk and injure the collecting system.

Plan recovery around possible stent discomfort, hematuria, and infectious complications. Confirm neuromuscular recovery before extubation if a neuromuscular blocking drug was used; this does not apply to cases without such blockade.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Ureteroscopy is used to diagnose or treat ureteral and renal stones, strictures, urothelial tumors, and other upper-tract findings. Retrograde access proceeds through the urethra and bladder; antegrade access may be considered in selected altered-anatomy or access situations.

Scope selection follows the target: rigid or semi-rigid scopes are generally used for distal ureteral conditions; flexible scopes are suited to upper-tract anatomy, including the renal pelvis and calyces.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review relevant imaging and obtain urinalysis and urine culture to assess for urinary infection. The procedure-specific source identifies preoperative infection as the most important predictor of postoperative urinary infectious complications.

An active UTI should be treated and resolved before ureteroscopy. If cloudy or purulent urine is encountered before scope placement, the source advises treating this as presumptive infection, obtaining a culture, postponing the procedure, and arranging appropriate drainage and subsequent reassessment.

Assess anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy and bleeding diathesis individually. The source describes these as relative contraindications requiring case-by-case assessment, while also noting that ureteroscopy can often be performed in anticoagulated patients; neither statement supports a blanket rule.

Consider infection-risk modifiers reported in the review, including longer operative time, diabetes, positive preoperative urine nitrites, and pre- or postoperative stenting. These are risk associations, not a patient-specific prediction.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Dorsal lithotomy with stirrups is typical. Confirm the side and ensure the table supports the patient, including when moved toward the end of the table for cystoscopy.

Cystoscopy generally precedes ureteroscopy to assess anatomy, visualize the bladder and ureteric orifice, and facilitate guidewire placement. A safety guidewire is generally placed in the renal pelvis and secured against displacement.

When fluoroscopy is used, arrange the C-arm and video tower for access and use static or pulsed imaging and the minimum necessary radiation exposure. Apply basic anesthetic monitoring standards; the procedure-specific sources do not define a separate monitoring protocol.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: General anesthesia is recommended by the ureteroscopy review, and reduced patient movement is a procedural advantage. Combined spinal-epidural anesthesia is described as an adequate alternative. The supplied evidence does not establish a routine airway device, ventilation strategy, or need for neuromuscular blockade.

If a neuromuscular blocking drug is used, quantitative monitoring is preferred and recovery should be confirmed at TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 before extubation, using the adductor pollicis site. These recommendations concern blockade management, not a requirement to use blockade for ureteroscopy.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Irrigation distends the urinary tract and supports visualization, but use the lowest flow that maintains adequate renal visualization. Excess flow may move stones; high intrarenal pressure may cause calyceal rupture and increase bacteremia risk.

Normal saline is preferred for irrigation in the procedure-specific review because it reduces tissue-damage risk if absorbed or extravasated. This is irrigation guidance, not a recommendation for an intravenous fluid type or volume.

Avoid forcing a guidewire, catheter, or access sheath against resistance. If access requires substantial force or dilation, consider stopping, stenting, and staging rather than risking mucosal injury, perforation, or disruption.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Urethral stricture treatment may involve dilation or direct-vision internal urethrotomy (DVIU); longer or recurrent strictures are generally better addressed with urethroplasty. Anesthetic setting varies from office local anesthesia to operating-room sedation, spinal, or general anesthesia.

For endoscopic treatment, dorsal lithotomy supports rigid cystoscopic access. Prioritize direct visualization and controlled dilation: false passage, urethral perforation, bleeding, and later recurrence are relevant procedural hazards.

Preprocedure assessment should establish stricture location and length, prior treatment, and whether urinary infection is present. The available procedure reviews do not establish a case-specific airway, anesthetic drug regimen, or physiologic target.

After endoscopic treatment, catheter use is common but duration is not settled; counsel and observe for hematuria, urinary infection, and recurrence. Recovery monitoring should follow the anesthetic and the patient's condition.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: CEA removes atherosclerotic plaque at the carotid artery. It may be performed under general, regional, or cooperative-patient general anesthesia; available evidence has not established that one approach produces better major outcomes.

The critical intraoperative concern is cerebral hypoperfusion during carotid clamping. Choose clinical or instrumental cerebral monitoring to fit the anesthetic and shunt strategy; awake clinical assessment is described as more sensitive than instrumental methods.

Avoid pressure falling below baseline during clamping, while recognizing that pressure augmentation must be individualized, particularly in patients with cardiac risk. After unclamping, postoperative hypertension is a concern because of cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome.

Recovery priorities are prompt comparison with the preoperative neurological state, blood-pressure surveillance, and recognition of neck hematoma or new neurological symptoms. The supplied sources do not establish a CEA-specific recovery observation schedule.

Heparin is described as being administered before carotid clamping. Whether to reverse residual anticoagulant effect with protamine varies between centers; evidence is insufficient to establish a definitive reversal strategy.

Antiplatelet therapy may increase blood loss, so coordinate bleeding-risk assessment with the surgical and anesthesia teams. The available review does not supply a universal perioperative antiplatelet regimen for an individual patient.

bullets: After anesthesia, reassess neurological status against baseline and continue postoperative blood-pressure monitoring. The CEA guideline review supports postoperative pressure monitoring but does not define duration, location, or a universal treatment threshold.

PACU or equivalent care should include continual evaluation appropriate to the patient’s condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. A receiving-team handoff and documentation are part of the ASA postanesthesia standards.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Dialysis graft placement creates an arteriovenous access using a tunneled PTFE graft. Available procedure-specific evidence describes local anesthesia as common; broader ESRD guidance favors local/MAC or regional techniques whenever feasible.
The dominant anesthetic concerns are ESRD-related electrolyte and volume disturbance, particularly hyperkalemia and fluid overload, alongside cardiovascular disease, anemia, and bleeding tendency.
Protect existing and future vascular access: document the access site, avoid using a functioning graft or fistula for routine vascular access, and preserve potential access veins and limbs.

Recovery priorities include reassessing oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and consciousness, and confirming the surgical team’s assessment of access function while monitoring fluid and electrolyte status.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: The operation establishes hemodialysis access by tunneling a PTFE graft between arterial and venous exposures and creating anastomoses. The available clinical series describes tunneling before anastomosis, with graft placement superficial enough to facilitate later access.

That series describes a straight forearm graft using radial-artery inflow and an antecubital vein, with loop configurations also reported. These are reported approaches, not a universal selection rule; anatomy and prior access history determine feasible sites.

Local anesthesia is described in the procedure-specific series; general anesthesia was used occasionally for patient-related reasons. ESRD anesthesia guidance supports local/MAC or regional approaches when appropriate, but the available sources do not establish one technique for every graft operation.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Review ESRD status, comorbid cardiovascular disease and diabetes, volume status, anemia and bleeding history. ESRD is associated with increased perioperative morbidity and mortality, and the source recommends multidisciplinary assessment.

Establish dialysis schedule and access type/site; assess whether preoperative dialysis is needed in light of volume and electrolyte status. The source specifically advises documenting access and routine dialysis needs.

Check relevant electrolytes, particularly potassium, and assess coagulation when considering regional techniques. The source cautions that uremic platelet and coagulation abnormalities may persist despite dialysis.

Preserve future access options: document existing access and avoid routine venipuncture or arterial-line placement in a functioning access extremity. Avoid subclavian central access because stenosis may compromise future AVF creation.
