sections.title: Preoperative assessment & obesity-related challenges
bullets: Risk is not defined by BMI alone. Review functional capacity, prior anesthetic and airway records, fat distribution, neck mobility, cardiopulmonary disease and the planned procedure or revision.

Screen for known or suspected obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS). Clarify home CPAP/BiPAP use, tolerance and settings; ask the patient to bring their device. Plan the recovery location before induction.

Assess hypertension, coronary disease, ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, diabetes, renal impairment and metabolic-associated liver disease. These comorbidities affect monitoring, fluids, drug titration and postoperative disposition.
Ask specifically about reflux, dysphagia, regurgitation, vomiting, gastroparesis, prior bariatric anatomy and GLP-1 therapy. A reported fasting interval alone does not settle aspiration risk.

Review oral intake, hydration, glycemia, anemia and nutritional concerns, especially after previous bypass or prolonged vomiting. Coordinate correction and perioperative medication plans rather than assuming all bariatric patients have identical requirements.

sections.title: GLP-1 medications & aspiration planning
bullets: Record the agent, indication, dose, last dose, recent dose increases and gastrointestinal symptoms. Escalation, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or other delayed-emptying conditions increase concern for retained gastric contents.

For increased risk, coordinate a liquid-only diet for 24 hours, an individualized anesthetic/aspiration plan and, when appropriate and expertise is available, gastric ultrasound. Diet instructions must also respect the institution’s fasting policy.

Dose escalation or significant ongoing gastrointestinal symptoms may justify deferring elective surgery until risk improves. Make the decision with the surgeon, anesthesia clinician, prescriber and patient; account for glycemic consequences if treatment is withheld.

A medication history does not replace day-of-surgery assessment. If retained contents are suspected, weigh delay against proceeding with appropriate aspiration precautions; do not assume prolonged fasting guarantees an empty stomach.

sections.title: NG/OG tubes, bougies & staple-line safety

sections.title: Drug dosing: TBW, LBW, IBW & adjusted weight
bullets: TBW/actual body weight is the measured weight. LBW estimates non-adipose mass. IBW is a height-based reference weight; adjusted body weight combines IBW with a fraction of excess weight. These terms are not interchangeable, and an adjustment formula is drug- and protocol-specific.

Propofol induction: LBW is a commonly recommended initial scalar, with titration to loss of consciousness and hemodynamic response. A full TBW-derived bolus can be excessive; a scalar is a starting approach, not a guaranteed adequate induction dose.

Propofol maintenance/TIVA: do not copy the induction LBW rule into the infusion. Published approaches differ: older pharmacokinetic reviews discuss TBW/allometric clearance, while the BJA Education/SOBA chart uses adjusted weight. Vecuronium and atracurium/cisatracurium: IBW-based dosing is supported in the cited pharmacokinetic review to avoid unnecessarily prolonged block from TBW dosing. This evidence is older; confirm the current local drug protocol and titrate with quantitative neuromuscular monitoring.

sections.title: Hemodynamics, pneumoperitoneum & monitoring
bullets: Obesity can be associated with increased blood volume/cardiac workload, hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction. OSA/OHS-related pulmonary hypertension and right-ventricular disease may make the patient less tolerant of hypoxemia, hypercarbia or major loading changes.

Discuss insufflation and position changes with the surgeon. If cardiopulmonary tolerance is poor, reassess insufflation pressure, positioning, anesthetic effect and reversible causes rather than treating hypotension with fluid alone.

sections.title: Liver retraction & vagal bradycardia

Stop or release the provoking stimulus; stop insufflation and release pneumoperitoneum when that is implicated. Assess oxygenation, ventilation, anesthetic/opioid effects and other reversible causes instead of assuming every bradycardia is benign or purely vagal.

Treat clinically significant bradycardia promptly under the local perioperative bradycardia/ACLS protocol; anticholinergic treatment may be appropriate. sections.title: Intraoperative management & surgical coordination
bullets: Use secure weight-appropriate positioning with protection from sliding, pressure injury and nerve compression. Recheck access and airway security when the table is tilted or surgical access changes.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and match blockade to surgical requirements. If deeper block is requested, plan reliable reversal and objective recovery rather than assuming elapsed time or apparent spontaneous breathing proves recovery.

Coordinate decompression, bougie placement, retraction, insufflation and any leak testing with the surgeon. Unexpected bleeding, airway-pressure changes or hemodynamic deterioration warrant reassessment rather than attribution to routine laparoscopy.

sections.title: Fluids, perfusion & venous thromboembolism
bullets: Aim for individualized euvolemia and adequate tissue perfusion. ERAS favors goal-directed fluid management where appropriate and avoidance of both excessive restriction and fluid overload.
Evaluate hypotension for anesthetic vasodilation, position/insufflation effects, bleeding and other causes. A fluid bolus is not the automatic answer to every reduction in blood pressure.

Use mechanical and pharmacologic VTE prevention according to bleeding risk, renal function, procedure and institutional policy. Prior VTE, immobility and other risk factors may influence extended prophylaxis; duration is individualized.

Plan early mobilization and postoperative hydration. Persistent tachycardia or dyspnea is not simply pain or dehydration until important causes such as bleeding, leak, respiratory compromise and VTE have been considered.

sections.title: Analgesia, nausea prevention & recovery
bullets: Favor multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia. Local infiltration or regional techniques can reduce opioid needs; consider organ function, maximum doses and the procedure-specific surgical plan.

Use risk-based multimodal PONV prophylaxis and a rescue plan. Vomiting is particularly undesirable after upper-GI surgery and should not be dismissed when accompanied by pain, tachycardia or inability to tolerate intake.
NSAID suitability differs by procedure and patient. In Roux-en-Y patients, marginal-ulcer risk is a specific concern; do not automatically transfer a generic NSAID-based pathway to a bypass patient.
Resume oral intake and mobilization according to the bariatric pathway. Persistent intolerance, dehydration or nutritional problems need follow-up rather than repeated symptomatic treatment alone.

sections.title: Extubation, CPAP/BiPAP & postoperative monitoring
bullets: Plan extubation as deliberately as induction. Use head-up positioning, adequate preoxygenation, awake airway control and objectively confirmed neuromuscular recovery; have equipment and assistance ready if re-intubation is necessary.

Continue prescribed home CPAP/BiPAP in the postoperative period when indicated. For increased desaturation risk, consider extubation directly to CPAP or HFNO; OHS or persistent hypoxemia may warrant bilevel/noninvasive ventilatory support and a higher-acuity setting.

CPAP is not automatically prohibited after bariatric surgery and is not mandatory for every patient. Match support to OSA/OHS, oxygenation, ventilation and surgical/clinical circumstances; persistent deterioration requires escalation, not repeated mask adjustments alone.

Monitor for obstruction, hypoventilation, residual block and opioid-related respiratory depression. Supplemental oxygen can conceal impaired ventilation; a reassuring oxygen saturation alone does not exclude hypercapnia or ventilatory failure.

Choose PACU, monitored ward or higher-acuity care based on respiratory events, OSA/OHS, comorbidities, opioid needs and recovery, rather than BMI alone. Continue head-up recovery, mobilization and coordinated VTE prevention.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: A small gastric pouch empties into a Roux limb, bypassing the remaining stomach and proximal small intestine. Anastomoses and altered anatomy add risks beyond a purely restrictive procedure.
Use the same ramped airway, rapid-desaturation and obesity-physiology precautions as other laparoscopic bariatric operations; individualize aspiration precautions.
No routine/blind NG passage across fresh reconstruction. Coordinate any necessary OG/bougie placement or leak testing with the surgeon.
Balance pneumoperitoneum, position and fluid management; use drug-specific weight scalars and objective block recovery.
Postoperative priorities include respiratory support, leak/bleeding surveillance, VTE prevention and longer-term nutrition; NSAID-related marginal-ulcer risk matters.

sections.title: Procedure anatomy & case-specific priorities
bullets: The stomach is divided into a small proximal pouch and an excluded remnant. A gastrojejunal connection carries food into the Roux limb; a downstream small-bowel connection reunites food with biliopancreatic secretions.

The excluded stomach and bypassed proximal bowel are not accessed by ordinary passage from the mouth. Before any tube intervention or return to surgery, establish the patient’s actual reconstruction and the surgeon’s intended route.

Compared with sleeve or band, the reconstruction is more complex and has greater vitamin/mineral deficiency risk. Previous bypass patients may present with obstruction, dehydration or nutritional problems even after substantial weight loss.
In the 2024 MBSAQIP-based study reported by ASMBS in 2026, Roux-en-Y represented 32.82% of analyzed procedures. This dated study estimate should not be substituted for a local case mix.

Evaluate hypotension for anesthetic vasodilation, position/insufflation effects, bleeding and other causes. A fluid bolus is not the automatic answer to every reduction in blood pressure.

Use mechanical and pharmacologic VTE prevention according to bleeding risk, renal function, procedure and institutional policy. Prior VTE, immobility and other risk factors may influence extended prophylaxis; duration is individualized.

Plan early mobilization and postoperative hydration. Persistent tachycardia or dyspnea is not simply pain or dehydration until important causes such as bleeding, leak, respiratory compromise and VTE have been considered.

sections.title: Analgesia, nausea prevention & recovery
bullets: Favor multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia. Local infiltration or regional techniques can reduce opioid needs; consider organ function, maximum doses and the procedure-specific surgical plan.

Use risk-based multimodal PONV prophylaxis and a rescue plan. Vomiting is particularly undesirable after upper-GI surgery and should not be dismissed when accompanied by pain, tachycardia or inability to tolerate intake.
NSAID suitability differs by procedure and patient. In Roux-en-Y patients, marginal-ulcer risk is a specific concern; do not automatically transfer a generic NSAID-based pathway to a bypass patient.
Resume oral intake and mobilization according to the bariatric pathway. Persistent intolerance, dehydration or nutritional problems need follow-up rather than repeated symptomatic treatment alone.

sections.title: Extubation, CPAP/BiPAP & postoperative monitoring
bullets: Plan extubation as deliberately as induction. Use head-up positioning, adequate preoxygenation, awake airway control and objectively confirmed neuromuscular recovery; have equipment and assistance ready if re-intubation is necessary.

Continue prescribed home CPAP/BiPAP in the postoperative period when indicated. For increased desaturation risk, consider extubation directly to CPAP or HFNO; OHS or persistent hypoxemia may warrant bilevel/noninvasive ventilatory support and a higher-acuity setting.

CPAP is not automatically prohibited after bariatric surgery and is not mandatory for every patient. Match support to OSA/OHS, oxygenation, ventilation and surgical/clinical circumstances; persistent deterioration requires escalation, not repeated mask adjustments alone.

Monitor for obstruction, hypoventilation, residual block and opioid-related respiratory depression. Supplemental oxygen can conceal impaired ventilation; a reassuring oxygen saturation alone does not exclude hypercapnia or ventilatory failure.

Choose PACU, monitored ward or higher-acuity care based on respiratory events, OSA/OHS, comorbidities, opioid needs and recovery, rather than BMI alone. Continue head-up recovery, mobilization and coordinated VTE prevention.

sections.title: Procedure-specific complications & follow-up
bullets: Early leak or hemorrhage can present with tachycardia and clinical deterioration. Evaluate pain, fever, falling hemoglobin, perfusion and respiratory findings with the surgical team rather than relying on a single reassuring observation.

Small-bowel obstruction and other bowel complications are recognized after bypass. New significant abdominal symptoms in a prior-bypass patient require attention to altered anatomy and aspiration risk.
Marginal ulcers are associated with NSAID and tobacco exposure. Confirm the postoperative analgesic plan rather than routinely adding NSAIDs to a bypass pathway.

Longer-term issues include micronutrient deficiencies, dumping and postoperative hypoglycemia. These affect the assessment of prior-bypass patients and the need for ongoing nutritional and medical follow-up.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: An adjustable silicone band restricts the proximal stomach without gastric resection or intestinal bypass. New placement is now uncommon, but existing bands and revision/removal cases remain clinically relevant.
Identify whether the case is placement, removal or revision and ask about dysphagia, regurgitation and vomiting; slippage, erosion or esophageal dilation may change risk.
Existing bands can retain material in the pouch/esophagus despite fasting and weight loss. Individualize aspiration precautions rather than assuming a lower current BMI means low risk.
Use ramped airway preparation and protected-airway planning; coordinate any calibration or gastric tube with the surgeon rather than passing a routine blind NG tube.
Recovery emphasizes airway/respiratory safety, nausea control and recognition of persistent swallowing or intake problems, with surgical follow-up for band-specific complications.

sections.title: Procedure anatomy & case-specific priorities
bullets: The band sits around the upper stomach, creating a small proximal pouch. A subcutaneous access port allows adjustment of restriction; there is no intestinal bypass in uncomplicated primary placement.

Banding has declined because weight loss is less than with other procedures and reoperation is frequent. It represented 0.28% of procedures in the 2024 MBSAQIP-based analysis reported by ASMBS in 2026.

Removal or conversion is not equivalent to uncomplicated new placement. Clarify the reason for revision, prior symptoms and planned final anatomy before adopting a standard primary-band anesthetic plan.

A 2013 case report describes aspiration after prolonged fasting, plausibly from retained pouch/esophageal contents. This supports caution but is not a validated universal fasting interval, a routine-deflation mandate or proof that every band patient needs identical induction.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & obesity-related challenges
bullets: Risk is not defined by BMI alone. Review functional capacity, prior anesthetic and airway records, fat distribution, neck mobility, cardiopulmonary disease and the planned procedure or revision.

Screen for known or suspected obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS). Clarify home CPAP/BiPAP use, tolerance and settings; ask the patient to bring their device. Plan the recovery location before induction.

Assess hypertension, coronary disease, ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, diabetes, renal impairment and metabolic-associated liver disease. These comorbidities affect monitoring, fluids, drug titration and postoperative disposition.
Ask specifically about reflux, dysphagia, regurgitation, vomiting, gastroparesis, prior bariatric anatomy and GLP-1 therapy. A reported fasting interval alone does not settle aspiration risk.

Review oral intake, hydration, glycemia, anemia and nutritional concerns, especially after previous bypass or prolonged vomiting. Coordinate correction and perioperative medication plans rather than assuming all bariatric patients have identical requirements.

Confirm weight-rated table and transfer equipment, appropriately sized blood-pressure cuff, positioning aids, vascular-access plan and staffing. Consider ultrasound-guided access and invasive monitoring when clinical risk or unreliable noninvasive measurements warrant it.

sections.title: GLP-1 medications & aspiration planning
bullets: Record the agent, indication, dose, last dose, recent dose increases and gastrointestinal symptoms. Escalation, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or other delayed-emptying conditions increase concern for retained gastric contents.

Most patients can continue GLP-1 therapy before elective surgery under multisociety guidance. Do not apply an automatic seven-day hold to every weekly formulation or cancel solely because a patient takes a GLP-1 drug.

For increased risk, coordinate a liquid-only diet for 24 hours, an individualized anesthetic/aspiration plan and, when appropriate and expertise is available, gastric ultrasound. Diet instructions must also respect the institution’s fasting policy.

Dose escalation or significant ongoing gastrointestinal symptoms may justify deferring elective surgery until risk improves. Make the decision with the surgeon, anesthesia clinician, prescriber and patient; account for glycemic consequences if treatment is withheld.

A medication history does not replace day-of-surgery assessment. If retained contents are suspected, weigh delay against proceeding with appropriate aspiration precautions; do not assume prolonged fasting guarantees an empty stomach.

sections.title: Airway difficulty, ramping & rapid desaturation
bullets: Anticipate difficult mask ventilation and upper-airway obstruction. Excess pharyngeal soft tissue, a large neck, reduced neck movement and loss of airway tone can compromise ventilation; BMI alone does not reliably predict difficult laryngoscopy.

Use ramped, head-up positioning as the default for bariatric airway management. SOBA recommends at least 30° head-up for preoxygenation where feasible; adapt to hemodynamic tolerance and positioning constraints rather than treating the angle as an absolute rule.

Start effective preoxygenation early with a tight mask seal. Consider positive-pressure support or CPAP when appropriate, and nasal oxygen/HFNO for peroxygenation; oxygen delivery during apnea does not replace ventilation when it is needed.

Reduced oxygen reserve and increased oxygen consumption shorten safe apnea time. Prepare adjuncts, two-person mask ventilation, rescue supraglottic airway, suction and an explicit failed-airway plan before induction.

Videolaryngoscopy is recommended first line by SOBA 2025. Choose a familiar blade and technique; maintain a low threshold to consider awake intubation when difficult ventilation/intubation or other airway risks are anticipated, not because of obesity alone.

A cuffed tracheal tube is the usual airway for laparoscopic bariatric surgery. Individualize rapid-sequence induction to aspiration risk while preserving oxygenation; a rescue device remains part of the plan even when not appropriate as the definitive airway.

sections.title: Pulmonary physiology & intraoperative ventilation
bullets: Obesity reduces functional residual capacity and expiratory reserve, limits chest-wall/diaphragm movement and increases oxygen demand. Supine positioning, induction and pneumoperitoneum compound these effects, promoting dependent atelectasis, ventilation–perfusion mismatch and rapid desaturation.

Set lung-protective tidal volume using height-derived predicted body weight, not actual body weight. ERAS describes approximately 6–8 mL/kg PBW as a starting range; titrate ventilation to the clinical situation rather than to excess adipose mass.

Individualize PEEP and recruitment to oxygenation, compliance/driving pressure and blood pressure. Do not use a mandatory PEEP of 10–15 cm H₂O for every patient; an oxygenation gain can be offset by hemodynamic compromise or overdistension.

Head-up/reverse Trendelenburg may improve respiratory mechanics. Pneumoperitoneum increases airway pressures and CO₂ load; trend end-tidal CO₂ and adjust minute ventilation, with blood gas assessment when clinically indicated.

New high airway pressure or hypoxemia requires assessment for reversible causes, including tube position/obstruction and mechanical problems; do not attribute every deterioration to body habitus. Interpret airway pressure alongside compliance, delivered volume and the operative events.

Minimize unnecessary circuit disconnection and loss of PEEP. OSA and especially OHS increase postoperative respiratory risk, so intraoperative ventilation and the extubation/monitoring plan should be linked.

sections.title: NG/OG tubes, bougies & staple-line safety
bullets: Avoid routine or blind NG placement. Bariatric anatomy and fresh staple lines/anastomoses make uncoordinated tube placement hazardous; any necessary tube should be agreed with the surgeon and passed with careful technique.

If decompression is requested during primary surgery, an OG route may be used. BJA Education advises removing the decompression tube once the stomach is decompressed because an unintended tube can be trapped in a staple line.

Do not confuse an OG decompression tube with the calibration bougie intentionally used to size a sleeve. Confirm with the surgeon which device is present, its intended position and the timing of insertion, movement and removal before stapling.

Bougie passage and leak-test tube maneuvers carry perforation/injury risk. Do not force a device against resistance or undertake unfamiliar maneuvers without appropriate experienced assistance and surgical coordination.

Routine postoperative nasogastric decompression is not supported by ERAS. If postoperative decompression becomes necessary, review the exact reconstruction and arrange surgeon-directed placement rather than a blanket “never tube” or “routine blind tube” rule.

sections.title: Drug dosing: TBW, LBW, IBW & adjusted weight
bullets: TBW/actual body weight is the measured weight. LBW estimates non-adipose mass. IBW is a height-based reference weight; adjusted body weight combines IBW with a fraction of excess weight. These terms are not interchangeable, and an adjustment formula is drug- and protocol-specific.

Propofol induction: LBW is a commonly recommended initial scalar, with titration to loss of consciousness and hemodynamic response. A full TBW-derived bolus can be excessive; a scalar is a starting approach, not a guaranteed adequate induction dose.

Propofol maintenance/TIVA: do not copy the induction LBW rule into the infusion. Published approaches differ: older pharmacokinetic reviews discuss TBW/allometric clearance, while the BJA Education/SOBA chart uses adjusted weight. Use an appropriate obesity-validated dosing model or local TIVA protocol and titrate to effect; avoid uncritical linear TBW dosing.

Fentanyl and remifentanil: LBW-based initial dosing is supported in obesity reviews, followed by effect-guided titration. TBW-scaled remifentanil can produce excessive concentrations; opioid sensitivity, OSA/OHS and co-administered sedatives remain important.

Succinylcholine: TBW/actual weight is the commonly recommended obesity scalar when this agent is otherwise appropriate. This does not remove its usual contraindications or replace the institution’s dosing guidance.

Rocuronium: do not apply a single scalar to every context. SOBA 2025 uses LBW in its rapid-sequence example; older non-emergency dosing literature favors IBW to reduce prolonged block. Use the intended airway strategy and institutional protocol, then quantitative monitoring for subsequent dosing and recovery.

Vecuronium and atracurium/cisatracurium: IBW-based dosing is supported in the cited pharmacokinetic review to avoid unnecessarily prolonged block from TBW dosing. This evidence is older; confirm the current local drug protocol and titrate with quantitative neuromuscular monitoring.

Sugammadex: the March 2026 US BRIDION label specifies ACTUAL body weight, with dose selected by depth of block. Do not substitute IBW/adjusted-weight research regimens as the US-label default; severe renal impairment requires particular caution because use is not recommended by that label.

Acetaminophen, antibiotics, anticoagulants and local anesthetics each have agent-specific limits and obesity guidance. Do not extrapolate an opioid or induction scalar to these drugs or multiply adult maximum doses by TBW; use the current drug reference and institutional protocol.

sections.title: Hemodynamics, pneumoperitoneum & monitoring
bullets: Obesity can be associated with increased blood volume/cardiac workload, hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction. OSA/OHS-related pulmonary hypertension and right-ventricular disease may make the patient less tolerant of hypoxemia, hypercarbia or major loading changes.

Pneumoperitoneum can increase vascular resistance/afterload and alter venous return; higher intra-abdominal pressure may reduce cardiac output. Reverse Trendelenburg and positive-pressure ventilation further change preload, so hypertension or hypotension must be interpreted in context.

Trend perfusion, blood pressure, rhythm, CO₂ and operative events, not a single number in isolation. Correct cuff sizing matters; select an arterial line for clinical indications rather than obesity alone.

Discuss insufflation and position changes with the surgeon. If cardiopulmonary tolerance is poor, reassess insufflation pressure, positioning, anesthetic effect and reversible causes rather than treating hypotension with fluid alone.

sections.title: Liver retraction & vagal bradycardia
bullets: Upper-abdominal traction, including liver displacement/retraction, can provoke a vagal bradycardic response. The specific liver-retraction evidence is historical and does not establish a modern bariatric incidence; describe it as a possible trigger, not an expected event in every sleeve.

Peritoneal stretch during insufflation is another recognized vagal trigger. A sudden heart-rate decrease temporally linked to traction or insufflation should prompt immediate communication with the surgeon and assessment of perfusion.

Stop or release the provoking stimulus; stop insufflation and release pneumoperitoneum when that is implicated. Assess oxygenation, ventilation, anesthetic/opioid effects and other reversible causes instead of assuming every bradycardia is benign or purely vagal.

Treat clinically significant bradycardia promptly under the local perioperative bradycardia/ACLS protocol; anticholinergic treatment may be appropriate. If circulatory arrest occurs, initiate resuscitation without delay. Routine prophylactic anticholinergic use for all laparoscopic cases is not established.

sections.title: Intraoperative management & surgical coordination
bullets: Use secure weight-appropriate positioning with protection from sliding, pressure injury and nerve compression. Recheck access and airway security when the table is tilted or surgical access changes.

Maintain an individualized anesthetic with short-acting agents where appropriate, multimodal analgesia and planned PONV prevention. Avoid letting residual sedation, opioid accumulation or incomplete neuromuscular recovery become the limiting factor at emergence.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and match blockade to surgical requirements. If deeper block is requested, plan reliable reversal and objective recovery rather than assuming elapsed time or apparent spontaneous breathing proves recovery.

Coordinate decompression, bougie placement, retraction, insufflation and any leak testing with the surgeon. Unexpected bleeding, airway-pressure changes or hemodynamic deterioration warrant reassessment rather than attribution to routine laparoscopy.

Monitor temperature and glycemia as indicated. Apply antimicrobial and thromboprophylaxis protocols matched to the patient and procedure; there is no single obesity dose rule that safely covers all medications.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: A sleeve component is combined with substantial small-bowel bypass. This is a less common, more complex operation with greater malabsorption than sleeve alone.
Plan for the shared obesity airway and cardiopulmonary risks, plus the requirements of a more involved reconstruction.
Coordinate all gastric tubes/bougies and avoid routine blind NG placement; identify the exact reconstructed anatomy.
Drug-specific dosing, individualized perfusion and ventilation, opioid-sparing recovery and objective neuromuscular reversal remain central.
Nutritional status deserves particular attention: protein/nutrient malabsorption, vitamin/mineral follow-up and postoperative intake problems are important in these patients.

sections.title: Procedure anatomy & case-specific priorities
bullets: BPD-DS combines a sleeve-shaped stomach with diversion of food into distal small bowel, substantially reducing the bowel length through which food and digestive secretions mix. It is not simply another name for a sleeve or Roux-en-Y bypass.

The operation is more complex and generally requires more operative time than simpler bariatric procedures. Match monitoring, positioning and recovery planning to the patient and reconstruction rather than a fixed duration estimate.

BPD-DS represented 1.27% of procedures in the 2024 MBSAQIP-based analysis reported by ASMBS in 2026. It belongs in the library, but should be identified as less common rather than a usual first-line case mix.

The degree of malabsorption creates a greater risk of vitamin and micronutrient deficiencies than other common operations. Ongoing supplementation and multidisciplinary follow-up are integral to care.

sections.title: NG/OG tubes, bougies & staple-line safety
bullets: Avoid routine or blind NG placement. Bariatric anatomy and fresh staple lines/anastomoses make uncoordinated tube placement hazardous; any necessary tube should be agreed with the surgeon and passed with careful technique.

If decompression is requested during primary surgery, an OG route may be used. BJA Education advises removing the decompression tube once the stomach is decompressed because an unintended tube can be trapped in a staple line.

Do not confuse an OG decompression tube with the calibration bougie intentionally used to size a sleeve. Confirm with the surgeon which device is present, its intended position and the timing of insertion, movement and removal before stapling.

Bougie passage and leak-test tube maneuvers carry perforation/injury risk. Do not force a device against resistance or undertake unfamiliar maneuvers without appropriate experienced assistance and surgical coordination.

Routine postoperative nasogastric decompression is not supported by ERAS. If postoperative decompression becomes necessary, review the exact reconstruction and arrange surgeon-directed placement rather than a blanket “never tube” or “routine blind tube” rule.

sections.title: Drug dosing: TBW, LBW, IBW & adjusted weight
bullets: TBW/actual body weight is the measured weight. LBW estimates non-adipose mass. IBW is a height-based reference weight; adjusted body weight combines IBW with a fraction of excess weight. These terms are not interchangeable, and an adjustment formula is drug- and protocol-specific.

Propofol induction: LBW is a commonly recommended initial scalar, with titration to loss of consciousness and hemodynamic response. A full TBW-derived bolus can be excessive; a scalar is a starting approach, not a guaranteed adequate induction dose.

Propofol maintenance/TIVA: do not copy the induction LBW rule into the infusion. Published approaches differ: older pharmacokinetic reviews discuss TBW/allometric clearance, while the BJA Education/SOBA chart uses adjusted weight. Use an appropriate obesity-validated dosing model or local TIVA protocol and titrate to effect; avoid uncritical linear TBW dosing.

Fentanyl and remifentanil: LBW-based initial dosing is supported in obesity reviews, followed by effect-guided titration. TBW-scaled remifentanil can produce excessive concentrations; opioid sensitivity, OSA/OHS and co-administered sedatives remain important.

Succinylcholine: TBW/actual weight is the commonly recommended obesity scalar when this agent is otherwise appropriate. This does not remove its usual contraindications or replace the institution’s dosing guidance.

Rocuronium: do not apply a single scalar to every context. SOBA 2025 uses LBW in its rapid-sequence example; older non-emergency dosing literature favors IBW to reduce prolonged block. Use the intended airway strategy and institutional protocol, then quantitative monitoring for subsequent dosing and recovery.

Vecuronium and atracurium/cisatracurium: IBW-based dosing is supported in the cited pharmacokinetic review to avoid unnecessarily prolonged block from TBW dosing. This evidence is older; confirm the current local drug protocol and titrate with quantitative neuromuscular monitoring.

Sugammadex: the March 2026 US BRIDION label specifies ACTUAL body weight, with dose selected by depth of block. Do not substitute IBW/adjusted-weight research regimens as the US-label default; severe renal impairment requires particular caution because use is not recommended by that label.

Acetaminophen, antibiotics, anticoagulants and local anesthetics each have agent-specific limits and obesity guidance. Do not extrapolate an opioid or induction scalar to these drugs or multiply adult maximum doses by TBW; use the current drug reference and institutional protocol.

sections.title: Hemodynamics, pneumoperitoneum & monitoring
bullets: Obesity can be associated with increased blood volume/cardiac workload, hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction. OSA/OHS-related pulmonary hypertension and right-ventricular disease may make the patient less tolerant of hypoxemia, hypercarbia or major loading changes.

Pneumoperitoneum can increase vascular resistance/afterload and alter venous return; higher intra-abdominal pressure may reduce cardiac output. Reverse Trendelenburg and positive-pressure ventilation further change preload, so hypertension or hypotension must be interpreted in context.

Trend perfusion, blood pressure, rhythm, CO₂ and operative events, not a single number in isolation. Correct cuff sizing matters; select an arterial line for clinical indications rather than obesity alone.

Discuss insufflation and position changes with the surgeon. If cardiopulmonary tolerance is poor, reassess insufflation pressure, positioning, anesthetic effect and reversible causes rather than treating hypotension with fluid alone.

sections.title: Liver retraction & vagal bradycardia
bullets: Upper-abdominal traction, including liver displacement/retraction, can provoke a vagal bradycardic response. The specific liver-retraction evidence is historical and does not establish a modern bariatric incidence; describe it as a possible trigger, not an expected event in every sleeve.

Peritoneal stretch during insufflation is another recognized vagal trigger. A sudden heart-rate decrease temporally linked to traction or insufflation should prompt immediate communication with the surgeon and assessment of perfusion.

Stop or release the provoking stimulus; stop insufflation and release pneumoperitoneum when that is implicated. Assess oxygenation, ventilation, anesthetic/opioid effects and other reversible causes instead of assuming every bradycardia is benign or purely vagal.

Treat clinically significant bradycardia promptly under the local perioperative bradycardia/ACLS protocol; anticholinergic treatment may be appropriate. If circulatory arrest occurs, initiate resuscitation without delay. Routine prophylactic anticholinergic use for all laparoscopic cases is not established.

sections.title: Intraoperative management & surgical coordination
bullets: Use secure weight-appropriate positioning with protection from sliding, pressure injury and nerve compression. Recheck access and airway security when the table is tilted or surgical access changes.

Maintain an individualized anesthetic with short-acting agents where appropriate, multimodal analgesia and planned PONV prevention. Avoid letting residual sedation, opioid accumulation or incomplete neuromuscular recovery become the limiting factor at emergence.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and match blockade to surgical requirements. If deeper block is requested, plan reliable reversal and objective recovery rather than assuming elapsed time or apparent spontaneous breathing proves recovery.

Coordinate decompression, bougie placement, retraction, insufflation and any leak testing with the surgeon. Unexpected bleeding, airway-pressure changes or hemodynamic deterioration warrant reassessment rather than attribution to routine laparoscopy.

Monitor temperature and glycemia as indicated. Apply antimicrobial and thromboprophylaxis protocols matched to the patient and procedure; there is no single obesity dose rule that safely covers all medications.

sections.title: Fluids, perfusion & venous thromboembolism
bullets: Aim for individualized euvolemia and adequate tissue perfusion. ERAS favors goal-directed fluid management where appropriate and avoidance of both excessive restriction and fluid overload.
Evaluate hypotension for anesthetic vasodilation, position/insufflation effects, bleeding and other causes. A fluid bolus is not the automatic answer to every reduction in blood pressure.

Use mechanical and pharmacologic VTE prevention according to bleeding risk, renal function, procedure and institutional policy. Prior VTE, immobility and other risk factors may influence extended prophylaxis; duration is individualized.

Plan early mobilization and postoperative hydration. Persistent tachycardia or dyspnea is not simply pain or dehydration until important causes such as bleeding, leak, respiratory compromise and VTE have been considered.

sections.title: Analgesia, nausea prevention & recovery
bullets: Favor multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia. Local infiltration or regional techniques can reduce opioid needs; consider organ function, maximum doses and the procedure-specific surgical plan.

Use risk-based multimodal PONV prophylaxis and a rescue plan. Vomiting is particularly undesirable after upper-GI surgery and should not be dismissed when accompanied by pain, tachycardia or inability to tolerate intake.
NSAID suitability differs by procedure and patient. In Roux-en-Y patients, marginal-ulcer risk is a specific concern; do not automatically transfer a generic NSAID-based pathway to a bypass patient.
Resume oral intake and mobilization according to the bariatric pathway. Persistent intolerance, dehydration or nutritional problems need follow-up rather than repeated symptomatic treatment alone.

sections.title: Extubation, CPAP/BiPAP & postoperative monitoring
bullets: Plan extubation as deliberately as induction. Use head-up positioning, adequate preoxygenation, awake airway control and objectively confirmed neuromuscular recovery; have equipment and assistance ready if re-intubation is necessary.

Continue prescribed home CPAP/BiPAP in the postoperative period when indicated. For increased desaturation risk, consider extubation directly to CPAP or HFNO; OHS or persistent hypoxemia may warrant bilevel/noninvasive ventilatory support and a higher-acuity setting.

CPAP is not automatically prohibited after bariatric surgery and is not mandatory for every patient. Match support to OSA/OHS, oxygenation, ventilation and surgical/clinical circumstances; persistent deterioration requires escalation, not repeated mask adjustments alone.

Monitor for obstruction, hypoventilation, residual block and opioid-related respiratory depression. Supplemental oxygen can conceal impaired ventilation; a reassuring oxygen saturation alone does not exclude hypercapnia or ventilatory failure.

Choose PACU, monitored ward or higher-acuity care based on respiratory events, OSA/OHS, comorbidities, opioid needs and recovery, rather than BMI alone. Continue head-up recovery, mobilization and coordinated VTE prevention.

sections.title: Procedure-specific complications & follow-up
bullets: As with other reconstructed bariatric procedures, acute deterioration requires assessment for leak, bleeding, respiratory compromise and VTE rather than assuming an uncomplicated recovery.
BPD-DS carries substantial malabsorption and nutritional risk; review prior supplementation, intake, hydration and laboratory concerns when patients return for other procedures.

Reflux and looser/frequent bowel movements are recognized disadvantages. Persistent intake intolerance or dehydration should prompt clinical review, not simply an assumption that symptoms are expected.

title: SADI-S
aliases: single anastomosis duodeno ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy combines a sleeve with a duodeno-ileal connection. It is a less common alternative related to, but distinct from, conventional duodenal switch.
Apply ramped airway preparation, rapid-desaturation precautions and individualized pneumoperitoneum/ventilation management.
Confirm whether this is primary surgery or a staged/revisional operation. Avoid blind NG placement and coordinate gastric devices with the surgeon.
Use agent-specific drug scalars, opioid-sparing analgesia and planned awake extubation with respiratory support when indicated.
Do not equate fewer anastomoses with no malabsorption: nutritional deficiencies, reflux and postoperative intolerance still require follow-up.

sections.title: Procedure anatomy & case-specific priorities
bullets: A sleeve is created and the proximal duodenum is connected to a distal ileal loop. Compared with conventional BPD-DS, the bowel reconstruction uses one intestinal anastomosis; the procedures should remain separate case references.
SADI-S represented 1.51% of analyzed procedures in the 2024 MBSAQIP-based study reported by ASMBS in 2026. It is less common than sleeve or Roux-en-Y in that dataset.

The procedure is intended to combine sleeve restriction/metabolic effects with altered intestinal nutrient transit. It does not eliminate vitamin/mineral deficiency risk and requires ongoing nutritional follow-up.

Confirm previous sleeve or other surgery and the actual reconstruction before tube placement or anesthetic planning. Primary, staged and revisional anatomy should not be inferred from the short label alone.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & obesity-related challenges
bullets: Risk is not defined by BMI alone. Review functional capacity, prior anesthetic and airway records, fat distribution, neck mobility, cardiopulmonary disease and the planned procedure or revision.

Screen for known or suspected obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS). Clarify home CPAP/BiPAP use, tolerance and settings; ask the patient to bring their device. Plan the recovery location before induction.

Assess hypertension, coronary disease, ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, diabetes, renal impairment and metabolic-associated liver disease. These comorbidities affect monitoring, fluids, drug titration and postoperative disposition.
Ask specifically about reflux, dysphagia, regurgitation, vomiting, gastroparesis, prior bariatric anatomy and GLP-1 therapy. A reported fasting interval alone does not settle aspiration risk.

Review oral intake, hydration, glycemia, anemia and nutritional concerns, especially after previous bypass or prolonged vomiting. Coordinate correction and perioperative medication plans rather than assuming all bariatric patients have identical requirements.

Confirm weight-rated table and transfer equipment, appropriately sized blood-pressure cuff, positioning aids, vascular-access plan and staffing. Consider ultrasound-guided access and invasive monitoring when clinical risk or unreliable noninvasive measurements warrant it.

sections.title: GLP-1 medications & aspiration planning
bullets: Record the agent, indication, dose, last dose, recent dose increases and gastrointestinal symptoms. Escalation, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or other delayed-emptying conditions increase concern for retained gastric contents.

Most patients can continue GLP-1 therapy before elective surgery under multisociety guidance. Do not apply an automatic seven-day hold to every weekly formulation or cancel solely because a patient takes a GLP-1 drug.

For increased risk, coordinate a liquid-only diet for 24 hours, an individualized anesthetic/aspiration plan and, when appropriate and expertise is available, gastric ultrasound. Diet instructions must also respect the institution’s fasting policy.

Dose escalation or significant ongoing gastrointestinal symptoms may justify deferring elective surgery until risk improves. Make the decision with the surgeon, anesthesia clinician, prescriber and patient; account for glycemic consequences if treatment is withheld.

A medication history does not replace day-of-surgery assessment. If retained contents are suspected, weigh delay against proceeding with appropriate aspiration precautions; do not assume prolonged fasting guarantees an empty stomach.

sections.title: Airway difficulty, ramping & rapid desaturation
bullets: Anticipate difficult mask ventilation and upper-airway obstruction. Excess pharyngeal soft tissue, a large neck, reduced neck movement and loss of airway tone can compromise ventilation; BMI alone does not reliably predict difficult laryngoscopy.

Use ramped, head-up positioning as the default for bariatric airway management. SOBA recommends at least 30° head-up for preoxygenation where feasible; adapt to hemodynamic tolerance and positioning constraints rather than treating the angle as an absolute rule.

Start effective preoxygenation early with a tight mask seal. Consider positive-pressure support or CPAP when appropriate, and nasal oxygen/HFNO for peroxygenation; oxygen delivery during apnea does not replace ventilation when it is needed.

Reduced oxygen reserve and increased oxygen consumption shorten safe apnea time. Prepare adjuncts, two-person mask ventilation, rescue supraglottic airway, suction and an explicit failed-airway plan before induction.

Videolaryngoscopy is recommended first line by SOBA 2025. Choose a familiar blade and technique; maintain a low threshold to consider awake intubation when difficult ventilation/intubation or other airway risks are anticipated, not because of obesity alone.

A cuffed tracheal tube is the usual airway for laparoscopic bariatric surgery. Individualize rapid-sequence induction to aspiration risk while preserving oxygenation; a rescue device remains part of the plan even when not appropriate as the definitive airway.

sections.title: Pulmonary physiology & intraoperative ventilation
bullets: Obesity reduces functional residual capacity and expiratory reserve, limits chest-wall/diaphragm movement and increases oxygen demand. Supine positioning, induction and pneumoperitoneum compound these effects, promoting dependent atelectasis, ventilation–perfusion mismatch and rapid desaturation.

Set lung-protective tidal volume using height-derived predicted body weight, not actual body weight. ERAS describes approximately 6–8 mL/kg PBW as a starting range; titrate ventilation to the clinical situation rather than to excess adipose mass.

Individualize PEEP and recruitment to oxygenation, compliance/driving pressure and blood pressure. Do not use a mandatory PEEP of 10–15 cm H₂O for every patient; an oxygenation gain can be offset by hemodynamic compromise or overdistension.

Head-up/reverse Trendelenburg may improve respiratory mechanics. Pneumoperitoneum increases airway pressures and CO₂ load; trend end-tidal CO₂ and adjust minute ventilation, with blood gas assessment when clinically indicated.

New high airway pressure or hypoxemia requires assessment for reversible causes, including tube position/obstruction and mechanical problems; do not attribute every deterioration to body habitus. Interpret airway pressure alongside compliance, delivered volume and the operative events.

Minimize unnecessary circuit disconnection and loss of PEEP. OSA and especially OHS increase postoperative respiratory risk, so intraoperative ventilation and the extubation/monitoring plan should be linked.

bullets: Removal of devitalized or infected burn tissue may range from a limited procedure to extensive excision; procedure duration alone does not predict physiologic risk.

Reassess altered drug response and neuromuscular-blocker safety at every operation; use multimodal procedural and postoperative analgesia.

sections.title: Burn size, timing & physiologic phase
bullets: Establish the injury date/time, mechanism, depth, total body surface area (TBSA), inhalation injury, associated trauma and planned excision/donor area. A short dressing procedure, major acute excision and late healed reconstruction are different anesthetic problems.

Early major-burn physiology is dominated by capillary leak, intravascular depletion and depressed cardiac output. Later hyperdynamic/hypermetabolic physiology can increase oxygen consumption, CO₂ production and drug clearance; phase transitions are approximate, not clock-based guarantees.
Current physiology overrides the calendar. Shock, sepsis, ongoing bleeding, renal/hepatic dysfunction or poor nutrition can coexist with the expected burn phase and change the anesthetic response.

Review prior anesthetics, airway findings, access sites, transfusions, current analgesic/sedative infusions and previous drug response. Repeated surgery creates changing airway anatomy, tolerance, procedural anxiety and cumulative practical challenges, not a reason to recycle an unchanged plan.

For healed contracture/reconstruction cases, distinguish residual scar/airway/functional problems from active burn-shock physiology. Do not automatically apply acute-resuscitation formulas or smoke-toxin assumptions to a remote, healed injury.

sections.title: Airway, inhalation injury & ventilation
bullets: Concerning findings include enclosed-space smoke exposure, facial/neck burns, soot, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridor, altered consciousness and respiratory distress. Facial burns or singed hair alone do not prove obstruction; assess the whole clinical picture.

Airway edema may progress over hours and worsen with resuscitation. Reassess frequently and secure a threatened airway before edema makes intubation difficult; urgency, oxygenation and anticipated difficult ventilation/intubation determine the approach.

Prepare advanced airway equipment and an explicit rescue plan. Existing airway burns, tenuous tube fixation and repeated transfers increase the consequences of accidental extubation; protect and reassess the airway throughout positioning and transport.

Lower-airway injury may cause bronchospasm, secretions/casts, impaired clearance, atelectasis and evolving gas-exchange failure. A normal initial chest radiograph does not exclude inhalation injury; bronchoscopy may help assess injury within the burn-team pathway.

Continue individualized lung-protective ventilation and required PEEP. Hypermetabolism increases CO₂ production; preserve oxygenation and avoid derecruitment during ventilator changes rather than using fixed settings for every burn patient.

Late facial or neck contracture can markedly reduce mouth opening and neck extension. Review earlier airway records and consider an awake airway strategy when indicated; a previously easy acute-burn intubation does not guarantee an easy reconstructive airway.

sections.title: Smoke exposure: carbon monoxide & cyanide
bullets: Conventional two-wavelength pulse oximetry can be falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Measure carboxyhemoglobin with blood co-oximetry when exposure is suspected; either venous or arterial blood may be used.

Interpret COHb alongside exposure history, symptoms and elapsed time after oxygen/removal from the fire. A falling level or apparently adequate PaO₂ does not alone establish that clinically important CO toxicity is absent.

Provide high-concentration oxygen promptly for suspected CO poisoning and obtain toxicology/Poison Control input for severity-based treatment, including whether hyperbaric consultation is appropriate. Do not use a single COHb cutoff as the entire decision.

Closed-space structural fires can also produce cyanide exposure. Soot plus altered mental status, cardiovascular instability or marked lactic acidosis raises concern, but lactate is not specific and not every smoke-exposed patient has cyanide poisoning.

The CYANOKIT label supports prompt hydroxocobalamin when clinical suspicion is high, alongside airway, oxygenation and circulatory support. Do not delay urgent treatment for a confirmatory cyanide test or lactate result; use the institutional toxicology pathway.

If hydroxocobalamin is given, communicate this to the laboratory and renal team: its red color can interfere with some assays and dialysis blood-leak detectors. Monitor renal function and interpret affected results with laboratory support.

sections.title: Resuscitation, ongoing losses & perfusion
bullets: Separate the initial burn-resuscitation requirement from maintenance needs and operative blood-loss replacement. Excision hemorrhage cannot be managed simply by restarting a burn formula.

The ABA 2024 guideline addresses adults with burns ≥20% TBSA during the first 48 hours. The recommended starting approach uses a 2 mL/kg/%TBSA first-24-hour volume estimate rather than routinely starting at 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, followed by response-guided rate titration. This is not an hourly dose or a fixed volume to infuse regardless of physiology.

Use the burn center’s timed resuscitation protocol and reconcile fluid already given. Follow urine output and the broader perfusion picture, including hemodynamics, lactate/base deficit trends and organ function; avoid both under-resuscitation and fluid creep.

Albumin may be considered during initial resuscitation, especially with larger burns, to reduce resuscitation volume and improve urine output. This is a specialist, patient-specific decision, not routine replacement of every crystalloid infusion.

After initial resuscitation, wound/evaporative losses, ongoing surgery, changing capillary permeability and mobilization of edema alter fluid needs. Reassess rather than carrying the first-day fluid rate forward indefinitely.

Electrical injury with deep muscle damage and rhabdomyolysis may need a different renal/perfusion strategy. Do not extrapolate one thermal-burn urine-output goal or an old mannitol/bicarbonate recipe to every electrical injury.

sections.title: Excision blood loss & transfusion planning
bullets: Major excision can bleed rapidly from broad surfaces and donor sites. Bleeding may be underestimated because blood mixes with irrigation, collects beneath the patient or remains hidden under bulky dressings.

Estimate risk with the surgeon using the area and depth to be excised, infection, timing, donor sites and expected duration. Published percentage-of-blood-volume estimates vary and should not be treated as a reliable individual blood-loss calculator.

For substantial anticipated loss, establish suitable access, arrange crossmatched blood and a clear escalation/massive-transfusion plan; arterial monitoring and serial laboratory assessment may be appropriate.

Follow perfusion, serial hemoglobin, coagulation and temperature together. A stable-patient transfusion threshold is not a reason to wait during active major hemorrhage; follow the institution’s hemorrhage and blood-product pathway.

Tourniquets, staged excision, compression and topical/infiltrated hemostatic agents may limit bleeding. Coordinate agent identity, concentration, total amount and timing with the surgeon rather than assuming topical treatment has no systemic relevance.
Continue surveillance after dressings are applied and during transfer. Apparent completion of the procedure does not establish that wound bleeding has stopped.

sections.title: Temperature preservation & exposure
bullets: Loss of the skin barrier, broad exposure, irrigation and fluid/blood administration create substantial hypothermia risk. Monitor core temperature throughout significant burn surgery and plan warming before exposing the patient.

Use a warmed operating room, warmed IV fluids/blood, appropriate active warming and insulation of areas not being treated. Minimize unnecessary exposure and coordinate warming devices with wound, graft and surgical-access constraints.
Hypothermia worsens the physiologic burden and can aggravate coagulopathy and blood loss. Temperature management is part of resuscitation, not a comfort-only intervention.

Later hypermetabolic burn patients may be febrile or hyperthermic. Follow measured temperature and the clinical context rather than indiscriminately heating an already hyperthermic patient; fever alone does not distinguish inflammation from infection.

sections.title: Neuromuscular blockers: major safety changes
bullets: After major burns, extrajunctional acetylcholine-receptor upregulation makes succinylcholine capable of causing severe, potentially fatal hyperkalemia. Use a conservative avoidance boundary after the first 24 hours rather than treating 24–48 hours as an assured safe window.

Risk may persist for months or longer and cannot be cleared by the calendar alone. Active wounds, impaired mobility and ongoing critical illness require particular caution; confirm the plan with the burn/anesthesia team rather than declaring succinylcholine safe at an arbitrary follow-up date.

Even in the first 24 hours, succinylcholine is not automatically appropriate: consider existing hyperkalemia, electrical/crush muscle injury and other contraindications. The early time window does not cancel patient-specific risk.

Resistance to nondepolarizing blockers develops with major burns, often becoming evident several days after injury. Larger doses or more frequent redosing may be required, but onset and duration remain variable.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and titrate to the actual surgical/airway need. Do not assume a standard rapid-sequence dose provides standard onset, or that a high administered dose means recovery is complete at emergence.

sections.title: Altered drug response & repeated anesthetics
bullets: Early low cardiac output and reduced renal/hepatic perfusion can decrease drug clearance and worsen sensitivity to hemodynamic depression. Titrate induction to current shock physiology rather than to a generic “burn patients need more” rule.

Later hypermetabolism, altered protein binding, expanded distribution volume and increased clearance may increase requirements for some drugs. Organ failure or sepsis can reverse that expectation; adjust to effect and current physiology.

Opioid and sedative tolerance may develop during prolonged care. Reconcile ongoing infusions and baseline requirements with the ICU/pain team; abrupt interruption can cause undertreatment or withdrawal.

Repeated operations should trigger reassessment of prior response, anxiety, emerging neuropathic pain, delirium and weaning needs. There is no single fixed anesthetic dose escalation that applies to every return to the OR.

sections.title: Background, procedural, donor-site & neuropathic pain
bullets: Assess background pain, breakthrough pain, procedural pain and neuropathic symptoms separately. Include donor sites, positioning, lines and associated injuries rather than asking only about the burned wound.

Use multimodal therapy tailored to physiology: acetaminophen with attention to liver function/total daily exposure, titrated opioids and selected adjuncts. NSAID decisions require renal, bleeding and graft-related risk assessment with the surgical team.

Ketamine may support monitored procedural sedation or serve as an opioid-sparing adjunct. Appropriate staff, monitoring and airway rescue remain necessary; its use does not guarantee preserved ventilation or hemodynamic stability.

Dexmedetomidine may help with analgosedation, anxiety or withdrawal-related needs, but bradycardia and hypotension matter. Consider neuropathic agents for a suitable pain phenotype rather than adding them routinely to every burn case.

Regional techniques may improve donor-site or extremity analgesia and reduce opioid needs. Match the block to the operative sites and weigh infection, coagulation, anticoagulation, access and postoperative assessment needs; neuraxial techniques require particular caution in unstable or infected patients.

Plan pain control beyond the incision: dressing changes, mobilization and later procedures can be intensely painful. Include specialist pain care, anticipatory dosing and nonpharmacologic measures such as psychological support or distraction.

sections.title: Access, monitoring & graft protection
bullets: Map usable sites before preparation and positioning. Edema, dressings and burned skin may limit peripheral IVs, arterial access, ECG contact, cuffs and oximetry; ultrasound guidance and a backup access plan may be needed.

Prefer intact skin when feasible and avoid pressure, shear or unnecessary adhesive trauma over wounds and fresh grafts. If monitoring/access must cross an affected area, coordinate protection and asepsis with the burn team rather than forgoing essential monitoring.

Select arterial and central access for the actual need: anticipated hemorrhage, repeated sampling, vasoactive support or limited access. Their placement is not mandatory solely because the patient has a burn.

Monitor temperature, ventilation and neuromuscular response as well as standard cardiovascular parameters. Oximeter placement limitations and possible CO exposure are separate problems; a good pulse waveform does not solve the COHb measurement limitation.

sections.title: Electrolytes, electrical injury & kidney function
bullets: Assess potassium, acid–base status, renal function and the broader injury pattern when muscle damage, electrical injury, crush injury or shock is present. A small skin wound can coexist with substantial deeper electrical injury.

Review ECG/rhythm and associated trauma after electrical exposure. Monitoring intensity depends on symptoms, ECG abnormalities, mechanism and clinical course; historical series should not be treated as a universal discharge or telemetry-duration rule.
Compartment compromise requires urgent surgical assessment. An escharotomy releases constricting skin; persistent deep-compartment pathology may require fasciotomy, not simply additional fluid.

sections.title: Infection, inflammation & nutrition
bullets: Loss of the skin barrier, invasive devices and repeated procedures increase infection risk. Distinguish colonization from invasive infection and assess the trend in organ function, wounds and hemodynamics rather than fever or tachycardia alone.

Major-burn inflammation and hypermetabolism can resemble sepsis. New deterioration requires evaluation of wound, pulmonary, line and other sources with the burn team; culture-directed treatment and source control may be needed.

Reconcile perioperative prophylaxis with ongoing antimicrobial treatment and local microbiology. Inhalation injury alone is not an automatic indication for routine prophylactic systemic antibiotics or steroids.

sections.title: Extubation, recovery & postoperative disposition
bullets: Extubation depends on airway patency/edema, gas exchange, ventilation, neuromuscular recovery, hemodynamics, metabolic status and anticipated ongoing bleeding or repeat surgery. Finishing a brief procedure does not make an unstable burn patient ready for extubation.

Consider continued ventilation/ICU care when inhalation injury, unresolved shock, major blood loss, significant edema or other organ dysfunction persists. Stable limited procedures and healed reconstruction may have different recovery needs.
Protect the tube, maintain required PEEP, continue essential infusions and warming, and hand over blood loss, fluids/products, latest laboratory results and evolving airway concerns during transfer.

Postoperative surveillance includes hidden wound bleeding, temperature, graft/limb assessment, renal/electrolyte trends and adequate analgesia. Coordinate pain and sedation plans with respiratory safety and rehabilitation needs.

sections.title: Evidence scope & clinical review
bullets: This adult reference is a clinical review draft, not a patient-specific order set. Current physiology, burn-center practice and specialist judgment determine management; pediatric burn resuscitation is outside its scope.

Consider continued ventilation/ICU care when inhalation injury, unresolved shock, major blood loss, significant edema or other organ dysfunction persists. Stable limited procedures and healed reconstruction may have different recovery needs.
Protect the tube, maintain required PEEP, continue essential infusions and warming, and hand over blood loss, fluids/products, latest laboratory results and evolving airway concerns during transfer.

Postoperative surveillance includes hidden wound bleeding, temperature, graft/limb assessment, renal/electrolyte trends and adequate analgesia. Coordinate pain and sedation plans with respiratory safety and rehabilitation needs.

sections.title: Airway, inhalation injury & ventilation
bullets: Concerning findings include enclosed-space smoke exposure, facial/neck burns, soot, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridor, altered consciousness and respiratory distress. Facial burns or singed hair alone do not prove obstruction; assess the whole clinical picture.

Prepare advanced airway equipment and an explicit rescue plan. Existing airway burns, tenuous tube fixation and repeated transfers increase the consequences of accidental extubation; protect and reassess the airway throughout positioning and transport.

Lower-airway injury may cause bronchospasm, secretions/casts, impaired clearance, atelectasis and evolving gas-exchange failure. A normal initial chest radiograph does not exclude inhalation injury; bronchoscopy may help assess injury within the burn-team pathway.

Continue individualized lung-protective ventilation and required PEEP. Hypermetabolism increases CO₂ production; preserve oxygenation and avoid derecruitment during ventilator changes rather than using fixed settings for every burn patient.

Late facial or neck contracture can markedly reduce mouth opening and neck extension. Review earlier airway records and consider an awake airway strategy when indicated; a previously easy acute-burn intubation does not guarantee an easy reconstructive airway.

sections.title: Smoke exposure: carbon monoxide & cyanide
bullets: Conventional two-wavelength pulse oximetry can be falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Measure carboxyhemoglobin with blood co-oximetry when exposure is suspected; either venous or arterial blood may be used.

Interpret COHb alongside exposure history, symptoms and elapsed time after oxygen/removal from the fire. A falling level or apparently adequate PaO₂ does not alone establish that clinically important CO toxicity is absent.

Provide high-concentration oxygen promptly for suspected CO poisoning and obtain toxicology/Poison Control input for severity-based treatment, including whether hyperbaric consultation is appropriate. Do not use a single COHb cutoff as the entire decision.

Closed-space structural fires can also produce cyanide exposure. Soot plus altered mental status, cardiovascular instability or marked lactic acidosis raises concern, but lactate is not specific and not every smoke-exposed patient has cyanide poisoning.

The CYANOKIT label supports prompt hydroxocobalamin when clinical suspicion is high, alongside airway, oxygenation and circulatory support. Do not delay urgent treatment for a confirmatory cyanide test or lactate result; use the institutional toxicology pathway.

If hydroxocobalamin is given, communicate this to the laboratory and renal team: its red color can interfere with some assays and dialysis blood-leak detectors. Monitor renal function and interpret affected results with laboratory support.

sections.title: Resuscitation, ongoing losses & perfusion
bullets: Separate the initial burn-resuscitation requirement from maintenance needs and operative blood-loss replacement. Excision hemorrhage cannot be managed simply by restarting a burn formula.

The ABA 2024 guideline addresses adults with burns ≥20% TBSA during the first 48 hours. The recommended starting approach uses a 2 mL/kg/%TBSA first-24-hour volume estimate rather than routinely starting at 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, followed by response-guided rate titration. This is not an hourly dose or a fixed volume to infuse regardless of physiology.

Use the burn center’s timed resuscitation protocol and reconcile fluid already given. Follow urine output and the broader perfusion picture, including hemodynamics, lactate/base deficit trends and organ function; avoid both under-resuscitation and fluid creep.

Albumin may be considered during initial resuscitation, especially with larger burns, to reduce resuscitation volume and improve urine output. This is a specialist, patient-specific decision, not routine replacement of every crystalloid infusion.

After initial resuscitation, wound/evaporative losses, ongoing surgery, changing capillary permeability and mobilization of edema alter fluid needs. Reassess rather than carrying the first-day fluid rate forward indefinitely.

Electrical injury with deep muscle damage and rhabdomyolysis may need a different renal/perfusion strategy. Do not extrapolate one thermal-burn urine-output goal or an old mannitol/bicarbonate recipe to every electrical injury.

sections.title: Excision blood loss & transfusion planning
bullets: Major excision can bleed rapidly from broad surfaces and donor sites. Bleeding may be underestimated because blood mixes with irrigation, collects beneath the patient or remains hidden under bulky dressings.

Estimate risk with the surgeon using the area and depth to be excised, infection, timing, donor sites and expected duration. Published percentage-of-blood-volume estimates vary and should not be treated as a reliable individual blood-loss calculator.

For substantial anticipated loss, establish suitable access, arrange crossmatched blood and a clear escalation/massive-transfusion plan; arterial monitoring and serial laboratory assessment may be appropriate.

Follow perfusion, serial hemoglobin, coagulation and temperature together. A stable-patient transfusion threshold is not a reason to wait during active major hemorrhage; follow the institution’s hemorrhage and blood-product pathway.

Tourniquets, staged excision, compression and topical/infiltrated hemostatic agents may limit bleeding. Coordinate agent identity, concentration, total amount and timing with the surgeon rather than assuming topical treatment has no systemic relevance.
Continue surveillance after dressings are applied and during transfer. Apparent completion of the procedure does not establish that wound bleeding has stopped.

sections.title: Temperature preservation & exposure
bullets: Loss of the skin barrier, broad exposure, irrigation and fluid/blood administration create substantial hypothermia risk. Monitor core temperature throughout significant burn surgery and plan warming before exposing the patient.

Use a warmed operating room, warmed IV fluids/blood, appropriate active warming and insulation of areas not being treated. Minimize unnecessary exposure and coordinate warming devices with wound, graft and surgical-access constraints.
Hypothermia worsens the physiologic burden and can aggravate coagulopathy and blood loss. Temperature management is part of resuscitation, not a comfort-only intervention.

Later hypermetabolic burn patients may be febrile or hyperthermic. Follow measured temperature and the clinical context rather than indiscriminately heating an already hyperthermic patient; fever alone does not distinguish inflammation from infection.

sections.title: Neuromuscular blockers: major safety changes
bullets: After major burns, extrajunctional acetylcholine-receptor upregulation makes succinylcholine capable of causing severe, potentially fatal hyperkalemia. Use a conservative avoidance boundary after the first 24 hours rather than treating 24–48 hours as an assured safe window.

Risk may persist for months or longer and cannot be cleared by the calendar alone. Active wounds, impaired mobility and ongoing critical illness require particular caution; confirm the plan with the burn/anesthesia team rather than declaring succinylcholine safe at an arbitrary follow-up date.

Even in the first 24 hours, succinylcholine is not automatically appropriate: consider existing hyperkalemia, electrical/crush muscle injury and other contraindications. The early time window does not cancel patient-specific risk.

Resistance to nondepolarizing blockers develops with major burns, often becoming evident several days after injury. Larger doses or more frequent redosing may be required, but onset and duration remain variable.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and titrate to the actual surgical/airway need. Do not assume a standard rapid-sequence dose provides standard onset, or that a high administered dose means recovery is complete at emergence.

sections.title: Altered drug response & repeated anesthetics
bullets: Early low cardiac output and reduced renal/hepatic perfusion can decrease drug clearance and worsen sensitivity to hemodynamic depression. Titrate induction to current shock physiology rather than to a generic “burn patients need more” rule.

Later hypermetabolism, altered protein binding, expanded distribution volume and increased clearance may increase requirements for some drugs. Organ failure or sepsis can reverse that expectation; adjust to effect and current physiology.

Opioid and sedative tolerance may develop during prolonged care. Reconcile ongoing infusions and baseline requirements with the ICU/pain team; abrupt interruption can cause undertreatment or withdrawal.

Repeated operations should trigger reassessment of prior response, anxiety, emerging neuropathic pain, delirium and weaning needs. There is no single fixed anesthetic dose escalation that applies to every return to the OR.

sections.title: Background, procedural, donor-site & neuropathic pain
bullets: Assess background pain, breakthrough pain, procedural pain and neuropathic symptoms separately. Include donor sites, positioning, lines and associated injuries rather than asking only about the burned wound.

Use multimodal therapy tailored to physiology: acetaminophen with attention to liver function/total daily exposure, titrated opioids and selected adjuncts. NSAID decisions require renal, bleeding and graft-related risk assessment with the surgical team.

Ketamine may support monitored procedural sedation or serve as an opioid-sparing adjunct. Appropriate staff, monitoring and airway rescue remain necessary; its use does not guarantee preserved ventilation or hemodynamic stability.

Dexmedetomidine may help with analgosedation, anxiety or withdrawal-related needs, but bradycardia and hypotension matter. Consider neuropathic agents for a suitable pain phenotype rather than adding them routinely to every burn case.

Regional techniques may improve donor-site or extremity analgesia and reduce opioid needs. Match the block to the operative sites and weigh infection, coagulation, anticoagulation, access and postoperative assessment needs; neuraxial techniques require particular caution in unstable or infected patients.

Plan pain control beyond the incision: dressing changes, mobilization and later procedures can be intensely painful. Include specialist pain care, anticipatory dosing and nonpharmacologic measures such as psychological support or distraction.

sections.title: Access, monitoring & graft protection
bullets: Map usable sites before preparation and positioning. Edema, dressings and burned skin may limit peripheral IVs, arterial access, ECG contact, cuffs and oximetry; ultrasound guidance and a backup access plan may be needed.

Prefer intact skin when feasible and avoid pressure, shear or unnecessary adhesive trauma over wounds and fresh grafts. If monitoring/access must cross an affected area, coordinate protection and asepsis with the burn team rather than forgoing essential monitoring.

Select arterial and central access for the actual need: anticipated hemorrhage, repeated sampling, vasoactive support or limited access. Their placement is not mandatory solely because the patient has a burn.

Monitor temperature, ventilation and neuromuscular response as well as standard cardiovascular parameters. Oximeter placement limitations and possible CO exposure are separate problems; a good pulse waveform does not solve the COHb measurement limitation.

sections.title: Electrolytes, electrical injury & kidney function
bullets: Assess potassium, acid–base status, renal function and the broader injury pattern when muscle damage, electrical injury, crush injury or shock is present. A small skin wound can coexist with substantial deeper electrical injury.

Rhabdomyolysis and pigmenturia can accompany muscle necrosis, with risk of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury. Follow clinical perfusion, laboratory trends and urine findings with the burn/critical-care team rather than using urine color alone.

Review ECG/rhythm and associated trauma after electrical exposure. Monitoring intensity depends on symptoms, ECG abnormalities, mechanism and clinical course; historical series should not be treated as a universal discharge or telemetry-duration rule.
Compartment compromise requires urgent surgical assessment. An escharotomy releases constricting skin; persistent deep-compartment pathology may require fasciotomy, not simply additional fluid.

sections.title: Infection, inflammation & nutrition

Review nutrition and glycemic management during prolonged care and repeated fasting. Malnutrition and catabolism influence healing, recovery and the practical plan for serial operations.

bullets: Urgent release of constricting burn eschar may be needed for threatened distal circulation or restricted chest-wall ventilation. This is not the same operation as a deep-compartment fasciotomy.

sections.title: Temperature preservation & exposure
