sections.title: Neuromuscular blockers: major safety changes
bullets: After major burns, extrajunctional acetylcholine-receptor upregulation makes succinylcholine capable of causing severe, potentially fatal hyperkalemia. Use a conservative avoidance boundary after the first 24 hours rather than treating 24–48 hours as an assured safe window.

Risk may persist for months or longer and cannot be cleared by the calendar alone. Active wounds, impaired mobility and ongoing critical illness require particular caution; confirm the plan with the burn/anesthesia team rather than declaring succinylcholine safe at an arbitrary follow-up date.

Even in the first 24 hours, succinylcholine is not automatically appropriate: consider existing hyperkalemia, electrical/crush muscle injury and other contraindications. The early time window does not cancel patient-specific risk.

Resistance to nondepolarizing blockers develops with major burns, often becoming evident several days after injury. Larger doses or more frequent redosing may be required, but onset and duration remain variable.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and titrate to the actual surgical/airway need. Do not assume a standard rapid-sequence dose provides standard onset, or that a high administered dose means recovery is complete at emergence.

sections.title: Altered drug response & repeated anesthetics
bullets: Early low cardiac output and reduced renal/hepatic perfusion can decrease drug clearance and worsen sensitivity to hemodynamic depression. Titrate induction to current shock physiology rather than to a generic “burn patients need more” rule.

Opioid and sedative tolerance may develop during prolonged care. Reconcile ongoing infusions and baseline requirements with the ICU/pain team; abrupt interruption can cause undertreatment or withdrawal.

Repeated operations should trigger reassessment of prior response, anxiety, emerging neuropathic pain, delirium and weaning needs. There is no single fixed anesthetic dose escalation that applies to every return to the OR.

sections.title: Background, procedural, donor-site & neuropathic pain
bullets: Assess background pain, breakthrough pain, procedural pain and neuropathic symptoms separately. Include donor sites, positioning, lines and associated injuries rather than asking only about the burned wound.

Ketamine may support monitored procedural sedation or serve as an opioid-sparing adjunct. Appropriate staff, monitoring and airway rescue remain necessary; its use does not guarantee preserved ventilation or hemodynamic stability.

Regional techniques may improve donor-site or extremity analgesia and reduce opioid needs. Match the block to the operative sites and weigh infection, coagulation, anticoagulation, access and postoperative assessment needs; neuraxial techniques require particular caution in unstable or infected patients.

Plan pain control beyond the incision: dressing changes, mobilization and later procedures can be intensely painful. Include specialist pain care, anticipatory dosing and nonpharmacologic measures such as psychological support or distraction.

sections.title: Access, monitoring & graft protection

bullets: Late reconstruction addresses healed scar and functional restriction; the major risks may be difficult airway, positioning, access and pain rather than acute burn shock.

sections.title: Procedure-specific anesthesia priorities
bullets: Confirm which contracture is being released, the expected change in positioning and whether grafting or flap coverage will be added. Reconstructive surgery may involve more than the visible scar.

Severe face/neck deformity may make conventional airway access difficult and can require a coordinated anesthesia/surgical strategy. A historical easy intubation is not sufficient reassurance after scar maturation.

Tailor active-burn precautions to present status. Review healing, mobility, organ function and medication history rather than assuming either persistent acute shock or complete normalization of every drug response.

sections.title: Burn size, timing & physiologic phase
bullets: Establish the injury date/time, mechanism, depth, total body surface area (TBSA), inhalation injury, associated trauma and planned excision/donor area. A short dressing procedure, major acute excision and late healed reconstruction are different anesthetic problems.

Early major-burn physiology is dominated by capillary leak, intravascular depletion and depressed cardiac output. Later hyperdynamic/hypermetabolic physiology can increase oxygen consumption, CO₂ production and drug clearance; phase transitions are approximate, not clock-based guarantees.
Current physiology overrides the calendar. Shock, sepsis, ongoing bleeding, renal/hepatic dysfunction or poor nutrition can coexist with the expected burn phase and change the anesthetic response.

Review prior anesthetics, airway findings, access sites, transfusions, current analgesic/sedative infusions and previous drug response. Repeated surgery creates changing airway anatomy, tolerance, procedural anxiety and cumulative practical challenges, not a reason to recycle an unchanged plan.

For healed contracture/reconstruction cases, distinguish residual scar/airway/functional problems from active burn-shock physiology. Do not automatically apply acute-resuscitation formulas or smoke-toxin assumptions to a remote, healed injury.

sections.title: Airway, inhalation injury & ventilation
bullets: Concerning findings include enclosed-space smoke exposure, facial/neck burns, soot, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridor, altered consciousness and respiratory distress. Facial burns or singed hair alone do not prove obstruction; assess the whole clinical picture.

Airway edema may progress over hours and worsen with resuscitation. Reassess frequently and secure a threatened airway before edema makes intubation difficult; urgency, oxygenation and anticipated difficult ventilation/intubation determine the approach.

Prepare advanced airway equipment and an explicit rescue plan. Existing airway burns, tenuous tube fixation and repeated transfers increase the consequences of accidental extubation; protect and reassess the airway throughout positioning and transport.

Lower-airway injury may cause bronchospasm, secretions/casts, impaired clearance, atelectasis and evolving gas-exchange failure. A normal initial chest radiograph does not exclude inhalation injury; bronchoscopy may help assess injury within the burn-team pathway.

Continue individualized lung-protective ventilation and required PEEP. Hypermetabolism increases CO₂ production; preserve oxygenation and avoid derecruitment during ventilator changes rather than using fixed settings for every burn patient.

Late facial or neck contracture can markedly reduce mouth opening and neck extension. Review earlier airway records and consider an awake airway strategy when indicated; a previously easy acute-burn intubation does not guarantee an easy reconstructive airway.

sections.title: Smoke exposure: carbon monoxide & cyanide
bullets: Conventional two-wavelength pulse oximetry can be falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Measure carboxyhemoglobin with blood co-oximetry when exposure is suspected; either venous or arterial blood may be used.

Interpret COHb alongside exposure history, symptoms and elapsed time after oxygen/removal from the fire. A falling level or apparently adequate PaO₂ does not alone establish that clinically important CO toxicity is absent.

Provide high-concentration oxygen promptly for suspected CO poisoning and obtain toxicology/Poison Control input for severity-based treatment, including whether hyperbaric consultation is appropriate. Do not use a single COHb cutoff as the entire decision.

Closed-space structural fires can also produce cyanide exposure. Soot plus altered mental status, cardiovascular instability or marked lactic acidosis raises concern, but lactate is not specific and not every smoke-exposed patient has cyanide poisoning.

The CYANOKIT label supports prompt hydroxocobalamin when clinical suspicion is high, alongside airway, oxygenation and circulatory support. Do not delay urgent treatment for a confirmatory cyanide test or lactate result; use the institutional toxicology pathway.

If hydroxocobalamin is given, communicate this to the laboratory and renal team: its red color can interfere with some assays and dialysis blood-leak detectors. Monitor renal function and interpret affected results with laboratory support.

sections.title: Resuscitation, ongoing losses & perfusion
bullets: Separate the initial burn-resuscitation requirement from maintenance needs and operative blood-loss replacement. Excision hemorrhage cannot be managed simply by restarting a burn formula.

The ABA 2024 guideline addresses adults with burns ≥20% TBSA during the first 48 hours. The recommended starting approach uses a 2 mL/kg/%TBSA first-24-hour volume estimate rather than routinely starting at 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, followed by response-guided rate titration. This is not an hourly dose or a fixed volume to infuse regardless of physiology.

Use the burn center’s timed resuscitation protocol and reconcile fluid already given. Follow urine output and the broader perfusion picture, including hemodynamics, lactate/base deficit trends and organ function; avoid both under-resuscitation and fluid creep.

Albumin may be considered during initial resuscitation, especially with larger burns, to reduce resuscitation volume and improve urine output. This is a specialist, patient-specific decision, not routine replacement of every crystalloid infusion.

After initial resuscitation, wound/evaporative losses, ongoing surgery, changing capillary permeability and mobilization of edema alter fluid needs. Reassess rather than carrying the first-day fluid rate forward indefinitely.

Electrical injury with deep muscle damage and rhabdomyolysis may need a different renal/perfusion strategy. Do not extrapolate one thermal-burn urine-output goal or an old mannitol/bicarbonate recipe to every electrical injury.

sections.title: Excision blood loss & transfusion planning
bullets: Major excision can bleed rapidly from broad surfaces and donor sites. Bleeding may be underestimated because blood mixes with irrigation, collects beneath the patient or remains hidden under bulky dressings.

Estimate risk with the surgeon using the area and depth to be excised, infection, timing, donor sites and expected duration. Published percentage-of-blood-volume estimates vary and should not be treated as a reliable individual blood-loss calculator.

For substantial anticipated loss, establish suitable access, arrange crossmatched blood and a clear escalation/massive-transfusion plan; arterial monitoring and serial laboratory assessment may be appropriate.

Follow perfusion, serial hemoglobin, coagulation and temperature together. A stable-patient transfusion threshold is not a reason to wait during active major hemorrhage; follow the institution’s hemorrhage and blood-product pathway.

Tourniquets, staged excision, compression and topical/infiltrated hemostatic agents may limit bleeding. Coordinate agent identity, concentration, total amount and timing with the surgeon rather than assuming topical treatment has no systemic relevance.
Continue surveillance after dressings are applied and during transfer. Apparent completion of the procedure does not establish that wound bleeding has stopped.

sections.title: Temperature preservation & exposure
bullets: Loss of the skin barrier, broad exposure, irrigation and fluid/blood administration create substantial hypothermia risk. Monitor core temperature throughout significant burn surgery and plan warming before exposing the patient.

Use a warmed operating room, warmed IV fluids/blood, appropriate active warming and insulation of areas not being treated. Minimize unnecessary exposure and coordinate warming devices with wound, graft and surgical-access constraints.
Hypothermia worsens the physiologic burden and can aggravate coagulopathy and blood loss. Temperature management is part of resuscitation, not a comfort-only intervention.

Later hypermetabolic burn patients may be febrile or hyperthermic. Follow measured temperature and the clinical context rather than indiscriminately heating an already hyperthermic patient; fever alone does not distinguish inflammation from infection.

sections.title: Neuromuscular blockers: major safety changes
bullets: After major burns, extrajunctional acetylcholine-receptor upregulation makes succinylcholine capable of causing severe, potentially fatal hyperkalemia. Use a conservative avoidance boundary after the first 24 hours rather than treating 24–48 hours as an assured safe window.

Risk may persist for months or longer and cannot be cleared by the calendar alone. Active wounds, impaired mobility and ongoing critical illness require particular caution; confirm the plan with the burn/anesthesia team rather than declaring succinylcholine safe at an arbitrary follow-up date.

Even in the first 24 hours, succinylcholine is not automatically appropriate: consider existing hyperkalemia, electrical/crush muscle injury and other contraindications. The early time window does not cancel patient-specific risk.

Resistance to nondepolarizing blockers develops with major burns, often becoming evident several days after injury. Larger doses or more frequent redosing may be required, but onset and duration remain variable.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and titrate to the actual surgical/airway need. Do not assume a standard rapid-sequence dose provides standard onset, or that a high administered dose means recovery is complete at emergence.

sections.title: Altered drug response & repeated anesthetics
bullets: Early low cardiac output and reduced renal/hepatic perfusion can decrease drug clearance and worsen sensitivity to hemodynamic depression. Titrate induction to current shock physiology rather than to a generic “burn patients need more” rule.

Later hypermetabolism, altered protein binding, expanded distribution volume and increased clearance may increase requirements for some drugs. Organ failure or sepsis can reverse that expectation; adjust to effect and current physiology.

Opioid and sedative tolerance may develop during prolonged care. Reconcile ongoing infusions and baseline requirements with the ICU/pain team; abrupt interruption can cause undertreatment or withdrawal.

Repeated operations should trigger reassessment of prior response, anxiety, emerging neuropathic pain, delirium and weaning needs. There is no single fixed anesthetic dose escalation that applies to every return to the OR.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Protect myocardial oxygen supply and ventricular function through induction, sternotomy, bypass and reperfusion. Avoid major hypotension and tachycardia.
Plan invasive monitoring, TEE, systemic anticoagulation and blood conservation for conventional on-pump CABG. Off-pump and minimally invasive approaches change the hazards.
Separation from bypass depends on rhythm, filling, biventricular function, graft-related ischemia, de-airing and metabolic recovery, not pressure alone.
Fast-track extubation is selective; ICU handoff must include ventricular function, pacing, vasoactive support and bleeding.

sections.title: Operation & approach
bullets: Coronary conduits bypass obstructed native arteries; clarify graft targets, conduit plan, prior sternotomy and whether surgery is on-pump, off-pump or minimally invasive.
The CPB sections below apply to on-pump surgery. Do not automatically apply CPB ACT targets, ventilation pauses or pump-separation assumptions to an off-pump operation.

sections.title: Coronary anatomy, ventricular reserve & comorbidity
bullets: Review coronary disease distribution, unstable angina/recent MI, LV ejection fraction and regional dysfunction, RV function, rhythm and current mechanical or vasoactive support.
Assess renal, pulmonary, cerebrovascular and peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, anemia and previous cardiac operations. These alter induction tolerance, access, transfusion risk and recovery.

sections.title: Antiplatelets & preoperative bleeding plan
bullets: Reconcile aspirin, the specific P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulants, last doses and recent coronary stenting/ACS. Balance ischemic risk against surgical bleeding with the cardiac team.

For elective CABG, the blood-management guideline supports generally continuing aspirin and allowing appropriate P2Y12 interruption: approximately 5 days for clopidogrel, at least 3 days for ticagrelor and 7 days for prasugrel. Urgency and recent stenting can change the plan; these are not patient-directed stop instructions.
After recent ACS or PCI, postoperative P2Y12 resumption is individualized once bleeding risk permits. Avoid losing the antiplatelet plan at the OR-to-ICU transition.

sections.title: New ischemia & postrevascularization assessment
bullets: Track ECG and TEE changes against baseline and operative events. New regional dysfunction after revascularization should prompt discussion of ischemia, graft problems, air and loading conditions.

Sternal retraction can produce vagal bradycardia/hypotension, whereas incision and sternotomy may provoke hypertension/tachycardia. Communicate the temporal relationship and correct the provoking event where possible.

If low output persists, reassess both ventricles, rhythm, filling and mechanical causes before simply escalating support. Difficult separation can require further surgical assessment or mechanical circulatory support.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & TEE
bullets: Match access and monitoring to ventricular reserve, surgical approach, anticipated bleeding and rescue requirements. Arterial pressure, reliable large-bore access, central access, ECG, temperature and serial blood gases are central to major open cardiac surgery.

TEE evaluates baseline and new ventricular dysfunction, filling, residual structural problems and de-airing. Check contraindications and use an appropriately trained operator; unavailable or contraindicated TEE requires an alternative imaging plan.

A pulmonary artery catheter is selected for the clinical question, not inserted automatically for every case. Interpret pressure, output and oxygenation measurements alongside echo and perfusion rather than treating CVP as a direct volume measurement.

Prepare external defibrillation/pacing capability and vasoactive support before induction. Discuss re-entry, peripheral cannulation and emergency bypass access when prior surgery or circulatory instability makes these relevant.

sections.title: Induction, oxygen delivery & ventricular protection
bullets: Titrate induction to the patient’s reserve and allow time for drug effect in low cardiac output. Avoid a large unopposed fall in vascular tone or contractility while also controlling the tachycardic/hypertensive response to airway instrumentation.

Protect myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance by addressing hypotension, tachycardia, hypoxemia, anemia and new ischemia in context. Blood pressure alone does not establish adequate cardiac output or oxygen delivery.

Use the actual valve or ventricular physiology to choose heart-rate and loading goals. The pressure-loaded LV in aortic stenosis and the volume-loaded LV in regurgitation should not receive an identical hemodynamic recipe.

With pulmonary hypertension or RV dysfunction, prevent avoidable hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive airway pressure. Balance RV filling against dilatation and septal shift rather than repeatedly giving fluid for every low-output state.

sections.title: Heparin, ACT & protamine
bullets: Establish baseline coagulation, recent antiplatelet/anticoagulant exposure and any HIT history. Confirm adequate anticoagulation before initiating CPB and repeat testing at protocol-defined intervals.

The 2024 European CPB guideline describes ACT >480 seconds for conventional uncoated circuits with cardiotomy suction. Assay and circuit characteristics matter: use the institution’s validated system-specific target, not a universal target copied from PCI, ECMO or another ACT device.

An inadequate ACT response requires confirmation of sampling/testing and an organized heparin-resistance assessment, including antithrombin availability. Acute HIT and alternative anticoagulants require a specialist perfusion/hematology strategy; direct thrombin inhibitors do not have a protamine-like reversal agent.

Coordinate protamine administration with the surgeon and perfusionist after separation. Watch for hypotension, pulmonary vascular/RV deterioration or hypersensitivity and retain a clear emergency return-to-bypass plan.

Persistent bleeding or prolonged ACT after reversal does not prove residual heparin. Temperature, platelets and factor deficits affect testing; excess protamine can itself impair coagulation. Use the cardiac bleeding algorithm and heparin-sensitive testing when available.

sections.title: CPB: perfusion, temperature & laboratory trends
bullets: During bypass, assess pump flow and oxygen delivery together with hemoglobin/hematocrit, venous saturation, gases, lactate and organ-perfusion indicators. A satisfactory pressure reading is not sufficient evidence that tissue oxygen delivery is adequate.

Follow potassium, acid–base status, glucose, calcium as clinically indicated and serial anticoagulation testing. Reconcile anesthetic delivery and ventilation transitions with the perfusionist rather than assuming the usual pre-bypass circuit is still delivering the anesthetic.

Coordinate cooling and controlled rewarming with the perfusion strategy. Avoid systemic hyperthermia; the CPB guideline recommends oxygenator arterial outlet temperature not exceeding 37°C, rather than deliberately heating above normal to qualify for separation.

Treat sudden perfusion or drainage problems as team events. Cannula malposition, obstruction, air, dissection and inadequate venous return require rapid circuit and patient assessment, not isolated escalation of vasoactive drugs.

sections.title: Separation from bypass & low-output differential
bullets: Before reducing support, coordinate ventilation, temperature, rhythm/pacing, electrolyte and acid–base correction, filling and de-airing. Assess the surgical result and both ventricles with TEE.

Distinguish inadequate preload, LV dysfunction, RV failure, ischemia, vasoplegia and a residual structural or dynamic lesion. Similar arterial pressures can conceal very different causes and treatments.

Review new regional wall-motion changes, valve function, intracardiac air and the effect of rhythm/AV synchrony. A postrepair mitral SAM/LVOT-obstruction pattern requires different management from primary pump failure.

Use volume, vasoactive or inotropic treatment for the identified physiology and reassess the response. Avoid forcing separation with escalating high-dose support when inadequate perfusion persists; discuss return to CPB or temporary mechanical support early.

sections.title: Blood conservation & postoperative bleeding
bullets: When time permits, identify and treat preoperative anemia and iron deficiency. Plan crossmatched blood, cell salvage and an institution-approved antifibrinolytic strategy for the expected surgical burden.

Use targeted laboratory/viscoelastic-guided treatment for bleeding while evaluating surgical hemostasis. Correct contributing hypothermia and residual anticoagulation; distinguish a mechanical bleeding source from diffuse coagulopathy.

Restrictive red-cell strategies reduce transfusion in suitable cardiac-surgery patients, but a trial threshold such as 7.5 g/dL is not an instruction to delay transfusion during active hemorrhage, ischemia or inadequate oxygen delivery.

Tranexamic acid is effective in cardiac blood conservation; dosing should account for the local regimen and patient risks, including renal function and seizures. Do not convert an evidence summary into a fixed dose for all procedures.
Postoperative instability with bleeding needs prompt multidisciplinary reassessment. Repeated empiric blood products must not delay evaluation for surgical re-exploration when indicated.

bullets: Use multimodal analgesia while limiting unnecessary high-dose opioid exposure. Regional techniques require an explicit assessment of systemic anticoagulation, bleeding risk, expertise and the planned postoperative pathway.

NSAIDs are not a routine CABG analgesic option: respect the coronary-revascularization warning/contraindication and renal, bleeding and cardiovascular risks. Do not transfer a VATS analgesic regimen unchanged into CABG.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Identify the dominant lesion: severe aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation require different pre-bypass heart-rate and loading goals.
With aortic stenosis, preserve coronary perfusion, adequate filling and sinus rhythm when possible; avoid major hypotension, tachycardia and marked bradycardia.
Open AVR usually involves CPB, systemic heparinization and postimplant TEE assessment of the valve and both ventricles.
Recovery depends on prosthetic function, ventricular performance, rhythm and bleeding rather than valve implantation alone.

sections.title: Open AVR versus other approaches
bullets: This reference addresses open surgical AVR. Clarify isolated AVR versus combined CABG/root surgery and prosthetic plan; transcatheter aortic valve replacement has a distinct procedural and rescue pathway.
Assess calcification, ventricular function and associated aortic or mitral disease before induction. The hemodynamic implications come from the lesion and myocardium, not simply the label AVR.

sections.title: Aortic stenosis: pressure-loaded LV
bullets: A hypertrophied, poorly compliant LV depends on adequate filling and coronary perfusion. Preserve sinus rhythm/atrial contribution when present and promptly evaluate new atrial fibrillation or other poorly tolerated rhythms.
Avoid abrupt loss of SVR and hypotension. Maintain sufficient preload without indiscriminate loading; both tachycardia and marked bradycardia can impair output in severe obstruction.

A preserved ejection fraction does not eliminate risk: diastolic dysfunction and supply-demand ischemia remain important. Review low-flow states with the cardiac/echo team rather than interpreting one valve gradient in isolation.

sections.title: Aortic regurgitation: forward flow
bullets: In significant AR, avoid pronounced bradycardia and excessive afterload that worsen regurgitant burden. Preserve forward output and contractility while maintaining adequate systemic perfusion.
Acute decompensation or severe ventricular dysfunction changes tolerance of induction and loading. Do not apply the chronic compensated-lesion plan unchanged to an unstable patient.

sections.title: Postimplant TEE & changed physiology
bullets: Assess prosthetic motion, residual/paravalvular regurgitation, gradients in the actual flow state, ventricular function and de-airing. Discuss unexpected findings before accepting separation.
Relieving the valve lesion does not immediately normalize ventricular hypertrophy or dysfunction. Continue careful loading, rhythm and coronary-perfusion management after bypass.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & TEE
bullets: Match access and monitoring to ventricular reserve, surgical approach, anticipated bleeding and rescue requirements. Arterial pressure, reliable large-bore access, central access, ECG, temperature and serial blood gases are central to major open cardiac surgery.

TEE evaluates baseline and new ventricular dysfunction, filling, residual structural problems and de-airing. Check contraindications and use an appropriately trained operator; unavailable or contraindicated TEE requires an alternative imaging plan.

A pulmonary artery catheter is selected for the clinical question, not inserted automatically for every case. Interpret pressure, output and oxygenation measurements alongside echo and perfusion rather than treating CVP as a direct volume measurement.

Prepare external defibrillation/pacing capability and vasoactive support before induction. Discuss re-entry, peripheral cannulation and emergency bypass access when prior surgery or circulatory instability makes these relevant.

sections.title: Induction, oxygen delivery & ventricular protection
bullets: Titrate induction to the patient’s reserve and allow time for drug effect in low cardiac output. Avoid a large unopposed fall in vascular tone or contractility while also controlling the tachycardic/hypertensive response to airway instrumentation.

Protect myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance by addressing hypotension, tachycardia, hypoxemia, anemia and new ischemia in context. Blood pressure alone does not establish adequate cardiac output or oxygen delivery.

Use the actual valve or ventricular physiology to choose heart-rate and loading goals. The pressure-loaded LV in aortic stenosis and the volume-loaded LV in regurgitation should not receive an identical hemodynamic recipe.

With pulmonary hypertension or RV dysfunction, prevent avoidable hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive airway pressure. Balance RV filling against dilatation and septal shift rather than repeatedly giving fluid for every low-output state.

sections.title: Heparin, ACT & protamine
bullets: Establish baseline coagulation, recent antiplatelet/anticoagulant exposure and any HIT history. Confirm adequate anticoagulation before initiating CPB and repeat testing at protocol-defined intervals.

The 2024 European CPB guideline describes ACT >480 seconds for conventional uncoated circuits with cardiotomy suction. Assay and circuit characteristics matter: use the institution’s validated system-specific target, not a universal target copied from PCI, ECMO or another ACT device.

An inadequate ACT response requires confirmation of sampling/testing and an organized heparin-resistance assessment, including antithrombin availability. Acute HIT and alternative anticoagulants require a specialist perfusion/hematology strategy; direct thrombin inhibitors do not have a protamine-like reversal agent.

Coordinate protamine administration with the surgeon and perfusionist after separation. Watch for hypotension, pulmonary vascular/RV deterioration or hypersensitivity and retain a clear emergency return-to-bypass plan.

Persistent bleeding or prolonged ACT after reversal does not prove residual heparin. Temperature, platelets and factor deficits affect testing; excess protamine can itself impair coagulation. Use the cardiac bleeding algorithm and heparin-sensitive testing when available.

sections.title: CPB: perfusion, temperature & laboratory trends
bullets: During bypass, assess pump flow and oxygen delivery together with hemoglobin/hematocrit, venous saturation, gases, lactate and organ-perfusion indicators. A satisfactory pressure reading is not sufficient evidence that tissue oxygen delivery is adequate.

Follow potassium, acid–base status, glucose, calcium as clinically indicated and serial anticoagulation testing. Reconcile anesthetic delivery and ventilation transitions with the perfusionist rather than assuming the usual pre-bypass circuit is still delivering the anesthetic.

Coordinate cooling and controlled rewarming with the perfusion strategy. Avoid systemic hyperthermia; the CPB guideline recommends oxygenator arterial outlet temperature not exceeding 37°C, rather than deliberately heating above normal to qualify for separation.

Treat sudden perfusion or drainage problems as team events. Cannula malposition, obstruction, air, dissection and inadequate venous return require rapid circuit and patient assessment, not isolated escalation of vasoactive drugs.

sections.title: Separation from bypass & low-output differential
bullets: Before reducing support, coordinate ventilation, temperature, rhythm/pacing, electrolyte and acid–base correction, filling and de-airing. Assess the surgical result and both ventricles with TEE.

Distinguish inadequate preload, LV dysfunction, RV failure, ischemia, vasoplegia and a residual structural or dynamic lesion. Similar arterial pressures can conceal very different causes and treatments.

Review new regional wall-motion changes, valve function, intracardiac air and the effect of rhythm/AV synchrony. A postrepair mitral SAM/LVOT-obstruction pattern requires different management from primary pump failure.

Use volume, vasoactive or inotropic treatment for the identified physiology and reassess the response. Avoid forcing separation with escalating high-dose support when inadequate perfusion persists; discuss return to CPB or temporary mechanical support early.

sections.title: Blood conservation & postoperative bleeding
bullets: When time permits, identify and treat preoperative anemia and iron deficiency. Plan crossmatched blood, cell salvage and an institution-approved antifibrinolytic strategy for the expected surgical burden.

Use targeted laboratory/viscoelastic-guided treatment for bleeding while evaluating surgical hemostasis. Correct contributing hypothermia and residual anticoagulation; distinguish a mechanical bleeding source from diffuse coagulopathy.

Restrictive red-cell strategies reduce transfusion in suitable cardiac-surgery patients, but a trial threshold such as 7.5 g/dL is not an instruction to delay transfusion during active hemorrhage, ischemia or inadequate oxygen delivery.

Tranexamic acid is effective in cardiac blood conservation; dosing should account for the local regimen and patient risks, including renal function and seizures. Do not convert an evidence summary into a fixed dose for all procedures.
Postoperative instability with bleeding needs prompt multidisciplinary reassessment. Repeated empiric blood products must not delay evaluation for surgical re-exploration when indicated.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Define stenosis versus regurgitation and assess pulmonary hypertension, RV function and rhythm before selecting hemodynamic goals.
Stenosis favors controlled heart rate and judicious filling; regurgitation favors forward flow without excessive afterload or marked bradycardia.
TEE defines the mechanism and evaluates the repair, residual MR/stenosis, ventricular function and systolic anterior motion (SAM).
Postrepair low output can reflect afterload mismatch, RV failure, ischemia or SAM/LVOT obstruction; these require different treatments.

sections.title: Repair, replacement & minimally invasive access
bullets: Clarify repair versus replacement, concomitant operations and sternotomy versus minimally invasive/robotic access. The latter may involve peripheral cannulation, lung isolation and restricted airway access.
TEE guides lesion assessment, cannula/balloon positioning where used, the surgical result and changes during separation. Assess suitability for probe placement in advance.

sections.title: Mitral stenosis: filling time & pulmonary circulation
bullets: Avoid tachycardia, which shortens diastole and raises the transmitral gradient. Preserve sinus rhythm when possible and coordinate treatment of rapid atrial arrhythmias.
Use fluid judiciously: an underfilled LV does not mean the patient can tolerate large volume loads into a high-pressure pulmonary circulation. Watch for pulmonary edema.
Prevent hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive lung inflation that increase PVR. Significant pulmonary hypertension makes RV protection central.

sources.label: Valvular heart disease and anaesthesia: lesion physiology review

sections.title: Mitral regurgitation & postrepair afterload
bullets: Maintain forward flow and contractility; avoid excessive SVR, volume overload and substantial bradycardia. The desired heart rate and pressure remain individualized to coronary disease and ventricular reserve.
Once regurgitation is corrected, the LV loses its low-pressure outlet into the left atrium. Latent dysfunction or afterload mismatch may become evident despite apparently favorable preoperative EF.
TEE and perfusion assessment guide inotropy, loading and afterload adjustment. Residual regurgitation, new obstruction and ischemia must not be mistaken for simple myocardial depression.

sections.title: SAM & dynamic LVOT obstruction after repair
bullets: TEE may show systolic anterior mitral motion, dynamic LVOT obstruction and associated MR. Assess the mechanism under representative loading rather than interpreting a single Doppler number alone.

For hemodynamically significant SAM, coordinated treatment commonly includes restoring appropriate filling, reducing inotropic stimulation, increasing vascular tone and carefully selected beta blockade. These measures differ from the usual response to primary systolic pump failure.

Reassess obstruction and MR after treatment; persistent significant SAM may require surgical revision. Avoid treating every postrepair hypotensive patient with escalating inotropes before checking the mechanism.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Assess the RV, pulmonary pressure, systemic congestion and any accompanying left-sided lesion; right-heart function often determines separation and recovery.
Maintain effective RV filling without worsening dilatation, TR and septal shift. CVP alone is not a reliable volume target.
Coordinate TEE, CPB and any pulmonary artery catheter with the surgeon to avoid interference or catheter entrapment.
After repair, reassess RV output, residual valve dysfunction and organ perfusion; be prepared for inotropic/pulmonary vascular support when indicated.

sources.label: Kaplan: valvular heart disease replacement and repair (2018 chapter)

sections.title: Primary versus secondary tricuspid disease
bullets: Clarify primary leaflet pathology versus functional regurgitation related to annular/RV dilatation and left-sided disease. Combined surgery changes both the bypass plan and postrepair physiology.
Repair versus replacement and the prosthetic plan are surgical decisions. Avoid treating chronic compensated TR, endocarditis and severe RV failure as the same anesthetic presentation.

sources.label: Kaplan: valvular heart disease replacement and repair (2018 chapter)

sections.title: RV reserve & venous congestion
bullets: Assess RV size/function, septal position, pulmonary hypertension and clinical end-organ congestion. Markedly elevated CVP does not establish adequate effective forward flow.
Balance preload with the consequences of overdistension. Use TEE and output/perfusion trends when available rather than fluid boluses directed only at a filling-pressure number.

sources.label: Kaplan: valvular heart disease replacement and repair (2018 chapter)

sections.title: Pulmonary vascular load & support
bullets: Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive airway pressure that may worsen RV afterload. Preserve systemic pressure needed for RV coronary perfusion.
Inotropic support and selected pulmonary vasodilators may be needed for RV dysfunction; monitor systemic hypotension and reassess forward flow after each intervention.

Kaplan: valvular heart disease replacement and repair (2018 chapter)

sections.title: Catheters, TEE & postrepair reassessment
bullets: A PAC may provide useful information but may need repositioning/removal for valve surgery. Coordinate its location with the surgeon and avoid entrapment by intracardiac suture lines.
Evaluate residual regurgitation/obstruction, RV dimensions and function, septal interaction and the left-sided result before final separation. Interpret TR in the actual loading and flow state.

bullets: Use a lesion-by-lesion plan: stenosis, regurgitation, LV dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension may impose competing goals.

sections.title: Practical lesion comparison
bullets: AS: preserve coronary perfusion and appropriate filling; avoid hypotension and extremes of rate. AR: avoid marked bradycardia and excessive afterload while preserving output.
MS: avoid tachycardia and pulmonary overcirculation/congestion. MR: support forward flow and anticipate changed LV loading after competent repair.
TR/RV dysfunction: avoid excessive PVR and RV overdistension; interpret venous pressure with echo and perfusion, not as a stand-alone fluid target.

sections.title: Induction, oxygen delivery & ventricular protection
bullets: Titrate induction to the patient’s reserve and allow time for drug effect in low cardiac output. Avoid a large unopposed fall in vascular tone or contractility while also controlling the tachycardic/hypertensive response to airway instrumentation.

Protect myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance by addressing hypotension, tachycardia, hypoxemia, anemia and new ischemia in context. Blood pressure alone does not establish adequate cardiac output or oxygen delivery.

Use the actual valve or ventricular physiology to choose heart-rate and loading goals. The pressure-loaded LV in aortic stenosis and the volume-loaded LV in regurgitation should not receive an identical hemodynamic recipe.

With pulmonary hypertension or RV dysfunction, prevent avoidable hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive airway pressure. Balance RV filling against dilatation and septal shift rather than repeatedly giving fluid for every low-output state.

sections.title: Heparin, ACT & protamine
bullets: Establish baseline coagulation, recent antiplatelet/anticoagulant exposure and any HIT history. Confirm adequate anticoagulation before initiating CPB and repeat testing at protocol-defined intervals.

The 2024 European CPB guideline describes ACT >480 seconds for conventional uncoated circuits with cardiotomy suction. Assay and circuit characteristics matter: use the institution’s validated system-specific target, not a universal target copied from PCI, ECMO or another ACT device.

An inadequate ACT response requires confirmation of sampling/testing and an organized heparin-resistance assessment, including antithrombin availability. Acute HIT and alternative anticoagulants require a specialist perfusion/hematology strategy; direct thrombin inhibitors do not have a protamine-like reversal agent.

Coordinate protamine administration with the surgeon and perfusionist after separation. Watch for hypotension, pulmonary vascular/RV deterioration or hypersensitivity and retain a clear emergency return-to-bypass plan.

Persistent bleeding or prolonged ACT after reversal does not prove residual heparin. Temperature, platelets and factor deficits affect testing; excess protamine can itself impair coagulation. Use the cardiac bleeding algorithm and heparin-sensitive testing when available.

sections.title: CPB: perfusion, temperature & laboratory trends
bullets: During bypass, assess pump flow and oxygen delivery together with hemoglobin/hematocrit, venous saturation, gases, lactate and organ-perfusion indicators. A satisfactory pressure reading is not sufficient evidence that tissue oxygen delivery is adequate.

bullets: Choose arterial monitoring sites around cannulation and anticipated clamping. Bilateral upper-extremity and/or femoral measurements may answer different perfusion questions during arch and lower-body arrest.

sections.title: Circulatory arrest & selective perfusion
bullets: Hypothermia reduces metabolic demand; antegrade cerebral perfusion is commonly used with moderate hypothermia. Temperature and flow choices depend on anticipated duration, anatomy and center expertise.

Unilateral versus bilateral cerebral perfusion requires assessment of collateral pathways and monitoring. Published temperature bands or experimental flow values are not guaranteed safe targets for an individual patient.
Longer lower-body ischemia and extensive descending-aortic involvement increase spinal/visceral concerns. Discuss the protection strategy rather than applying routine CSF drainage to every arch case.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Assess severe LV failure together with RV reserve, PVR, congestion and end-organ function; the RV must deliver blood to fill the LVAD.
TEE assesses shunts, aortic regurgitation, thrombus, cannula position, de-airing, unloading and septal position.
Low device flow can reflect hypovolemia, RV failure, excessive afterload, suction or a mechanical problem. Do not assume every low-flow alarm needs fluid.
Coordinate device initiation and settings with the implant team; persistent RV failure may require temporary right-sided support.

sections.title: Preimplant assessment & device plan
bullets: Review RV function, pulmonary pressures, inotropes/mechanical support, renal/hepatic injury, rhythm and anticoagulation. Plan induction and rescue around the patient’s very limited reserve.
Identify the exact pump and local implant protocol. Contemporary devices differ in speed, flow estimation and alarm behavior; do not copy one device’s operating values into another.

sections.title: TEE before and during pump initiation
bullets: Before bypass, assess LV/RV size and function, intracardiac thrombus, aortic valve function, TR and PFO/other shunts. Unloading may expose clinically important right-to-left shunting.

During initiation, assess de-airing, inflow/outflow paths, degree of LV unloading and septal position. Communicate cannula or structural concerns rather than attempting to solve all low flow by changing speed.
Significant AR can create recirculation from aorta back into the LV instead of effective systemic flow. The surgical team should address clinically important AR and shunts in the implant plan.

sections.title: RV failure versus inadequate preload
bullets: The LVAD does not bypass the need for RV output. RV dilatation and reduced pulmonary forward flow may underfill the LV despite high venous pressures.
Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia and excessive RV loading; use selected inotropic and pulmonary vascular support as indicated. Refractory RV failure may require RVAD or VA-ECMO support.
Excessive unloading can shift the septum and promote suction/arrhythmias. Reassess volume, RV function and pump speed with the implant team, using TEE rather than a console number alone.

Handoff includes device identity/settings, RV function, current support, residual valve/shunt findings, bleeding and the anticoagulation plan. Device-specific operating instructions remain essential.

bullets: Establish baseline coagulation, recent antiplatelet/anticoagulant exposure and any HIT history. Confirm adequate anticoagulation before initiating CPB and repeat testing at protocol-defined intervals.

bullets: When time permits, identify and treat preoperative anemia and iron deficiency. Plan crossmatched blood, cell salvage and an institution-approved antifibrinolytic strategy for the expected surgical burden.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Recipients may arrive with inotropes, LVAD or ECMO support; plan induction and re-entry around severe limited reserve and bleeding risk.
Pulmonary hypertension places the donor RV at risk during reperfusion and separation. TEE guides biventricular and anastomotic assessment.

sections.title: Recipient, donor timing & reoperation
bullets: Review PVR, RV function, renal/hepatic function, current support and prior surgery. Vascular anatomy and indwelling devices may constrain access.

sections.title: Reperfusion & donor RV protection
bullets: The donor RV must adapt to the recipient’s pulmonary circulation. Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive airway pressures; use appropriate inotropic and pulmonary vasodilator support.

sections.title: Denervation, rhythm & drug response
bullets: Immediately after transplantation, autonomic connections to the graft are interrupted. Reflex heart-rate responses are altered and atropine may not provide the expected chronotropic effect.
For clinically important bradycardia/low output, be prepared for pacing and direct-acting support under the transplant protocol rather than depending on indirect sympathomimetics.

These immediate-transplant considerations should not be generalized into a claim that every remote transplant recipient has identical drug responses; reinnervation and other clinical factors can vary.

sections.title: Graft dysfunction, vasoplegia & ICU
bullets: Distinguish donor RV failure, LV dysfunction, residual/anastomotic problems and vasoplegia with echo and perfusion assessment. More fluid is not necessarily helpful when the RV is already distended.
Escalate early for persistent graft dysfunction despite appropriate support; temporary mechanical circulatory support, including VA ECMO, may be required.
Coordinate immunosuppression/infection prevention and ICU support. Extubation depends on perfusion, gas exchange and bleeding; it should not be pursued merely to meet a fast-track time target.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & TEE
bullets: Match access and monitoring to ventricular reserve, surgical approach, anticipated bleeding and rescue requirements. Arterial pressure, reliable large-bore access, central access, ECG, temperature and serial blood gases are central to major open cardiac surgery.

TEE evaluates baseline and new ventricular dysfunction, filling, residual structural problems and de-airing. Check contraindications and use an appropriately trained operator; unavailable or contraindicated TEE requires an alternative imaging plan.

A pulmonary artery catheter is selected for the clinical question, not inserted automatically for every case. Interpret pressure, output and oxygenation measurements alongside echo and perfusion rather than treating CVP as a direct volume measurement.

Prepare external defibrillation/pacing capability and vasoactive support before induction. Discuss re-entry, peripheral cannulation and emergency bypass access when prior surgery or circulatory instability makes these relevant.

sections.title: Induction, oxygen delivery & ventricular protection
bullets: Titrate induction to the patient’s reserve and allow time for drug effect in low cardiac output. Avoid a large unopposed fall in vascular tone or contractility while also controlling the tachycardic/hypertensive response to airway instrumentation.

Protect myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance by addressing hypotension, tachycardia, hypoxemia, anemia and new ischemia in context. Blood pressure alone does not establish adequate cardiac output or oxygen delivery.

Use the actual valve or ventricular physiology to choose heart-rate and loading goals. The pressure-loaded LV in aortic stenosis and the volume-loaded LV in regurgitation should not receive an identical hemodynamic recipe.

With pulmonary hypertension or RV dysfunction, prevent avoidable hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive airway pressure. Balance RV filling against dilatation and septal shift rather than repeatedly giving fluid for every low-output state.

sections.title: Airway & lung isolation
bullets: Confirm whether lung isolation is required for exposure, contamination control or the planned airway/bronchial reconstruction. A double-lumen tube and a bronchial blocker have different suction, access and postoperative-airway advantages.

With a difficult airway, securing a suitable single-lumen airway first and then placing a blocker may be preferable to forcing a bulky double-lumen tube. Match the plan to the operation and rescue options.

Confirm position with flexible bronchoscopy and reassess after lateral positioning and when oxygenation, ventilation or surgical exposure changes. Auscultation alone does not reliably establish correct lung-isolation-device position.
Coordinate device/cuff location and withdrawal with bronchial stapling or airway surgery. Avoid trapping an airway device or suction catheter in a staple line.

sections.title: One-lung ventilation: protective strategy
bullets: Use predicted/ideal body weight, not actual body weight, to select tidal volume. Contemporary review ranges commonly begin around 4–6 mL/kg for OLV, then individualize to compliance, gas exchange, pressures and the operative context.

Individualize PEEP and keep airway/distending pressures as low as reasonably compatible with adequate ventilation. Excess PEEP may overdistend the dependent lung, impair venous return and worsen shunt; too little can promote derecruitment.

Titrate FiO2 to the clinical oxygenation requirement; use 100% oxygen during significant desaturation while evaluating the cause. No single FiO2 or PEEP setting is correct throughout every thoracic procedure.

Mild hypercapnia may be tolerated, but severe hypercarbia/acidosis is particularly undesirable with pulmonary hypertension, RV dysfunction, arrhythmias or raised intracranial pressure. Assess arterial gases when end-tidal CO2 may poorly reflect arterial CO2.

Recruitment is a selective maneuver, not an automatic high-pressure step. Consider hemodynamic tolerance, emphysema, air leak and surgical repair; recruitment can transiently worsen oxygenation and blood pressure.

sections.title: OLV hypoxemia: clinical troubleshooting
bullets: Abrupt severe desaturation is an emergency: notify the surgeon, pause the procedure and restore two-lung ventilation with FiO2 1.0 when feasible while urgently evaluating the cause. Do not persist with OLV solely to preserve exposure.
Check the airway/circuit and use bronchoscopy to reassess tube or blocker position, obstruction and secretions; consider bleeding, bronchospasm and loss of dependent-lung ventilation.
Assess blood pressure, cardiac output, hemoglobin and gas exchange as well as the ventilator. A low oxygen saturation may coexist with inadequate oxygen delivery from circulatory failure.

For persistent hypoxemia, individualize dependent-lung recruitment/PEEP and discuss oxygen insufflation or low-level CPAP to the operative lung, or intermittent two-lung ventilation. These interventions may interfere with the operation and require explicit coordination.

sections.title: Hemodynamics, fluids & hemorrhage
bullets: Aim for adequate organ perfusion without unnecessary positive fluid balance. Avoid both indiscriminate loading and rigid restriction that produces hypovolemia or kidney injury.
Differentiate vasodilation, bleeding and ventricular dysfunction when pressure falls. Treat the cause; hypotension under anesthesia is not automatically a fluid deficit.

Assess anticipated vascular injury and conversion risk before positioning limits access. Major pulmonary, hilar or chest-wall bleeding requires rapid surgical communication, suitable access and blood availability.
Interpret dynamic preload indices cautiously with an open thorax, low tidal volumes, arrhythmia or major changes in intrathoracic pressure; integrate imaging and perfusion trends when available.

sections.title: Analgesia, breathing & postoperative destination
bullets: Effective pain control supports cough, deep breathing and mobilization. Match regional coverage to the actual incision, port sites and drains rather than to the procedure name alone.

For VATS, PROSPECT supports paravertebral or erector spinae plane analgesia, with serratus plane block as a second-choice option. Acetaminophen and an NSAID/COX-2 agent are considered when not contraindicated, with opioids for rescue.

Open thoracotomy or thoracoabdominal surgery may need a different analgesic strategy, including epidural or paravertebral approaches when appropriate. Anticoagulation, infection, hypotension risk and anatomy determine suitability; blocks are not interchangeable.

Extubation requires adequate gas exchange, respiratory strength, alertness, hemostasis and analgesia, not simply completion of surgery. Decide monitored ward versus higher-acuity care from reserve, extent of resection, ongoing support and complications.

Postoperative surveillance includes atelectasis, secretion retention, pneumonia, air leak, respiratory failure and arrhythmia. Reassess unexpected dyspnea or rising oxygen needs rather than attributing them automatically to pain.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: A major thoracoabdominal operation with approach-dependent lung isolation, prolonged exposure and pulmonary risk.
Assess dysphagia, obstruction and aspiration risk; plan positioning and airway access before turning or robotic docking.
Protect organ/conduit perfusion without fluid overload; vasodilation and true hypovolemia require different responses.
Analgesia, respiratory readiness and postoperative support are central to safe recovery.

sections.title: Approach & access constraints
bullets: Confirm abdominal, thoracic and cervical phases, lateral versus prone positioning, anastomotic location and robotic access. Airway and line access may become restricted during later phases.
Use a DLT or blocker when required; selected prone minimally invasive procedures may use two-lung ventilation. Agree on conversion and oxygenation-rescue plans in advance.

sections.title: Airway strategy & postoperative aspiration concerns
bullets: Review dysphagia, regurgitation and obstructing disease. Standard fasting guidance for low-risk elective patients does not establish an empty esophagus or stomach in this setting; individualize the aspiration-prevention and induction plan.
A difficult airway may favor securing a single-lumen tube with an awake technique when indicated, followed by a bronchial blocker. Confirm isolation bronchoscopically.

Do not insert an NG/OG tube blindly through suspected obstruction or a fresh surgical reconstruction. Coordinate whether, how and when a tube is placed with the surgeon; tube placement can itself cause injury or provoke regurgitation.

After reconstruction, altered gastroesophageal anatomy can increase aspiration concerns. Respiratory support and postoperative airway decisions must account for the reconstructed conduit, not just the preoperative airway.

sections.title: Perfusion, fluids & anesthetic hypotension
bullets: Balance conduit/systemic perfusion against pulmonary edema and kidney injury. Very restrictive fluids can be harmful, just as large unnecessary positive balances can be harmful.

Use a cause-directed response to hypotension; vasopressors may be appropriate for vasodilation rather than repeated fluid loading. Do not describe any vasopressor as universally risk-free for conduit perfusion.
Dynamic preload indices may be unreliable with an open chest and other nonstandard conditions. Integrate perfusion trends and the operative phase.

sections.title: Analgesia & respiratory support after reconstruction
bullets: Thoracic epidural, paravertebral or selected fascial-plane techniques may be considered according to approach, coagulation and hemodynamic tolerance. Abdominal and thoracic incisions may need different coverage.
Extubation in the OR is possible in selected stable patients; continued ventilation/ICU is appropriate when physiology requires it. No single approach guarantees early extubation.

Postoperative NIV/CPAP decisions require team discussion because aspiration and conduit/anastomotic concerns exist. Do not turn these concerns into an absolute prohibition of needed respiratory rescue.

sections.title: Pulmonary reserve & functional assessment
bullets: Review respiratory symptoms, functional capacity, oxygen/ventilatory support, prior lung treatment and cardiac comorbidity. For planned lung resection, assess FEV1 and DLCO and estimate postoperative reserve for the actual extent of resection.

Low predicted postoperative function or limited exercise capacity warrants further multidisciplinary assessment, often including exercise testing. Do not decide operability from one historical spirometry cutoff in isolation.
Review pulmonary hypertension and RV function when relevant. Removing or excluding part of the pulmonary vascular bed, hypoxemia and excessive airway pressure can increase RV stress.

sections.title: Airway & lung isolation
bullets: Confirm whether lung isolation is required for exposure, contamination control or the planned airway/bronchial reconstruction. A double-lumen tube and a bronchial blocker have different suction, access and postoperative-airway advantages.

sections.title: One-lung ventilation: protective strategy
bullets: Use predicted/ideal body weight, not actual body weight, to select tidal volume. Contemporary review ranges commonly begin around 4–6 mL/kg for OLV, then individualize to compliance, gas exchange, pressures and the operative context.

Individualize PEEP and keep airway/distending pressures as low as reasonably compatible with adequate ventilation. Excess PEEP may overdistend the dependent lung, impair venous return and worsen shunt; too little can promote derecruitment.

Titrate FiO2 to the clinical oxygenation requirement; use 100% oxygen during significant desaturation while evaluating the cause. No single FiO2 or PEEP setting is correct throughout every thoracic procedure.

Mild hypercapnia may be tolerated, but severe hypercarbia/acidosis is particularly undesirable with pulmonary hypertension, RV dysfunction, arrhythmias or raised intracranial pressure. Assess arterial gases when end-tidal CO2 may poorly reflect arterial CO2.

Recruitment is a selective maneuver, not an automatic high-pressure step. Consider hemodynamic tolerance, emphysema, air leak and surgical repair; recruitment can transiently worsen oxygenation and blood pressure.

sections.title: OLV hypoxemia: clinical troubleshooting
bullets: Abrupt severe desaturation is an emergency: notify the surgeon, pause the procedure and restore two-lung ventilation with FiO2 1.0 when feasible while urgently evaluating the cause. Do not persist with OLV solely to preserve exposure.
Check the airway/circuit and use bronchoscopy to reassess tube or blocker position, obstruction and secretions; consider bleeding, bronchospasm and loss of dependent-lung ventilation.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Assess airway, cardiac and great-vessel compression separately; positional symptoms and CT findings guide risk.
High-risk induction needs a prearranged rescue position, airway/surgical expertise and, when indicated, extracorporeal support ready before deterioration.
Maintaining spontaneous ventilation may be appropriate, but it is not a guarantee against collapse. Selected adult studies challenge blanket assumptions about paralysis.
Continue vigilance after resection and during recovery for airway, respiratory or hemodynamic deterioration.

sections.title: Symptoms, imaging & risk anatomy
bullets: Review orthopnea, stridor, syncope, supine intolerance, SVC symptoms and prior anesthetic tolerance. Lack of symptoms does not exclude important compression.
Review CT for tracheal/main-bronchial narrowing and location, vascular/cardiac compression and effusion. Airway diameter alone does not describe the cardiovascular risk.
Identify the position that improves symptoms and whether a tube or rigid bronchoscope could actually pass beyond the obstructed segment.

sections.title: Individualized induction, not a blanket rule
bullets: Avoid unplanned deep sedation in a high-risk patient. Consider awake/local techniques, staged induction and preserving spontaneous ventilation when the anatomy and team plan support them.

Small adult observational studies found that controlled positive pressure and paralysis did not necessarily worsen airway caliber and sometimes improved it. This does not prove routine induction safe or exclude cardiovascular collapse.

Expiratory obstruction and air trapping can occur despite improved inspiratory patency; allow adequate exhalation and follow hemodynamics. Positive pressure may worsen venous return when the heart/great vessels are compressed.

sections.title: Rescue capability before induction
bullets: Agree on repositioning, rigid bronchoscopy and surgical decompression options with the relevant teams before airway manipulation. Equipment elsewhere in the hospital is not equivalent to immediate rescue capability.
Selected very-high-risk patients may require planned ECMO/CPB access or support before induction. VA versus VV depends on cardiovascular involvement as well as airway obstruction.
If SVC obstruction compromises upper-body venous access, plan lower-extremity access as appropriate; ensure emergency drugs can reach the circulation.

bullets: Reassess ventilation, airway mechanics and circulation after surgical decompression; the end of resection does not eliminate perioperative cardiopulmonary risk.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Distinguish thymoma compression from myasthenia gravis; either or both may influence the plan.
Assess bulbar and respiratory weakness, prior crisis and medication timing; optimize MG with neurology when feasible.
MG produces unpredictable neuromuscular-blocker response, especially sensitivity to nondepolarizers. Use quantitative monitoring and a deliberate reversal plan.
Extubation depends on strength, airway protection and gas exchange, not only a train-of-four result.

sections.title: Approach & mediastinal anatomy
bullets: Clarify VATS, robotic or open access, lung-isolation needs and insufflation. Large thymoma may also compress airway or vessels; use the mediastinal-mass risk framework when present.

sections.title: MG assessment & medication continuity
bullets: Assess dysphagia/dysarthria, respiratory weakness, previous crisis, current disease control and FVC where appropriate. Antibody results alone do not establish clinical optimization.

Coordinate with neurology; anticholinesterases and glucocorticoids are generally continued, with steroid supplementation when indicated. Missed doses during long operations may contribute to end-of-case weakness.
Discuss postoperative ventilation in patients with significant bulbar/respiratory symptoms or other risk factors rather than promising routine immediate extubation.

sections.title: Neuromuscular blockers & reversal
bullets: Avoid neuromuscular blockers when a suitable technique allows; when required, use carefully titrated dosing and quantitative monitoring. MG patients can be profoundly sensitive to nondepolarizing blockade.
Succinylcholine response is complicated by resistance, possible phase-II block and anticholinesterase-related prolongation. It is not a straightforward substitute for a nondepolarizing strategy.

Rocuronium with sugammadex is a commonly favored strategy when blockade is necessary, but residual weakness and rare incomplete recovery remain possible. Confirm quantitative recovery and clinical respiratory/bulbar function.

sources.label: BJA Education: perioperative management of myasthenia gravis

sections.title: Delayed extubation & crisis assessment
bullets: Confirm effective cough, ventilation, airway reflexes and strength, with quantitative TOF recovery at least 0.9 before extubation. A normal ratio does not exclude MG-related respiratory weakness.
Evaluate persistent weakness for residual block, missed medication, myasthenic crisis and other causes. Suspected crisis needs neurology/critical-care involvement and appropriate ventilatory support.

bullets: Review obstructive versus restrictive disease, baseline gases, oxygen/ventilatory needs, PH, RV function and infection status. The physiology and induction reserve vary substantially.
Discuss planned single/bilateral sequence and the circumstances for ECMO or CPB support before induction. Instability during PA clamping may require extracorporeal rescue.

sections.title: Lung isolation & pulmonary artery clamping
bullets: A DLT commonly facilitates isolation, suction and sequential transplantation; a blocker may be an alternative. Reconfirm positioning throughout major manipulation.
OLV and PA clamping can worsen oxygenation and RV loading. Reassess RV function and circulation rather than treating hypotension only with volume.

sections.title: Reperfusion & graft ventilation
bullets: Coordinate controlled reperfusion, de-airing and ventilation with the surgeon. Sudden changes in perfusion, pulmonary vascular load and graft function can destabilize circulation.
Use a graft-protective strategy that considers donor lung size, compliance and gas exchange. Avoid transferring fixed ventilation settings from the diseased native lung to the new graft.
TEE may help assess pulmonary vascular anastomoses and biventricular function when hypoxemia or instability persists. Primary graft dysfunction is only one potential cause.

sections.title: Fluid balance, airway exchange & ICU
bullets: The newly implanted lung has impaired lymphatic drainage and is vulnerable to edema. Balance blood/fluid replacement against overload and reassess ongoing perfusion and bleeding.
If changing from a DLT to a single-lumen tube, plan for airway edema and a controlled exchange with appropriate visualization/rescue equipment.
ICU handoff includes graft ventilation, oxygenation, ECMO status, ventricular support, bleeding and anastomotic concerns. Ongoing graft dysfunction may require continued extracorporeal support.

sources.label: Review of anesthesia for lung transplantation

sections.title: Pulmonary reserve & functional assessment
bullets: Review respiratory symptoms, functional capacity, oxygen/ventilatory support, prior lung treatment and cardiac comorbidity. For planned lung resection, assess FEV1 and DLCO and estimate postoperative reserve for the actual extent of resection.

Low predicted postoperative function or limited exercise capacity warrants further multidisciplinary assessment, often including exercise testing. Do not decide operability from one historical spirometry cutoff in isolation.
Review pulmonary hypertension and RV function when relevant. Removing or excluding part of the pulmonary vascular bed, hypoxemia and excessive airway pressure can increase RV stress.

sections.title: Airway & lung isolation
bullets: Confirm whether lung isolation is required for exposure, contamination control or the planned airway/bronchial reconstruction. A double-lumen tube and a bronchial blocker have different suction, access and postoperative-airway advantages.

With a difficult airway, securing a suitable single-lumen airway first and then placing a blocker may be preferable to forcing a bulky double-lumen tube. Match the plan to the operation and rescue options.

Confirm position with flexible bronchoscopy and reassess after lateral positioning and when oxygenation, ventilation or surgical exposure changes. Auscultation alone does not reliably establish correct lung-isolation-device position.
Coordinate device/cuff location and withdrawal with bronchial stapling or airway surgery. Avoid trapping an airway device or suction catheter in a staple line.

sections.title: One-lung ventilation: protective strategy
bullets: Use predicted/ideal body weight, not actual body weight, to select tidal volume. Contemporary review ranges commonly begin around 4–6 mL/kg for OLV, then individualize to compliance, gas exchange, pressures and the operative context.

Individualize PEEP and keep airway/distending pressures as low as reasonably compatible with adequate ventilation. Excess PEEP may overdistend the dependent lung, impair venous return and worsen shunt; too little can promote derecruitment.

Titrate FiO2 to the clinical oxygenation requirement; use 100% oxygen during significant desaturation while evaluating the cause. No single FiO2 or PEEP setting is correct throughout every thoracic procedure.

Mild hypercapnia may be tolerated, but severe hypercarbia/acidosis is particularly undesirable with pulmonary hypertension, RV dysfunction, arrhythmias or raised intracranial pressure. Assess arterial gases when end-tidal CO2 may poorly reflect arterial CO2.

Recruitment is a selective maneuver, not an automatic high-pressure step. Consider hemodynamic tolerance, emphysema, air leak and surgical repair; recruitment can transiently worsen oxygenation and blood pressure.

sections.title: OLV hypoxemia: clinical troubleshooting
bullets: Abrupt severe desaturation is an emergency: notify the surgeon, pause the procedure and restore two-lung ventilation with FiO2 1.0 when feasible while urgently evaluating the cause. Do not persist with OLV solely to preserve exposure.
Check the airway/circuit and use bronchoscopy to reassess tube or blocker position, obstruction and secretions; consider bleeding, bronchospasm and loss of dependent-lung ventilation.
Assess blood pressure, cardiac output, hemoglobin and gas exchange as well as the ventilator. A low oxygen saturation may coexist with inadequate oxygen delivery from circulatory failure.

For persistent hypoxemia, individualize dependent-lung recruitment/PEEP and discuss oxygen insufflation or low-level CPAP to the operative lung, or intermittent two-lung ventilation. These interventions may interfere with the operation and require explicit coordination.

sections.title: Hemodynamics, fluids & hemorrhage
bullets: Aim for adequate organ perfusion without unnecessary positive fluid balance. Avoid both indiscriminate loading and rigid restriction that produces hypovolemia or kidney injury.
Differentiate vasodilation, bleeding and ventricular dysfunction when pressure falls. Treat the cause; hypotension under anesthesia is not automatically a fluid deficit.

Assess anticipated vascular injury and conversion risk before positioning limits access. Major pulmonary, hilar or chest-wall bleeding requires rapid surgical communication, suitable access and blood availability.
Interpret dynamic preload indices cautiously with an open thorax, low tidal volumes, arrhythmia or major changes in intrathoracic pressure; integrate imaging and perfusion trends when available.

sections.title: Analgesia, breathing & postoperative destination
bullets: Effective pain control supports cough, deep breathing and mobilization. Match regional coverage to the actual incision, port sites and drains rather than to the procedure name alone.

For VATS, PROSPECT supports paravertebral or erector spinae plane analgesia, with serratus plane block as a second-choice option. Acetaminophen and an NSAID/COX-2 agent are considered when not contraindicated, with opioids for rescue.

Open thoracotomy or thoracoabdominal surgery may need a different analgesic strategy, including epidural or paravertebral approaches when appropriate. Anticoagulation, infection, hypotension risk and anatomy determine suitability; blocks are not interchangeable.

Extubation requires adequate gas exchange, respiratory strength, alertness, hemostasis and analgesia, not simply completion of surgery. Decide monitored ward versus higher-acuity care from reserve, extent of resection, ongoing support and complications.

Postoperative surveillance includes atelectasis, secretion retention, pneumonia, air leak, respiratory failure and arrhythmia. Reassess unexpected dyspnea or rising oxygen needs rather than attributing them automatically to pain.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Differentiate bedside chemical instillation from VATS pleurodesis with possible additional lung surgery.
Adequate pleural apposition is important; a nonexpanding trapped lung changes the treatment plan.
Pain, hypoxemia and respiratory complications require active planning and monitoring.
Drain handling depends on the indication: avoid blindly copying a clamping instruction into a patient with an ongoing air leak.

sources.label: Chemical pleurodesis: indications and complications review
PROSPECT 2021: VATS pain recommendations

sections.title: Effusion versus pneumothorax
bullets: Confirm recurrent effusion versus recurrent/persistent pneumothorax and whether the procedure includes bleb/wedge resection. The anesthesia and ventilation burden differ.
Chemical bedside pleurodesis does not automatically require the general anesthesia or OLV used for VATS. Apply the lung-isolation details below only when the operation needs them.

sources.label: Chemical pleurodesis: indications and complications review

sections.title: Lung expansion & alternatives
bullets: Assess whether drainage permits lung re-expansion and symptom relief. Nonexpanding trapped lung limits successful pleurodesis and may favor a tunneled pleural catheter strategy.
The procedural team determines the intervention based on disease, prognosis and operative fitness; this reference is not an instruction to use talc in every recurrent effusion.

sources.label: Chemical pleurodesis: indications and complications review

sections.title: Pain, talc & inflammatory complications
bullets: Pleuritic pain is common and may need multimodal analgesia. Monitor for increasing oxygen requirement or respiratory distress rather than treating all discomfort as expected.
Talc-associated severe respiratory injury is uncommon but important; particle characteristics and the patient’s reserve matter. Avoid using historical complication rates as an individual prediction.

sources.label: Chemical pleurodesis: indications and complications review

sections.title: Drain plan & postoperative reassessment
bullets: For pneumothorax with ongoing air leakage, clamping can create tension physiology. Confirm the surgeon’s drainage plan and do not apply an effusion-slurry clamping schedule indiscriminately.
Monitor for re-expansion pulmonary edema, pneumothorax and persistent air leak when dyspnea or hypoxemia develops after drainage or pleurodesis.

sources.label: Chemical pleurodesis: indications and complications review

sections.title: Pulmonary reserve & functional assessment
bullets: Review respiratory symptoms, functional capacity, oxygen/ventilatory support, prior lung treatment and cardiac comorbidity. For planned lung resection, assess FEV1 and DLCO and estimate postoperative reserve for the actual extent of resection.

Low predicted postoperative function or limited exercise capacity warrants further multidisciplinary assessment, often including exercise testing. Do not decide operability from one historical spirometry cutoff in isolation.
Review pulmonary hypertension and RV function when relevant. Removing or excluding part of the pulmonary vascular bed, hypoxemia and excessive airway pressure can increase RV stress.

sources.label: BJA Education: anaesthesia for pneumonectomy
Review of anesthesia for lung transplantation

sections.title: Airway & lung isolation
bullets: Confirm whether lung isolation is required for exposure, contamination control or the planned airway/bronchial reconstruction. A double-lumen tube and a bronchial blocker have different suction, access and postoperative-airway advantages.

With a difficult airway, securing a suitable single-lumen airway first and then placing a blocker may be preferable to forcing a bulky double-lumen tube. Match the plan to the operation and rescue options.

Confirm position with flexible bronchoscopy and reassess after lateral positioning and when oxygenation, ventilation or surgical exposure changes. Auscultation alone does not reliably establish correct lung-isolation-device position.
Coordinate device/cuff location and withdrawal with bronchial stapling or airway surgery. Avoid trapping an airway device or suction catheter in a staple line.
