sections.title: One-lung ventilation: protective strategy
bullets: Use predicted/ideal body weight, not actual body weight, to select tidal volume. Contemporary review ranges commonly begin around 4–6 mL/kg for OLV, then individualize to compliance, gas exchange, pressures and the operative context.

Individualize PEEP and keep airway/distending pressures as low as reasonably compatible with adequate ventilation. Excess PEEP may overdistend the dependent lung, impair venous return and worsen shunt; too little can promote derecruitment.

Titrate FiO2 to the clinical oxygenation requirement; use 100% oxygen during significant desaturation while evaluating the cause. No single FiO2 or PEEP setting is correct throughout every thoracic procedure.

Mild hypercapnia may be tolerated, but severe hypercarbia/acidosis is particularly undesirable with pulmonary hypertension, RV dysfunction, arrhythmias or raised intracranial pressure. Assess arterial gases when end-tidal CO2 may poorly reflect arterial CO2.

Recruitment is a selective maneuver, not an automatic high-pressure step. Consider hemodynamic tolerance, emphysema, air leak and surgical repair; recruitment can transiently worsen oxygenation and blood pressure.

sections.title: OLV hypoxemia: clinical troubleshooting
bullets: Abrupt severe desaturation is an emergency: notify the surgeon, pause the procedure and restore two-lung ventilation with FiO2 1.0 when feasible while urgently evaluating the cause. Do not persist with OLV solely to preserve exposure.
Check the airway/circuit and use bronchoscopy to reassess tube or blocker position, obstruction and secretions; consider bleeding, bronchospasm and loss of dependent-lung ventilation.
Assess blood pressure, cardiac output, hemoglobin and gas exchange as well as the ventilator. A low oxygen saturation may coexist with inadequate oxygen delivery from circulatory failure.

For persistent hypoxemia, individualize dependent-lung recruitment/PEEP and discuss oxygen insufflation or low-level CPAP to the operative lung, or intermittent two-lung ventilation. These interventions may interfere with the operation and require explicit coordination.

sources.label: BJA Education 2023: hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation

sections.title: Hemodynamics, fluids & hemorrhage
bullets: Aim for adequate organ perfusion without unnecessary positive fluid balance. Avoid both indiscriminate loading and rigid restriction that produces hypovolemia or kidney injury.
Differentiate vasodilation, bleeding and ventricular dysfunction when pressure falls. Treat the cause; hypotension under anesthesia is not automatically a fluid deficit.

Assess anticipated vascular injury and conversion risk before positioning limits access. Major pulmonary, hilar or chest-wall bleeding requires rapid surgical communication, suitable access and blood availability.
Interpret dynamic preload indices cautiously with an open thorax, low tidal volumes, arrhythmia or major changes in intrathoracic pressure; integrate imaging and perfusion trends when available.

sections.title: Analgesia, breathing & postoperative destination
bullets: Effective pain control supports cough, deep breathing and mobilization. Match regional coverage to the actual incision, port sites and drains rather than to the procedure name alone.

For VATS, PROSPECT supports paravertebral or erector spinae plane analgesia, with serratus plane block as a second-choice option. Acetaminophen and an NSAID/COX-2 agent are considered when not contraindicated, with opioids for rescue.

Open thoracotomy or thoracoabdominal surgery may need a different analgesic strategy, including epidural or paravertebral approaches when appropriate. Anticoagulation, infection, hypotension risk and anatomy determine suitability; blocks are not interchangeable.

Extubation requires adequate gas exchange, respiratory strength, alertness, hemostasis and analgesia, not simply completion of surgery. Decide monitored ward versus higher-acuity care from reserve, extent of resection, ongoing support and complications.

Postoperative surveillance includes atelectasis, secretion retention, pneumonia, air leak, respiratory failure and arrhythmia. Reassess unexpected dyspnea or rising oxygen needs rather than attributing them automatically to pain.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Define chest-wall extent, concomitant lung resection and reconstruction; respiratory mechanics and analgesia needs may be substantial.
Lung isolation is approach-dependent, not mandatory for every chest-wall operation.
Prepare for bleeding, positioning constraints and possible postoperative ventilation.
Protect respiratory function with effective analgesia and reassess the stability of the reconstruction.

sections.title: Defect, resection & reconstruction
bullets: Clarify tumor/trauma indication, ribs or sternum involved, adjacent lung resection and anticipated prosthetic or soft-tissue reconstruction.
The reconstructive goal includes stability and protection of underlying organs; extensive defects can impair mechanics and increase postoperative support needs.

sources.label: Chest-wall reconstruction: multicenter surgical experience

sections.title: Ventilation depends on intrathoracic work
bullets: A DLT may be used for planned lung resection or relevant intrathoracic injury; isolated chest-wall work may use a single-lumen airway. Confirm the operation rather than defaulting to OLV.
When OLV is needed, apply protective ventilation and bronchoscopic device checks as detailed below.

sections.title: Bleeding, mechanics & analgesic coverage
bullets: Estimate blood availability/access needs from the operative extent. The possibility of re-exploration for bleeding remains even with apparently successful reconstruction.
Regional/systemic analgesia must match incision and drain distribution; extensive resection can change the feasibility of familiar blocks.

sources.label: Chest-wall reconstruction: multicenter surgical experience

sections.title: Postoperative surveillance
bullets: Assess respiratory mechanics, gas exchange, cough and pain when deciding extubation and ICU care. Reconstruction does not guarantee normal chest-wall function immediately.
Unexpected chest pain/swelling, respiratory deterioration or fever warrants assessment for bleeding, pneumothorax, infection or reconstruction-related problems.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Although diagnostic and often brief, mediastinoscopy can cause major bleeding, airway obstruction or innominate-artery compression.
Review any mediastinal mass for airway and cardiovascular compression before induction.
Prepare access and rapid surgical rescue according to anatomy and risk, not the small neck incision.
Reassess airway, respiratory and hemodynamic status before recovery disposition.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: adult mediastinal masses and mediastinoscopy
2024 review: perioperative mediastinal mass syndrome

sections.title: Cervical access & adjacent structures
bullets: Cervical mediastinoscopy accesses the pretracheal space toward the carina for diagnostic sampling. Important vessels and airway structures are close to the operative field.
Lung isolation is not routine for standard cervical mediastinoscopy. A combined or converted thoracic procedure may require a different airway strategy.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: adult mediastinal masses and mediastinoscopy
BJA Education 2023: hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation

sections.title: Compression assessment
bullets: Assess positional symptoms and review CT anatomy. Major airway, SVC or cardiac compression may require the dedicated high-risk mediastinal-mass plan.
Lower-extremity access may be appropriate with significant SVC obstruction. Plan drug delivery and hemorrhage resuscitation accordingly.

sources.label: 2024 review: perioperative mediastinal mass syndrome
OpenAnesthesia: adult mediastinal masses and mediastinoscopy

sections.title: Hemorrhage & arterial compression
bullets: Major hemorrhage may require emergent thoracotomy. Plan large-bore access, blood and rapid conversion support for the patient’s risk.

Innominate-artery compression is a recognized complication. Correlate abrupt monitoring changes with instrument position and promptly communicate concern rather than treating every pressure change as systemic anesthetic hypotension.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: adult mediastinal masses and mediastinoscopy

sections.title: Airway obstruction & recovery
bullets: For significant preexisting airway compromise, have the planned bronchoscopic/surgical rescue resources available before manipulation. A conventional tube may not bypass distal compression.
Use monitored recovery appropriate to residual compression, airway events, bleeding and gas-exchange concerns.

sources.label: 2024 review: perioperative mediastinal mass syndrome
OpenAnesthesia: adult mediastinal masses and mediastinoscopy

sections.title: SVC obstruction & cardiac compression
bullets: Airway compression and cardiovascular compression are separate problems. A patent tube does not correct impaired venous return, pulmonary artery obstruction or cardiac compression.
Review imaging and symptoms for SVC and cardiac involvement and plan access/support accordingly.

sources.label: 2024 review: perioperative mediastinal mass syndrome
2023 review: evolution of mediastinal-mass anesthesia
OpenAnesthesia: adult mediastinal masses and mediastinoscopy

sections.title: Sedation & positioning tolerance
bullets: Supine intolerance, orthopnea or syncope should change planning before sedation. Preserve access to the position that relieves symptoms and avoid unplanned deep sedation in a high-risk patient.
Use a staged individualized induction when significant compression is present rather than treating the procedure as routine merely because the incision is small.

sources.label: 2024 review: perioperative mediastinal mass syndrome

sections.title: Ventilation with central compression
bullets: Spontaneous breathing is not a guarantee of airway or cardiovascular safety. Selected adult evidence shows that positive pressure can improve airway caliber, but this does not remove the risk of impaired circulation.
Allow adequate expiration when central obstruction is present; air trapping can reduce venous return and cause hemodynamic deterioration.

sources.label: 2023 review: evolution of mediastinal-mass anesthesia

sections.title: When ordinary airway rescue is insufficient
bullets: Rigid bronchoscopy may help bypass obstruction when anatomy allows. It cannot solve every distal obstruction or cardiovascular compression problem.
Selected extreme-risk cases may need preplanned extracorporeal access/support. Standby equipment without a feasible, timely cannulation plan may be inadequate.

sources.label: 2024 review: perioperative mediastinal mass syndrome
OpenAnesthesia: adult mediastinal masses and mediastinoscopy

sections.title: Vascular injury readiness
bullets: Clarify how rapid surgical access and resuscitation would occur if a major vessel is injured. Access, blood availability and team readiness should reflect the imaging and expected dissection.
After an abrupt deterioration, correlate instrument position and operative events with oxygenation, ventilation and circulation rather than assuming a medication effect.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: adult mediastinal masses and mediastinoscopy

sections.title: Postprocedure observation & handoff
bullets: Communicate airway/vascular compression, any intraoperative obstruction or hemorrhage and ongoing support needs to the recovery team.
Persistent positional symptoms, respiratory compromise or hemodynamic instability warrants a higher-acuity postoperative plan.

sources.label: 2024 review: perioperative mediastinal mass syndrome
OpenAnesthesia: adult mediastinal masses and mediastinoscopy

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: TEVAR and open descending/thoracoabdominal repair have different airway, perfusion and hemorrhage requirements.
Assess spinal-cord, cerebral, renal and visceral perfusion risks from coverage/clamping and baseline vascular disease.
CSF drainage is selected by risk and center protocol; it carries hemorrhage and infection hazards and is not routine for every TEVAR.
Delayed leg weakness or focal neurologic changes require immediate escalation, even after an initially normal examination.

sources.label: Perioperative management of thoracic endovascular repair
Thoracoabdominal aortic repair: anesthesia review
2025 review: cerebral and spinal cord protection in aortic arch surgery

sections.title: Endovascular versus open repair
bullets: Clarify coverage or clamp extent, branch-vessel involvement, prior aortic repair and planned revascularization. These determine ischemic risk and access strategy.
Open repair may require OLV, distal perfusion and major transfusion preparation; routine TEVAR should not automatically inherit an open-repair anesthetic.

sources.label: Perioperative management of thoracic endovascular repair
Thoracoabdominal aortic repair: anesthesia review

sections.title: Organ reserve & baseline examination
bullets: Review renal function, cardiac/pulmonary reserve, prior stroke, peripheral access anatomy and baseline leg neurologic function. Communicate preexisting deficits.
Assess how coverage, left subclavian involvement and previous infrarenal repair may affect collateral spinal circulation.

sources.label: Perioperative management of thoracic endovascular repair
Thoracoabdominal aortic repair: anesthesia review

sections.title: Monitoring & vascular access
bullets: Choose arterial sites around clamping/cannulation and branch coverage. Coordinate femoral access with the surgical team and preserve the ability to monitor perfusion in relevant territories.
Use invasive monitoring, serial laboratory assessment and blood availability appropriate to open repair, instability or rupture risk.

sources.label: Thoracoabdominal aortic repair: anesthesia review
Perioperative management of thoracic endovascular repair

sections.title: Airway & ventilation
bullets: Open descending repair commonly needs lung isolation. Confirm placement bronchoscopically and use a protective OLV strategy.
TEVAR anesthesia is individualized to stability, imaging/immobility needs and rescue capability; not every case requires lung isolation.

sources.label: Thoracoabdominal aortic repair: anesthesia review
BJA Education 2023: hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation
Perioperative management of thoracic endovascular repair

sections.title: Spinal-cord perfusion & CSF drainage
bullets: Spinal perfusion depends on arterial inflow and downstream pressure, including CSF/venous pressure. Avoid sustained hypotension and support oxygen delivery in patients at risk.
Selected high-risk patients may benefit from CSF drainage. Placement/removal must be coordinated with anticoagulation and performed within a specialist protocol with drainage limits.
Overdrainage can cause intracranial/spinal bleeding and other serious complications. Do not present a high rescue drainage rate as a routine bedside instruction.

sources.label: Thoracoabdominal aortic repair: anesthesia review
Perioperative management of thoracic endovascular repair

sections.title: Anticoagulation & neuraxial coordination
bullets: Reconcile antiplatelet/anticoagulant exposure, stents, mechanical valves and any CSF drain. Use current drug-specific institutional neuraxial timing rather than a blanket one-week hold for all agents.
Heparin targets and reversal depend on the operation and circuit/perfusion technique. Do not substitute conventional CPB ACT thresholds for every endovascular repair.

sources.label: Perioperative management of thoracic endovascular repair
Thoracoabdominal aortic repair: anesthesia review
EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP 2024: adult cardiopulmonary bypass guideline (2025 publication)

sections.title: Clamping, reperfusion & blood loss
bullets: Open clamping changes proximal afterload and distal organ perfusion; release can expose vasodilation, acidosis and bleeding. Coordinate timing and support with surgeon/perfusionist.
Use suitable access, warming, blood and cell salvage where appropriate. Correct perfusion and coagulopathy while the surgeon assesses mechanical bleeding.

sources.label: Thoracoabdominal aortic repair: anesthesia review
EACTS/EACTAIC 2024: adult cardiac patient blood management

sections.title: Renal & visceral protection
bullets: Minimize avoidable hypotension and nephrotoxic exposure and follow renal/perfusion trends. TEVAR adds contrast considerations; open repair adds clamp-related visceral ischemia.
Fluid support must fit cardiac reserve and measured perfusion. Renal protection is not achieved by a single prophylactic drug or fixed fluid volume.

sources.label: Perioperative management of thoracic endovascular repair
Thoracoabdominal aortic repair: anesthesia review

sections.title: New postoperative neurologic deficit
bullets: New paraparesis/paraplegia is time-sensitive. Activate the aortic-team rescue pathway for perfusion augmentation, oxygen-delivery assessment and drain evaluation/placement when safe and indicated.
A focal cerebral deficit needs immediate stroke/neurologic evaluation. Severe headache or neurologic change with a CSF drain also raises concern for bleeding, not simply inadequate drainage.

sources.label: Perioperative management of thoracic endovascular repair

sections.title: ICU, pain & serial assessment
bullets: Plan the monitoring environment for serial neurologic examinations, blood pressure goals, renal function, bleeding and drain management. Delayed spinal injury is possible.
Open repair requires substantial pain and respiratory planning; coordinate regional options with anticoagulation, perfusion goals and any spinal drain.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Confirm configuration and purpose: VV supports respiratory gas exchange; VA adds direct circulatory support.
Use imaging-guided cannulation, a bleeding/vascular-rescue plan and configuration-specific monitoring.
Monitor VV recirculation and gas exchange; with peripheral VA, watch upper-body oxygenation, LV distension and limb perfusion.
Weaning and decannulation require organ-recovery assessment and a specialist trial, not merely improved saturation.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline
ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: VV versus VA support
bullets: VV returns oxygenated blood to the venous circulation and provides no direct hemodynamic support. It may indirectly improve RV function by correcting gas exchange and pulmonary vasoconstriction.
VA returns blood to the arterial circulation and supports perfusion but may increase LV afterload. Central/peripheral and hybrid configurations create different monitoring and rescue needs.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline
ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: Cannulation plan & induction risk
bullets: Clarify urgency, cannulation sites, support already in place and whether the patient can tolerate sedation/induction. Assign cannulation, imaging, perfusion and emergency roles explicitly.
Prepare for hemodynamic changes and occult cannulation bleeding when support begins. Titrate resuscitation to physiology rather than assuming every flow limitation is hypovolemia.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline
ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: Imaging & cannula position
bullets: Use ultrasound for vascular access and appropriate echo/fluoroscopy for guidewire/cannula guidance. Dual-lumen VV positioning particularly requires live imaging; misplaced wires/cannulae can perforate the heart.
Reassess position and drainage/return when flow or oxygenation changes. Secure cannulae and maintain position awareness during transfer and surgery.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline
ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: VV blood flow, sweep & recirculation
bullets: Blood flow is a major determinant of extracorporeal oxygen delivery; sweep gas primarily controls CO2 removal. Overall oxygenation also depends on hemoglobin, native cardiac output, recirculation and metabolic demand.
Avoid abrupt large reductions in PaCO2 at initiation. Titrate support with serial gases and physiologic assessment.

Recirculation returns oxygenated blood directly to the drainage limb and reduces effective delivery. Worsening saturation despite increased pump flow should prompt assessment, not endless flow escalation.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline

sections.title: Peripheral VA: differential oxygenation
bullets: When recovering native cardiac output ejects poorly oxygenated pulmonary venous blood, the upper body may remain hypoxemic despite apparently good lower-body oxygenation.
Right-radial gases/right-hand oximetry help detect this pattern in typical femoral VA configurations. Assess native lung function and discuss configuration changes when refractory.

sources.label: ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: VA afterload & LV distension
bullets: Assess pulse pressure, aortic-valve opening, LV size/stasis and pulmonary edema. VA flow can increase afterload and impair LV ejection.
Persistent LV distension or pulmonary edema requires specialist unloading assessment. Options depend on physiology and configuration; adjusting flow must preserve organ perfusion.

sources.label: ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: Distal limb perfusion & vascular injury
bullets: Femoral arterial cannulation can compromise distal flow. Plan distal perfusion and serial clinical/Doppler or NIRS assessment according to configuration and local protocol.
Monitor for bleeding, ischemia, compartment compromise and vascular injury during cannulation and after decannulation. A working circuit does not establish adequate limb perfusion.

sections.title: Anticoagulation, bleeding & thrombosis
bullets: Use the ECMO service’s anticoagulation strategy and serial coagulation/platelet/fibrinogen assessment. CPB ACT targets are not transferable to ECMO.
Life-threatening bleeding may require reducing or holding anticoagulation while closely monitoring thrombosis/circuit risks. Low-flow trials need particular attention to circuit clotting.

sections.title: Lung protection & organ monitoring
bullets: Use lung-protective ventilation while the circuit provides gas exchange; do not reflexively restore injurious ventilator settings for a circuit-related problem.
Follow perfusion, gases, neurologic status, renal function and hemoglobin along with circuit parameters. Thermodilution output may be unreliable during ECMO.

sections.title: Weaning trial & decannulation
bullets: VV weaning tests native oxygenation and ventilatory reserve through a monitored sweep reduction/off-sweep strategy while preserving safe circuit flow.
VA weaning assesses cardiac recovery and perfusion during a carefully supervised reduction in support, using echo, pressures, gases and vasoactive requirements. A normal EF alone is not sufficient.

Before removal, agree on anticoagulation timing, airway/sedation support, blood availability, vascular closure and postremoval surveillance. Continue assessment for bleeding, thrombosis and limb complications.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Distinguish a stable effusion from hemodynamic tamponade; induction and positive pressure can precipitate collapse in the latter.
Preserve venous return, contractility and compensatory vascular tone until decompression.
In unstable tamponade, coordinate immediate drainage capability before induction; local drainage may be appropriate.
After decompression, reassess support needs and watch for bleeding or ventricular/pulmonary deterioration.

sections.title: Effusion versus tamponade
bullets: Hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate and pericardial pressure, not fluid volume alone. Review echo and clinical perfusion rather than classifying risk by effusion size only.
Elevated CVP in tamponade reflects external compression and is not a reliable measure of usable cardiac preload.

sources.label: BJA Education: pericardial effusion and tamponade

sections.title: Preoperative status & urgency
bullets: Assess hypotension, compensatory tachycardia, dyspnea, rhythm and any associated bleeding or anticoagulation. The need for urgent decompression changes the sequence of preparation.
Do not delay life-saving drainage to obtain optional monitoring or complete an elective-style workup.

sources.label: BJA Education: pericardial effusion and tamponade

sections.title: Drainage approach & local anesthesia
bullets: Confirm subxiphoid versus other surgical approach and whether local anesthesia or general anesthesia is planned. Severe unstable tamponade may be drained under local anesthesia.
For general anesthesia in significant tamponade, have the surgeon and drainage equipment ready before induction rather than treating rescue as an afterthought.

sources.label: BJA Education: pericardial effusion and tamponade

sections.title: Monitoring & access
bullets: Establish reliable large-bore IV access, resuscitation drugs and appropriate arterial monitoring when feasible without harmful delay. Central access is desirable in some cases but must not delay urgent drainage.
Prepare defibrillation and vasoactive support before induction and track response through decompression.

sources.label: BJA Education: pericardial effusion and tamponade

sections.title: Induction: preserve compensation
bullets: Avoid abrupt vasodilation, myocardial depression and bradycardia. Titrate a hemodynamically appropriate technique while preserving the compensations maintaining output.
Volume can support venous return when depleted but is a bridge, not definitive treatment of tamponade. Decompression resolves the obstructive physiology.

sources.label: BJA Education: pericardial effusion and tamponade

sections.title: Ventilation before drainage
bullets: Positive-pressure ventilation can reduce venous return. Limit excessive inspiratory pressure/PEEP until decompression while maintaining oxygenation and ventilation.
Spontaneous-breathing techniques may be selected, but no technique removes the need for immediate surgical rescue in severe tamponade.

sources.label: BJA Education: pericardial effusion and tamponade

sections.title: Peri-induction deterioration
bullets: Sudden collapse requires urgent communication and decompression while supporting circulation. Repeated anesthetic or vasoactive adjustments cannot substitute for relieving the mechanical obstruction.
Reassess ventilation pressure, rhythm and circulating volume as the team proceeds with definitive drainage.

sources.label: BJA Education: pericardial effusion and tamponade

sections.title: After decompression
bullets: Expect rapid hemodynamic change; reduce support or deepen anesthesia as appropriate rather than continuing pre-drainage doses unchanged.
Rapid relief of a large chronic effusion can be followed by ventricular dysfunction or pulmonary edema. Persistent hypotension after drainage needs a new differential, including bleeding.

sources.label: BJA Education: pericardial effusion and tamponade

sections.title: Bleeding & ongoing drainage
bullets: Assess the nature of the effusion and surgical bleeding, with blood/coagulation support appropriate to the cause and medication exposure.
Confirm the postoperative drain and recurrence-surveillance plan with the surgeon.

sources.label: BJA Education: pericardial effusion and tamponade

sections.title: Extubation & monitored recovery
bullets: Extubation depends on recovered perfusion, ventilation and airway readiness; unstable physiology warrants continued support and higher-acuity care.
Continue surveillance for recurrent tamponade, arrhythmia, bleeding and respiratory deterioration after apparently successful drainage.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: A shared-airway procedure whose risk depends on obstruction, bleeding and the intended intervention, not simply flexible versus rigid scope.
Agree on ventilation method, scope/airway exchanges and rescue before starting.
Jet ventilation requires a patent expiratory route; air trapping and barotrauma remain major hazards.
Laser/thermal intervention requires a specific fire-prevention plan and coordinated oxygen delivery.

sections.title: Diagnostic versus therapeutic bronchoscopy
bullets: Clarify biopsy, tumor debulking, stenting, foreign-body work or another intervention. Rigid bronchoscopy generally needs general anesthesia; selected flexible procedures may use topical anesthesia and sedation.
Confirm whether obstruction or a mediastinal mass creates risk during induction before choosing a routine sedation pathway.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy: shared-airway review

sections.title: Obstruction, bleeding & reserve
bullets: Review location/severity of narrowing, gas exchange, positional symptoms and bleeding risk. An apparently easy upper airway does not exclude critical distal obstruction.
Plan the ability to suction blood/secretions and protect ventilation if the intervention worsens obstruction.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy: shared-airway review

sections.title: Shared-airway communication
bullets: Agree on who controls the airway at each phase, ventilation pauses, scope changes and the response to loss of ventilation. Maintain direct communication during every transition.
Airway leak can compromise both ventilation and anesthetic delivery. A technique independent of volatile delivery may be appropriate for an open airway.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy: shared-airway review

sections.title: Ventilation options
bullets: Options include controlled ventilation through the scope, spontaneous-assisted ventilation, intermittent apnea and jet ventilation. Choose for the anatomy, procedure and expertise, not by a universal preference.
Monitor chest movement, pressures and gas exchange; end-tidal CO2 may be difficult to interpret in an open system. Arterial/transcutaneous assessment may be helpful when needed.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy: shared-airway review

sections.title: Jet ventilation: expiratory safety
bullets: High-pressure gas delivery with obstructed expiration can cause air trapping, hypotension, pneumothorax or barotrauma. Confirm an adequate expiratory path and allow sufficient exhalation.
Driving pressure, frequency and inspiratory timing are device- and patient-specific. Historical settings from a narrative review should not be used as a universal jet-ventilator prescription.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy: shared-airway review

sections.title: Desaturation or ventilatory failure
bullets: Notify the bronchoscopist, restore a workable oxygenation/ventilation route and assess scope position, obstruction, secretions, blood and fragments.
Consider pneumothorax/air trapping and circulatory compromise as well as inadequate ventilation. Coordinate withdrawal or exchange of the scope when needed.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy: shared-airway review

sections.title: Airway bleeding
bullets: Bleeding can obstruct gas exchange before the measured volume appears large. Prioritize airway clearance, ventilation and surgical hemostasis with the bronchoscopy team.
Prepare escalation to advanced airway isolation or surgical rescue according to the anticipated lesion and resources.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy: shared-airway review

sections.title: Laser / thermal airway work
bullets: Use the institution’s airway-fire prevention pathway: coordinate oxidizer delivery with the proceduralist, avoid nitrous oxide and manage combustible materials/equipment appropriately.

Do not confuse emergency oxygen escalation for hypoxemia with permission to continue an ignition source in an oxygen-enriched airway. Stop thermal energy while correcting oxygenation and re-establishing a safe plan.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy: shared-airway review

sections.title: Topical anesthesia & sedation
bullets: Track total topical/local-anesthetic exposure and systemic sedatives across both teams. Titrate to reserve while maintaining the planned airway and ventilatory strategy.
In a high-risk obstructed airway, deeper sedation is not a substitute for a definitive rescue plan.

sources.label: Anaesthesia for bronchoscopy: shared-airway review

sections.title: Recovery & airway reassessment
bullets: Evaluate airway patency, bleeding, ventilation and respiratory reserve before removing support. Persistent obstruction, edema or major intervention may require postoperative ventilation/critical care.
Communicate stent/intervention details, airway difficulty, bleeding and any ongoing respiratory concerns at handoff.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Choose sedation or general anesthesia according to ischemia, hemodynamic stability, respiratory status and procedural needs.

sections.title: Diagnostic study versus intervention
bullets: Clarify diagnostic catheterization, planned PCI or unstable rescue intervention and the anticipated need for circulatory support. Procedure complexity and patient condition determine anesthetic involvement.
A stable patient needing light sedation is different from acute MI with respiratory distress, cardiogenic instability or an inability to tolerate the procedure.

sources.label: Anesthesia for cardiac catheterization procedures (2014 review)

sections.title: Ischemia, ventricular function & respiratory status
bullets: Review active ischemia, ventricular failure, rhythm, hemodynamic support and oxygenation. Minimize avoidable delay in an urgent reperfusion pathway.
Assess airway and aspiration concerns, renal function, contrast history and recent medication exposure as time permits.

sources.label: Anesthesia for cardiac catheterization procedures (2014 review)

sections.title: Remote-site setup
bullets: Ensure reliable IV access, oxygen, suction, monitoring, emergency drugs and an airway-rescue plan despite restricted space and equipment around the patient.
Communicate with the cardiologist before deepening sedation or changing ventilation because induction can materially alter the patient’s circulation.

sources.label: Anesthesia for cardiac catheterization procedures (2014 review)

sections.title: Monitoring during sedation or anesthesia
bullets: Use monitoring appropriate to depth and physiologic risk, including ventilation monitoring during moderate/deep sedation unless precluded by the procedure. Invasive pressure may be indicated in unstable patients.
Recognize unintended progression from sedation to general anesthesia and be prepared to manage airway and hemodynamic consequences.

sources.label: Anesthesia for cardiac catheterization procedures (2014 review)

sections.title: Sedation versus intubation
bullets: There is no single best technique for all catheterization procedures. Titrate drugs to ventricular reserve, respiratory status and the need for patient immobility/cooperation.
Respiratory failure, severe instability or uncontrolled airway risk may require a secured airway. Prepare vasoactive support and coordinate timing with the intervention.

sources.label: Anesthesia for cardiac catheterization procedures (2014 review)

sections.title: Maintaining myocardial and systemic perfusion
bullets: Avoid unnecessary hypotension, hypoxemia and marked sympathetic stress in ischemic patients. Escalate new ECG/rhythm or pressure changes promptly to the interventional team.
Treat decompensated physiology with a cause-directed approach rather than repeated sedation adjustments.

sections.title: Antithrombotics: procedure-specific plan
bullets: Reconcile antiplatelet and anticoagulant exposure with the cardiologist. Procedural agent, ACT target where used and reversal decisions depend on the intervention and drugs.

sections.title: Contrast & renal considerations
bullets: Review prior contrast reactions and renal dysfunction; communicate these to the interventional team and limit avoidable contrast exposure.
Hydration must fit ventricular reserve and congestion risk. Do not apply a large prophylactic fluid load indiscriminately in decompensated heart failure.

bullets: New instability during PCI requires immediate procedural and anesthetic reassessment, including ischemia/thrombosis, rhythm disturbance, respiratory failure and bleeding.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Separate primary hyperparathyroidism from renal secondary/tertiary disease; calcium, renal reserve and bone turnover change perioperative risk.
Assess hypercalcemia, dehydration, kidney dysfunction and rhythm effects before induction; severe symptomatic disease needs coordinated stabilization.
Coordinate gland exploration, intraoperative PTH sampling and any nerve monitoring without turning a laboratory criterion into an anesthesia target.
After removal, watch for hypocalcemia and hungry bone syndrome as well as neck hematoma and vocal-cord dysfunction.

sections.title: Focused exploration versus multigland surgery
bullets: Confirm focused removal versus bilateral exploration, reoperation, MEN-related multigland disease or renal hyperparathyroidism. Surgical extent and comorbidity determine anesthesia and admission needs.

General anesthesia with a tracheal tube is commonly used; selected focused procedures can use local/cervical techniques in experienced teams. Do not apply a minimal-sedation pathway to complex exploration or patients unlikely to tolerate it.

sources.label: StatPearls: Parathyroidectomy (2024)

sections.title: Calcium, hydration & cardiac assessment
bullets: Review calcium trend, renal function, electrolytes, symptoms and ECG as indicated. Hypercalcemia can accompany dehydration, weakness, confusion and conduction/rhythm abnormalities; correct clinically significant depletion while accounting for heart and kidney function.
Hypercalcemic crisis requires urgent endocrine input and resuscitation coordinated with definitive surgery. A single total-calcium number is not a complete assessment of physiologic stability.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
NCI PDQ: genetics of endocrine and neuroendocrine neoplasias (2024)

sections.title: Renal disease & high bone-turnover context
bullets: In secondary/tertiary disease, review dialysis, potassium, fluid balance, anemia and medication burden with nephrology. Calcium management must reflect kidney function and the expected postoperative shift rather than a routine primary-hyperparathyroidism pathway.
Identify significant skeletal disease and protect positioning. High bone turnover creates a different calcium-replacement burden from an uncomplicated isolated adenoma.

sources.label: StatPearls: Parathyroidectomy (2024)

sections.title: Monitoring, access & escalation
bullets: Use standard anesthetic monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation and circulation. Choose arterial monitoring, reliable additional IV access and serial laboratory testing for anticipated instability, major surgery or rapid metabolic change rather than for the endocrine label alone.

Agree who communicates hormone-related interventions, key surgical transitions and abnormal laboratory results. Have the required rescue drugs, blood access and postoperative monitoring destination ready before a predictable high-risk phase.

sections.title: Positioning, airway access & exposure
bullets: Check cervical mobility before extending the neck. Pad pressure points, protect eyes, secure the airway and IVs, and recheck ventilation after final positioning and draping. Avoid forcing extension in cervical disease.

Account for restricted airway access after the table turns. Extensive central/lateral neck dissection, reoperation or substernal disease changes the duration and airway plan; it is not interchangeable with a small focused operation.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
StatPearls: Parathyroidectomy (2024)

sections.title: Nerve-monitoring tube & neuromuscular blockade
bullets: If laryngeal EMG monitoring is planned, position the tube electrodes correctly at the vocal cords and verify contact after neck positioning. Tube movement, electrode contact and residual blockade can cause poor signals; loss of signal is not automatically surgical nerve injury.

Coordinate adequate intubating conditions with recovery before stimulation. Neuromuscular blockers suppress EMG amplitude, so agree on the induction/reversal strategy and any additional doses rather than applying an indiscriminate “never use relaxant” rule.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring; a usable surgical EMG signal is not proof of complete systemic recovery. When blockade was used, confirm adductor-pollicis train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation.

sections.title: Intraoperative PTH & communication
bullets: Confirm the team’s baseline and post-excision sampling sequence and laboratory turnaround. Interpretation depends on the surgical protocol and biochemical context; anesthesia should keep timing and sample handling reliable.

A satisfactory intraoperative PTH fall supports the surgical assessment but does not remove the need for postoperative calcium surveillance. Avoid inferring that immediate biochemical success excludes later hungry bone syndrome.

sources.label: StatPearls: Parathyroidectomy (2024)

sections.title: Hemodynamic changes after gland removal
bullets: If hypotension, dysrhythmia or myocardial dysfunction develops, consider calcium change alongside bleeding, anesthetic effects and volume status. Check appropriate laboratory values and treat the cause rather than assuming all hypotension is hypovolemia.
Continue quantitative neuromuscular assessment because electrolyte abnormalities can alter response. Confirm adequate recovery before extubation.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)
APSF: neuromuscular blockade guideline summary (2023)

sections.title: Analgesia, nausea & smooth recovery
bullets: Use multimodal analgesia with acetaminophen, local infiltration or a selected superficial cervical plexus technique, and NSAID/COX-2 therapy when renal, bleeding and other risks permit. Reserve titrated opioids for additional need, particularly with OSA or airway concerns.

Plan risk-based PONV prevention and prompt treatment. Aim for a controlled emergence without severe coughing or retching, but do not sacrifice ventilation or airway protection merely to suppress the response.

sources.label: BJA Education: thyroid and parathyroid anaesthesia (2024)

sections.title: Neck hematoma: recognize & act
bullets: Look for DESATS: difficulty swallowing/discomfort, rising early-warning score, swelling, anxiety, tachypnea/difficulty breathing and stridor. Stridor may be late; a small hematoma can still produce dangerous airway compression and venous congestion.

Call surgical and senior anesthesia help, give oxygen and assess the airway with the patient head-up. Rapidly expanding swelling or airway compromise requires immediate emergency management; do not delay decompression for imaging or routine transfer.

For airway compromise from suspected hematoma, trained clinicians should open and evacuate the wound using the local emergency protocol. SCOOP means skin exposure, cut sutures, open skin, open muscles including the strap layer, and pack the wound. Merely opening superficial skin may not decompress the deeper collection.

If compromise persists, proceed with expert airway management, limited attempts and immediate front-of-neck rescue capability. Definitive surgical hemostasis and close monitored care are still required after initial decompression. The thyroid consensus is the direct source; adapt through the local neck-surgery pathway for parathyroid cases.

sections.title: Hypoparathyroidism versus hungry bone syndrome
bullets: Hungry bone syndrome reflects rapid skeletal uptake of calcium after removal of the high-PTH stimulus; it is distinct from simply losing all parathyroid function. Both can produce clinically important postoperative hypocalcemia.

Watch for perioral/fingertip paresthesia, cramps, tetany, laryngospasm, arrhythmia or seizures. Arrange serial biochemical assessment and an individualized calcium/vitamin-D plan; severe symptomatic hypocalcemia warrants urgent monitored treatment.

sources.label: StatPearls: Parathyroidectomy (2024)

sections.title: Monitoring and discharge ownership
bullets: The observation plan should reflect calcium trajectory, renal disease, surgical extent and ability to obtain follow-up, not only a short uncomplicated operation. Document who will check labs and adjust calcium/calcitriol.

Provide separate return precautions for neck swelling/airway symptoms and for hypocalcemia. Persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism requires follow-up rather than assumptions based only on the operative note.

bullets: Cortisol excess combines hypertension, glucose intolerance, myopathy, infection and VTE risk; obesity and OSA may complicate airway and recovery.
Distinguish overt Cushing syndrome from mild autonomous cortisol secretion and identify preoperative cortisol-lowering drugs.
Protect fragile skin/bone, optimize major metabolic abnormalities and prepare for the actual adrenal exposure.

bullets: Assess and optimize hypertension, diabetes/hyperglycemia, hypokalemia and cardiovascular disease. Severe hypercortisolism may warrant endocrine-directed medical treatment before surgery; document its effects on the perioperative steroid plan.

Check current medications and recent hormone testing. Cortisol-lowering drugs or receptor blockade can alter interpretation and replacement needs; coordinate rather than continuing or withholding them by rote.

bullets: Look for obesity, OSA, weakness and limited reserve. Avoid heavy unsupervised premedication, preoxygenate effectively and anticipate greater sensitivity to respiratory depression in recovery.

sections.title: Approach, position & pneumoperitoneum
bullets: Confirm transperitoneal versus retroperitoneal access, side, unilateral versus bilateral resection and possible conversion to open surgery. Suspected invasive malignancy or adjacent-organ involvement changes exposure and bleeding preparation.

Secure airway, IVs and pressure points before lateral/prone positioning or robot docking. Pneumoperitoneum and positioning can reduce compliance and alter venous return; use lung-protective ventilation and individualized PEEP, CO₂ management and hemodynamic assessment.

Hemodynamic or ventilatory deterioration after insufflation warrants reassessment of pressure, positioning, bleeding and CO₂ absorption. Coordinate pauses or undocking if needed; do not keep treating a mechanical problem with escalating drug doses alone.

sections.title: Positioning, skin and skeletal fragility
bullets: Handle and tape fragile skin carefully, pad pressure points and avoid excessive joint stress. Osteoporosis and myopathy can make positioning injuries more likely even during minimally invasive surgery.
Recheck support and access after positioning; do not allow the drive for surgical exposure to override pressure protection.

sources.label: Adrenal gland surgery anesthesia review (2014/2015)

sections.title: Blood loss, fluids & hemodynamic differential
bullets: Prepare access and blood availability for the planned exposure and tumor complexity. An endocrine explanation for instability must not distract from hemorrhage, impaired venous return, anesthetic effects or cardiac dysfunction.

Use physiology-guided balanced crystalloid and blood replacement when needed, avoiding both depletion and overload. Urine output and blood pressure alone are imperfect volume indicators, especially during pneumoperitoneum or in catecholamine cardiomyopathy.

sections.title: Infection and VTE prevention
bullets: Hypercortisolism increases infection and thrombotic risk. Agree on mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with the surgical team, balancing bleeding and any regional-catheter considerations.

Risk does not disappear immediately when cortisol production falls. Early mobilization and a documented postoperative prophylaxis plan are important; do not apply one extended-anticoagulation duration to every patient.

sections.title: After resection: glucocorticoid coverage
bullets: AAES recommends empirical postoperative glucocorticoid replacement after unilateral adrenalectomy for overt Cushing syndrome. Document the perioperative dosing plan, taper owner and testing strategy before surgery.

For MACS, postoperative morning cortisol or corticotropin testing can guide replacement. Replacement may be temporary while the axis recovers; do not label every patient permanently steroid dependent.

sections.title: Adrenal insufficiency versus other causes of deterioration
bullets: Hypotension, weakness, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, fever or confusion after resection should trigger evaluation for adrenal insufficiency as well as hemorrhage, sepsis and cardiac causes. Do not let steroid replacement delay parallel resuscitation and investigation.

bullets: Use controlled, titratable anesthesia while maintaining cerebral perfusion and oxygenation. TIVA may improve the operative field, but no single low MAP is appropriate for all patients; account for baseline pressure, cardiovascular disease and intracranial pathology.

sections.title: Post-resection diuresis is not always DI
bullets: Successful treatment can rapidly release retained fluid associated with GH excess, often within the first 48 hours. This can resemble AVP-D on a urine-output chart.
Check thirst, sodium, urine concentration, paired osmolality, glucose and fluid exposure. Do not give repeated DDAVP solely because a urine-volume threshold was crossed.

sections.title: AVP deficiency: assess before treating polyuria
bullets: Arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D; central diabetes insipidus) causes inappropriately dilute polyuria. Assess urine output trend, fluid balance, thirst, serum sodium and paired serum/urine osmolality rather than diagnosing from urine volume alone.

A proposed postoperative screen is urine output >300 mL/hour for 3 consecutive hours with urine specific gravity <1.005 plus excessive thirst, serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg or sodium >145 mmol/L. These are assessment criteria, not an automatic DDAVP order; sodium may remain normal with intact thirst and water access.

Exclude mobilization of perioperative fluids, hyperglycemia/osmotic diuresis, mannitol/diuretics and rapid fluid loss after successful acromegaly surgery. Glucocorticoid replacement can unmask AVP-D that cortisol deficiency had obscured.

If thirst is intact and drinking is safe, allow access to water with surveillance. Significant losses, rising sodium, impaired consciousness or inability to drink may require individualized fluid replacement and desmopressin. Initially use reassessment-driven dosing rather than automatic repeated doses; monitor sodium and urine response.

sections.title: Delayed hyponatremia, DDAVP & discharge checks
bullets: Delayed SIAD-related hyponatremia often develops after initial recovery, commonly around postoperative day 7 within a reported day 4–14 window. Arrange a sodium check around one week and give explicit symptom/return instructions, even if inpatient sodium was normal.

Before labeling hyponatremia SIAD, assess adrenal insufficiency, thyroid deficiency, medications including desmopressin, fluid exposure and volume status. Severe symptoms, confusion or seizures require urgent hospital assessment and controlled correction.

Do not apply a blanket postoperative fluid restriction to a patient with active AVP-D or impaired thirst. Excess DDAVP plus fluid intake can cause dangerous hyponatremia, especially if a later antidiuretic phase develops.

sections.title: Emergence, OSA & skull-base repair
bullets: Clear blood/secretions, verify pack removal and quantitative recovery if relaxants were used, and plan awake extubation with a defined reintubation strategy for difficult airways or OSA. A smooth wake-up should still allow prompt neurologic and visual assessment.

Postoperative CPAP/noninvasive positive pressure needs an individualized agreement with the skull-base team: defect/repair integrity, CSF-leak risk and OSA severity matter. Do not prescribe a universal restart date or simply leave significant obstruction untreated; provide an appropriate monitored rescue plan.

New visual loss, diplopia, depressed consciousness, major epistaxis or suspected CSF rhinorrhea requires urgent neurosurgical assessment. Avoid nose blowing and straining according to the repair-specific instructions.

bullets: Hypothalamic disease and endocrine dysfunction may coexist with obesity and impaired reserve. Individualize airway management and postoperative respiratory observation.

For an endonasal operation, use the shared-airway/skull-base precautions, avoid blind nasal instrumentation after repair and agree on CPAP/positive-pressure rescue. A transcranial case needs its own neurosurgical positioning and emergence plan.

Agree who communicates hormone-related interventions, key surgical transitions and abnormal laboratory results. Have the required rescue drugs, blood access and postoperative monitoring destination ready before a predictable high-risk phase.

sections.title: Perfusion, fluid and metabolic surveillance
bullets: Preserve oxygenation and perfusion, and track glucose, sodium, urine output and fluid administration during prolonged or complex surgery. Record baseline and changes so postoperative endocrine assessment is meaningful.
Coordinate sudden polyuria or hemodynamic changes with the surgeon and endocrinology. Do not treat presumed AVP-D without checking dilution, glucose and fluid/medication causes.

sections.title: Hypothalamic dysfunction & temperature
bullets: Hypothalamic injury may complicate appetite/weight, autonomic function and longer-term endocrine recovery. Monitor temperature and overall physiology; avoid attributing unexplained deterioration to “expected endocrine changes” without assessment.
Use the actual lesion and operative course to set postoperative observation intensity. The mixed-age endocrine literature does not establish one universal adult postoperative pathway.

sections.title: AVP deficiency: assess before treating polyuria
bullets: Arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D; central diabetes insipidus) causes inappropriately dilute polyuria. Assess urine output trend, fluid balance, thirst, serum sodium and paired serum/urine osmolality rather than diagnosing from urine volume alone.

A proposed postoperative screen is urine output >300 mL/hour for 3 consecutive hours with urine specific gravity <1.005 plus excessive thirst, serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg or sodium >145 mmol/L. These are assessment criteria, not an automatic DDAVP order; sodium may remain normal with intact thirst and water access.

Exclude mobilization of perioperative fluids, hyperglycemia/osmotic diuresis, mannitol/diuretics and rapid fluid loss after successful acromegaly surgery. Glucocorticoid replacement can unmask AVP-D that cortisol deficiency had obscured.

If thirst is intact and drinking is safe, allow access to water with surveillance. Significant losses, rising sodium, impaired consciousness or inability to drink may require individualized fluid replacement and desmopressin. Initially use reassessment-driven dosing rather than automatic repeated doses; monitor sodium and urine response.

sources.label: JCEM: Disorders of salt and water balance after pituitary surgery (2022/2023)

sections.title: Adipsic AVP deficiency: absent thirst is dangerous
bullets: Damage near thirst-regulating structures can produce absent thirst despite hypernatremia. A patient who is not asking for water may still be losing substantial free water.

Use prescribed fluid intake, careful intake/output, weights and frequent sodium assessment with specialist-directed desmopressin when adipsia or impaired consciousness prevents self-regulation. Do not rely on drink-to-thirst instructions alone.

sources.label: JCEM: Disorders of salt and water balance after pituitary surgery (2022/2023)

sections.title: Changing water balance over time
bullets: Some patients develop an initial polyuric phase, a subsequent antidiuretic/SIAD phase and then recurrent or persistent AVP-D. This triphasic sequence is possible, not inevitable.
Reassess desmopressin and fluid orders as physiology changes; unchanged dosing across an antidiuretic phase can lead to water retention and hyponatremia.

sections.title: Delayed hyponatremia, DDAVP & discharge checks
bullets: Delayed SIAD-related hyponatremia often develops after initial recovery, commonly around postoperative day 7 within a reported day 4–14 window. Arrange a sodium check around one week and give explicit symptom/return instructions, even if inpatient sodium was normal.

Before labeling hyponatremia SIAD, assess adrenal insufficiency, thyroid deficiency, medications including desmopressin, fluid exposure and volume status. Severe symptoms, confusion or seizures require urgent hospital assessment and controlled correction.

Do not apply a blanket postoperative fluid restriction to a patient with active AVP-D or impaired thirst. Excess DDAVP plus fluid intake can cause dangerous hyponatremia, especially if a later antidiuretic phase develops.

sections.title: Neurologic recovery & postoperative escalation
bullets: Assess consciousness, vision, focal findings, airway and endocrine status together. New neurologic or visual deterioration requires urgent neurosurgical evaluation, not solely adjustment of replacement hormones.
Match the postoperative unit to neurologic, respiratory and metabolic needs. Significant sodium instability, impaired thirst or ongoing support requires close monitored care.

sections.title: Long-term replacement and follow-up
bullets: Document glucocorticoid, thyroid and any desmopressin plan, including who will monitor and change them. Replacement requirements may change after surgery and require continuing endocrine review.

Education must be tailored to cognition and thirst function, with caregiver support where needed. Arrange early sodium follow-up and emergency advice for dehydration, confusion, seizures or adrenal-insufficiency symptoms.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Prevent fasting and intraoperative hypoglycemia; general anesthesia masks the usual warning symptoms.
Use an explicit glucose/dextrose monitoring plan before fasting, through manipulation and after removal.
Octreotide is not universally protective: it can worsen hypoglycemia and requires demonstrated response before routine use.
A glucose rise after resection is not proof of complete cure; both recurrent hypoglycemia and postoperative hyperglycemia require follow-up.

sections.title: Localization, MEN1 and extent of pancreatic resection
bullets: Confirm a localized sporadic lesion versus multifocal/MEN1 disease and the plan for enucleation, limited pancreatectomy or major resection. Blood loss, analgesia and pancreatic-function implications vary with extent.
Pancreas-sparing techniques may be appropriate when anatomy permits, but the anesthesia plan must allow for a more extensive operation if localization or duct/vascular relationships require it.

sections.title: Before fasting: prevent neuroglycopenia
bullets: Review the timing/severity of hypoglycemia, prior seizures or confusion and current diet/medical therapy. Avoid unplanned prolonged fasting; arrange IV glucose when needed and measure glucose during the fasting interval.
The target is safe glucose control, not permitting hypoglycemia to make an operative response easier to interpret. Make rescue glucose and reliable IV access available before induction.

sections.title: Diazoxide and somatostatin-analogue cautions
bullets: Document response to prescribed diazoxide or somatostatin analogues and agree on continuation with endocrinology. Do not initiate a new perioperative drug solely because it appears in an older case report.

ENETS advises a closely monitored short-acting octreotide trial before long-acting therapy when an SSA is being considered: glucagon suppression and variable receptor expression can paradoxically worsen hypoglycemia.

sections.title: Frequent glucose measurements & infusion safety
bullets: Use frequent measured glucose checks; older anesthesia reviews describe intervals of 15–30 minutes intraoperatively, with more frequent reassessment for instability, manipulation, resection or changes in insulin/dextrose. Individualize rather than treating an interval as a guarantee of safety.
Track infusion concentration, rate and line reliability. Dextrose requirement can change abruptly; do not stop protective glucose merely to look for a diagnostic rebound after resection.

sections.title: Anesthetic technique and masked symptoms
bullets: Choose general anesthesia/airway management for the planned pancreatic exposure and patient risk. Under anesthesia, neuroglycopenic symptoms and adrenergic signs are unreliable; laboratory surveillance remains essential.

Use titratable anesthesia and hemodynamic assessment rather than choosing outdated volatile agents for their metabolic effects. No single anesthetic drug regimen is established as mandatory for insulinoma.

sections.title: Tumor manipulation and severe hypoglycemia
bullets: Manipulation may release insulin and worsen hypoglycemia. Alert the surgeon, verify glucose promptly and treat with titrated IV glucose while reassessing infusion and measurement reliability.
Do not delay treatment to preserve interpretation of resection success. Continued clinical concern after an apparent correction warrants repeat measurement and evaluation for ongoing insulin effect.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum, ventilation & perfusion
bullets: For minimally invasive exposure, anticipate reduced respiratory compliance and altered venous return. Secure the airway and access, adjust lung-protective ventilation and coordinate insufflation when instability occurs.
Use individualized fluid and blood replacement for perfusion; an older recommendation for liberal fluid therapy is not a universal modern insulinoma requirement.

sections.title: After removal: glucose can rise, but cure is not immediate proof
bullets: Reduce/titrate dextrose according to measured glucose and ongoing need. Transient hyperglycemia may follow removal and can require carefully titrated insulin; avoid overshoot and subsequent hypoglycemia.

Rebound hyperglycemia is an unreliable stand-alone marker of complete tumor removal. Follow the surgical/endocrine plan for assessment of residual disease, especially with multifocal or MEN1-associated tumors.

sections.title: Analgesia and pancreatic surgical risk
bullets: Use approach-appropriate multimodal analgesia and regional options where suitable. A small enucleation and a Whipple do not need identical pain, fluid or disposition plans.
For extensive pancreatic surgery, consider coagulation, bleeding, epidural-related hypotension and postoperative anticoagulation when selecting regional analgesia.

sections.title: Glucose surveillance beyond PACU
bullets: Continue glucose surveillance after surgery: requirements may normalize over hours or days, and either hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia can persist. A normal first PACU result is not a reason to stop monitoring.
Choose postoperative observation based on glucose stability, resection extent, hemodynamics and comorbidity. Document dextrose/insulin changes and an explicit overnight monitoring plan.

bullets: Restart intake through the surgical pathway and coordinate it with glucose therapy. Do not stop IV support before intake and metabolic stability are established.

Provide a follow-up plan for recurrent symptoms and glucose abnormalities. MEN1/multifocal disease requires continued specialist surveillance rather than reassurance from one postoperative glucose rise.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Identify the secreted hormone and clinical syndrome; nonfunctioning, insulin-secreting and diarrheal/acid-secretory tumors need different preparation.
VIPoma may cause profound volume, potassium and bicarbonate loss; gastrinoma requires ongoing acid suppression.
Glucagonoma adds nutritional and thrombotic concerns, while insulinoma requires a dedicated hypoglycemia pathway.
Match anesthesia to enucleation, distal/other pancreatic resection or Whipple; a neuroendocrine label does not define surgical magnitude.

sections.title: Functioning versus nonfunctioning PanNET
bullets: Review hormone assays, symptoms, treatment response, metastatic burden and hereditary context. Hormone syndrome and anatomic operation are separate axes of risk.
Nonfunctioning tumors can still require major pancreatic surgery; conversely a small functional tumor can create major metabolic instability before any incision.

sources.label: ENETS: functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor guidance (2023)

sections.title: VIPoma: diarrhea, depletion and acidosis
bullets: Secretory diarrhea may produce severe dehydration, hypokalemia and bicarbonate-loss metabolic acidosis. Stabilize volume/electrolytes and the hormonal syndrome before elective surgery when feasible.

ENETS supports somatostatin-analogue therapy for preoperative stabilization and IV fluid/electrolyte treatment when diarrhea is severe. Quantify ongoing losses rather than replacing only the presenting deficit.

sections.title: Gastrinoma: acid suppression and aspiration context
bullets: Maintain effective PPI therapy through the perioperative period, using an appropriate route when oral therapy is interrupted. Abrupt withdrawal can provoke serious rebound acid-related complications.

Assess ulcer disease, bleeding, vomiting or obstruction and the resulting aspiration/volume risk. Continue postoperative acid suppression through the specialist plan; curative-intent surgery is not an automatic reason to stop immediately.

sections.title: Glucagonoma: metabolic, nutritional and VTE risk
bullets: Assess hyperglycemia, weight loss, skin disease and nutritional deficits. Specialist therapy may include somatostatin analogues and targeted nutritional support rather than treating the tumor as only a glucose problem.
Plan thromboprophylaxis for increased DVT/PE risk while respecting bleeding and neuraxial timing. Do not copy historical “high-dose heparin” wording into a universal prophylactic dose.

sections.title: Insulinoma and less common hormone syndromes
bullets: For insulinoma, use frequent glucose testing, planned dextrose support and the dedicated insulinoma reference. Somatostatin analogues can worsen hypoglycemia in some patients.

Ectopic ACTH secretion may cause severe hypercortisolism; GHRH secretion can cause acromegaly; PTHrP secretion can cause hypercalcemia. Stabilize the actual syndrome with endocrinology rather than giving a generic “NET premedication.”

sections.title: Carcinoid syndrome is not synonymous with every PanNET
bullets: If a mediator syndrome such as flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm or carcinoid heart disease is suspected, evaluate it explicitly. Do not automatically apply a carcinoid-crisis regimen to every pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.

Perioperative octreotide practices and evidence vary; coordinate a syndrome-specific crisis/rescue plan. The older ENETS consensus acknowledges limited evidence and no universal prophylactic regimen, so prophylaxis must not be presented as a guarantee against crisis.

Account for prolonged abdominal exposure or pneumoperitoneum/robot docking. Reassess perfusion and ventilation as position and insufflation change.

bullets: Replace measured volume/electrolyte losses while protecting organ perfusion and avoiding overload. Repeated potassium, acid-base and glucose assessment should follow the dominant syndrome and operative course.

Communicate tumor manipulation/removal because hormone output and treatment requirements can change. Update infusions according to measurements rather than continuing pre-resection rates automatically.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: This is a cross-cutting surgical-planning reference: more than one active hormone disorder may matter even when only one organ is being operated on.
MEN1 classically involves parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic/duodenal neuroendocrine tumors.
MEN2A includes medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and parathyroid disease; MEN2B has a different phenotype without the same increased parathyroid risk.
Exclude functioning pheochromocytoma before relevant surgery in MEN2; when present, coordinate treatment before thyroidectomy to avoid catecholamine crisis.

sections.title: Start with a hormone and procedure inventory
bullets: List the planned operation, known tumors, biochemical activity, prior resections and current replacement. The organ on the booking form may not be the dominant anesthetic hazard.
Coordinate endocrinology, anesthesia and the operating team; genetics/surveillance findings can change sequencing and the need for bilateral or tissue-preserving surgery.

sections.title: MEN1: parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic physiology
bullets: Assess calcium/volume/renal effects of hyperparathyroidism, pituitary hormone excess or deficiency and functional pancreatic/duodenal tumor syndromes. Multiple abnormalities can coexist.
Do not assume a previous parathyroid or pancreatic operation eliminates recurrence/multifocal risk. Review the current surveillance and biochemical status.

sections.title: MEN2A: medullary thyroid, pheochromocytoma and parathyroid
bullets: Review medullary thyroid cancer status, catecholamine screening and calcium/parathyroid disease. A thyroid operation should not proceed on the assumption that its airway risks are the only anesthesia concern.
Pheochromocytoma may be bilateral or discovered before thyroid disease. Confirm the actual biochemical results and preparation rather than relying only on absence of hypertension.

sections.title: MEN2B is not the MEN2A triad
bullets: MEN2B includes medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma with features such as mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus and gastrointestinal ganglioneuromatosis. Clinically significant parathyroid disease is not increased as it is in MEN2A.
For this adult library, assess current airway, gastrointestinal and endocrine consequences. Pediatric prophylactic-thyroidectomy age recommendations are outside this anesthesia reference’s scope.

sections.title: Pheochromocytoma screening and surgical sequence
bullets: GeneReviews recommends plasma-free or urine-fractionated metanephrine assessment before surgery in MEN2 phenotypes. If functioning pheochromocytoma is identified, adrenal treatment should precede thyroidectomy when feasible within the coordinated plan.

Life-threatening urgent surgery needs individualized expert management, not a simplified elective sequence. A known catecholamine tumor requires an explicit preparation and rescue strategy even when another organ is the surgical target.

sections.title: Catecholamine preparation and induction
bullets: When functional PPGL is present, establish specialist-directed alpha blockade and appropriate volume preparation; beta blockade, if needed, follows adequate alpha blockade. Review cardiomyopathy and relevant provoking medications.
Prepare for induction/manipulation hypertension and post-resection hypotension, with appropriate arterial/access monitoring and titratable drugs. The dedicated PPGL case gives the operational detail.

sections.title: Prior adrenal or pituitary surgery and replacement
bullets: Review remaining adrenal tissue, cortisol reserve, thyroid replacement and desmopressin needs. Previous operations can create deficiencies in addition to the syndrome’s tumor-related hormone excess.
If adrenal and thyroid axes are deficient, ensure glucocorticoid coverage before new thyroid replacement. Document postoperative dose adjustment and monitoring responsibilities.

bullets: Assess symptomatic hypercalcemia, hydration and renal function when parathyroid disease is present. After parathyroid removal, plan for hypocalcemia/hungry bone surveillance rather than assuming the preoperative calcium problem simply disappears.
Protect fragile bone/skin and consider renal function when selecting medications, fluids and analgesia. Match the plan to actual manifestations, not the syndrome name alone.

bullets: Insulinoma requires fasting protection and frequent glucose checks; gastrinoma requires uninterrupted effective acid suppression; VIPoma requires volume/electrolyte stabilization. These are not interchangeable NET pathways.
Coordinate the expected post-resection change with the team and adjust support to measured response. Multifocal MEN1 disease requires follow-up beyond an immediate glucose or symptom change.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: CRT patients often have advanced HF; maintain perfusion and avoid excessive myocardial depression during a potentially longer implant.
Local anesthesia with MAC is common; GA may be appropriate for patient tolerance, complexity, airway or testing needs.
Identify the exact system and dependence; external pacing/defibrillation must remain available throughout.
Assess capture, rhythm, pocket/access complications and the final device program before leaving monitored care.

sections.title: Patient physiology and implant plan
bullets: Review indication, rhythm, LV/RV function, HF status, medications, infection risk and ability to lie flat. Clarify first implant, upgrade, revision or replacement.
Confirm the planned device and lead route. Transvenous, leadless and subcutaneous systems have different access and analgesic requirements.

sources.label: AME Medical Journal: anesthesia for EP procedures (2025 narrative review)

sections.title: Pacing dependence, magnet response & EMI
bullets: Review underlying rhythm, interrogation, battery status, pacing dependence and the exact pacemaker/ICD/CRT or leadless model. Dependence and adequacy of the underlying rhythm may change with anesthetic depth.

An ICD magnet generally suspends tachyarrhythmia therapy without creating asynchronous pacing. Pacemaker magnet responses are model-specific; Micra has no magnet response. Coordinate reprogramming when dependence, EMI or inaccessible/sterile generator position makes a magnet unsuitable.

bullets: Obstruction, ileus and ongoing vomiting can retain large volumes despite fasting. Consider gastric decompression when appropriate; a tube does not empty every compartment or abolish aspiration risk.

bullets: Assess recent dose escalation, nausea/vomiting, bloating, constipation and coexisting motility disease. Most low-risk elective patients can continue GLP-1 therapy under the multisociety approach.

sections.title: Perfusion, fluids & electrolytes
bullets: Account for vomiting, bowel preparation, poor intake, bleeding and measured gastric/wound losses. Give fluid for evidence of hypovolemia or fluid responsiveness and reassess; do not replace a presumed fixed “third-space deficit.”

Avoid both excess crystalloid and under-resuscitation. Balanced crystalloid is often appropriate; distinguish vasodilatory hypotension from hemorrhage or low output and use vasoactive support when indicated. Correct potassium, sodium and acid-base disturbances with attention to renal function.

bullets: CO₂ insufflation reduces respiratory compliance/FRC, increases CO₂ load and can alter SVR and venous return; the direction of cardiac-output change depends on pressure, position and volume status. Use predicted/ideal, not actual, body weight for lung-protective tidal volume.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum, positioning & ventilation
bullets: CO₂ insufflation reduces respiratory compliance/FRC, increases CO₂ load and can alter SVR and venous return; the direction of cardiac-output change depends on pressure, position and volume status. Use predicted/ideal, not actual, body weight for lung-protective tidal volume.

Individualize PEEP and minute ventilation to mechanics, oxygenation and CO₂. Reverse Trendelenburg may worsen hypotension; Trendelenburg may worsen airway pressures and edema. Sudden severe bradycardia during insufflation warrants immediate communication, stopping the stimulus/deflation and treatment as clinically indicated.

sections.title: Perfusion, fluids & electrolytes
bullets: Account for vomiting, bowel preparation, poor intake, bleeding and measured gastric/wound losses. Give fluid for evidence of hypovolemia or fluid responsiveness and reassess; do not replace a presumed fixed “third-space deficit.”

Avoid both excess crystalloid and under-resuscitation. Balanced crystalloid is often appropriate; distinguish vasodilatory hypotension from hemorrhage or low output and use vasoactive support when indicated. Correct potassium, sodium and acid-base disturbances with attention to renal function.

sections.title: Blood loss and glucose
bullets: Arrange blood support and invasive monitoring according to extent, vascular dissection and comorbidities. Track temperature and coagulation during substantial bleeding.

sections.title: Analgesia and surgical tubes
bullets: Choose incision-appropriate multimodal analgesia, with epidural or regional alternatives for selected open cases. Account for hypotension, coagulation and respiratory reserve.

bullets: New pain, fever, bleeding or hemodynamic deterioration warrants assessment for pancreatic leak, intra-abdominal infection or hemorrhage. Monitor glycemia and nutritional/exocrine needs.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & temperature

sections.title: Extubation, respiratory recovery & disposition
bullets: Before extubation, assess wakefulness, airway protection, ventilation, oxygenation, temperature, perfusion and ongoing bleeding. If neuromuscular blockers were used, verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; head lift alone is insufficient.

Plan monitored or ICU recovery for persistent shock, major resuscitation, respiratory failure or an open abdomen. CPAP/NIV for postoperative hypoxemia requires an appropriate patient with low aspiration risk, skilled monitoring and prompt escalation if it fails.

bullets: Agree before starting how to stop the procedure and regain airway access. Treat obstruction/apnea promptly with depth adjustment, airway support and assisted ventilation as needed; summon help early when deterioration persists.

title: Acute Upper GI Bleed / Endoscopic Hemostasis

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: This is hemorrhage and aspiration-risk management, not simply a routine EGD with more sedation.
Resuscitate and coordinate timely hemostasis; ongoing hematemesis, altered consciousness or inability to protect the airway may justify intubation.
Do not routinely intubate every upper-GI bleeder: induction and ventilation also carry risk.
Plan for rebleeding, anticoagulant decisions and ICU/monitored recovery when physiology or the intervention requires it.

bullets: Review ongoing blood loss, mentation, circulation, cardiopulmonary disease, antithrombotics, hemoglobin and relevant coagulation/electrolyte results. Arrange type/cross and access suitable for severity.

sections.title: Selective intubation, not routine prophylaxis
bullets: The 2026 ESGE update advises against routine prophylactic intubation for acute UGIH. Select patients with ongoing active hematemesis, agitation or encephalopathy with inadequate airway control for airway protection.
