sections.title: Resuscitation and transfusion context
bullets: Use blood and fluid according to perfusion, ongoing loss and comorbidities; a restrictive stable-patient strategy is not a reason to withhold needed blood in uncontrolled hemorrhagic shock.

The guideline uses a hemoglobin below 7 g/dL trigger for stable patients without cardiovascular disease and a higher threshold in cardiovascular disease. Individualize to active ischemia, physiology and the current transfusion protocol.

bullets: After hemodynamic resuscitation, ESGE recommends early endoscopy within 24 hours for peptic-ulcer bleeding; persistent instability despite resuscitation may require more urgent intervention.

bullets: Coordinate withholding or reversal according to the agent, severity, renal function and thrombotic indication. Needed hemostasis should not be delayed solely to normalize every coagulation result.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview

Inability to handle secretions, proximal impaction or a full stomach can create substantial aspiration risk.
Complete esophageal obstruction, esophageal batteries and sharp objects require emergent endoscopic management, not delay simply to complete fasting.

sections.title: Object, location and complete obstruction
bullets: Clarify object type, timing, location, symptoms, inability to swallow saliva and any respiratory compromise. Adult foreign-body guidance is not a pediatric dosing or timing protocol.

ESGE recommends emergent endoscopy, preferably within 2 hours and at latest within 6 hours, for complete esophageal obstruction, esophageal batteries or sharp-pointed objects. Other objects have different urgency.

sources.label: ESGE adult upper-GI foreign body guideline (2016)

sections.title: Aspiration protection and difficult access
bullets: High-risk features include full stomach, proximal esophageal location, food impaction and inability to cooperate. Consider tracheal intubation when aspiration/protection needs justify it.

sources.label: ESGE adult upper-GI foreign body guideline (2016)

sections.title: Preparation without inappropriate delay
bullets: Arrange effective suction, appropriate retrieval expertise and emergency assistance. Pharmacologic attempts to dislodge a food bolus should not delay indicated endoscopy.

sources.label: ESGE adult upper-GI foreign body guideline (2016)

sections.title: Protective devices and instrumentation
bullets: The endoscopist may use an overtube, cap or protective hood for retrieval. These protect tissues and may reduce contamination but do not substitute for indicated tracheal airway protection.

sources.label: ESGE adult upper-GI foreign body guideline (2016)

sections.title: Perforation, bleeding and retained objects

sources.label: ESGE adult upper-GI foreign body guideline (2016)

sections.title: Observation and underlying cause
bullets: Uncomplicated successful retrieval may permit discharge after adequate recovery; difficult extraction, high-risk objects or extensive mucosal injury may warrant observation.

bullets: Review dysphagia, regurgitation, esophageal dilation, prior treatment and pulmonary consequences. An empty stomach does not exclude retained material in a dilated esophagus.

Coordinate diet/fasting and any clearance procedure with the POEM team. Published practices vary; no single reported 24- or 48-hour protocol guarantees clearance, and prophylactic endoscopy itself may carry aspiration risk.

sources.label: POEM anesthesia review (2021/2022; heterogeneous practice)

sections.title: Induction and secure tube positioning
bullets: Plan an aspiration-risk induction, commonly RSI when appropriate, with effective suction and a difficult-airway contingency. Technique must account for physiologic and airway limitations.
Secure tube depth and fixation before the endoscopist occupies the head. Confirm that scope manipulation has not displaced or obstructed the breathing circuit or tube.

sources.label: POEM anesthesia review (2021/2022; heterogeneous practice)

sections.title: CO₂ load and mechanical changes
bullets: Track ETCO₂ trends, oxygenation, airway pressures and respiratory compliance during insufflation. Adjust ventilation as tolerated; an arterial blood gas may help when CO₂ load or physiology makes ETCO₂ less reliable.

Examine the abdomen, neck and chest when pressures or CO₂ rise. A tense abdomen, subcutaneous emphysema or respiratory/circulatory compromise should not be managed solely by increasing minute ventilation.

sources.label: POEM anesthesia review (2021/2022; heterogeneous practice)

sections.title: Capnoperitoneum and capnothorax response
bullets: Alert the endoscopist, reduce/stop insufflation and coordinate luminal suction or a procedural pause while supporting ventilation and perfusion. Exclude tube/circuit problems and other causes of deterioration.

Tense capnoperitoneum or tension capnothorax may require urgent decompression by the appropriately equipped team. Treat clinical compromise promptly; case-series pressure/ETCO₂ cutoffs are not mandatory prerequisites for rescue.

sources.label: POEM anesthesia review (2021/2022; heterogeneous practice)

sections.title: Bleeding, leak and prolonged procedure
bullets: Monitor for hemorrhage, mucosal injury and uncontrolled leak as well as gas complications. Establish escalation to surgery/critical care when endoscopic rescue is insufficient.
Maintain temperature, hydration and analgesia/PONV management appropriate to duration and patient reserve; avoid excessive opioids when respiratory recovery is a concern.

sources.label: POEM anesthesia review (2021/2022; heterogeneous practice)

sections.title: Extubation and post-POEM surveillance
bullets: Extubate when awake with adequate airway protection, ventilation and resolved clinically important gas effects. Significant neck gas, respiratory compromise or persistent hypercarbia may require additional assessment or continued ventilation.
Persistent chest/abdominal pain, dyspnea, fever, hypoxemia or instability requires evaluation for aspiration, leak or thoracic gas complications. Follow the POEM team’s observation and feeding plan.

bullets: Before starting, verify oxygen, suction, bag-mask ventilation, airway devices, resuscitation equipment, trained assistance and the transfer route. Arrange the patient, scope, tubing and monitors so the airway remains reachable.

Agree how the endoscopist will stop, withdraw the scope and help reposition the patient if ventilation or resuscitation is needed. High-flow oxygen may support oxygenation in selected patients but does not prevent aspiration or substitute for ventilation monitoring.

bullets: MAC describes an anesthesia service, not a fixed depth of sedation. Moderate/deep sedation can progress to apnea or loss of airway reflexes; the anesthesia plan must include rescue and possible conversion to GA.

bullets: Antegrade and retrograde deep enteroscopy differ in preparation and airway implications; procedures may be prolonged.
Moderate/deep sedation or GA is individualized to route, duration, therapeutic work and patient reserve.

bullets: Clarify oral versus anal approach, expected duration, prior surgery/adhesions and whether diagnostic examination or treatment is planned. Review the indication such as bleeding or retained capsule.
Assess fasting/prep losses, obstruction symptoms and cardiopulmonary reserve; a long procedure can magnify sedation and positioning burdens.

sections.title: Sedation and airway strategy
bullets: Conscious/moderate sedation, deep sedation and GA are recognized options. Choose based on patient tolerance, route, duration, complexity and available expertise rather than a single universal technique.
Antegrade work shares the upper airway; prolonged procedures and retained contents may favor a secured airway. Maintain a clear conversion and repositioning plan.

sections.title: Frailty, OSA and physiologic reserve
bullets: Review previous sedation problems, OSA/obesity, baseline oxygen/ventilatory support and cardiopulmonary reserve. Frail or older patients often need smaller, slower sedative increments with time to assess the effect.

Assess fasting losses, bowel preparation, renal/hepatic dysfunction and concurrent sedating medicines. Hypotension or apnea may reflect excessive drug effect, but persistent deterioration also requires a procedural differential.

sources.label: BSG adult endoscopy sedation guideline (2023/2024)

sections.title: Diagnostic versus therapeutic bleeding risk
bullets: Confirm the actual planned intervention: diagnostic examination/biopsy, EUS without sampling and stent-only ERCP differ from sphincterotomy, EUS sampling, polypectomy and EMR/ESD. A low-risk booking may become therapeutic.

Balance bleeding against thrombosis with the prescribing/procedural team, particularly for coronary stents or mechanical valves. Do not give a blanket “stop all blood thinners” instruction; drug, renal function, intervention and current guidance determine interruption, bridging and restart.

sections.title: Therapeutic escalation and complication response
bullets: Polypectomy, hemostasis or difficult retrieval may increase risk beyond diagnostic enteroscopy. Announce instability and evaluate bleeding, perforation and ventilatory problems promptly.
An inadequate or incomplete examination does not justify persisting through unsafe sedation or physiologic deterioration; agree a pause, alternative technique or staged approach.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Routine swallowed capsule examination generally does not need anesthesia; distinguish it from endoscopic capsule deployment.
Swallowing difficulty, altered mentation or impaired gastric emptying may make oral ingestion unsafe or ineffective.
Evaluate stricture/obstruction and retention risk before capsule use; do not label capsule testing risk-free.
Sedation/anesthesia and its recovery requirements apply when endoscopic placement is needed, not automatically to every swallowed capsule.

sections.title: Swallowed capsule versus endoscopic deployment
bullets: Clarify whether the patient will swallow the capsule or undergo EGD-assisted placement. A swallowed camera is not a reason by itself to provide IV sedation.
Dysphagia, Zenker’s diverticulum or impaired gastric emptying may favor endoscopic placement; anesthesia planning then follows the patient’s airway and procedural risk.

sections.title: Obstruction and capsule-retention risk
bullets: Review Crohn’s disease, prior obstruction/resection, radiation, known stricture/mass and relevant NSAID exposure. Suspected obstruction warrants specialist evaluation before routine ingestion.
The GI team may use patency testing or enterography. A failed patency study or demonstrated stricture requires an alternative plan, not automatic administration of the diagnostic capsule.

sources.label: ASGE capsule endoscopy and deep enteroscopy quality indicators (2022)

sections.title: Aspiration and deployment
bullets: For difficult swallowing or altered consciousness, evaluate aspiration risk before asking the patient to ingest the capsule. Rare airway entry can occur.
If endoscopic deployment is chosen, prepare the same monitoring, suction and rescue capability as for EGD with the selected sedation/GA technique.

sections.title: When anesthesia standards apply
bullets: The anesthesia-room and sedation monitoring sections below apply to endoscopic placement or other actual anesthesia care, not to an unsedated ambulatory capsule study.
For routine oral ingestion, follow the GI service’s device instructions, preparation and sensor/recorder workflow; avoid unnecessary sedation-related burdens.

sections.title: Passage, MRI and symptoms
bullets: Avoid MRI until capsule passage is confirmed according to the device/GI team’s instructions. Lack of observed passage after an incomplete study requires follow-up, often imaging.
Abdominal pain, vomiting, inability to pass stool/gas or marked bloating before passage warrants urgent assessment for retention/obstruction rather than waiting for a routine result.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Define the operation and urgency first: short vaginal instrumentation, prolonged laparoscopy, or major open pelvic resection require different plans.
Assess aspiration, pregnancy possibility, anemia/bleeding, cardiopulmonary reserve and expected access restrictions.
Prioritize lithotomy nerve protection, Trendelenburg/CO₂ physiology, blood readiness and hysteroscopic fluid tracking when applicable.
Plan opioid-sparing analgesia, PONV prevention, safe emergence, urinary care, VTE prevention and the appropriate recovery location.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum & Trendelenburg physiology
bullets: CO₂ insufflation and head-down positioning reduce FRC/compliance, increase airway pressures and CO₂ load, and alter SVR and venous return. Cardiac output responses depend on insufflation pressure, position, volume status and ventricular reserve; decreases are not inevitable in every patient.

Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight, individualize PEEP and minute ventilation, and reassess ETT depth after positioning. Sudden bradycardia with insufflation requires communication, stopping the stimulus/deflation and treatment; unexplained hypoxemia or collapse warrants evaluation for hemorrhage, gas embolism or thoracic gas complications.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: laparoscopic and robotic surgery (2024 educational review)

sections.title: Hemorrhage recognition & resuscitation
bullets: For substantial anticipated bleeding, establish suitable access, type/crossmatch and a blood-delivery plan before incision. During active hemorrhage activate the local pathway early, follow perfusion and serial laboratory trends, and address hypothermia, hypocalcemia, fibrinogen/platelet deficits and coagulopathy as indicated.

A normal initial hemoglobin does not exclude acute major blood loss. Resuscitation and definitive surgical control proceed together; vasopressors may support perfusion but do not replace blood or correction of the bleeding source.

sections.title: Procedure families & boundaries
bullets: Use the procedure-specific reference rather than assuming all gynecologic cases need GA, steep Trendelenburg or a blood crossmatch. Local/MAC or neuraxial techniques may suit selected brief vaginal procedures; laparoscopy commonly requires controlled ventilation and a secured airway.

Cesarean delivery and postpartum hemorrhage remain in Obstetrics. Existing cerclage and postpartum tubal-ligation routes are retained as related pregnancy/postpartum procedures; this expansion does not replace those references.

bullets: Confirm indication, approach, pregnancy possibility and testing with consent under local policy. Review anemia, bleeding history, anticoagulants, obesity/OSA, cardiopulmonary reserve, renal function, prior pelvic operations and baseline neurologic symptoms.

Investigate and treat iron-deficiency anemia and nutritional deficits before elective major surgery when time permits. Urgent hemorrhage or source control should not wait for completion of an elective optimization pathway.

sections.title: Anesthetic technique & aspiration assessment
bullets: Choose local anesthesia with or without sedation, neuraxial anesthesia or GA according to procedure, duration, patient preference and rescue needs. MAC is an anesthesia service, not a fixed depth; sedation can progress to apnea and requires airway-rescue capability.

Assess vomiting, pain/opioids, reflux, obstruction, fasting and gestational stage individually. Early pregnancy alone does not establish delayed gastric emptying or mandate identical full-stomach management for every patient; active vomiting, shock or an emergency may still justify a protected-airway/rapid-sequence strategy.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & thermal care
bullets: Use appropriate ECG, blood pressure, oxygenation and ventilation monitoring; exhaled CO₂ is expected during moderate/deep sedation unless precluded or invalidated. Monitor temperature when clinically significant changes are intended, anticipated or suspected.

Match venous access, arterial monitoring and blood availability to hemorrhage risk and physiologic reserve, not the procedure name alone. Warm patients and substantial fluid/blood infusions; reassess hemoglobin, electrolytes, glucose and acid-base status as indicated.

sections.title: Lithotomy, pressure points & nerve protection
bullets: Document mobility limits and neuropathy; lift and lower legs together with adequate personnel. Protect the fibular head, heels and calves, avoid excessive hip flexion/abduction or external rotation, and avoid traction/compression on the brachial plexus or tucked arms.

Minimize time in lithotomy and steep Trendelenburg, reassess supports and perfusion when feasible, and avoid prolonged hypotension or concentrated calf pressure. Severe postoperative leg pain, swelling or weakness can signal compartment syndrome even with palpable pulses; obtain urgent assessment rather than attributing it automatically to a block.

sources.label: DGGG/OEGGG/SGGG positioning consensus (2020/2021; stated validity ended July 2025)

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & fluid balance
bullets: Target euvolemia with reassessment of perfusion and measured losses; avoid both indiscriminate crystalloid loading and rigid restriction during bleeding. Distinguish vasodilation from hypovolemia or low cardiac output before choosing fluid, blood or vasoactive support.

Account for poor intake, bowel preparation, ascites drainage and irrigation absorption when relevant. Oliguria during pneumoperitoneum or pelvic manipulation is not by itself a mandate for repeated fluid boluses; inspect the catheter, hemodynamics and surgical context.

sources.label: Gynecologic oncology ERAS implementation review (2021; summarizes 2016/2019 guidance)
ERAS Society vulvar and vaginal surgery recommendations (2020)

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV prevention
bullets: Use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia with acetaminophen and an NSAID when renal function, bleeding risk and other contraindications permit. Local infiltration or an appropriate regional block may reduce incisional pain; blocks do not reliably eliminate visceral pelvic pain.

Assess PONV risk and use multimodal prophylaxis from different drug classes when indicated; consider propofol-based anesthesia and opioid reduction. Choose rescue antiemetics from a different class where possible and account for QT risk, sedation, urinary retention and other patient-specific effects.

sources.label: ERAS gynecologic oncology implementation update (2023; not the 2026 update)

sections.title: Emergence, airway safety & disposition
bullets: Before extubation, confirm consciousness, airway protection, gas exchange, temperature and hemodynamic stability. After neuromuscular blockade verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; prolonged Trendelenburg also requires assessment for airway edema and a safe reintubation plan.

Arrange observation or higher-acuity care for persistent shock, major bleeding, airway swelling or respiratory compromise. Discharge requires controlled pain/nausea, appropriate bleeding assessment and procedure-specific voiding/catheter and return-precaution plans.

sections.title: VTE prevention & postoperative recovery
bullets: Assess cancer, prior VTE, obesity, immobility and bleeding risk. Coordinate mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with surgical hemostasis, renal function and neuraxial timing; do not apply an automatic anticoagulant hold/restart schedule.

After major open pelvic cancer surgery, evaluate extended prophylaxis under the oncology pathway; the 2023 ERAS update supports 28 days in high-risk patients, not routine extension for every minor or minimally invasive case. Mobilize and resume nutrition as feasible, with exceptions for instability or specific reconstruction requirements.

bullets: Urgent adnexal surgery commonly presents with severe pain, vomiting and uncertain fasting.
Assess pregnancy and possible ectopic pregnancy, volume depletion and other causes of instability.
Normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion; anesthesia preparation should support timely surgical evaluation.
Expect laparoscopy with possible conversion, individualized aspiration precautions and postoperative reassessment.

sections.title: Time-sensitive diagnosis & preservation
bullets: Torsion is a surgical emergency: coordinate prompt gynecologic assessment, pregnancy testing where appropriate and available imaging without creating avoidable delays. Ovarian salvage/detorsion decisions belong to the surgical team; a dark appearance alone does not prove irreversible loss.

Distinguish pain-related tachycardia or dehydration from hemorrhage, sepsis or pregnancy-related pathology. Normal imaging flow cannot independently rule out torsion when clinical suspicion remains high.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum & Trendelenburg physiology
bullets: CO₂ insufflation and head-down positioning reduce FRC/compliance, increase airway pressures and CO₂ load, and alter SVR and venous return. Cardiac output responses depend on insufflation pressure, position, volume status and ventricular reserve; decreases are not inevitable in every patient.

Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight, individualize PEEP and minute ventilation, and reassess ETT depth after positioning. Sudden bradycardia with insufflation requires communication, stopping the stimulus/deflation and treatment; unexplained hypoxemia or collapse warrants evaluation for hemorrhage, gas embolism or thoracic gas complications.

sections.title: Uterine perforation & concealed injury
bullets: Unexpected loss of resistance, a sudden fluid-deficit increase, abdominal distension, bleeding or instability should trigger concern for perforation. Under anesthesia, pain may be absent; quantify bleeding and ask about instrument/energy use and possible extrauterine injury.

Stop and reassess with the surgical team; bowel, bladder or vascular injury may require laparoscopy/laparotomy and resuscitation. Stable suspected perforation and perforation with electrosurgery, ongoing bleeding or organ injury are not interchangeable scenarios.

sections.title: Uterotonics & hemorrhage medication cautions
bullets: Uterotonics treat appropriate uterine-atony scenarios, not every surgical bleeding source. Methylergonovine is contraindicated in hypertension/toxemia and can cause coronary vasospasm; routine IV use is unsafe. Do not assume its role in rescue bleeding supports prophylactic use: SFP advises against prophylactic methylergonovine for D&E at 20–24 weeks.

Carboprost can cause bronchoconstriction; its label contraindicates active pulmonary disease and cautions with an asthma history, so select alternatives or follow a specialist protocol where relevant. Oxytocin/misoprostol selection and TXA use should follow the indication-specific hemorrhage pathway; direct evidence for TXA in abortion hemorrhage is limited and partly extrapolated.

Rapid IV oxytocin can cause hypotension, flushing and reflex tachycardia, with potential ischemia or arrhythmia in vulnerable patients. Follow the product-specific and indication-specific protocol; avoid an unplanned rapid bolus and communicate administration to anesthesia.

Misoprostol can cause shivering and fever. Consider timing and the full clinical picture rather than automatically diagnosing infection from fever alone, while still evaluating persistent fever, instability or other evidence of sepsis.

sections.title: Encephalopathy, sodium & postoperative examination

sections.title: Ascites, decompression & renal risk

sections.title: Donor-specific safety & consent
bullets: Review the donor program’s assessment, consent and ability to withdraw without pressure. Confirm the extent of donation, vascular/biliary anatomy, expected remnant and contingency plan with an experienced team.

Healthy baseline status does not make hemorrhage, embolism or postoperative dysfunction trivial. Monitoring and blood conservation should protect the donor rather than prioritize recipient or scheduling goals.

sections.title: Hemodynamics without a rigid CVP target
bullets: CVP has important limitations and does not consistently correlate with blood loss in healthy donors. Tailor venous-pressure reduction, monitoring and fluid/vasoactive support to the donor and transection phase instead of enforcing one number.

Use the center’s balanced-fluid protocol and preserve renal/hepatic perfusion. Donor studies are heterogeneous; they do not establish one universal anesthetic, central-line requirement or fluid formula.

sections.title: Major bleeding & transfusion readiness
bullets: Match crossmatched blood, access, rapid infusion and cell-salvage planning to vascular involvement, portal collaterals and surgical extent. Cell-salvage use in malignancy or contamination requires institutional selection and processing policy, not an automatic blanket ban or mandate.

During uncontrolled bleeding, activate the hemorrhage protocol and pursue source control while following perfusion and serial hemoglobin/coagulation trends. Warm products, monitor ionized calcium, potassium and acid-base status, and move toward targeted therapy when timely tests are available.

sections.title: Venous air / gas embolism: recognition & response
bullets: Open hepatic veins and low venous pressure can permit air entrainment; laparoscopic venous injury can also allow CO₂ embolism. Sudden ETCO₂ fall, hypoxemia, hypotension or arrhythmia warrants immediate team assessment alongside hemorrhage, circuit and cardiac causes; none is diagnostic alone.

Alert the surgeon, stop air entry or insufflation and occlude/flood the source as appropriate; give 100% oxygen, stop nitrous oxide if used, and support ventilation/circulation. Use resuscitation for arrest and consider echo. Aspiration through an already suitably positioned catheter or repositioning may help in selected circumstances, but must not delay source control or CPR.

sections.title: Access, monitoring & temperature
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring and temperature assessment when significant change is anticipated. Major resection, shock or substantial anticipated transfusion often warrants an arterial line, adequate large-bore access and repeated point-of-care laboratory assessment.

Prepare rapid blood delivery, warming and appropriate vasoactive infusions before high-risk phases. Choose central access and additional cardiac monitoring for the individual procedure and reserve; they are not obligatory for every routine cholecystectomy.

sections.title: Perfusion, renal protection & fluid balance
bullets: Avoid both excessive crystalloid loading and rigid under-resuscitation. Reassess actual blood/fluid losses, perfusion and fluid responsiveness, interpreting dynamic measures within their limitations rather than treating CVP as a direct blood-volume measurement.

Balance organ perfusion against hepatic venous congestion; use vasoactive support for vasodilation when indicated. Track renal function and electrolytes and avoid unnecessary nephrotoxins; oliguria requires clinical assessment, not automatic repeated boluses.

sections.title: Rebalanced coagulation & targeted transfusion
bullets: Cirrhosis can predispose to both hemorrhage and thrombosis. INR alone does not measure overall bleeding risk, and prophylactic plasma solely to normalize chronic cirrhotic INR is not recommended; anticoagulant-related INR elevation and active massive hemorrhage require different assessment.

Integrate surgical bleeding, platelets, fibrinogen, temperature, ionized calcium and acid-base status. TEG/ROTEM can guide targeted transfusion in major bleeding/transplantation but does not reliably predict every procedure-related bleed or certify neuraxial safety. Avoid a universal platelet/INR target for all HPB procedures.

sections.title: Drug handling, analgesia & regional choices
bullets: Hepatic dysfunction can change clearance, protein binding and sensitivity; titrate rather than simply excluding every hepatically metabolized drug. Avoid unnecessary prolonged sedation, reassess neuromuscular blockade quantitatively and account for simultaneous renal dysfunction.

Use multimodal analgesia suited to hepatic/renal reserve and the incision. Acetaminophen requires an appropriate hepatic plan; NSAIDs may be unsuitable with renal injury or bleeding risk. Epidural benefit must be weighed against hypotension and evolving post-resection coagulation, including a safe catheter-removal plan.

sections.title: Glucose, electrolytes & acid-base trends
bullets: Monitor glucose during major hepatic/pancreatic procedures and severe liver dysfunction. Stress hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia with poor hepatic reserve can both occur; use measured values and a local protocol rather than assuming a single predictable direction.

Trend potassium, ionized calcium, sodium, lactate and other electrolytes according to severity and transfusion. Interpret poor lactate clearance in the context of perfusion and liver function; protect against excessively rapid sodium correction in chronically hyponatremic patients.

sections.title: Emergence & postoperative surveillance
bullets: Extubate only when consciousness, airway protection, ventilation, oxygenation, temperature and perfusion are adequate. If neuromuscular blockade was used, verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; shock, edema or respiratory failure may require continued ventilation.

Handoff bleeding, transfusion, glucose/electrolyte trends, liver/renal function, drains and analgesia. Escalate persistent lactate elevation, worsening bilirubin/coagulation, hypoglycemia, encephalopathy, fever or abdominal findings for possible organ failure, bleeding or bile/pancreatic leak.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Infected obstruction needs antibiotics, resuscitation and timely drainage coordinated together.
Shock, AKI, encephalopathy and vomiting change both induction risk and the appropriate procedural setting.
ERCP is generally favored when feasible; instability or altered anatomy may favor a different drainage approach.
The urgency and extent of intervention are individualized: unstable patients may need decompression rather than prolonged definitive stone work.

sections.title: Timing and extent of biliary drainage
bullets: The 2021 ASGE guideline conditionally favors ERCP within 48 hours, but that is not permission to wait in deteriorating septic shock. Persistent shock may require more urgent source control; pancreatitis with cholangitis has separate ACG guidance for ERCP within 24 hours.

For instability, coagulopathy or major antithrombotic concerns, discuss drainage alone rather than adding extensive sphincterotomy/stone removal. Percutaneous drainage may be appropriate when ERCP is infeasible or a lesser-sedation approach is needed.

sections.title: Shock, resuscitation & airway readiness
bullets: Assess blood pressure/perfusion, lactate, renal function, acid-base status and respiratory reserve; administer indicated antibiotics and treat hypovolemia while preparing vasoactive support. Induction may remove compensatory sympathetic tone and cause profound hypotension.

Protect the airway when consciousness, vomiting, obstruction or procedure requirements warrant it. GA is not dictated solely by the word cholangitis; choose technique and location to permit prompt airway/circulatory rescue, recognizing restricted access during prone/semi-prone ERCP.

bullets: Handoff drainage method, stent/drain function, cultures, antibiotics, hemodynamics and organ support. Continued hypotension may reflect persistent sepsis, incomplete drainage, bleeding or another procedural complication.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Enucleation spares pancreatic tissue but can still cause duct injury, fistula or hemorrhage.
Determine whether the lesion is hormonally active; insulinoma and other endocrine syndromes require their existing specific pathways.
Match monitoring, access and ventilation to lesion location and open versus minimally invasive approach.
Continue postoperative glucose and surgical-complication surveillance; a limited resection is not a guarantee of uncomplicated recovery.

sections.title: Tumor location, duct relationship & evidence limits
bullets: Review the intended approach and relationship to major ducts/vessels with the surgeon. The feasibility of tissue-sparing resection depends on anatomy and tumor biology; selection thresholds from a single-center series are not universal anesthesia rules.

Published open-enucleation outcomes document pancreatic fistula and bleeding despite parenchymal preservation. The cited 2025 series spans several decades and does not establish a modern laparoscopic complication rate or an anesthesia protocol.

sections.title: Hormone-specific preparation without duplication
bullets: Use the existing Insulinoma Resection or Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumor Resection reference for hormone-specific stabilization, glucose checks, dextrose and electrolyte planning. Do not infer hormone activity from tumor size or the fact that enucleation is planned.

Coordinate tumor manipulation/removal with glucose monitoring and communicate postoperative changes to recovery. The operative reference supplements, rather than replaces, the endocrine syndrome plan.

sections.title: Major bleeding & transfusion readiness
bullets: Match crossmatched blood, access, rapid infusion and cell-salvage planning to vascular involvement, portal collaterals and surgical extent. Cell-salvage use in malignancy or contamination requires institutional selection and processing policy, not an automatic blanket ban or mandate.

During uncontrolled bleeding, activate the hemorrhage protocol and pursue source control while following perfusion and serial hemoglobin/coagulation trends. Warm products, monitor ionized calcium, potassium and acid-base status, and move toward targeted therapy when timely tests are available.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum & surgical position
bullets: CO₂ absorption, reduced compliance and increased abdominal pressure change ventilation and circulation. Titrate minute ventilation/PEEP, check airway pressures and tube position, and recognize that reverse Trendelenburg may reduce venous return.

Sudden bradycardia during insufflation requires immediate communication, stopping the stimulus/deflation and appropriate treatment. Prolonged or unexpected hypoxemia, hypercarbia or collapse requires evaluation for gas complications, hemorrhage and cardiopulmonary causes.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Most pancreatitis is not an immediate operation; anesthesia risk depends on organ failure and the actual drainage/debridement plan.
Assess respiratory failure, AKI, perfusion, glucose, electrolytes and aspiration risk before transport or induction.
Use reassessed, moderate fluid resuscitation rather than indiscriminate high-volume loading.
Stable necrosis often permits delayed intervention; sepsis or clinical deterioration requires multidisciplinary reassessment.

sections.title: Fluid resuscitation and organ dysfunction
bullets: ACG favors lactated Ringer’s and moderately aggressive early hydration with frequent reassessment of vitals, BUN/hematocrit and clinical volume status. This is not a mandate for large unmonitored volumes, especially with renal or cardiac dysfunction.

Consider pulmonary edema/ARDS, pleural effusions, AKI, hypocalcemia and glucose disturbances when planning anesthesia. A falling urine output or rising BUN should prompt reassessment of perfusion and illness, not automatic limitless fluid administration.

sections.title: Infected versus sterile necrosis & intervention timing
bullets: Antibiotics are for suspected/confirmed infection, not routine prophylaxis for sterile pancreatitis. In stable necrosis, the 2024 ACG highlights advise deferring surgical/radiologic/endoscopic intervention approximately 4–6 weeks when feasible.

Clinical deterioration, uncontrolled infection or another emergency changes that plan; coordinate gastroenterology, interventional radiology, surgery and critical care. Pancreatitis with cholangitis requires urgent biliary drainage rather than waiting for necrosis maturation.

sections.title: Procedure, airway and postoperative organ support
bullets: Clarify endoscopic drainage/necrosectomy, percutaneous drainage or open surgery, expected duration/position and airway access. Existing ventilator/vasopressor needs and transport risks may dominate the anesthetic.

Continue close postoperative monitoring for hemorrhage, perforation, persistent sepsis and respiratory/renal failure. A technically successful drainage procedure does not immediately reverse established multiorgan dysfunction.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: TIPS reduces portal pressure but increases systemic venous return/preload and can unmask cardiac or RV failure.
Review cardiac assessment, pulmonary hypertension, renal function and baseline encephalopathy.
Select sedation or GA according to airway, urgency and patient risk, with interventional-suite rescue capability.
Watch for bleeding, gas embolism, heart failure, liver dysfunction and new/worsened encephalopathy afterward.

sections.title: Cardiopulmonary selection & preparation
bullets: Elective TIPS assessment includes echocardiography and evaluation for LV/RV dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension; abnormal findings may need cardiology/right-heart assessment. Severe heart failure, severe untreated valvular disease and moderate-to-severe pulmonary hypertension are major contraindications requiring specialist resolution.

Also consider uncontrolled infection, refractory overt encephalopathy, biliary obstruction and anatomic barriers. Urgent rescue decisions require a multidisciplinary risk-benefit plan, not automatic application of a single elective score or pressure cutoff.

sections.title: Shunt opening & right-heart stress
bullets: Opening the shunt increases venous return and cardiac output and may precipitate congestion, pulmonary edema or RV failure. Communicate shunt creation and reassess filling, oxygenation and perfusion rather than treating every fall in pressure with large fluid boluses.

Individualize invasive/cardiac monitoring and vasoactive support to cardiac reserve. The ALTA consensus does not show one sedation technique improves outcomes for every TIPS patient; airway protection and rescue access guide the anesthetic choice.

sources.label: ALTA North American practice-based TIPS recommendations (2022 consensus)

sections.title: Venous air / gas embolism: recognition & response
bullets: Open hepatic veins and low venous pressure can permit air entrainment; laparoscopic venous injury can also allow CO₂ embolism. Sudden ETCO₂ fall, hypoxemia, hypotension or arrhythmia warrants immediate team assessment alongside hemorrhage, circuit and cardiac causes; none is diagnostic alone.

Alert the surgeon, stop air entry or insufflation and occlude/flood the source as appropriate; give 100% oxygen, stop nitrous oxide if used, and support ventilation/circulation. Use resuscitation for arrest and consider echo. Aspiration through an already suitably positioned catheter or repositioning may help in selected circumstances, but must not delay source control or CPR.

sources.label: WFSA air embolism and anesthesia (2016 educational tutorial)

sections.title: Encephalopathy and post-TIPS observation
bullets: Document baseline neurologic status and risk factors including prior encephalopathy, advanced dysfunction, renal impairment and hyponatremia. New confusion may be encephalopathy but still requires evaluation for medication, respiratory, metabolic or bleeding causes.

ALTA recommends at least overnight in-hospital observation, with acuity matched to indication and complexity. Reassess labs and clinical signs of cardiac decompensation, hepatic failure or bleeding; severe persistent encephalopathy may require specialist treatment and shunt reassessment.

sources.label: ALTA North American practice-based TIPS recommendations (2022 consensus)

sections.title: Hepatic reserve & patient assessment
bullets: Review cirrhosis/portal hypertension, bilirubin, albumin, coagulation, platelets, renal function, sodium, nutrition and functional capacity. Distinguish hepatocellular injury tests from synthetic function and the amount/function of liver expected to remain.

Assess ascites, encephalopathy, infection, cardiomyopathy and pulmonary complications. Hepatopulmonary syndrome involves abnormal pulmonary vascular dilation/hypoxemia; portopulmonary hypertension adds pulmonary vascular and RV risk. They require different evaluation and are not interchangeable diagnoses.

sources.label: Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)
Portal hypertension perioperative considerations (2023 ANZCA review)

sections.title: Aspiration, induction & ventilation
bullets: Assess vomiting, obstruction, ascites, encephalopathy, fasting and urgency. Choose airway protection and induction technique for the actual risk, with adequate preoxygenation and vasoactive/blood support available when perfusion is fragile.

Use controlled ventilation for major surgery with lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight and individualized PEEP. Ascites, pleural effusions, abdominal exposure and pneumoperitoneum can alter mechanics; protect oxygenation without ignoring RV and venous-pressure effects.

OpenAnesthesia adult liver transplantation (2023 educational review)

sections.title: Access, monitoring & temperature
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring and temperature assessment when significant change is anticipated. Major resection, shock or substantial anticipated transfusion often warrants an arterial line, adequate large-bore access and repeated point-of-care laboratory assessment.

Prepare rapid blood delivery, warming and appropriate vasoactive infusions before high-risk phases. Choose central access and additional cardiac monitoring for the individual procedure and reserve; they are not obligatory for every routine cholecystectomy.

sources.label: ASA Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Perfusion, renal protection & fluid balance
bullets: Avoid both excessive crystalloid loading and rigid under-resuscitation. Reassess actual blood/fluid losses, perfusion and fluid responsiveness, interpreting dynamic measures within their limitations rather than treating CVP as a direct blood-volume measurement.

Balance organ perfusion against hepatic venous congestion; use vasoactive support for vasodilation when indicated. Track renal function and electrolytes and avoid unnecessary nephrotoxins; oliguria requires clinical assessment, not automatic repeated boluses.

sources.label: ERAS Society liver surgery guideline (2022)

sections.title: Rebalanced coagulation & targeted transfusion
bullets: Cirrhosis can predispose to both hemorrhage and thrombosis. INR alone does not measure overall bleeding risk, and prophylactic plasma solely to normalize chronic cirrhotic INR is not recommended; anticoagulant-related INR elevation and active massive hemorrhage require different assessment.

Integrate surgical bleeding, platelets, fibrinogen, temperature, ionized calcium and acid-base status. TEG/ROTEM can guide targeted transfusion in major bleeding/transplantation but does not reliably predict every procedure-related bleed or certify neuraxial safety. Avoid a universal platelet/INR target for all HPB procedures.

sections.title: Drug handling, analgesia & regional choices
bullets: Hepatic dysfunction can change clearance, protein binding and sensitivity; titrate rather than simply excluding every hepatically metabolized drug. Avoid unnecessary prolonged sedation, reassess neuromuscular blockade quantitatively and account for simultaneous renal dysfunction.

Use multimodal analgesia suited to hepatic/renal reserve and the incision. Acetaminophen requires an appropriate hepatic plan; NSAIDs may be unsuitable with renal injury or bleeding risk. Epidural benefit must be weighed against hypotension and evolving post-resection coagulation, including a safe catheter-removal plan.

sources.label: ERAS Society liver surgery guideline (2022)

sections.title: Glucose, electrolytes & acid-base trends
bullets: Monitor glucose during major hepatic/pancreatic procedures and severe liver dysfunction. Stress hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia with poor hepatic reserve can both occur; use measured values and a local protocol rather than assuming a single predictable direction.

Trend potassium, ionized calcium, sodium, lactate and other electrolytes according to severity and transfusion. Interpret poor lactate clearance in the context of perfusion and liver function; protect against excessively rapid sodium correction in chronically hyponatremic patients.

sources.label: Major liver resection perioperative review (2024)

sections.title: Emergence & postoperative surveillance
bullets: Extubate only when consciousness, airway protection, ventilation, oxygenation, temperature and perfusion are adequate. If neuromuscular blockade was used, verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; shock, edema or respiratory failure may require continued ventilation.

Handoff bleeding, transfusion, glucose/electrolyte trends, liver/renal function, drains and analgesia. Escalate persistent lactate elevation, worsening bilirubin/coagulation, hypoglycemia, encephalopathy, fever or abdominal findings for possible organ failure, bleeding or bile/pancreatic leak.

sections.title: VTE prevention, nutrition & mobilization
bullets: An elevated INR does not protect against VTE. Coordinate mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with bleeding, renal function and neuraxial procedures using the current institutional pathway.

Use individualized PONV prevention, early mobilization and enteral intake when clinically appropriate. Adapt recovery milestones to obstruction, reconstruction, ongoing shock and complications rather than applying one ERAS pathway indiscriminately.

Reassess airway, aspiration risk, organ dysfunction and ICU needs rather than reusing the patient’s earlier elective plan.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Start with baseline neurologic function, pathology and the risk of losing cerebral or spinal cord perfusion.
Match pressure, ventilation and anesthetic goals to the condition rather than applying one universal neuro target.
Coordinate airway access, position, monitoring modalities, blood readiness and immediate rescue communication.
Plan smooth emergence and timely neurologic assessment without forcing unsafe extubation.

sections.title: Cord perfusion & immediate signal-loss response
bullets: For a significant monitoring change, immediately announce it, pause the provoking surgical maneuver and initiate the agreed team response. Check surgical compression/hardware/traction, technical leads/stimulation and anesthetic/physiologic causes in parallel; do not wait to notify the surgeon until an anesthesia checklist is finished.

Reassess arterial pressure at the correct reference level, oxygenation/ventilation, blood loss/hemoglobin, temperature, anesthetic delivery and residual/new neuromuscular blockade. Restore agreed perfusion and correct reversible abnormalities with the team; no single universal rescue MAP or alarm percentage applies to all modalities and lesions.

sources.label: Intraoperative spinal cord injury clinical practice guideline (2024)

sections.title: SSEP / MEP / EMG-compatible anesthesia
bullets: Agree modalities and baseline acquisition before incision and, when useful, before/after positioning. TIVA is commonly chosen for robust evoked potentials; volatile agents and nitrous oxide can suppress signals, while neuromuscular blockade especially affects myogenic MEP/EMG rather than sensory conduction itself.

Keep anesthetic concentrations and physiology stable and communicate all boluses or blocker doses. TIVA still requires reliable delivery, hypnosis assessment and awareness prevention; neither TIVA nor a preserved SSEP guarantees intact motor function.

sections.title: Brain versus spine and related endocrine routes
bullets: Brain cases emphasize ICP/CPP, venous drainage, seizures and neurologic examination. Spine cases add cord perfusion, prone/approach-specific exposure, signal preservation and positioning injury.

Transsphenoidal pituitary surgery and adult craniopharyngioma retain their existing endocrine-aware references. This category reuses those routes without duplicating hormone-replacement, DI or sodium-management content.

sections.title: Baseline neurologic status & preparation
bullets: Document consciousness, pupils, language, strength/sensation and relevant pre-existing deficits before anesthesia when feasible. Review imaging, urgency, seizures, antithrombotics, cardiopulmonary disease, renal function and prior airway/cervical issues.

Clarify the surgical/monitoring plan and usual antiseizure, steroid, Parkinson or chronic pain medications. Continue or modify medications through an explicit specialist plan; mapping-related changes are not permission for indiscriminate withholding.

sections.title: Airway control & restricted access
bullets: Choose airway technique for aspiration risk, consciousness, cervical stability and anticipated access after fixation/positioning. Use the approach most likely to secure oxygenation safely while limiting unnecessary cervical movement; awake intubation is selective, not mandatory for every cervical case.

Secure and recheck the ETT, circuit and lines before draping, pinning or turning prone. Plan rescue, release of fixation or repositioning with the team; sedation with limited access still requires capnography and the ability to rescue apnea or obstruction.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & reference level
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring, temperature surveillance when indicated and access matched to hemorrhage or vasoactive needs. Arterial pressure monitoring is often useful for major cranial/cord-risk surgery; it must not create avoidable delay in emergency reperfusion or decompression.

Document the arterial transducer reference level, especially with the head elevated; pressure measured at heart level may overestimate brain-level arterial pressure. Recheck airway/lines after positioning and arrange access to blood, laboratory testing and emergency equipment.

sources.label: ASA Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: CPP, pressure targets & venous drainage
bullets: The usual bedside model is CPP = MAP − ICP; brain-level arterial pressure, venous pressure and autoregulation affect interpretation. Hypotension can reduce perfusion even when ICP is not rising. Agree targets for the actual pathology and operative phase rather than using one number for all neurosurgery.

Keep the head/neck positioned to support venous drainage without excessive rotation, flexion or external compression. Coordinate head elevation and PEEP with oxygenation and perfusion; zero PEEP or indiscriminate volume loading is not a universal neuroprotective strategy.

sections.title: Brain relaxation, CO₂ & osmotherapy
bullets: Avoid hypoxemia and unintended hypercapnia; confirm PaCO₂ when ETCO₂ may be misleading. Routine profound or prolonged hyperventilation can reduce cerebral blood flow. A brief rescue strategy for threatened herniation is different from prophylactic hypocapnia in every craniotomy.

Mannitol or hypertonic saline may be used for a defined indication with surgical/neurocritical coordination. Monitor perfusion, sodium/osmolality, renal function and volume consequences; neither drug nor a fixed regimen is automatically appropriate for every swollen brain.

sections.title: Head fixation, stimulation & position
bullets: Coordinate analgesia/anesthesia for laryngoscopy, pin placement, incision and emergence while protecting perfusion. If local/scalp block is used, track total dose and communicate timing; sudden hemodynamic changes still need assessment rather than automatic anesthetic deepening.

Protect eyes and pressure points, secure lines and preserve airway access as far as practical. With the head above the heart, consider venous air entrainment risk; communicate any need to release fixation or reposition during an emergency.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & metabolic care
bullets: Maintain appropriate intravascular volume and cerebral/cord perfusion without excessive fluid loading. Use measured bleeding, hemoglobin and physiology to guide blood/fluid therapy; deliberate hypotension is not a default blood-conservation strategy in a perfusion-vulnerable patient.

Avoid unnecessary hypo-osmolar fluid in intracranial disease, and monitor glucose, sodium, hemoglobin, temperature and acid-base status according to case severity. Treat hypoglycemia when present; a blanket prohibition on all glucose-containing fluid would be unsafe.

sections.title: Analgesia, PONV & examination quality
bullets: Provide multimodal analgesia matched to the incision and patient, considering local/scalp or appropriate regional techniques. Check cumulative local-anesthetic exposure and bleeding considerations; opioid-sparing care should not mean inadequate analgesia.

Prevent and treat PONV while avoiding unnecessary sedation that obscures the neurologic exam. Balance smooth emergence and blood-pressure control with ventilation, airway protection and reliable assessment.

sections.title: Emergence, neurologic examination & disposition
bullets: Aim for a smooth, timely neurologic exam when safe, but do not force immediate extubation in a patient with impaired airway protection, brainstem dysfunction, severe swelling, shock or respiratory failure. Verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis after neuromuscular blockade.

Handoff baseline and new deficits, pupils/mental status, blood-pressure goals, drain settings, bleeding, seizures and airway concerns. New weakness, delayed awakening or respiratory deterioration requires urgent assessment for reversible physiology and surgical/neurologic complications.

sections.title: Head fixation, stimulation & position
bullets: Coordinate analgesia/anesthesia for laryngoscopy, pin placement, incision and emergence while protecting perfusion. If local/scalp block is used, track total dose and communicate timing; sudden hemodynamic changes still need assessment rather than automatic anesthetic deepening.

Protect eyes and pressure points, secure lines and preserve airway access as far as practical. With the head above the heart, consider venous air entrainment risk; communicate any need to release fixation or reposition during an emergency.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & metabolic care
bullets: Maintain appropriate intravascular volume and cerebral/cord perfusion without excessive fluid loading. Use measured bleeding, hemoglobin and physiology to guide blood/fluid therapy; deliberate hypotension is not a default blood-conservation strategy in a perfusion-vulnerable patient.

Avoid unnecessary hypo-osmolar fluid in intracranial disease, and monitor glucose, sodium, hemoglobin, temperature and acid-base status according to case severity. Treat hypoglycemia when present; a blanket prohibition on all glucose-containing fluid would be unsafe.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Review rupture history, seizure status, lesion vascularity and staged embolization/resection plans.
Prepare for rapid intracranial bleeding and abrupt changes during vascular control.
Maintain perfusion intraoperatively and coordinate postoperative pressure limits carefully.
Post-resection edema or hemorrhage may occur; new deficits require urgent assessment rather than a single assumed mechanism.

sections.title: Vascular anatomy and resection risk
bullets: Clarify lesion size, venous drainage, previous embolization and expected operative blood loss. Plan suitable access, arterial monitoring, crossmatched blood and communication around feeder/venous control.

Neuromonitoring and the baseline examination help identify ischemic injury, but no monitoring modality eliminates risk. Treat surgical bleeding and physiologic deterioration promptly while the team reassesses flow and perfusion.

sections.title: Post-resection pressure and edema
bullets: Agree explicit postoperative BP and fluid goals with the neurosurgical team based on lesion and operative findings. Avoid sudden hypertension, but do not import very low single-center protocol targets as a universal standard.

The cited Helsinki series is retrospective and uncontrolled; it supports vigilance, not a proven one-size BP recipe. Edema, hemorrhage or an arterial occlusion can require different responses, so investigate new deficits and tailor care to imaging and physiology.

sections.title: Seizure prevention & rescue
bullets: Reconcile seizure history, recent events and antiseizure medication timing; continue indicated therapy unless the epilepsy team deliberately modifies it for recording. Have a communicated rescue plan before cortical stimulation.

If a seizure occurs, alert the surgeon and stop stimulation, support oxygenation/ventilation and protect the patient. Exposed-cortex irrigation with chilled sterile solution may stop stimulation-induced activity; persistent/generalized seizures require prompt medication and airway rescue under the local protocol even if recording must be interrupted.

sections.title: Baseline neurologic status & preparation
bullets: Document consciousness, pupils, language, strength/sensation and relevant pre-existing deficits before anesthesia when feasible. Review imaging, urgency, seizures, antithrombotics, cardiopulmonary disease, renal function and prior airway/cervical issues.

Clarify the surgical/monitoring plan and usual antiseizure, steroid, Parkinson or chronic pain medications. Continue or modify medications through an explicit specialist plan; mapping-related changes are not permission for indiscriminate withholding.

sections.title: Airway control & restricted access
bullets: Choose airway technique for aspiration risk, consciousness, cervical stability and anticipated access after fixation/positioning. Secure and recheck the ETT, circuit and lines before draping, pinning or turning prone. Plan rescue, release of fixation or repositioning with the team; sedation with limited access still requires capnography and the ability to rescue apnea or obstruction.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & reference level
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring, temperature surveillance when indicated and access matched to hemorrhage or vasoactive needs. Arterial pressure monitoring is often useful for major cranial/cord-risk surgery; it must not create avoidable delay in emergency reperfusion or decompression.

Document the arterial transducer reference level, especially with the head elevated; pressure measured at heart level may overestimate brain-level arterial pressure. Recheck airway/lines after positioning and arrange access to blood, laboratory testing and emergency equipment.

sections.title: CPP, pressure targets & venous drainage
bullets: The usual bedside model is CPP = MAP − ICP; brain-level arterial pressure, venous pressure and autoregulation affect interpretation. Keep the head/neck positioned to support venous drainage without excessive rotation, flexion or external compression. Coordinate head elevation and PEEP with oxygenation and perfusion; zero PEEP or indiscriminate volume loading is not a universal neuroprotective strategy.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Assess hemorrhage location/size, neurologic deterioration, hydrocephalus and need for urgent surgery.
Use smooth individualized BP control while protecting CPP, especially with severe disease or elevated ICP.
Rapidly reconcile and reverse clinically relevant anticoagulation under the current protocol.
Do not transfer mild-to-moderate medical ICH targets or nonsurgical platelet recommendations indiscriminately to emergency surgery.

sections.title: ICH blood-pressure qualifiers
bullets: For mild-to-moderate spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP 150–220 mmHg, the 2022 guideline supports a target near 140 with maintenance 130–150 in selected patients; lowering below 130 can be harmful.

Safety/efficacy of intensive lowering is not well established in large/severe ICH or patients needing decompression. Coordinate BP with ICP/CPP and neurologic status rather than automatically applying the medical-ICH range during high-risk surgery.

sources.label: AHA/ASA spontaneous ICH guideline (2022)

sections.title: Anticoagulants versus antiplatelets
bullets: Stop and promptly reverse significant anticoagulation using the actual drug, timing, renal function and current local protocol; reversal-agent availability and newer evidence must be checked rather than relying on a fixed 2022 drug list.

For aspirin-associated ICH requiring emergency neurosurgery, platelet transfusion may be considered. In aspirin-treated spontaneous ICH without emergency surgery, routine platelet transfusion can be harmful. Desmopressin benefit remains uncertain; do not extrapolate one scenario to all patients.

sources.label: AHA/ASA spontaneous ICH guideline (2022)

sections.title: Hydrocephalus, edema and urgent deterioration
bullets: Hydrocephalus contributing to reduced consciousness may require ventricular drainage. Cerebellar hemorrhage with deterioration, brainstem compression or obstructed CSF pathways requires urgent neurosurgical assessment.

Bolus hyperosmolar therapy may transiently reduce ICP when indicated; routine prophylactic continuous therapy has uncertain outcome benefit. Corticosteroids should not be used to treat elevated ICP from spontaneous ICH.

sources.label: AHA/ASA spontaneous ICH guideline (2022)

sections.title: EVD leveling, drainage & transport
bullets: Verify ordered drainage height, reference point, patency and open-versus-clamped plan. Level an EVD at the external auditory meatus with an appropriate leveling device; relevel after position changes and never connect a pressurized flush system.

Do not routinely clamp every EVD for transport. Agree a plan using clamp tolerance, ICP and drainage needs; prevent overdrainage during movement and restore ordered settings with trained monitoring. Accurate fluid-coupled pressure measurement and simultaneous open drainage are not interchangeable states.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Adult deformity combines prolonged surgery, possible major bleeding and high-risk cord monitoring.
Assess restrictive respiratory mechanics, frailty, anemia and cardiac reserve rather than borrowing a pediatric scoliosis protocol.
Plan blood conservation, eye/pressure protection and a coordinated signal-loss response.
Postoperative respiratory support and higher-acuity care depend on reserve and intraoperative events.

sections.title: Major spine / cranial hemorrhage readiness
bullets: Correct elective anemia when feasible and plan crossmatch, large-bore access, warming, cell salvage and antifibrinolytic use for high-blood-loss operations. TXA selection and regimen should account for renal function, seizure/thrombotic context and the procedure rather than copying a universal dose.

During major loss, reassess hemoglobin, coagulation, platelets/fibrinogen, ionized calcium and temperature. Restoring MAP with fluid/pressors alone does not restore oxygen-carrying capacity; transfusion decisions integrate bleeding, perfusion and neurologic risk.

sections.title: Adult reserve and correction magnitude
bullets: Review pulmonary limitations, exercise tolerance, previous fusion, osteoporosis/frailty, nutrition and anemia. Complex deformity and osteotomy merit a high-risk multidisciplinary plan.

Coordinate surgical staging, correction steps, anticipated transfusion and postoperative bed availability. TXA/cell salvage may reduce transfusion needs but do not replace hemorrhage control or adequate perfusion.

sections.title: Respiratory and neurologic recovery after long fusion
bullets: Reassess ventilation, facial/airway edema, blood loss and metabolic status before extubation. Significant restrictive disease, large resuscitation or neurologic concern may require continued ventilation or ICU monitoring.

Document motor/sensory and visual assessment when the patient is alert. Severe new deficit or visual symptoms requires urgent specialist evaluation, not reassurance based on earlier normal intraoperative signals.

sections.title: Prone positioning, eyes & peripheral nerves
bullets: Before and after turning, verify the airway, ventilation, lines, neutral neck alignment and padded pressure points. Keep the abdomen free of avoidable compression and avoid excessive arm abduction or plexus stretch; reassess supports throughout a long case.

Avoid direct eye pressure and periodically confirm eye/head position. For high-risk prolonged or high-blood-loss spine surgery, discuss visual-loss risk, preserve perfusion and oxygen delivery, and assess vision when awake; new visual symptoms require urgent ophthalmologic evaluation. No device or fixed transfusion threshold guarantees prevention.

sections.title: SSEP / MEP / EMG-compatible anesthesia
bullets: Agree modalities and baseline acquisition before incision and, when useful, before/after positioning. TIVA is commonly chosen for robust evoked potentials; volatile agents and nitrous oxide can suppress signals, while neuromuscular blockade especially affects myogenic MEP/EMG rather than sensory conduction itself.

Keep anesthetic concentrations and physiology stable and communicate all boluses or blocker doses. TIVA still requires reliable delivery, hypnosis assessment and awareness prevention; neither TIVA nor a preserved SSEP guarantees intact motor function.

sections.title: Cord perfusion & immediate signal-loss response
bullets: For a significant monitoring change, immediately announce it, pause the provoking surgical maneuver and initiate the agreed team response. Check surgical compression/hardware/traction, technical leads/stimulation and anesthetic/physiologic causes in parallel; do not wait to notify the surgeon until an anesthesia checklist is finished.

Reassess arterial pressure at the correct reference level, oxygenation/ventilation, blood loss/hemoglobin, temperature, anesthetic delivery and residual/new neuromuscular blockade. Restore agreed perfusion and correct reversible abnormalities with the team; no single universal rescue MAP or alarm percentage applies to all modalities and lesions.

sections.title: Intramedullary versus extrinsic compression
bullets: Clarify lesion location, surgical dissection planes and expected monitoring with the neurophysiology team. Intramedullary tumors and marked myelopathy are high-risk contexts; preserved sensory signals alone do not establish motor-pathway safety.

The older surgical chapter supports complementary sensory/motor monitoring, not a universal amplitude threshold or instruction to continue resection despite signal loss. Use the current team protocol and surgeon/neurophysiologist assessment.

sources.label: Intraoperative spinal cord injury clinical practice guideline (2024)

sections.title: Major spine / cranial hemorrhage readiness
bullets: Correct elective anemia when feasible and plan crossmatch, large-bore access, warming, cell salvage and antifibrinolytic use for high-blood-loss operations. TXA selection and regimen should account for renal function, seizure/thrombotic context and the procedure rather than copying a universal dose.

During major loss, reassess hemoglobin, coagulation, platelets/fibrinogen, ionized calcium and temperature. Restoring MAP with fluid/pressors alone does not restore oxygen-carrying capacity; transfusion decisions integrate bleeding, perfusion and neurologic risk.

sections.title: Postoperative function and escalation
bullets: Arrange serial motor/sensory exams and individualized perfusion goals in an appropriate monitored setting. Document any intraoperative signal change and response precisely.
New deficits require urgent evaluation for residual compression, hematoma, ischemia or other reversible causes. A completed resection does not remove the need for prompt postoperative rescue.

sections.title: Baseline neurologic status & preparation
bullets: Document consciousness, pupils, language, strength/sensation and relevant pre-existing deficits before anesthesia when feasible. Review imaging, urgency, seizures, antithrombotics, cardiopulmonary disease, renal function and prior airway/cervical issues.

Clarify the surgical/monitoring plan and usual antiseizure, steroid, Parkinson or chronic pain medications. Continue or modify medications through an explicit specialist plan; mapping-related changes are not permission for indiscriminate withholding.

sections.title: Airway control & restricted access
bullets: Choose airway technique for aspiration risk, consciousness, cervical stability and anticipated access after fixation/positioning. Use the approach most likely to secure oxygenation safely while limiting unnecessary cervical movement; awake intubation is selective, not mandatory for every cervical case.

Secure and recheck the ETT, circuit and lines before draping, pinning or turning prone. Plan rescue, release of fixation or repositioning with the team; sedation with limited access still requires capnography and the ability to rescue apnea or obstruction.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & reference level
bullets: Use standard anesthesia monitoring, temperature surveillance when indicated and access matched to hemorrhage or vasoactive needs. Arterial pressure monitoring is often useful for major cranial/cord-risk surgery; it must not create avoidable delay in emergency reperfusion or decompression.

Document the arterial transducer reference level, especially with the head elevated; pressure measured at heart level may overestimate brain-level arterial pressure. Recheck airway/lines after positioning and arrange access to blood, laboratory testing and emergency equipment.

sections.title: Prone positioning, eyes & peripheral nerves
bullets: Before and after turning, verify the airway, ventilation, lines, neutral neck alignment and padded pressure points. Keep the abdomen free of avoidable compression and avoid excessive arm abduction or plexus stretch; reassess supports throughout a long case.

Avoid direct eye pressure and periodically confirm eye/head position. For high-risk prolonged or high-blood-loss spine surgery, discuss visual-loss risk, preserve perfusion and oxygen delivery, and assess vision when awake; new visual symptoms require urgent ophthalmologic evaluation. No device or fixed transfusion threshold guarantees prevention.

sections.title: SSEP / MEP / EMG-compatible anesthesia
bullets: Agree modalities and baseline acquisition before incision and, when useful, before/after positioning. TIVA is commonly chosen for robust evoked potentials; volatile agents and nitrous oxide can suppress signals, while neuromuscular blockade especially affects myogenic MEP/EMG rather than sensory conduction itself.

Keep anesthetic concentrations and physiology stable and communicate all boluses or blocker doses. TIVA still requires reliable delivery, hypnosis assessment and awareness prevention; neither TIVA nor a preserved SSEP guarantees intact motor function.

sections.title: Cord perfusion & immediate signal-loss response
bullets: For a significant monitoring change, immediately announce it, pause the provoking surgical maneuver and initiate the agreed team response. Check surgical compression/hardware/traction, technical leads/stimulation and anesthetic/physiologic causes in parallel; do not wait to notify the surgeon until an anesthesia checklist is finished.

Reassess arterial pressure at the correct reference level, oxygenation/ventilation, blood loss/hemoglobin, temperature, anesthetic delivery and residual/new neuromuscular blockade. Restore agreed perfusion and correct reversible abnormalities with the team; no single universal rescue MAP or alarm percentage applies to all modalities and lesions.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & metabolic care
bullets: Maintain appropriate intravascular volume and cerebral/cord perfusion without excessive fluid loading. Use measured bleeding, hemoglobin and physiology to guide blood/fluid therapy; deliberate hypotension is not a default blood-conservation strategy in a perfusion-vulnerable patient.

Avoid unnecessary hypo-osmolar fluid in intracranial disease, and monitor glucose, sodium, hemoglobin, temperature and acid-base status according to case severity. Treat hypoglycemia when present; a blanket prohibition on all glucose-containing fluid would be unsafe.

sections.title: Analgesia, PONV & examination quality
bullets: Provide multimodal analgesia matched to the incision and patient, considering local/scalp or appropriate regional techniques. Check cumulative local-anesthetic exposure and bleeding considerations; opioid-sparing care should not mean inadequate analgesia.

Prevent and treat PONV while avoiding unnecessary sedation that obscures the neurologic exam. Balance smooth emergence and blood-pressure control with ventilation, airway protection and reliable assessment.

sections.title: Emergence, neurologic examination & disposition
bullets: Aim for a smooth, timely neurologic exam when safe, but do not force immediate extubation in a patient with impaired airway protection, brainstem dysfunction, severe swelling, shock or respiratory failure. Verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis after neuromuscular blockade.

Handoff baseline and new deficits, pupils/mental status, blood-pressure goals, drain settings, bleeding, seizures and airway concerns. New weakness, delayed awakening or respiratory deterioration requires urgent assessment for reversible physiology and surgical/neurologic complications.

sections.title: Evidence scope & clinical-review boundary
bullets: Adult clinical-review draft, not an independently approved protocol. TBI, aSAH, spontaneous ICH, ischemic stroke and chronic spine disease have different targets; do not transfer one guideline’s pressure or drug recommendations indiscriminately to another.

Institutional handbook numbers are not universal mandates; the 2026 AHA/ASA stroke guideline takes precedence over older conflicting post-thrombectomy BP targets. Older mapping reviews and low-level rescue evidence are labeled. Device-specific instructions, local protocols and clinician signoff remain necessary.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Rapidly identify the immediate threat: airway obstruction, perfusion failure, hemorrhage, herniation, seizure or cord compression.
Activate the appropriate surgical/neurocritical response while correcting oxygenation and circulation.
Signal loss and postoperative deficits require immediate team assessment, not delayed notification after isolated checks.
Acute high-SCI hypotension and chronic autonomic dysreflexia have different mechanisms and treatments.

sections.title: Anterior cervical hematoma / airway emergency
bullets: New neck swelling, voice change, dysphagia, stridor, respiratory distress or rapidly increasing anxiety after anterior cervical surgery warrants immediate airway assessment and activation of surgical/anesthesia help. Airway compromise can progress rapidly; absence of dramatic external swelling does not exclude danger.

Support oxygenation, bring difficult-airway and front-of-neck rescue equipment, and coordinate urgent wound decompression/hematoma evacuation when indicated. In critical obstruction, rescue cannot wait for routine imaging or transport; repeated unsuccessful intubation attempts must not delay decompression or emergency airway access by trained clinicians.

sections.title: Seizure prevention & rescue
bullets: Reconcile seizure history, recent events and antiseizure medication timing; continue indicated therapy unless the epilepsy team deliberately modifies it for recording. Have a communicated rescue plan before cortical stimulation.

If a seizure occurs, alert the surgeon and stop stimulation, support oxygenation/ventilation and protect the patient. Exposed-cortex irrigation with chilled sterile solution may stop stimulation-induced activity; persistent/generalized seizures require prompt medication and airway rescue under the local protocol even if recording must be interrupted.

sections.title: Sitting / head-elevated surgery: gas embolism
bullets: Venous air embolism can occur whenever exposed venous channels lie above the heart, not only in sitting cases. Discuss shunt assessment, detection strategy and rescue beforehand; sudden ETCO₂ fall, hypotension or hypoxemia may be a clue but is not specific.

Alert the surgeon, stop air entrainment, give 100% oxygen, stop nitrous oxide if used and support circulation/ventilation. Consider echo and aspiration through an already suitable catheter if available; repositioning is context dependent and must not delay source control or CPR.

sections.title: Neurogenic shock versus autonomic dysreflexia
bullets: High acute SCI can produce hypotension and bradycardia from sympathetic disruption, but exclude hemorrhage and other shock causes. Support perfusion with individualized volume/vasoactive care; acute-SCI augmentation guidance is not a universal target for chronic spine surgery.

In susceptible chronic SCI, commonly at/above T6, sudden severe hypertension with or without bradycardia suggests autonomic dysreflexia. Stop/remove the trigger, assess bladder/bowel/pressure or surgical stimulation, deepen appropriate anesthesia/analgesia and treat persistent hypertension with the local short-acting rescue protocol.

sections.title: Herniation, hydrocephalus and new cord deficits
bullets: A falling level of consciousness, new pupillary abnormality or acute neurologic deficit requires immediate assessment and neurosurgical escalation. Maintain oxygenation/perfusion and use indicated ICP rescue while definitive decompression or CSF diversion is arranged.

Postoperative new weakness, cauda equina symptoms or severe pain may indicate compression/hematoma. Do not assume residual anesthesia or a block is the explanation without urgent evaluation; activate imaging and surgical rescue according to the clinical situation.

sections.title: CPP, pressure targets & venous drainage
bullets: The usual bedside model is CPP = MAP − ICP; brain-level arterial pressure, venous pressure and autoregulation affect interpretation. Hypotension can reduce perfusion even when ICP is not rising. Agree targets for the actual pathology and operative phase rather than using one number for all neurosurgery.

Keep the head/neck positioned to support venous drainage without excessive rotation, flexion or external compression. Coordinate head elevation and PEEP with oxygenation and perfusion; zero PEEP or indiscriminate volume loading is not a universal neuroprotective strategy.

sections.title: Brain relaxation, CO₂ & osmotherapy
bullets: Avoid hypoxemia and unintended hypercapnia; confirm PaCO₂ when ETCO₂ may be misleading. Routine profound or prolonged hyperventilation can reduce cerebral blood flow. A brief rescue strategy for threatened herniation is different from prophylactic hypocapnia in every craniotomy.

Mannitol or hypertonic saline may be used for a defined indication with surgical/neurocritical coordination. Monitor perfusion, sodium/osmolality, renal function and volume consequences; neither drug nor a fixed regimen is automatically appropriate for every swollen brain.

sections.title: Head fixation, stimulation & position
bullets: Coordinate analgesia/anesthesia for laryngoscopy, pin placement, incision and emergence while protecting perfusion. If local/scalp block is used, track total dose and communicate timing; sudden hemodynamic changes still need assessment rather than automatic anesthetic deepening.

Protect eyes and pressure points, secure lines and preserve airway access as far as practical. With the head above the heart, consider venous air entrainment risk; communicate any need to release fixation or reposition during an emergency.
